docs.title: The Easterling Steppe
docs.text:
The Khorun is the old geographic name for the immense belt of plains, grassland, forest-steppe, river country, lake basins, and colder northern margins stretching across much of Eorania. Western travelers more often call the same broad region the Easterling Steppe, and commonly call its peoples Easterlings.

Neither name describes a single country, ethnicity, or way of life. The Khorun is a continental system crossed by migrations, confederacies, river routes, caravan roads, watersheds, hunting grounds, grazing corridors, farming districts, fortified markets, and ecological frontiers. Horse pastoralism is powerful here, but it is not universal: settled farmers, fishers, river traders, hunters, craftsmen, and towns all belong to the Khorun world.

docs.title: Peoples of the Khorun
docs.text:
Five peoples are especially important in the present age, though none exhausts the region's population.

  • The Sigyn are an old western people whose aristocratic houses, ancestral landscapes, horse-breeding traditions, and mixed pastoral and settled communities preserve some of the deepest visible continuities in the western Khorun.
  • The Chulkas are highly mobile pastoral confederations whose clans and political followings have been driven westward in large numbers by the recent rise of the Khazgui.
  • The Khazgui are the ascendant power of the eastern Khorun. Under Hu Khan, conquest is turning an older steppe confederation into a wider military and tributary order.
  • The Uldat inhabit the river and forest-steppe systems of northeastern Eorania. Their towns, farms, fisheries, markets, boat routes, and warrior rulers link mobile peoples to settled production and long-distance trade.
  • The Ordai are wild-herd hunters of the northern and northwestern grassland and forest-steppe mosaic. Their seasonal bands gather for great hunts, exchange, diplomacy, marriage, and war.

Countless smaller clans, tributary communities, mixed settlements, local peoples, and frontier populations live among and between these larger cultural poles.

docs.title: A Region in Motion
docs.text:
The present Khorun is being reshaped by the rise of Hu Khan. Khazgui expansion has absorbed eastern communities and displaced major Chulkas confederations westward. Those movements in turn place new pressure on Sigyn lands, Uldat markets, Ordai hunting corridors, the Torgai Basin, and the roads leading toward the western realms.

The result is not a single Easterling invasion. Chulkas bands may arrive as refugees, raiders, caravan guards, settlers, mercenaries, or allies. Sigyn houses may resist them, employ them, or bargain with them. Uldat towns may profit from the upheaval even while fearing Khazgui tribute demands. Ordai bands may fight anyone whose herds, farms, or wars disrupt the migrations on which they depend.

docs.title: Trade and Interdependence
docs.text:
No one people commands everything needed to dominate the Khorun. Pastoral peoples supply horses, livestock, hides, escorts, and military labor. Ordai hunters move meat, hides, animal products, and knowledge of wild migration corridors. Uldat river communities supply grain, storage, metalwork, textiles, boats, markets, and access to imported goods. Khazgui expansion increasingly seeks to control these flows rather than merely conquer grazing land.

This interdependence makes river crossings, winter pasture, markets, migration bottlenecks, caravan routes, and lake basins as politically important as open battlefield victories.

docs.title: Torgai
docs.text: In northeastern Eorania, the Torgai Basin is one of the great contact zones of the Khorun. Its waters, marshes, reedlands, pasture, fisheries, river mouths, and trade approaches attract overlapping populations rather than belonging cleanly to one people. Uldat merchants and fishers, pastoral camps, hunters, displaced Chulkas, caravan traffic, and Khazgui agents may all meet there.

docs.title: Chulkas
docs.text: The Chulkas are one of the major peoples of The Easterling Steppe. They are among the most mobile pastoral peoples of the Khorun, organized through clans, allied followings, and confederations whose size and composition can change rapidly with fortune and leadership.

docs.title: Standard
docs.text: Blazon: Chequy vert and argent, a lion Or. (A gold lion on a green-and-white checkered field.)

docs.title: Confederations and Belonging
docs.text:
Chulkas identity is enduring, but political belonging is flexible. A successful confederation may draw in allied clans, client groups, refugees, dependents, and outsiders who accept its obligations. A failed one may fragment just as quickly. Leaders therefore depend not only on ancestry but on generosity, alliance-making, military success, access to pasture and trade, and their ability to keep followers together.

This political elasticity has helped the Chulkas survive repeated migrations and reversals. It also makes outsiders prone to mistaking one Chulkas host for the whole people.

docs.title: Life on the Move
docs.text:
For many Chulkas households, seasonal movement is a normal part of life. Herds, remounts, tents, pack animals, kin camps, and negotiated access to grazing and water shape both wealth and politics. Horses are central, but sheep, cattle, other livestock, caravan income, raiding, toll-taking, and military service all contribute to Chulkas fortunes.

Their mobility also makes them natural intermediaries across the Khorun. Chulkas may appear as caravan escorts, guides, traders, mercenaries, livestock dealers, raiders, or armed migrants—sometimes several of these in the course of one generation.

docs.title: Religion on the Move
docs.text:
Chulkas traditions belong to the wider Khorun religious family, but mobility itself shapes their sacred world. Recurring camps, wintering places, graves, water, pasture, migration routes, and assembly grounds form a network of meaningful places rather than one fixed ancestral territory. Genealogy, songs, remembered graves, ancestral possessions, and reputation allow a clan's history to travel with it.

The camp is an ordinary sacred center. Household fires, livestock enclosures, standards, hospitality, and repeated occupation establish a temporary order of belonging. Larger confederations can likewise accumulate religious identity through shared oaths, feasts, victories, standards, graves, songs, and remembered leaders without becoming permanent churches or states.

Hospitality, alliance, adoption, patronage, and sworn relationship are especially important. Generosity is also a religious measure of leadership: a chief who cannot distribute livestock, booty, food, pasture access, protection, gifts, and opportunity may lose more than political popularity. Ancestry matters, but fortune, judgment, followers, and continuing obligation matter with it.

Heaven and the open sky are prominent in many Chulkas traditions. Weather, celestial signs, seasonal fortune, herd fertility, and omen-reading receive close attention, although different clans and confederations do not necessarily describe Heaven in the same way.

The present displacement caused by Khazgui expansion is consequently a religious crisis as well as a political and ecological one. Lost pasture can mean lost access to graves, recurring camps, known spirit relationships, and the routes through which a community understands its own history. Chulkas leaders and specialists disagree over whether present disaster reflects failed obligation, lost favor, curse, bad leadership, or simply an enemy that has learned to organize war more effectively.

docs.title: Warfare
docs.text:
Chulkas warfare prizes strategic mobility and adaptability. Mounted archery, scouting, feigned withdrawal, raiding, pursuit, rapid concentration, and deep remount reserves allow a confederation to fight over enormous distances. Their forces usually grow from real clan and political followings rather than a rigid permanent state army, allowing bands to separate, combine, hire themselves abroad, or follow different leaders as circumstances change.

That flexibility is a strength, but it can also become a weakness when rival chiefs, exhausted pasture, or disputed spoils pull a confederation apart.

docs.title: Recent Displacement
docs.text:
The Chulkas formerly occupied much more of the central Khorun. The rise of the Khazgui under Hu Khan has broken or displaced major confederations and driven large numbers westward.

This is not one orderly migration. Different Chulkas groups are seeking wintering grounds, pasture, caravan work, mercenary employment, alliances, and permanent settlement in different places. Their movement has intensified conflict with Sigyn houses, Ordai hunters, Uldat markets, and western realms while also creating new alliances and trade relationships.

In the current era, Chulkas activity threatens the Eastward Road used by Zorah and its merchants, though not every Chulkas group has an interest in disrupting the road. Some profit more by guarding it.

docs.title: Ordai
docs.text: The Ordai are a major people of the northern and northwestern Khorun, where open grassland gives way irregularly to forest-steppe. Although they are accomplished riders, their way of life is not built primarily around vast domesticated herds. Much of Ordai society follows the movements of the great wild herds on which hunting, trade, prestige, and seasonal gathering depend.

docs.title: The Seasonal Round
docs.text:
For much of the year Ordai communities travel in comparatively small bands, spreading across hunting country without exhausting local game. At appointed seasons, many bands gather at traditional grounds for great communal hunts, exchange, marriages, councils, diplomacy, celebrations, and the settlement of disputes.

These gatherings are more than festivals or hunting camps. Because no permanent ruler can speak for all Ordai, the greatest seasonal assemblies are the principal occasions on which many bands can act collectively. Hunting access and migration corridors are negotiated, blood-feuds may be suspended or settled, foreign envoys received, marriages arranged, trade privileges recognized, compensation exchanged, and collective war debated. For a few weeks a gathering ground may function like the political center of a dispersed people; when the bands depart, that center effectively disappears until the next great assembly.

Ordai wealth includes horses, portable goods, hides, preserved meat, crafted animal products, trade goods, and rights recognized by custom over particular hunting grounds or migration bottlenecks. Their survival depends less on owning every mile of land than on continued access to the routes by which wild herds move through it.

docs.title: The Herd Roads
docs.text:
The Ordai distinguish strongly between customary rights to use a place and permanent ownership of the routes followed by the great herds. Bands, families, or communities may possess recognized camping places, hunting precedence, water access, or seasonal use-rights, but no hereditary claim is considered sufficient by itself to close a major herd road to the wider people.

Ordai tradition presents this principle as ancient, but its present political importance was sharpened by centuries of contact with neighboring pastoral and settled societies. Sigyn houses and other powerful neighbors increasingly treated pasture, estates, and ancestral territorial claims as inheritable possessions. To the Ordai, allowing the same logic to enclose the paths of migrating game would eventually destroy the hunting life itself.

Disputes over herd roads therefore became matters for the great assemblies rather than merely local quarrels. The resulting custom is one of the sharpest differences between the Ordai and their Sigyn cousins: Sigyn aristocratic legitimacy is often tied to ancestral places and territorial claims, while Ordai collective politics places special limits on turning the movement corridors of wild herds into hereditary private domains.

docs.title: Religion of the Wild Herds
docs.text:
Ordai traditions belong to the wider Khorun religious family, but their religious life is particularly shaped by wild herds, predators, communal hunts, seasonal aggregation, and recurring landscapes. The Ordai do not generally understand animals or land as existing simply for human possession. Their religious problem is instead how people may take what they need without destroying the relationships that make future return possible.

This does not make the Ordai passive preservationists. They hunt intensively, manipulate herd movement, compete with predators, and use the landscape pragmatically. Correct distribution, avoidance of waste, generosity, respect for dangerous places, and continuity of the herd matter at least as much as the act of killing itself. A great communal hunt therefore joins religion, subsistence, and politics: scouting, coordination, slaughter, butchery, allocation, hospitality, prestige, and household need are parts of one undertaking.

Some bands, families, lineages, or specialists maintain strong relationships with particular animals, but not every Ordai has a totem and there is no universal totem system. Wolves, great cats, raptors, ravens, vultures, and other predators or scavengers may be understood locally as rivals, teachers, fellow hunters, omens, dangerous powers, or beings bound to particular places.

Sacred landscape likewise does not imply ownership. Herd bottlenecks, calving grounds, springs, hunt sites, old camps, aggregation grounds, cliffs, and predator places can impose obligations on those who use them without becoming hereditary private property.

Ordai funerary customs characteristically favor elevated exposure. Platforms, scaffolds, trees, high stone shelves, and related practices allow wind, sun, raptors, scavengers, and predators to participate in the body's return to the landscape. Practice is not uniform, and later treatment of bones or possessions differs among communities.

docs.title: Leadership
docs.text:
The Ordai have no single office that governs every part of life. A respected band leader may not command a communal hunt. A renowned warrior may have little authority in a marriage dispute. Hunt leaders, diplomats, elders, band leaders, religious specialists, and warrior associations gain influence through different kinds of achievement and obligation.

This plural authority often confuses foreign rulers, who may conclude a treaty with one leader only to discover that the agreement never bound the people they assumed it did. Agreements meant to affect many bands are therefore most secure when recognized at one of the great seasonal assemblies.

Status rests heavily on achievement made useful to others: hunting skill, generosity, courage, diplomacy, leadership in communal undertakings, and reputation within warrior or social associations.

docs.title: Warfare
docs.text:
Ordai warfare grows naturally from the skills of the hunt. Scouting, tracking, concealment, pursuit, encirclement, knowledge of terrain, and sudden concentration are as useful against enemies as against migrating game.

War parties commonly gather around leaders with proven reputations rather than permanent military offices. Mounted fighting is important, but Ordai forces are not simply another formal cavalry tradition. Their strength lies in mobility, fieldcraft, and the ability of dispersed bands to gather rapidly when a hunting ground, herd road, or communal gathering place is threatened.

docs.title: Neighbors and Pressure
docs.text:
The Ordai share old cultural affinities with the Sigyn, visible in parts of their material culture and language, though the precise ancestry of the two peoples is uncertain. Their histories have diverged sharply: where many Sigyn communities developed aristocratic houses, pastoral estates, and more settled lifeways, the Ordai remained organized around wild-herd ecology and seasonal aggregation. Long-running disputes over whether migration corridors can be converted into hereditary pasture or estate land have helped make that divergence political as well as economic.

Relations with the Chulkas are particularly volatile. Domestic herds and heavy grazing can disrupt the movements of wild game, turning an ordinary migration of pastoralists into an existential threat to Ordai bands. Yet the same peoples trade horses, hides, meat, guides, captives, and information. The present Chulkas displacement is especially dangerous because refugee confederations seeking new pasture may unintentionally block or degrade herd roads that the Ordai regard as a collective necessity.

Uldat markets provide important outlets for Ordai products and neutral places for exchange and diplomacy, while Uldat farms and river settlements can also occupy crucial hunting bottlenecks. The expanding Khazgui present a different problem: defeating an Ordai band does not necessarily subject the people, because authority and population are widely dispersed. A conqueror seeking lasting control must eventually reckon with the seasonal assemblies and the corridors that bring distant bands together.

docs.title: Sigyn
docs.text: The Sigyn are one of the major peoples of The Easterling Steppe and among the Khorun peoples most familiar to western travelers. They are an old western people whose noble houses, ancestral landscapes, horse-breeding traditions, and burial grounds claim roots far deeper than the confederations now moving across the central steppe.

docs.title: Standard
docs.text:
Blazon: Argent, a sunwheel gules. (A red sunwheel on a white field.)

The device is simple, high-contrast, and easily reproduced as a cavalry standard, shield mark, brand, or embroidered badge.

docs.title: Houses and Ancestral Lands
docs.text:
Sigyn society is strongly shaped by old aristocratic houses. Noble prestige rests on ancestry, reputation, retainers, celebrated horses, and long association with particular pastures, settlements, burial mounds, and ancestral places. These claims can endure even when a house no longer controls every tract it remembers as its own.

Noble authority is not absolute. Councils, customary obligations, local communities, and the practical need to retain followers constrain even powerful houses. Feuds and rival claims are common enough that Sigyn politics cannot be reduced to a single ruler or confederation.

docs.title: Ways of Life
docs.text:
The Sigyn are not uniformly nomadic. Some communities move livestock seasonally between recognized grazing grounds; others combine herding with farming; still others live much of the year in permanent villages, winter settlements, or estate networks while maintaining strong equestrian traditions.

Across these variations, horses remain important markers of wealth and status. Old metalwork, animal motifs, elaborate tack, inherited ornaments, and the burial-mound landscapes of the western Khorun reinforce Sigyn claims to antiquity.

docs.title: Religion and the Ancestral Landscape
docs.text:
Sigyn traditions belong to the wider Khorun religious family, but their strongest emphasis falls on ancestry, burial, and inherited obligation. Burial mounds, cemeteries, house graves, remembered estates, battle sites, springs, groves, genealogy, lament, and old heirlooms can carry both political and sacred weight. A great mound may be simultaneously a tomb, a place of remembrance, an oath site, evidence in an inheritance dispute, and a dangerous place when the dead have not been properly settled.

Genealogists, lamenters, ritual speakers, funerary custodians, healers, omen-readers, spirit-workers, and household elders may all exercise religious authority. Horses are especially entangled with elite memory and burial; sacrificing a prestigious horse is a costly statement rather than an everyday rite. Some noble houses also cultivate distinctive religious associations with falconry or particular raptors.

Ancestry does not legitimate a house by itself. Sigyn tradition expects the living to remain worthy of inherited claims through protection of dependents, hospitality, oath-keeping, proper remembrance, and settlement of obligations. Murder, broken oaths, desecrated graves, and failed compensation can therefore disturb spiritual as well as political order.

Long contact with Atharism has transformed much of western Sigyn religious life. Conversion and intermarriage are old, and many Sigyn have abandoned human sacrifice under Atharite influence, although strong traditionalists and extraordinary funerals of great rulers may preserve it. Converted families may still visit ancestral mounds, preserve genealogical observances, or maintain local customs, while Atharite cremation creates an enduring tension with traditions in which burial places anchor house identity.

docs.title: Warfare
docs.text:
The most prestigious Sigyn warriors are armored cavalry drawn from noble households and their retainers. Lance and sword traditions carry particular status, while mounted archery, lighter riders, scouting, and pursuit remain important parts of war. More settled districts can also provide infantry, militia, and fortified local defense.

A great Sigyn muster therefore resembles an alliance of house forces more than a standardized state army. This gives experienced houses formidable local military depth, but old rivalries can make united action difficult.

docs.title: The Present Crisis
docs.text:
The westward displacement of the Chulkas and expansion of the Khazgui have made old Sigyn land claims newly dangerous. Some houses resist incoming peoples, some employ Chulkas riders, some negotiate settlement, and others consider accommodation with Khazgui power against their own rivals.

The Vyrkari of Khoryv are closely related to the Sigyn by ancestry, language, and material culture, but developed into a distinct frontier horse-host society under different historical pressures. Western observers sometimes confuse the two because of that kinship.

docs.title: Uldat
docs.text: The Uldat are a major people of the northeastern Khorun, where great rivers, forest-steppe, wetlands, farming country, and overland routes meet. Western travelers who imagine every Easterling living from horseback are often surprised by Uldat towns, granaries, fisheries, workshops, riverboats, and fortified markets.

docs.title: River and Steppe
docs.text:
Uldat life joins two worlds. Permanent villages and towns cultivate grain, keep livestock, fish rivers and lakes, store surpluses, work metal and cloth, and conduct long-distance trade. Beyond them lie grazing districts, tributary communities, seasonal camps, and mobile warrior households whose politics remain deeply connected to the wider Khorun.

Across much of Uldat country, towns and mobile warrior elites are mutually dependent. Towns provide storage, craftsmen, markets, boats, revenue, and imported goods. Warrior rulers and their followings provide cavalry, protection, diplomacy with mobile neighbors, tribute collection, and control of the roads and river approaches on which those towns depend.

This dual polity is a common Uldat pattern rather than an invariant constitution. Some polities lean heavily toward powerful towns, merchants, or councils; others toward aristocratic warrior households, tributary hinterlands, or mobile rulers. The wider result is less a single compact kingdom than a chain of political nodes: fortified settlements, crossings, ports, market towns, agricultural districts, and dependent routes linked by shifting obligations.

docs.title: Wealth and Status
docs.text:
Uldat wealth takes many forms. Land, grain stores, herds, workshops, river craft, toll rights, merchant connections, and control of crossings can all support powerful families. Town officers, merchants, craftsmen, landholders, and warrior retainers therefore compete for influence within the same political world.

This mixture makes Uldat politics difficult for outsiders to read. A mounted lord with an impressive following may still depend on a town council, merchant house, granary keeper, or boat-owning family that appears far less imposing on the road—and in some Uldat polities those settled interests may dominate outright.

docs.title: Religion of Rivers and Crossroads
docs.text:
Uldat traditions belong to the wider Khorun religious family, but rivers and towns make their religious life unusually layered and plural. Confluences, crossings, harbors, bridges, wells, markets, cemeteries, islands, town gates, and civic meeting places can accumulate overlapping sacred relationships. The same river may matter differently to boatmen, farmers, merchants, warrior households, foreigners, and older local communities.

A single household may maintain ancestral and local river customs while also participating in Atharism, southern religious traditions, foreign merchant cults, or practices brought by migrants and captives. This does not mean every tradition regards the others as equally legitimate, but Uldat life makes religious brokerage and coexistence difficult to avoid. Healers, diviners, spirit-workers, priests, sorcerers, and other specialists often learn to work alongside—or compete with—people whose explanations of the supernatural differ sharply from their own.

Ancient Khorun concern with oath and hospitality extends readily into commercial life. Contracts, partnerships, loans, shipping ventures, employment, guild obligations, merchant guarantees, inns, and civic safe-conduct can acquire sacred seriousness as well as legal force. Towns themselves may become spiritually consequential through generations of shared walls, wells, markets, cemeteries, guarantees, and public memory.

Uldat funerary practice is correspondingly diverse. River communities must deal not only with their own ancestors but with drowned travelers, foreigners, epidemic victims, executed criminals, unknown bodies, and people whose remains are never recovered. Different towns solve these problems differently, and imported religions add still more possibilities.

docs.title: Warfare
docs.text:
The Uldat fight for nodes and corridors. Walls, ferries, bridges, portages, boatyards, granaries, markets, and river mouths are often more important than possession of empty countryside.

Town militias and disciplined infantry defend settlements and crossings while mobile warrior households supply cavalry for reconnaissance, field fighting, tribute collection, and diplomacy. The balance differs from polity to polity. Boats can move troops and supplies quickly along favorable waterways. Uldat rulers also employ foreign riders, especially Chulkas, when they need mobility beyond their own forces—an effective practice that has caused more than one political disaster.

docs.title: Torgai and the Present Crisis
docs.text:
The Uldat are strongly connected to the Torgai Basin in northeastern Eorania, but Torgai is not simply an Uldat possession. Its fisheries, marshes, pasture, river approaches, and markets draw many peoples, making the basin both profitable and dangerous.

The rise of Hu Khan has divided Uldat rulers and towns. Some see Khazgui expansion as an existential threat. Others believe tribute or alliance could preserve trade and destroy local rivals. At the same time, displaced Chulkas bring horses, labor, mercenaries, customers, and disorder into Uldat markets.

For the Khazgui, Uldat towns are tempting prizes precisely because they can turn conquest into grain, revenue, transport, workshops, and sustained campaigning.

docs.title: Khazgui
docs.text: The Khazgui are the rapidly ascendant power of the eastern Khorun. Once one among the great eastern steppe confederations, they are being transformed under Hu Khan into something larger: a conquest order capable of absorbing defeated peoples and using their skills, settlements, and wealth to sustain further expansion.

docs.title: The Bloodsun
docs.text:
Blazon: Azure, a sun Or cradled by a crescent gules. (A golden sun held within the horns of a red crescent on a blue field.)

Western heralds dislike the red crescent on blue, but the Bloodsun belongs to a steppe standard tradition rather than Loranian armory. Khazgui riders have little reason to care whether Meropolitan scholars approve of its tinctures.

docs.title: Hu Khan's Order
docs.text:
Khazgui clan and kinship ties remain important, but Hu Khan increasingly demands service that cuts across older loyalties. Command, promotion, tribute, military obligation, and access to conquered wealth bind ambitious followers directly to the expanding order.

Defeated peoples are not always driven away or destroyed. Farmers may continue producing grain, craftsmen may be set to work for new masters, merchants may reopen routes under tribute, and local warriors may be reorganized into subject contingents. Translators, guides, engineers, administrators, and other specialists can become as valuable to conquest as horsemen.

This capacity to incorporate outsiders is one reason Khazgui power has grown faster than older rivals expected.

docs.title: Heaven, Victory, and Service
docs.text:
Khazgui traditions belong to the wider Khorun religious family, but Hu Khan's conquests are rapidly changing how many eastern peoples understand Heaven and political order. His supporters increasingly treat repeated victory, disciplined rule, protected trade, rewarded service, and successful incorporation of defeated peoples as signs that Heaven favors the new order.

This is not yet a settled theology. Heaven need not be understood as one humanlike god, and even Khazgui observers disagree over what Hu Khan's success proves. His enemies and skeptics attribute his victories variously to military genius, fortune, sorcery, ruthless administration, ancestry, or other powers. Rumors that Hu Khan is part Oni remain rumors rather than an established explanation of his success.

Service itself is acquiring religious significance. Oaths, standards, ranks, offices, rewards, and repeated public recognition can bind soldiers, administrators, translators, craftsmen, subject warriors, and other useful people into an order that crosses older ancestry. At present, demonstrated performance matters more than a settled doctrine of hereditary divine right, leaving the eventual succession to Hu Khan as a political and religious problem no one has yet solved.

Khazgui conquest does not normally require every subject to worship alike. Local gods, ancestors, temples, spirit-workers, priests, and foreign religions may be preserved, patronized, regulated, or appropriated so long as their communities obey. The expanding court therefore attracts diviners, astrologers, healers, shamans, mystics, sorcerers, foreign priests, and occult specialists from many peoples.

Songs, standards, battle sites, possessions, victories, and stories are already gathering around Hu Khan personally. Whether this becomes a lasting cult, what religious meaning his eventual death will acquire, and whether Heaven truly granted him any mandate remain unanswered.

docs.title: Warfare
docs.text:
Cavalry remains the heart of Khazgui military power, but their greatest advantage is increasingly organizational. Messengers, signals, coordinated commands, remount systems, service obligations, and the use of subject forces allow Khazgui armies to operate at a scale that looser confederations struggle to match.

Captured towns, crossings, workshops, and storehouses may be preserved as supply and administrative nodes. Khazgui commanders therefore fight not only for pasture and plunder but for the routes and productive centers that make repeated campaigning possible.

docs.title: Rise to Power
docs.text:
The Khazgui have only recently achieved their present prominence. Their expansion has broken or displaced major Chulkas confederations and driven large populations westward, setting off conflicts far beyond the lands directly conquered by Hu Khan.

The resulting upheaval reaches Sigyn houses, Uldat river polities, Ordai hunting grounds, Torgai, the western roads, and ultimately the realms beyond the Khorun.

Hu Khan is rumored to be part Oni. Whether this is literal ancestry, political myth, or frightened foreign gossip remains uncertain.

docs.title: Hu Khan
docs.text:
Hu Khan is the leader associated with the recent rise of the Khazgui to dominance on the eastern steppe.

His campaigns and political victories have pushed the Chulkas out of much of the central steppe and contributed to their westward displacement.

docs.title: Oni Blood
docs.text: Hu Khan is widely rumored to possess Oni blood. Whether the claim reflects literal ancestry, supernatural transformation, deliberate political myth, or frightened enemy propaganda is unknown.

docs.title: The Great Cities
docs.text:
The Five Great Cities are an ancient and internationally recognized class of sovereign metropolitan powers. They are not a league, alliance, or common political order. Their rulers have fought one another for centuries and may disagree on nearly everything except that the Five occupy a rank unlike ordinary kingdoms, principalities, and lesser city-states.

Their deep origins are different. Meropolis and Zorah became principal heartlands of the Heryoi imperial world; Al-Anwar was recurrently incorporated but never comfortably absorbed; Khemet remained a powerful rival outside ordinary Heryoi control; and distant Zamboula belonged to the same ancient network through diplomacy and long-distance trade rather than conquest. The Five were already interconnected before their present religious alignments emerged.

Great City status is not a population category. The Five differ in resident population and territorial form, but each preserves exceptional institutions and capabilities that make it politically consequential on roughly the scale of an entire Hetaireian Princedom. Their exact populations remain uncertain.

Great City rulers and ambassadors traditionally claim unusually high diplomatic precedence, and treaties are commonly made in the city's own name. Surrounding territories, ports, estates, dependencies, and client communities are understood as attached to the metropolis rather than as transforming it into an ordinary territorial kingdom.

The shared prestige also produces a notorious metropolitan chauvinism. Great City elites commonly regard younger territorial states as provincial, even when those states are rich, sophisticated, and militarily formidable. Meropolis shares this attitude despite its intimate religious and political ties to the Hetaireian Realms.

docs.title: Meropolis
docs.text:
Epithet: The Holy City Motto: “Rise From The Flame Eternal.” Symbol: Golden phoenix on purple.

Meropolis is the sacred-institutional center of the Hetaireia. Its power rests on religious legitimacy, archives, authentication, learned personnel, inherited Heryoi institutions, pilgrimage, diplomacy, and a growing capacity for direct military action.

docs.title: Al-Anwar
docs.text:
Epithet: The Golden City Motto: “Riches And Glory Beyond Compare.” Symbol: White crescent on gold.

Al-Anwar is the premier maritime and commercial power of the Sea of Ardan, ruled by dynastic merchant houses whose political culture treats commercial mastery as evidence of fitness to govern.

docs.title: Zorah
docs.text:
Epithet: The Ancient City Motto: “Ride Well, Shoot Far, Speak Truth.” Symbol: Gold eight-pointed star on red.

Zorah may be the oldest city in the world. Its absolute Shahdom claims continuity with Ardan's temporal imperial sovereignty and derives strategic power from the difficult routes linking the western world to the Sea of Thieves and the Eastward Road.

docs.title: Khemet
docs.text:
Epithet: The Undying City Motto: “Drink From The River Of Life Everlasting.” Symbol: Gold sphinx on blue.

Khemet is the great hydraulic and river-transit power of the Menaru. Its ancient law, mortuary institutions, and memories of the necromantic Cult of the Undying give the city a reputation at once learned, abundant, and deeply unsettling.

docs.title: Zamboula
docs.text:
Epithet: The Black City Motto: “Our Ancestors Named The Stars.” Symbol: Black panther on orange.

Zamboula is an isolated center of rare magical knowledge, black-stone infrastructure, astronomy, and divination. Its visible government is an eight-seat magocracy patterned symbolically on the Eightfold Method.

docs.title: Al-Anwar
docs.text: Epithet: The Golden City Motto: “Riches And Glory Beyond Compare.”

docs.title: Heraldry
docs.text:
Blazon: Or, a crescent argent. (A white crescent on a gold field.)

Meropolitan heralds consider the white-on-gold device improper by later armorial standards, but Al-Anwar is ancient enough that its civic emblem predates many of those conventions.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Al-Anwar is one of the Great Cities and the premier maritime and commercial power of the Sea of Ardan. Its wealth rests not simply on producing goods but on making distant markets interoperable: brokers, warehouses, commercial courts, credit, foreign quarters, shipping networks, caravan infrastructure, information, and reliable transactional institutions allow merchants from incompatible jurisdictions to do business through the city.

Its elite ideal might be described as rule by philosopher-merchants. Wealth alone does not command respect. The exemplary Al-Anwari merchant is expected to demonstrate judgment, foresight, nerve, logistical ability, legal knowledge, solvency, and the capacity to understand how distant events will affect markets before rivals do.

docs.title: Government
docs.text:
Al-Anwar is governed by an entrenched oligarchy of dynastic Great Houses. These houses resemble enduring commercial firms as much as hereditary noble lineages: capital, ships, warehouses, correspondents, clients, information networks, and accumulated reputation pass across generations.

The ruling order is neither wholly closed nor readily accessible. A new house may rise over generations through wealth, civic service, marriages, patronage, commercial victories, and indispensable alliances; an old house may eventually decline out of political consequence. Both processes are slow, and incumbent houses resist newcomers fiercely.

The city's chief executive office is auctioned for a fixed term, but only among candidates accepted as qualified by the oligarchic establishment. The winning bid goes into the civic treasury. Office brings real executive, diplomatic, military, and patronage power, but does not permit the purchaser to dissolve the oligarchy or treat the city as private property.

docs.title: Commercial Honor
docs.text:
Al-Anwari commercial ethics are severe but not sentimental. A merchant who outbargains another, exploits an opponent's ignorance, writes a superior contract, or profits from desperation may be admired rather than condemned. Being fleeced can be treated as evidence that the victim lacked sufficient wit.

The line is crossed when someone attacks the institutions that make trade possible. Forged civic seals, falsified official records, counterfeited recognized weights, and repudiation of explicit obligations threaten the credibility from which every house profits.

Elite culture therefore places enormous weight on face, family standing, fulfilled promises, reciprocal obligation, visible success, and the ability to answer humiliation. The exact Al-Anwari word for this complex of honor, reputation, and social standing remains unsettled.

docs.title: Patronage
docs.text:
Great Houses conspicuously endow temples, fountains, hospitals, schools, caravanserais, walls, harbors, relief funds, and other public works. Such generosity is not assumed to be disinterested. Patronage converts money into prestige, gratitude, dependents, clients, political influence, and remembered obligation.

To Al-Anwari eyes, gaining social capital from generosity does not invalidate the generosity. It proves that wealth has been mastered well enough to create public consequence.

docs.title: Religion and Foreign Communities
docs.text:
Al-Anwar is publicly and institutionally Behdin, but it maintains unusually broad chartered toleration for foreign merchant communities. Resident trading groups may retain shrines, burial customs, communal institutions, and limited internal rules so long as they obey civic law and do not threaten public order.

The settlement is pragmatic rather than relativist. Al-Anwar does not need foreigners to share its beliefs; it needs them to trust that business conducted in the city can be enforced.

docs.title: Trade and Maritime Power
docs.text:
Al-Anwar dominates large-scale commerce across the Sea of Ardan. Its naval strength, commercial enclaves, treaty relationships, credit, merchant houses, and shipping networks reinforce one another.

Its wider mercantile empire is organized less around large contiguous inland conquests than around ports, islands, anchorages, commercial enclaves, client rulers, toll privileges, caravan stations, and other strategic nodes.

This dominance is a major reason Zorah jealously protects its independent access toward the Sea of Thieves, the land bridge, and the Eastward Road. Unrestricted Al-Anwari penetration of those routes could turn Zorah from a rival commercial power into a dependent node in an Al-Anwari network.

docs.title: Military Power
docs.text:
Al-Anwar maintains professional civic security, fortifications, harbor forces, arsenals, and a permanent naval core. It does not normally maintain a comparably large standing field army, which its ruling culture tends to regard as an inefficient peacetime use of capital.

In major wars the city relies heavily on mercenary companies, contracted troops, house retainers, armed merchant vessels, private naval capacity, and specialist brokers able to assemble and supply forces rapidly. The navy is the major standing-force exception because seamanship, dockyards, pilots, and experienced crews cannot be improvised at the beginning of a war.

The system can fail. Delayed mobilization, bidding wars for mercenaries, contractor defection, rivalry among houses, and commanders gaining leverage during emergencies are recurring strategic dangers.

docs.title: Slavery
docs.text: Slavery is legal and commercially normalized but is not the ideological foundation of Al-Anwari society. Enslaved people can be bought, sold, transported, financed, and employed like other market assets; individual houses vary in how central enslaved labor is to their own enterprises.

docs.title: History
docs.text:
Al-Anwar was already an old and sophisticated city when Heryos imperial power reached the Swordlands. It was incorporated at times but remained recurrently resistant and difficult to absorb, preserving a distinct civic and mercantile identity through later imperial transformations.

Its rivalry with Zorah and Meropolis is ancient enough to have existed in the age of Ardan.

docs.title: Khemet
docs.text: Epithet: The Undying City Motto: “Drink From The River Of Life Everlasting.”

docs.title: Heraldry
docs.text: Blazon: Azure, a sphinx Or. (A golden sphinx on a blue field.)

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Khemet is one of the Great Cities and a major power of central Rorania. Its wealth and durability rest on the Menaru, one of Rorania's great permanent rivers. Rising in the Rakhan mountain spine, the river flows north through increasingly arid country before reaching the Sea of Ardan. Its floodplain forms an intensely fertile ribbon through otherwise dry lands, giving literal force to Khemet's ancient language of the River of Life.

Khemet converts irrigation, flood management, river transport, concentrated agricultural surplus, organized labor, mortuary institutions, and the portage traffic of the Kharset into unusual metropolitan power.

Where the upper Menaru leaves the Rakhan highlands for the northern dry country, it cuts through the Kharset, a long gorge-and-cataract complex of narrow channels, rocky islands, rapids, and successive falls. Boats and cargo moving between the uplands and lower Menaru must use portages and transshipment routes around its roughest reaches.

docs.title: Government and Law
docs.text:
Khemet is a kritarchy: ultimate civic sovereignty rests in its highest court or judicial college rather than a monarch, priesthood, or merchant oligarchy. Executive and administrative officials exercise delegated authority within a deeply precedent-heavy legal order.

Water rights, irrigation duties, land tenure, inheritance, debt, temple property, mortuary obligations, river access, portage rights, and public labor have accumulated immense bodies of jurisprudence. Khemite political culture prefers to say that judges discover, reconcile, and apply the law rather than create it, even when a new judgment plainly changes how future cases will be decided.

The senior judiciary tends to be old because mastery of Khemite law requires decades of training, precedent, and reputation, not because age itself confers sovereign authority.

The Deathspeakers are institutionally separate from the government.

docs.title: The Deathspeakers
docs.text:
Khemet’s defining mortuary institution is the order of Deathspeakers, spirit-specialists concerned with the proper relationship between the living and the dead.

Modern Deathspeakers serve primarily as mediums, exorcists, tomb-keepers, and guardians against disturbed or hostile dead. They may communicate with ghosts and shades, maintain funerary wards, investigate hauntings, or deal with dangerous spiritual entities such as Guardians and Revenants when they are encountered.

Khemites distinguish this tradition sharply from Necromancy. Deathspeakers do not legitimately animate corpses, raise zombies, create undead servants, or seek to preserve mortal life through undeath. Outsiders do not always accept that distinction.

The old corruption of Khemet is remembered precisely as a violation of this boundary: mortuary specialists and rulers ceased tending the dead and began attempting to defeat death itself.

docs.title: The Cult of the Undying
docs.text:
Ancient Khemet's characteristic magical horror was Necromancy, not Diabolism. The most infamous expression was the Cult of the Undying, an ancient movement obsessed with achieving immortality regardless of the cost.

Its greatest initiates transformed themselves into the Undying, intelligent and extraordinarily resilient undead who retained memory, ambition, magical knowledge, and long-term agency after death. Many became powerful Necromancers and surrounded themselves with ancient artifacts, undead servants, tomb complexes, and accumulated occult knowledge.

The Cult did not merely raise corpses. It represented a systematic rejection of mortality itself: death treated not as a boundary to be respected but as a technical problem to be overcome.

Some Khemite and Atharite traditions claim that modern Deathspeakers descend from the legitimate mortuary institutions that resisted or survived the Cult. Others remain suspicious that the distinction is too convenient. The extent to which ancient Deathspeaker institutions were complicit, conquered, corrupted, or opposed remains disputed.

docs.title: Religion
docs.text:
Khemet belongs formally to the southern Atharite communion known as The Behdin. Old Khemite mortuary customs survive alongside it in an uneasy mixture of accepted tradition, tolerated local practice, and recurrent suspicion.

Deathspeaking is not understood locally as Necromancy or as a separate rival religion. A Deathspeaker may be a devout Atharite while practicing a mortuary discipline that is neither ordinary priestly rite nor corpse-animation. The broader Behdin framework permits inherited local institutions to survive when their relationships are genuinely reordered under Atharite doctrine; Khemet is the clearest major example of that process.

docs.title: The City After Dark
docs.text:
Khemet's reputation for nocturnal danger is exaggerated, but not invented.

Busy riverfronts, major roads, guarded districts, temples, markets, and wealthy quarters can remain active after sunset. The worst dangers cluster around old tomb precincts, buried or abandoned hydraulic works, ancient neighborhoods, ruined compounds, and other liminal parts of the city.

The supernatural substrate is real. Restless dead, failed immortality workings, damaged tomb wards, necromantic contamination, sealed Undying, abandoned laboratories, and other legacies of the ancient crisis still survive in places. Not every strange event is a Necromancer or active cult, and ordinary criminals, smugglers, kidnappers, assassins, and grave robbers readily exploit the city's reputation.

Deathspeakers are part of why the problem is not worse.

docs.title: Slavery and Labor
docs.text:
Slavery is a deeply established part of Khemite society and is especially important on estates, in agriculture, households, major works, and other labor-intensive sectors of the Menaru economy. It exists alongside large populations of free peasants, tenants, dependents, seasonal workers, and people owing legally defined labor obligations.

As with nearly every Khemite institution, status and obligation are governed by elaborate law rather than one simple division between free and enslaved.

docs.title: Historical Importance
docs.text:
Khemet was an ancient metropolitan rival of the Heryoi imperial world rather than an ordinary imperial province. Atharite histories later made the city a notorious example of necromantic corruption because of the Cult of the Undying.

How much of that memory accurately describes ancient Khemet as a whole, rather than the triumph of one dreadful movement within a larger civilization, remains a matter of scholarly and religious dispute.

docs.title: Meropolis
docs.text: Epithet: The Holy City Motto: “Rise From The Flame Eternal.”

docs.title: Heraldry
docs.text:
Blazon: Purpure, a phoenix Or. (A golden phoenix on a purple field.)

The phoenix is both a civic emblem and a fitting expression of Meropolis's religious-historical identity: survival through imperial collapse, Ardan's revolution, and the city's motto all reinforce the image.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Meropolis is one of the Great Cities and the principal urban stronghold of the northern Atharite tradition. Although geographically situated among the southern cities, it is the exceptional metropolis aligned with the northern church and functions as the political and ecclesiastical center of the Hetaireia.

Meropolis stands at the western foot of Mount Kromon, so close to the isolated sacred mountain that the city's upper districts, sanctuaries, walls, and waterworks climb onto or are cut into its lower slopes without the city literally occupying the mountain itself. The Nelorelis, the “First Water,” issues from a great perennial spring at Kromon and descends through or immediately beside Meropolis before flowing south toward the Sea of Ardan. Downstream river traffic, coastal harbors, and converging overland routes make Meropolis a natural hinge between Szovij and the northern Hetaireian world, the Sea of Ardan, and the drier southern and eastern approaches. The city is therefore strongly maritime-connected without being a literal coastal metropolis.

The sacred spring is the symbolic heart and principal natural water source of Meropolis, but the mature Great City does not depend upon one outlet alone. Wells, cisterns, reservoirs, channels, and later waterworks supplement the Nelorelis and distribute water through a metropolis built against Kromon's foot and across the surrounding hills.

Its importance rests on overlapping inheritances: the seat of the Pontis, prestigious archives, authentication, learned personnel, inherited Heryoi institutions, pilgrimage, diplomacy, and increasingly direct military power. Meropolis's scarce resource is not raw population or territory but recognized legitimacy and institutional interoperability.

Meropolis does not possess a monopoly on imperial continuity. Princes, cities, religious houses, archives, and local communities across the Hetaireian Realms preserve other genuine fragments of the old order. Meropolitan claims carry exceptional prestige, but continuity itself remains politically contestable.

docs.title: Sacred Origins
docs.text:
Atharite tradition identifies Mount Kromon and the site of Meropolis as the birthplace of mankind. According to the sacred account, Athar created the First Man there, and the first water ever drunk by a human being was drawn from the Nelorelis, the holy river rising from Kromon. The city's sanctity therefore reaches, in Atharite belief, far deeper than Ardan, the Heryoi Empire, or any surviving institution.

The First Man's descendants include Lovar, Rovar, and Eovar, remembered as ancestral patriarchs associated with the early dispersal and division of mankind. The historical truth of this account is not settled outside Atharite doctrine, and other peoples preserve different origin traditions. Within Atharism, however, Meropolis's claim to be the first homeland of humanity is foundational sacred history rather than a later civic legend.

Mount Kromon, its spring, and the Nelorelis are consequently holy places in their own right. Pilgrimage to Meropolis is directed not only toward the Pontis, Ardanic relics, archives, and great sanctuaries, but toward a landscape believed to have witnessed the beginning of human life. The sacred character of the site is understood to predate the Heryoi Empire, Ardan, and the present ecclesiastical order; later civilizations inherited, monumentalized, and reinterpreted an already ancient holy place.

docs.title: Religion and Government
docs.text:
Meropolis is a hierocracy in sovereignty. Ultimate public authority rests in the Pontis and the sacred institutional order, but the city is not administered as if every civic task were performed directly by priests.

Government is distributed among the Pontis and High Ministry, inherited civil offices, professional administrators, municipal and corporate bodies, and influential great families. The Pontis is head of state as well as supreme Hetaireian religious authority, but ordinary administration depends on institutions older and broader than his personal household.

The High Ministry is an ecclesiastical governing body rather than a quiet technocratic cabinet. Its deliberations can be boisterous, doctrinally charged, factional, theatrical, and occasionally physically confrontational without being unserious. Senior clerics are expected to argue matters of faith, law, discipline, appointment, and policy with intensity.

Meropolis also contains hereditary great families with estates, patronage networks, ecclesiastical connections, and claims to ancient Heryoi ancestry. They possess enormous political influence but no separate sovereign senate. Their power lies in the offices, clients, wealth, marriages, and institutions they control.

Meropolis is therefore a hierocracy in sovereignty, a bureaucracy in administration, and a corporate city in everyday governance.

In Hetaireian political theory, the Princes of the northern Realms belong to an inherited Ardanic princely order rather than possessing wholly independent Kingship. In practice, Pontifical authority remains a bundle of powers whose reach varies by subject. The Pontis possesses final Hetaireian doctrinal authority subject to scripture and exercises enormous influence over upper clerical legitimacy, transregional recognition of rites and clergy, arbitration, princely recognition, and matters where religion intersects with marriage, legitimacy, oaths, sanctuary, sacrilege, clerical status, and ecclesiastical property.

His ordinary secular jurisdiction outside Meropolis is much narrower. The Pontis does not normally legislate the daily law of every Principality, and even prestigious Meropolitan judgments often require local actors for enforcement.

docs.title: Archives and Authentication
docs.text:
Meropolis contains some of the most prestigious archives in the Hetaireian world. Clerics, Princes, cities, noble houses, merchants, and litigants may seek Meropolitan confirmation of seals, genealogies, ecclesiastical status, ancient privileges, marriages, oaths, or disputed documents.

The city does not hold every record and cannot make a false claim true merely by decree. Its power lies in expertise, continuity, reputation, and the fact that recognition in Meropolis can make a claim intelligible across many otherwise incompatible jurisdictions.

docs.title: Ardan's Crown
docs.text:
Meropolis preserves Ardan's crown as a genuine sacred relic. It is associated with Ardan's sanctity, memory, and the sacred-institutional continuity of the post-imperial world rather than treated as living royal regalia for a later temporal ruler.

Zorah preserves Ardan's scepter as living accession regalia and uses it to support the Shahdom's claim to temporal imperial continuity. The divided regalia have become one of the clearest material symbols of the ancient succession dispute: Meropolis preserves the sacred crown; Zorah wields the temporal scepter.

docs.title: Language and People
docs.text:
The ancient Heryos who settled around Meropolis developed into the northern Heryoi branch. Their language changed over centuries into Meropolitan, the modern language of the city.

In Meropolitan, mer denotes a great water: a body or course of water understood as geographically or culturally major. In ordinary modern usage the term most often refers to seas, oceans, and very large lakes, but the sacred Nelorelis is traditionally reckoned among the Great Waters despite being a river. Meropolis, from mer-o-polis, is therefore conventionally understood as “City of the Great Water.” “Sea-City” remains a natural secondary reading because of the city's long relationship with the Sea of Ardan and the narrower tendency of later everyday usage.

Meropolitan is also the principal transregional learned and clerical language of the Hetaireian world. Clergy, scholars, scribes, record-keepers, diplomats, and many elites use it across Realm boundaries, but it is not a universal everyday common tongue.

See Languages.

docs.title: Historical Role
docs.text:
The Heryos and their imperial heirs were deeply entangled with Meropolis. The steppe conquerors were culturally transformed by contact with the sophisticated southern cities, especially Meropolis and Zorah.

When the late imperial order became corrupted by diabolism and eldritch cults, Ardan overthrew its sacred and political foundations. He nevertheless retained useful imperial machinery where it could serve survival and the spread of Athar's Way. The New Ardanic Empire that followed therefore combined inherited Heryos institutions with a revolutionary source of legitimacy.

The New Empire later contracted over generations rather than disappearing at once. Fiscal, military, and territorial centralization decayed faster than the transregional Atharite religious network. Meropolis consequently remained a center of religious recognition, records, learning, and political memory even as effective universal government disappeared.

After Ardan's death or Ascension, his wife Polema became the principal southern claimant opposed to Theron in the original succession and religious crisis. Polema later died without issue. Zorahn tradition holds that Ardan's temporal dynastic claim then continued through a son of Ardan's sister, while northern tradition often treats the direct line as having ended with Polema.

docs.title: Roads, Sanctuaries, and the Wider Hetaireia
docs.text:
Meropolis's practical connection to the Realms depends on networks rather than continuous territorial control. Sanctuaries, hospices, shrines, clerical houses, pilgrimage routes, safe-conducts, messengers, ferries, ports, and protected roads allow people and information to move between defended settlements through dangerous country.

The Hetaireia does not own the road system. Local Princes, cities, communities, merchants, monasteries, and other institutions maintain most routes. Meropolis contributes a transregional layer of recognized religious sites, credentials, sanctuary, hospitality, arbitration, and communication that helps those local systems interoperate.

docs.title: The Hiera Tagmata
docs.text:
Meropolis is also the center of the controversial modern expansion of Pontifical armed power. The Hiera Tagmata, or Sacred Regiments, grew from older and widely accepted rights to defend the Pontis, the High Ministry, sacred institutions, and the city itself.

The oldest and most prestigious regiment is the cavalry-centered Vyrkar Guard. The wider Tagmata are a more recent dynastic project whose authority outside Meropolis is being accumulated through precedent rather than one universally accepted grant.

Growing Chulkan pressure around Meropolis and increasing southern Behdin power make the expansion defensible. The same regiments also give the Pontis unprecedented direct coercive capacity, which makes many Princes wary even when they accept his religious authority.

docs.title: Social Notes
docs.text:
Slavery is effectively prohibited in Meropolis, following the broader Hetaireian norm. Foreign households, trafficking disguised under other legal statuses, and disputed external claims can create edge cases, but slavery has no legitimate place in Meropolitan civic law.

Married clergy also make clerical households important participants in Meropolitan politics. Office is not formally hereditary, but education, literacy, patronage, marriage, wealth, and institutional connections allow clerical families to accumulate influence across generations. The increasingly hereditary drift of the Pontificate is the most politically consequential example.

Meropolitan elites also share the characteristic Great City assumption that younger territorial polities are provincial. This produces a recurring tension with the Hetaireian Princedoms: Meropolis depends upon them politically and religiously while many Meropolitans still treat their courts and local institutions as peripheral to the true metropolitan center.

docs.title: Zamboula
docs.text:
Epithet: The Black City Motto: “Our Ancestors Named The Stars.”

Zamboula is an ancient black-stone city on the edge of the southern wilderness and one of the Great Cities. Its influence rests on rare magical knowledge, astronomy, divination, inherited supernatural infrastructure, and learned institutions whose expertise is difficult to reproduce elsewhere.

docs.title: Geography and Isolation
docs.text:
Zamboula lies at the western edge of the immense Mahrad desert system. The desert and the approaches to the Rakhan separate it from the denser road, caravan, and political networks surrounding the other Great Cities. Overland travel eastward depends heavily on established caravan routes, reliable wells, and oasis districts; travel away from those routes becomes dangerous and logistically expensive very quickly.

This geography gives Zamboula an unusual degree of isolation for a Great City. Sea travel and long-distance caravans prevent it from being cut off, but neither erases the cost of distance. The same barrier helps limit routine northern access to the southern Roranian interior and makes Zamboula an important western gate to lands that are otherwise difficult for outsiders to reach.

docs.title: Heraldry and Civic Emblem
docs.text:
Blazon: Tenné, a panther sable. (A black panther on an orange field.)

Here panther refers to the natural great cat rather than the fantastical beast depicted under that name in some western heraldic traditions. The orange/tawny field places Zamboula visibly outside ordinary Meropolitan armorial fashion.

docs.title: The Black Stone
docs.text:
Zamboula is built around immense black structures that appear carved from single masses rather than assembled by masonry. The Zamboulans claim their ancestors possessed lost rituals capable of shaping the stone.

There is evidence that at least some structures predate the present city. Their geometry is subtly wrong: interiors do not always seem to correspond with exterior dimensions, and people standing at certain intersections report auditory or visual distortions.

Black-stone monoliths and ruins of apparently related material are also reported far beyond Zamboula, especially across the southern coasts and islands: among the Wolilalika, on Hakori islands, throughout parts of the Pingrit Archipelago, and at other isolated maritime sites. Many of these structures are locally believed to predate human settlement. Their meanings differ sharply from place to place; some communities treat them as sacred, while others avoid them as cursed.

docs.title: Government: The Eightfold College
docs.text:
Zamboula is openly a magocracy. Supreme civic sovereignty rests collectively in eight recognized master magi whose seats correspond symbolically to the eight points of the Octogram.

The seats do not represent eight magical schools, ministries, castes, or elemental specializations. Zamboulan political philosophy instead draws on the same principle as ritual magic: no significant working is accomplished through one Element alone, and no single person is considered sufficient to govern the city alone.

Six members exercise ordinary votes. Time is the longest-serving member of the College, presides over its proceedings, and does not ordinarily vote. Fate is assigned by lot whenever membership changes and likewise casts no ordinary vote, but resolves an otherwise equal division among the six voting members.

Membership is normally for life. Candidates must first reach the highest recognized levels of magical learning, reputation, and civic standing before they can be considered for a vacancy. Exact academic ranks, office titles, and nomination procedures vary among institutions and remain obscure to most foreigners.

docs.title: The Mundungu
docs.text:
The Mundungu are Zamboula's dominant learned-magical estate. They include sorcerers, astrologers, diviners, occult philosophers, physicians, ritual specialists, and other highly trained practitioners. They are distinct from Atharite Speakers and are not a priesthood by definition.

Mundungu scholarship carries enormous prestige because access to advanced training, restricted texts, ancient sites, observatories, and rare ritual knowledge is concentrated in their institutions and patronage networks.

docs.title: Religion
docs.text:
Zamboula is nominally part of The Behdin, but its religious culture is chronically heterodox and often considered heretical elsewhere in the southern world. The Behdin's decentralized structure means no single authority can permanently and uncontestedly expel the city from the faith.

Southern synods, theologians, temples, and coalitions have repeatedly condemned particular Zamboulan teachers or doctrines, while Zamboula disputes their universal jurisdiction.

Older Zamboulan occult traditions include a form of Diabolism centered on Starspawn habitation rather than Devi-style external demon bargains. In these traditions the central danger is not opening a gate to something outside Creation, but making a mortal, bloodline, or institution habitable to something already trapped within it.

docs.title: Society and Slavery
docs.text:
Zamboulan elite culture presents the city as an island of extraordinary learning and civilization surrounded by peoples it considers comparatively primitive.

Slavery is structurally central to the city's political economy and elite way of life. Enslaved labor is used on great estates, in households, workshops, construction, transport, and other sectors; large agricultural estates or plantation-like systems are likely important, though their exact crops and geography remain to be established.

The institution should not be mistaken for proof that every Zamboulan is personally cruel or involved in occult practice. Most inhabitants remain ordinary artisans, laborers, soldiers, sailors, merchants, clerks, priests, householders, enslaved people, and farmers living under institutions they did not design.

docs.title: Historical Memory
docs.text: Zamboulan tradition claims the city preserves the western remnant of a much older learned civilization whose sages possessed knowledge of stars, ritual, and black-stone construction unavailable elsewhere. The exact extent and chronology of that civilization remain uncertain, but Zamboula's antiquity and role as a distant diplomatic and commercial peer of the ancient Great Cities are not dependent on Heryoi imperial incorporation.

docs.title: Zorah
docs.text: Epithet: The Ancient City Motto: “Ride Well, Shoot Far, Speak Truth.” Symbol: A gold eight-pointed star on red.

docs.title: Heraldry
docs.text:
Blazon: Gules, a mullet of eight points Or. (A gold eight-pointed star on a red field.)

The red-and-gold device is ancient, simple, and immediately recognizable.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Zorah is an ancient city on the southern coast of the land bridge joining Lorania, Rorania, and Eorania. It may be the oldest city in the world, though Meropolitan claims to primacy remain part of learned dispute.

The city occupies the eastern-facing end of the Great Cities' land bridge and stands at the western end of important trade with Devi and the farther east. It is associated with explorers, caravan interests, cavalry traditions, maritime risk-taking, and merchants who take an active role in opening and protecting difficult routes.

docs.title: Government and Imperial Claim
docs.text:
Zorah is an absolute monarchy under Shah Arslan. Zorahn constitutional doctrine does not ordinarily claim that the Shah is a newly restored Emperor. Instead, it holds that the Shahdom itself is the uninterrupted continuation of Ardan's temporal imperial sovereignty.

The claim rests on a genuine dynastic tradition. After Ardan's death or Ascension, his wife Polema became the principal southern claimant in the succession crisis. She did not remarry and died without issue. Zorahn genealogy holds that the dynastic claim then passed to a son of Ardan's sister and continued collaterally into the later royal line.

Northern and Hetaireian traditions may define “Ardan's line” more narrowly and regard the direct dynasty as having ended with Polema. The dispute is therefore not simply a fabricated Zorahn genealogy but a disagreement over what constitutes legitimate continuity.

Zorah also possesses Ardan's scepter, regarded as genuine living accession regalia of temporal sovereignty. Meropolis preserves Ardan's crown as a sacred relic rather than living royal regalia. The divided regalia have become a material expression of the old schism: Meropolis emphasizes sacred and institutional continuity, while Zorah emphasizes temporal and dynastic continuity.

docs.title: Religion
docs.text:
Before conversion, the people of Zorah practiced a dualistic fire faith. The Lord of Eternal Light, Ormahn, was opposed by his twin Angrahn, Lord of Infinite Darkness. Both were said to have been born of a blind and deaf Universal Mother representing the neutral substrate of existence.

This theology proved unusually compatible with Atharism. Zorahn syncretists identify Ormahn with Athar and reinterpret Angrahn as a personification of the Outer Darkness rather than a true god.

The Behdin does not constitutionally belong to the Shah. Nevertheless, Zorahn aristocrats and court clergy commonly argue that Ardanic descent, Polema's temporal succession, and custody of the imperial scepter impose upon the Shah a hereditary duty—and, in Zorahn eyes, a corresponding right—to protect the southern Atharite world, defend its institutions, preserve religious peace, and intervene against grave disorder.

Other major Behdin centers concede essentially no constitutional authority to this theory. They may acknowledge the authenticity of the dynasty, scepter, and historical continuity while denying that any of those facts gives the Shah standing over their clergy, councils, monasteries, or religious policy. The merchant princes of Al-Anwar are especially likely to treat Zorahn claims of universal guardianship as a source of amusement rather than obedience. Smaller rulers or religious institutions may defer to Zorah for political, military, or patronage reasons, but such deference is particular rather than a recognized right of the Shahdom over The Behdin as a whole.

docs.title: People and Language
docs.text:
The southern descendants of the ancient Heryos developed into the Heryan branch associated especially with Zorah.

The modern Zorahn language descends from that branch. See Languages.

docs.title: Trade and Rivalries
docs.text:
Zorah competes with Al-Anwar and Meropolis over tariffs, trade routes, and influence across the land bridge. These rivalries are ancient enough to have existed in the age of Ardan. The bloodshed associated with repeated wars among the three cities is one explanation for the name Swordlands.

Zorah's commercial strategy is shaped by the fact that Al-Anwar dominates the Sea of Ardan. Zorah therefore guards the routes Al-Anwar does not control: access toward the Sea of Thieves, the land bridge, and the Eastward Road. Its restrictive tariffs and route controls are not merely fiscal greed; Zorahn rulers fear that unrestricted Al-Anwari access would reduce Zorah to a subordinate node in a larger Al-Anwari network.

Under normal conditions, the Eastward Road provides the principal overland connection toward Eorania. The great mountain barrier farther east and south prevents merchants from simply bypassing the road through alternate passes.

When Chulkas pressure makes the Eastward Road unusable, merchants face a stark choice: lose access to eastern goods or attempt dangerous sea voyages around the southern routes. That crisis greatly increases the value of Zorah's ports, shipping interests, and knowledge of eastern maritime trade.

One especially notorious destination is Lautang, the northwestern Pingrit stilt-city near the Lautara channel. Lautang is far enough away that the voyage is costly and dangerous, but its black markets carry smuggled, stolen, restricted, and difficult-to-source eastern goods.

docs.title: Slavery
docs.text: Slavery is legal and socially normalized in Zorah, but it is not the central ideological foundation of the Shahdom. Enslaved labor appears in households, estates, agriculture, transport, and other sectors alongside free and dependent labor.

docs.title: Historical Notes
docs.text: Zorah was one of the great southern urban cultures that transformed the conquering Heryos in turn and later became a principal metropolitan heartland of the Heryoi imperial world.
