docs.title: The Hetaireian Princedoms
docs.text:
The Hetaireian Princedoms are the many decentralized polities of northern Atharite civilization. Their peoples share a broad Hetaireian order centered religiously on the Hetaireia and the Pontis in Meropolis, but they do not form a single state, ethnicity, language, or uniform legal system.

Hetaireian identity sits beside older and more immediate loyalties: village, city, clan, dynasty, Principality, language, people, and Realm. What makes the north a civilization is less uniformity than interoperability. Travelers crossing political boundaries can still recognize Hetaireian clergy and rites, marriage and burial customs, oath traditions, sanctuaries, pilgrimage networks, religious calendars, seals and credentials, and familiar forms of political legitimacy.

docs.title: Realms and Principalities
docs.text:
Albia, Clovia, Dorado, Nibelung, Szovij, and Khoryv are Realms: broad historical and cultural affinity regions rather than single states. A Realm may contain many independent or semi-independent Principalities, and need not possess a capital, supreme ruler, or common constitution.

A Principality is the polity or inherited jurisdiction ruled by a Prince. It need not resemble a modern territorial state. A Prince's authority may consist of overlapping lands, offices, revenues, cities, enclaves, customary rights, client lordships, immunities, and jurisdictions whose boundaries do not coincide neatly.

The broad political scale is therefore Hetaireian civilization → Realm → Principality → locally variable jurisdictions. Beneath a Principality may lie lordships, marches, clan territories, chartered cities, temple estates, castellanies, valleys, islands, leagues, or other arrangements. No single hierarchy applies everywhere.

The six Realms are:

  • Albia
  • Nibelung
  • Dorado
  • Clovia
  • Szovij
  • Khoryv

Within each Realm, Principalities usually share a recognizable family resemblance in language, history, legal vocabulary, elite custom, warfare, ecclesiastical style, road practice, architecture, and material culture. These similarities form a common cultural grammar rather than a standardized constitution.

docs.title: Why Princes, Not Kings
docs.text:
The title Prince is not a lesser grade of King. It descends from the Principalities of the New Ardanic Empire, whose rulers retained their old office and title as imperial territorial government gradually fragmented.

A legitimate Prince normally rests on two foundations: locally valid accession and Pontifical recognition. Local law determines how a ruler comes to power. Depending on the Principality, that may involve heredity, eligible-kindred selection, assembly approval, civic consent, military acclamation, possession, regalia, clerical participation, or several of these at once. There is no universal Hetaireian succession law.

The Pontis normally recognizes and universalizes an already meaningful local claim rather than creating one from nothing. Recognition places a ruler securely within the wider Hetaireian order, but political legitimacy is not perfectly binary: locally accepted but unrecognized rulers, disputed Princes, rival claimants, and usurpers all occur.

Kingship carries a different constitutional meaning. A King claims non-derivative temporal sovereignty outside the inherited Ardanic princely order. Such a claim inherently rejects Pontifical temporal supremacy, although it does not by itself require rejection of Athar, Ardan's Theosis, or the Pontis's religious office. Meropolis will normally regard the claim as grave insubordination, and the resulting dispute may also become religious.

docs.title: The Pontis and the Princes
docs.text:
The Pontis is universally important without being a northern emperor. His authority is strongest in doctrine, recognition of clergy and rites, marriage and legitimacy, ecclesiastical affairs, authentication, arbitration, sanctuary, oaths, and disputes that cross political boundaries. He does not ordinarily legislate the secular law of every Principality or directly administer their populations.

Pontifical influence generally grows as a problem becomes more transregional. A village quarrel may never concern Meropolis; a dispute between Princes in different Realms has much stronger reason to seek Hetaireian mediation because no shared secular authority stands above them.

This creates a dense political order rather than a chain of command. Princes, Speakers, cities, noble houses, temples, clans, merchant interests, and the High Ministry bargain through law, custom, reputation, religious standing, finance, marriage, arbitration, and force.

docs.title: Law and Jurisdiction
docs.text:
Hetaireian law is jurisdictionally plural. A person can simultaneously stand within princely, ecclesiastical, civic, household, kin, professional, military, or special jurisdictions. Which authority has the better claim may depend not only on where something happened but on the people involved, their status and oaths, the subject of the dispute, and the protected place or institution concerned.

Arguments over jurisdiction are therefore ordinary politics, not proof that the system has broken down. Hetaireian coherence comes largely from shared procedures that let different legal worlds interact: recognizable oaths, witnesses, seals, clerical credentials, safe-conducts, appeals, arbitration, documentary authentication, and negotiated transfers of cases.

The same pluralism shapes violence. Feud, vengeance, compensation, outlawry, ecclesiastical penance, civic punishment, and princely justice coexist. Princes continually seek to expand the idea of the Prince's peace, turning some injuries from private or kin disputes into offenses against public order, but the success of that project varies enormously.

docs.title: Roads, Hospitality, and the Dangerous World
docs.text:
The Hetaireian Realms are not blankets of safe settlement. Monsters, hostile spirits, eldritch remnants, predatory beings, bandits, and other dangers make wilderness travel materially more hazardous than in an ordinary human world. Civilization survives as defended concentrations of settlement linked by protected corridors.

Major roads, rivers, passes, pilgrimage ways, and coastal routes remain usable because people keep them usable. Patrols, fortified inns, temple hospices, bridge-towns, ferries, shrines, watchtowers, escorts, settlements, and beacon systems create chains of relative security. A road may remain physically visible long after it has ceased to be functionally open.

This gives rulers a widely understood obligation: keep the road. A Prince who cannot protect important routes, suppress persistent threats, maintain crossings, or keep travelers moving is visibly failing at rule. Reopening a monster-haunted pass or restoring an abandoned corridor can be an act of state-building as important as winning a battle.

The Hetaireia contributes to this system less by owning roads than by maintaining a transregional network of sanctuaries, hospices, clerical houses, recognized safe-conducts, pilgrimage sites, and religious protections. Some important sanctuaries possess genuine supernatural defenses, relics, wards, miraculous phenomena, or powerful theurgists, but such protections are exceptional rather than ubiquitous.

Hospitality consequently carries unusual moral force. Turning a peaceful traveler in genuine need back into dangerous darkness when shelter can reasonably be offered is widely regarded as a grave failure of guest-right. Exact rituals and obligations vary greatly between Realms.

docs.title: Arms, Peace, and Frontier Service
docs.text:
Hetaireian society does not assume a universal princely monopoly on violence. Self-defense, household defense, feud, civic force, princely war, outlaw-hunting, monster-hunting, contracted military service, and ecclesiastically authorized force can all be legitimate in the proper circumstances. The tolerated scale of private violence varies sharply between Principalities.

Peace is correspondingly layered. Guest-right, sanctuary, market peace, road peace, pilgrimage protection, safe-conducts, truces, sacred days, and princely peace can forbid violence that might otherwise be permissible. Violating a protected peace may be more serious than the same physical act elsewhere because it attacks the institution guaranteeing safety.

Ordinary defensive fortification is widespread. Farms, villages, temples, inns, mills, and isolated communities may need walls, palisades, towers, shutters, ditches, or refuges simply to survive. Political suspicion falls instead on fortifications and armed followings capable of sustaining autonomous coercive power against other humans.

Where persistent danger overwhelms ordinary settled administration, Marches may develop. A frontier is a material condition; a March is an institutional response to it. Marcher status brings exceptional rights together with exceptional obligations of patrol, warning, refuge, fortification, provisioning, and rapid response. Marches can face foreign enemies, raiders, monsters, supernatural corruption, or dangerous internal wilderness.

A Marcher is therefore not a universal noble rank but a prestigious Hetaireian classification of frontier service. Nobles, freemen, cities, clans, military hosts, temples, monasteries, and other institutions can possess marcher standing. Sustained frontier service can become a road to land, office, privilege, and even nobility.

docs.title: Professional Violence
docs.text:
The dangerous world supports many people whose livelihood depends on controlled violence without creating a universal adventurers' guild. Caravan guards, monster-hunters, road wardens, scouts, bounty hunters, ghoul-clearers, curse-breakers, exorcists, sanctioned sorcerers, ruin-guides, and mercenary companies are socially intelligible professions.

Their legitimacy depends on purpose and authority. Clearing a ghoul nest, guarding a caravan, hunting an outlaw, or defending a bridge can be honorable contracted work; using the same armed company for robbery or an unauthorized private seizure can turn respected professionals into brigands. Reputation, patronage, discipline, oath-keeping, and observance of protected places matter greatly.

docs.title: Imperial Memory
docs.text:
The Hetaireian order is the product of several historical layers. Heryos conquest and institution-building created much of the old administrative framework. Ardan preserved useful machinery while replacing the sacred and constitutional legitimacy of the old empire. The New Ardanic Empire then fragmented gradually: taxation, military command, infrastructure, and territorial government localized faster than the transregional religious network.

The result was not six clean successor kingdoms. Principalities, cities, temples, aristocratic houses, local communities, and Meropolis inherited different pieces of imperial law, office, archives, roads, boundaries, and memory. Old Provinces influenced later Realm identities, but there is no assumed one-to-one Province-to-Realm succession.

That uneven inheritance helps explain both Hetaireian unity and Hetaireian fragmentation: the Realms share enough institutional ancestry to understand one another while possessing centuries of divergent local development.

docs.title: Albia
docs.text: Motto: “Albia Forever.”

docs.title: Heraldry
docs.text:
Blazon: Vert, a triskelion argent. (A white triskelion on a green field.)

The Albian triskelion is ancient enough that its original meaning is forgotten. In the current era, many Atharites interpret its threefold design as representing Athar, Ardan, and mankind.

The triskelion is a broad Albian emblem rather than the personal arms of every Prince. Local peoples, dynasties, clans, cities, and confederations retain their own devices, and the highland Tuatha are not incorporated into a single Albian armorial system.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Albia is one of the Hetaireian Realms, but it is not a tightly unified state or a single ethnicity. Successive migrations and conquests, persistent kin structures, religiously porous highlands, island geography, and weak political integration have produced a dense patchwork of peoples, clans, Princes, island communities, and local identities.

The Bryth, Cymbraeth, Fian, Caledonians, and Manaw are among the most important identities conventionally grouped as Albian, while numerous Tuatha clans remain interspersed through the southern highlands. These categories are not equivalent administrative provinces and do not exhaust every local identity.

The Realm is regarded as a backwater by many of its peers, yet its longbowmen and sailors are widely respected.

docs.title: Northern Coastlands — Brythia
docs.text: The Bryth dominate much of Albia's northern coastlands. They descend substantially from Firelander invaders and settlers who crossed the northern sea and established themselves among older Albian populations.

docs.title: Central Lowlands — Cymbraeth
docs.text: The Cymbraeth inhabit much of central Albia's settled lowlands. Their pastoral villages, fields, grazing lands, streams, and old local communities have repeatedly fallen under stronger Princes without losing their cultural identity.

docs.title: Western Coast — Fian
docs.text: The Fian inhabit much of the western coast. Firelander raids from the sea and conflict with particularly aggressive Tuatha clans in the western hills have helped produce a martial culture famous for cattle-raiding, warrior companies, bardic memory, and a taste for both fighting and lamentation.

docs.title: Southern Highlands — Caledonians and Eídne
docs.text:
The Caledonians and Eídne clans inhabit the cold southern highlands. The distinction between them is often more religious than ethnic: neighboring clans may speak closely related dialects, intermarry, share ancestry and customs, yet be classified differently according to whether they follow Atharism or retain the older Tuathan religion.

The other major Tuatha confederations lie farther east and are not native to Albia.

docs.title: Northern Islands — Manaw
docs.text: The Manaw inhabit islands and maritime communities along Albia's northern waters. Their culture grew from generations of contact and intermarriage among islanders, coastal Albians, Firelander settlers, raiders, merchants, and sailors. Mainlanders often regard the sea as Albia's northern boundary; the Manaw regard it as a road.

docs.title: History
docs.text:
Albia's northern and western coasts have long suffered raids from the Firelanders. Around five centuries after the Ascension of Ardan, Firelander invaders occupied significant territory, especially in the northern coastlands. Their descendants became the Bryth, while other waves of settlement and intermarriage contributed to the mixed maritime culture of the Manaw.

Older Albian populations survived conquest in several forms. The Cymbraeth remained rooted in the central lowlands despite repeated political subjugation. The Fian developed along the embattled western coast, while the southern highlands preserved both Atharite Caledonian clans and Eídne communities following older traditions.

Prince Eodric's conversion to Atharism in 689 AA is the decisive event in the full public conversion of Brythia and an important milestone in Albia's place within the Hetaireian princely order.

Older traditions remain persistent. Human heads were once placed on pikes as territorial markers. The priesthood has outlawed the practice, but it reportedly survives in the highlands and isolated districts.

docs.title: Political Structure
docs.text:
Albia is very loosely unified. Princes, clan chiefs, island lords, local dynasties, and confederations compete continually, and princely jurisdictions overlap older kin, clan, and local structures. A strong Prince may dominate a broad territory; a minor Prince may govern little more than a hall, its immediate lands, rights, and dependents.

Cultural identity does not map cleanly onto political allegiance. A Brythian Prince may rule Cymbraeth subjects; neighboring Caledonian and Eídne clans may share kinship while following different religions; Fian warrior companies may cross princely boundaries; and Manaw sea-lords may maintain stronger ties across the water than to any mainland court.

docs.title: Tanistry
docs.text:
Among Atharite Albians, some form of tanistry is the normal principle of princely succession. The ruler is expected to come from a legitimate royal or chiefly kindred, but strict father-to-eldest-son primogeniture is unusual. Fitness, adulthood, reputation, kinship, and the willingness of important chiefs, nobles, warriors, clergy, or assemblies to accept a candidate all matter.

There is no single Albian law of tanistry. In some Principalities a successor is designated during the ruler's lifetime and succession is comparatively orderly. Elsewhere the choice remains informal until a death, and an unpopular candidate may be rejected even after an apparent settlement. The Fian preserve especially forceful clan-based customs close to the older Tuathan Choosing of Spears, while Brythian practice places greater weight on public acclamation and the assent of leading landholders, reflecting Firelander assembly traditions.

Albian scholars disagree over the origin of tanistry. Tuathan traditionalists regard it as a domesticated descendant of the ancient Choosing of Spears; Brythian chroniclers emphasize Firelander customs of recognizing rulers through assemblies; Atharite clerics credit post-conversion law and mediation with regularizing succession before it could become feud. The modern institution likely reflects all three influences.

The principle is therefore shared more widely than the procedure: royal blood establishes eligibility, but recognition establishes rule. Pontifical recognition gives a successful local claimant standing within the wider Hetaireian order but does not replace Albian accession custom.

docs.title: Fosterage, Hostages, and Kinship
docs.text:
Fosterage is deeply embedded across much of Albia. A child raised in another household can acquire durable quasi-kin whose claims of loyalty, protection, feud, marriage, succession, and political obligation may matter almost as much as genealogical descent.

Fosterage also provides one of the strongest social bridges across the religiously divided highlands. Caledonian and Eídne clans may foster children across the Atharite/Tuathan boundary. Hosts are expected to respect the foster-child's religion; coercive conversion or forced ritual participation is a serious breach of trust.

Fosterage and hostage-taking can overlap without becoming identical. A child may simultaneously be pupil, fosterling, alliance-bond, and political surety. Even an honorable hostage remains under the protection of the receiving household. If the guarantor breaks faith, escalation may mean tighter confinement, ransom, transfer, prolonged detention, or a change in legal status; mutilating or killing a blameless foster-hostage is exceptional and can itself be regarded as a grave dishonor.

These customs make reputation and reciprocal trust political resources. A house known to abuse fosterlings or hostages may win an immediate quarrel while making future alliances far harder to secure.

docs.title: Retinues and Violence
docs.text:
Albia has no universal retinue system. Kinship, fosterage, household membership, personal oath, land, gifts, wages, booty, patronage, and local obligation can all bind warriors to a leader in different combinations.

The Realm's weak political integration also means that feud, clan retaliation, princely justice, ecclesiastical peace, and contracted military service overlap visibly. Exact tolerances differ sharply between regions and Principalities. The shared Hetaireian order supplies procedures for mediation and recognition without erasing local Albian honor cultures.

docs.title: Brythia
docs.text:
Motto: “Right Conquers Might.” Symbol: White Wyrm.

The Bryth are Firelander-descended northern coastlanders whose heroic tradition centers on Wulfhere, slayer of the legendary White Wyrm.

docs.title: Cymbraeth
docs.text:
Motto: “We Are The Land.” Symbol: White Ram.

The Cymbraeth are pastoral central lowlanders famous for cultural persistence through repeated conquest and political subjugation.

docs.title: Fian
docs.text:
Motto: “Song And Sword.” Symbol: Harp.

The Fian are western coastal warriors, poets, cattlemen, and raiders whose songs are said to be sadder than their battles.

docs.title: Caledon
docs.text:
Motto: “Touch Not The Cat.” Symbol: Mountain lynx.

The Caledonians are Atharite highland clans closely related by blood, language, and custom to neighboring Eídne.

docs.title: Manaw
docs.text:
Motto: “By Wind And Oar.” Symbol: Black galley.

The Manaw are a mixed island and maritime people shaped by generations of Firelander and Albian contact.

docs.title: Eídne
docs.text:
The Eídne are the Tuatha confederation native to Albia's southern highlands. They preserve older religious traditions and remain closely intertwined by blood, language, and custom with neighboring Caledonian clans.

The Eídne High Kingship and its Choosing of Spears are specifically Eídne institutions, not a universal Tuathan political system. Other Tuatha confederations preserve their own structures farther east.

docs.title: Religion
docs.text:
Albia is part of the Atharite north, but religious history differs sharply among its peoples.

Brythia is fully Atharite in public identity. The conversion of Eodric completed the Brythian embrace of Atharism. Secret survivals of the Northern Gods may exist among some families, but they are remnants rather than the public Brythian faith.

The Cymbraeth and Fian contain substantial Atharite populations while preserving local customs and older cultural traditions. The Manaw are likewise shaped by both Atharite mainland influence and Firelander ancestry.

In the southern highlands, religious identity is particularly important. Caledonian clans are broadly Atharite, while neighboring Eídne clans preserve the older highland religion. The boundary between the two remains socially and genealogically porous.

docs.title: Brythia
docs.text:
Motto: “Right Conquers Might.” Symbol: White Wyrm.

The Bryth are descendants of major Firelander groups that invaded and colonized the northern coastlands of Albia. Over generations the conquerors became identified with the country they ruled, developing a distinct Brythian culture rather than remaining simply an overseas Firelander population.

docs.title: The White Wyrm
docs.text:
The great hero of old Brythian legend is Wulfhere, who lived before the full conversion of Brythia to Atharism. In the heroic songs, an ancient White Wyrm became a threat no ordinary warband could overcome. Wulfhere, already the foremost warrior of his age, went against it himself.

He slew the Wyrm, but suffered mortal wounds in the victory and died soon afterward. The story became one of the central legends of Brythian heroic culture: brute strength, terror, and even death do not determine what is rightfully possible for a person bound by courage and duty.

The White Wyrm is therefore the common Brythian badge. Outsiders sometimes mistake it for a sacred or protective dragon. Brythian tradition instead treats it as the image of the foe Wulfhere overcame.

Later Atharite poets reinterpret Wulfhere's sacrifice through the language of righteousness and the Uncreated Flame, while older versions of the tale are more concerned with fame, obligation, courage, and the defense of one's people.

docs.title: Heraldry
docs.text:
The White Wyrm appears on Brythian communal banners, carvings, military standards, and noble devices, but it is not the personal coat of arms of every Brythian prince.

Dynasties claiming descent from Wulfhere sometimes use a more explicit device showing a white wyrm transfixed by a spear, preserving the memory of the killing itself. Other houses use unrelated dynastic arms while displaying the White Wyrm when acting in an explicitly Brythian capacity.

docs.title: Conversion and Rule
docs.text:
The conversion of Prince Eodric of Brythia to Atharism in 689 AA is treated as the decisive event in the full public conversion of the Brythian people.

Modern Brythia is firmly Atharite. Individual families or secret circles may preserve remnants of the Northern Gods, but Reaver worship is no longer the normal or public Brythian faith.

Despite conversion, the Bryth retain a fierce warrior ethos shaped by their raiding, conquest, and heroic-age traditions.

docs.title: Political Position
docs.text:
Brythia is one of several competing peoples within loosely unified Albia. Brythian princes range greatly in power and have historically dominated or subjugated neighboring Cymbraeth communities without creating a permanently centralized Albian monarchy.

The northern coastlands also maintain close and complicated relations with the Manaw islands and with the Firelanders across the sea.

docs.title: Caledon
docs.text:
Motto: “Touch Not The Cat.” Symbol: Mountain lynx.

The Caledonians inhabit the cold, misty southern highlands of Albia. Their ancestors include older highland populations who survived the invasions that transformed the northern coastlands and central lowlands.

docs.title: Highland Identity
docs.text:
Life in the rocky highlands has produced a reputation for physical toughness, tenacity, clan loyalty, and martial skill. Caledon is not a single people in the sense of a unified kingdom or homogeneous ethnicity; it is a broad Atharite highland identity shared by many competing clans and local communities.

The Caledonians are extremely close to the surviving Tuatha. In many districts the distinction is principally religious rather than ethnic. A Caledonian clan and a neighboring Tuatha clan may speak closely related dialects, intermarry, share distant ancestors, dress similarly, and recognize many of the same customary practices.

The principal divide is that Caledonian clans broadly accept Atharism and participate in the Hetaireian religious order, while Tuatha clans preserve the older highland religion. Conversion can therefore change how a clan is classified over generations without replacing its ancestry or local culture.

docs.title: Political Position
docs.text: Caledon is not a single tightly governed highland province. It contains competing clans and princes operating within Albia's very loose political framework. Some valleys acknowledge Atharite princes; others are dominated by clan chiefs; still others sit within shifting zones of influence between Caledonian and Tuatha confederations.

docs.title: Emblem
docs.text: The Caledonian symbol is the mountain lynx. Its skin is worn proudly, including as scabbards for broad swords. The lynx is a Caledonian badge rather than a universal emblem of the highlands: Tuatha clans retain their own signs, sacred devices, and war-badges.

docs.title: Religion
docs.text:
Caledonian identity is strongly associated with Atharism, but highland religious life remains deeply entangled with older custom. Kinship with Tuatha clans, local sacred places, inherited taboos, and traditional seasonal practice can survive even where formal worship is Atharite.

This means the religious frontier rarely forms a clean geographic line. Atharite and Tuatha clans can be interspersed throughout the same highland districts.

docs.title: Cymbraeth
docs.text:
Motto: “We Are The Land.” Symbol: White ram.

The Cymbraeth are the old pastoral people of central Albia. They inhabit settled lowlands of fields, grazing country, streams, wooded hills, old villages, and small market communities. Their history is marked less by conquest than by surviving it.

docs.title: The Land Remains
docs.text:
Brythian princes and other ambitious rulers have repeatedly conquered, taxed, garrisoned, or claimed Cymbraeth districts. Such rule has rarely produced lasting cultural assimilation. Dynasties change, borders shift, halls burn and are rebuilt, but the Cymbraeth remain rooted in the same valleys, fields, kin-groups, burial grounds, and customary boundaries.

Their motto, “We Are The Land,” expresses this attachment. Cymbraeth identity is strongly local: a person's valley, village, family holding, grazing rights, and ancestral community may matter as much as allegiance to a distant prince.

docs.title: Pastoral Life
docs.text:
Sheep, cattle, wool, dairying, orchards, and mixed farming are central to much of Cymbraeth life. Outsiders sometimes stereotype them as provincial, overly attached to custom, and lacking the martial glamour of other Albian peoples. Cymbraeth tradition instead prizes continuity, hospitality, practical judgment, memory, and stubborn independence.

They are not unwarlike. Local levies and household retainers have resisted raids and princely abuses for generations, but warfare is not the central ideal around which Cymbraeth culture understands itself.

docs.title: Music and Memory
docs.text:
Music, recitation, genealogy, seasonal festivals, and local storytelling remain important. The crwth, a bowed stringed instrument, is particularly associated with Cymbraeth musical tradition and appears in feast halls, village celebrations, and the households of local patrons.

The crwth is a cultural badge rather than the principal heraldic emblem.

docs.title: Emblem
docs.text:
The shared Cymbraeth badge is the white ram. It reflects the pastoral economy of the central lowlands, but also carries a more admired meaning within Cymbraeth culture: patience, stubbornness, and refusal to be permanently driven from one's ground.

The ram may appear on communal banners and regional devices, while individual princes and families use their own arms.

docs.title: Political Position
docs.text: The Cymbraeth possess numerous local lords, princes, landholding families, and community institutions rather than one ruler who speaks for the entire people. Brythian princes have often ruled Cymbraeth populations, but political subjection has not normally erased local identity.

docs.title: Religion
docs.text: Most Cymbraeth communities participate in Atharism, although older local practices, holy places, customary observances, and traditions inherited from pre-Brythian Albia remain embedded in village life.

docs.title: Erinor
docs.text:
Erinor is an old geographical and ethnographic term found in earlier Albian chronicles and foreign writings. It was once used loosely for older populations of central and western Albia who were neither absorbed into Brythian culture nor identified with the southern highlands.

The term is no longer a precise description of a single modern people. Current usage distinguishes principally between the Cymbraeth of the central lowlands and the Fian of the western coast, whose histories and cultures developed differently despite their shared inheritance from older Albian populations.

Older texts may therefore describe people as Erinor where a modern writer would identify them more specifically as Cymbraeth, Fian, or another local population.

docs.title: Legacy
docs.text: Several cultural traits once generalized as “Erinor” are now understood more specifically. The famous harp tradition, bardic warrior-poetry, and the saying that their fighting is happy while their songs are sad belong especially to the Fian. The long history of surviving repeated conquest and political subjugation without cultural assimilation belongs especially to the Cymbraeth.

docs.title: Fian
docs.text:
Motto: “Song And Sword.” Symbol: Harp.

The Fian inhabit much of the western coast of Albia, a hard country of inlets, grazing land, rough hills, scattered strongholds, and exposed settlements. Their history has been shaped by repeated Firelander raids from the sea, feuds among local clans, and conflict with aggressive Tuatha communities in the western hills.

docs.title: Cultural Character
docs.text:
The Fian are famous for combining martial enthusiasm with a deeply melancholic poetic tradition. A common Albian saying claims:

“When Athar made the Fian, he created them mad—for all their fighting is happy, and all their songs are sad.”

Cattle-raiding, feud, personal courage, hospitality, boast, satire, lament, and reputation all occupy prominent places in Fian social life. Outsiders sometimes mistake their willingness to fight for simple savagery; the Fian themselves place equal importance on memory, eloquence, generosity, and the ability to preserve a person's deeds in song.

docs.title: Bards and the Harp
docs.text:
Bards are respected as poets, genealogists, satirists, praise-singers, and keepers of communal memory. The harp is the principal Fian cultural badge and appears in noble, bardic, military, and communal contexts.

The harp's importance is not a sign that the Fian imagine themselves as peaceful. Rather, it represents the belief that a deed without memory dies quickly, while a deed placed into song can outlive the warrior who performed it.

docs.title: Warrior Companies
docs.text:
Fian martial life is not confined to princely household troops. Indeed, their very name comes from the ancient Albian "Fianna," meaning something similar to "Warband." These independent or semi-independent warrior companies may gather around a renowned captain, noble heir, exile, champion, or poet-warrior. Their loyalties can cross clan and princely boundaries, making them useful in war and troublesome in peace.

The relationship between a fianna, a clan, and a prince varies widely. Some companies become respected military followings; others degenerate into raiding bands or attach themselves to frontier lords.

docs.title: Emblem
docs.text: The common Fian badge is the harp. Individual houses and clans use their own arms, but the harp is widely recognized as a sign of shared Fian identity.

docs.title: Political Position
docs.text:
The Fian are divided among many princes, clan chiefs, captains, and local dynasties. Coastal warfare and raiding encourage temporary coalitions rather than permanent unity. A prince who proves weak may find his own retainers drifting toward a more successful kinsman or war-leader.

Western Fian districts also maintain complicated relations with nearby Tuatha clans. Trade, fosterage, intermarriage, feud, raiding, and religious hostility can all occur between the same communities within a few generations.

docs.title: Religion
docs.text: The Fian include substantial Atharite populations, but older customs remain strong and contact with Tuatha communities is frequent. Religious affiliation can vary sharply between neighboring districts and noble families.

docs.title: Manaw
docs.text:
Motto: “By Wind And Oar.” Symbol: Black galley.

The Manaw are the maritime people of Albia's northern islands and sea-roads. Their culture grew from centuries of contact among island communities, coastal Albians, Firelander settlers and raiders, merchants, refugees, pirates, and intermarried noble houses.

Mainlanders often regard the northern sea as the edge of Albia. The Manaw are more likely to regard it as a road connecting islands, ports, kin-groups, markets, raiding grounds, and distant allies.

docs.title: The Northern Islands
docs.text:
The principal Manaw islands lie in the waters between northern Albia and southern Svealund, with smaller islands and island groups extending farther toward the Firelands. The exact political loyalties of these islands vary, but together they form a chain of anchorages, channels, sheltered harbors, fishing grounds, and sea-roads linking northern Albia to the wider northern maritime world.

This geography makes the Manaw natural intermediaries between Firelanders and the Loranian mainland. Timber from Svealund and Albia, metal goods, food, livestock, mercenaries, captives, pilgrims, settlers, and news all pass through Manaw waters. The same routes that support ordinary commerce have also carried generations of Firelander raiders and colonists toward northern Albia.

The islands are not a single uniform archipelago. Some are broad enough to support farming, grazing, woods, monasteries, towns, and competing lordships; others are little more than rocky or grassy islands around a harbor, channel, or fishing ground. Many smaller rocks, skerries, and local anchorages exist below the scale of ordinary continental maps.

docs.title: Maritime Life
docs.text:
Sailing is central to Manaw identity. Fishing, coastal trade, shipbuilding, piloting, seasonal voyaging, mercenary service, and raiding all blur into one another more readily than mainland moralists prefer.

A successful Manaw sea-lord may be merchant, prince, pirate-hunter, raider, and foreign envoy at different points in the same career. Island communities often maintain ties in several directions at once rather than orienting themselves exclusively toward a single mainland court.

docs.title: Mixed Inheritance
docs.text:
The Manaw are not simply Firelanders who settled offshore, nor are they merely island Bryth. Generations of intermarriage and cultural exchange have produced a distinct society with both Albian and Firelander inheritance.

Names, ship terminology, family traditions, and local law can therefore vary considerably between islands. Some noble houses emphasize Firelander ancestry, while others claim descent from older island dynasties or mainland Albian princes.

docs.title: Emblem
docs.text:
The common Manaw badge is the black galley, usually represented as an old-fashioned single-masted sea-going vessel with prominent oars.

The galley symbolizes mobility, seafaring skill, and the Manaw understanding of the sea as a route rather than a barrier. Individual island lords and dynasties use their own arms alongside the shared badge.

docs.title: Political Position
docs.text:
The Manaw do not answer to a single island king or unified prince. Sea-lords, island princes, merchant families, monasteries, harbor communities, and clan-based dynasties compete and cooperate across the northern waters.

Their political relationships with Brythia are especially close and contentious. Marriage, trade, naval service, piracy, tribute, and inherited claims can tie the same Manaw house to several Brythian princes at once.

Control of a strategically placed island, harbor, or pilotage route may matter as much as possession of a large tract of land. Some Manaw communities profit heavily from serving as middlemen in the timber routes between Svealund, Albia, and the Firelands.

docs.title: Religion
docs.text: Atharism is established among much of the Manaw, particularly in princely and mercantile centers, but Firelander ancestry and long maritime isolation have preserved older customs and family traditions in some islands.

docs.title: Buried Crown
docs.text:
The Buried Crown is one of the greatest sacred sites of the Tuathan Old Ways and is especially important to the Eídne of the southern Albian highlands.

At first glance, the site appears to be a vast prehistoric ring of standing stones set among the high valleys. The Eídne still gather there for major religious ceremonies, oaths, divination, political assemblies, and rites connected to moments of exceptional communal importance.

docs.title: The Visible Crown
docs.text:
The standing stones form the visible Crown from which the site takes its modern name. Some remain upright, others lean or have fallen, and still others barely emerge above the surrounding earth.

The stones are treated as sacred in their own right. They are not normally carved over, quarried, or moved, even when their original markings are weathered beyond recognition. Offerings may be placed at their bases, hung from nearby trees, buried in the surrounding earth, or deposited in nearby waters.

No living Tuatha tradition credibly claims that the Eídne or any other known Tuathan ancestors built the monument. The Buried Crown was already ancient when the forebears of the present highland peoples first encountered it. Within the Old Ways, this does not diminish its sanctity. A sacred place need not have been made by one's own ancestors in order to belong to the sacred world.

docs.title: The Buried Complex
docs.text:
The visible ring is only the uppermost portion of a much larger prehistoric ritual complex buried beneath the highlands.

Many of the apparent standing stones are actually the exposed crowns of enormous pillars extending deep below the present ground level. Beneath them lie buried chambers, passages, retaining walls, and other structures whose full extent has never been established.

The surviving landscape therefore gives a profoundly misleading impression of the original monument. What now appears to be a circle of monoliths may once have been the highest part of an enormous ceremonial complex, with much of its architecture deliberately or naturally covered by earth in prehistoric times.

Why the complex was buried is unknown. Tuathan traditions disagree, and no surviving written record reaches anywhere near the site's construction. Some stories say the earth rose to protect it, others that its builders buried their own holy place before departing, and still others that something beneath the Crown was meant never to be uncovered.

None of these explanations is treated as settled fact.

docs.title: Religious Use
docs.text:
The Buried Crown remains an active holy place rather than an abandoned ruin.

Eídne ritual specialists use the site for divination, oath-taking, seasonal observances, and ceremonies involving the great clans. Major political acts can also acquire religious force when performed before the stones, particularly where the legitimacy of a ruler, treaty, feud-settlement, or communal obligation is at stake.

The site does not belong personally to the High King. Even powerful Eídne rulers are expected to approach it as custodians and petitioners rather than owners.

The precise rites performed there vary by occasion and are not all public. The Buried Crown's relationship to the Choosing of Spears is particularly important but remains only partly defined.

docs.title: Antiquity and Interpretation
docs.text:
To Atharite scholars, the Buried Crown is one of the clearest surviving signs that sophisticated monumental cultures existed in the Albian highlands before any reliable written history.

To the Eídne, its unknown builders are less important than the fact that the place itself has endured. Its unknowable age is part of its authority. The monument is sacred not because the Tuatha can explain it, but because generations of diviners, chiefs, oath-takers, and worshippers have recognized that it was sacred before them and will remain so after them.

The name Buried Crown refers both to the visible ring of stones and to the far greater monument concealed beneath it.

docs.title: Clovia
docs.text: Motto: “Grace Through Honor.”

docs.title: Heraldry
docs.text:
Blazon: Purpure, a rose argent. (A white rose on a purple field.)

The White Rose is the shared emblem of Clovia's old provincial identity. It predates the modern political fragmentation of the Realm and is used by Princes, cities, communities, and institutions that otherwise possess very different arms of their own.

The rose should therefore be understood as a broad Clovian badge, not the personal arms of a single ruling house. A Longard Prince, Tusci city, Sapaudi pass-fortress, or Liguri merchant republic may all display the White Rose when emphasizing their place within Clovia while retaining their own local heraldry.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Clovia was one of the richest provinces of the old imperial order and remains one of the most powerful Hetaireian Realms. Its rolling hills, vineyards, cultivated woodlands, fortified towns, mineral wealth, mountain passes, and Sea of Ardan ports support disciplined armies and prosperous merchant houses.

Clovia's unusually dense imperial inheritance is not controlled by one successor. Princes, noble houses, cities, temples, merchant corporations, mountain communities, archives, and conquest-settler institutions all possess different pieces of old authority and different claims about what those inheritances mean. Clovian politics is consequently marked by contested continuity: ancient privilege, reconstructed law, revived office, genuine custom, forged genealogy, civic charter, and successful conquest can all become arguments about legitimacy.

Clovia shares a substantial western and northwestern land frontier with Albia. Farther southwest, its frontier with Dorado is organized around the Anora river-and-estuary system and the old marcher country of Flagros rather than a broad Dorado–Albia land boundary. The northern mountain wall rises beyond Clovia's settled interior, the forests and territories of Nibelung lie to the east, and the Sea of Ardan bounds the south. In the northeastern marches, a strip of Clovian territory lies between the Nibelung forest frontier and the river boundary facing Szovij.

Clovian nobles are stereotyped as proud and boastful, but even rivals tend to concede their reputation for courage, refinement, and personal honor.

docs.title: Clovian Identity
docs.text:
Clovian is a broad provincial, political, and civilizational identity rather than the name of a single ethnicity. Many inhabitants of the central counties, river valleys, market towns, and old imperial settlements use no narrower people-name at all; they are simply Clovians, or identify first with a city, valley, Prince, county, or dynasty.

Other identities cut across this larger Clovian world. Longard, Tusci, Royeux, Sapaudi, and Liguri describe peoples or regional cultures produced by very different historical processes. They do not form five administrative provinces, and their boundaries do not consistently match princely borders.

docs.title: Political and Legal Structure
docs.text:
Clovia is a cultural-political region of many Principalities rather than a unified kingdom. Princes rule jurisdictions of widely varying size, and powerful cities, merchant houses, mountain communities, old aristocratic lineages, ecclesiastical institutions, and military settlers complicate any attempt to divide the Realm neatly.

There is no formal office of supreme Clovian Prince. Exceptionally powerful rulers may nevertheless be called High Princes in ordinary political speech when their military strength, wealth, or network of dependents makes them the dominant figure across a large area. The designation is informal and can shift as fortunes change.

Clovia's wealth and documentary inheritance make jurisdiction especially elaborate. Charters, genealogies, seals, civic privileges, inherited offices, toll rights, ecclesiastical immunities, commercial agreements, old provincial boundaries, princely grants, and conquest claims can overlap in the same district. Courts and political actors therefore spend substantial effort determining not merely what rule applies, but whose law, privilege, or forum has standing.

This does not make Clovia uniquely lawless. On the contrary, Clovians often respond to political fragmentation by producing more records, more genealogical arguments, more contracts, and more legal claims. Documentary culture is itself a weapon of competition.

Meropolitan authentication and arbitration are valuable precisely because Clovian actors possess so many rival claims of continuity, but the Pontis does not replace the Realm's local courts and institutions.

docs.title: Economy
docs.text:
Northern Clovia contains productive veins of silver and gold, while the central and western hills produce grain, fruit, and renowned wines. The southern coast opens onto the Sea of Ardan and supports long-distance commerce, shipbuilding, banking, warehousing, and rival merchant cities.

Tusci wine and artwork are prestigious exports. Longard military power is supported by eastern marcher estates and access to mineral wealth. Royeux merchants seek to dominate coastal commerce, though Liguri cities vigorously resist any attempt to place Clovia's southern trade under a single monopoly. Sapaudi communities profit from livestock, mining, caravan service, and control of the northern passes.

Clovia's dense cities, commercial networks, and literate institutions give guilds, financiers, merchant houses, civic governments, lawyers, notaries, and professional companies unusual political weight. Wealth and office can create influence that does not fit neatly into hereditary aristocratic hierarchy.

docs.title: Roads, Passes, and Marches
docs.text:
Clovia's prosperity depends on keeping movement possible through a dangerous world. Old imperial roads and bridges, defended river crossings, coastal shipping, fortified towns, and Sapaudi passes form the skeleton of long-distance trade.

The Sapaudi expression that the passes are the doors of Clovia is therefore literal politics as well as symbolism. A fortress or community able to keep a high pass open may exercise toll, escort, refuge, military, and jurisdictional functions simultaneously.

Eastern Longard territories display another form of marcher institution. Persistent frontier conflict can justify unusually broad military privileges, fortified estates, armed households, patrol obligations, and rapid mobilization. Such privileges can outlive the emergency that produced them and become part of later disputes between Princes, towns, and military houses.

docs.title: Longard
docs.text:
Motto: “By the Sword.” Symbol: A crown transfixed by a sword.

The Longards descend from Svealish mercenaries hired by a Tusci Prince. When the mercenary hosts became too numerous and dangerous to control, they were granted land in eastern Clovia in exchange for sparing their employer.

Over roughly the last two centuries, Longard Princes and military settlers have become a major power in the eastern and northeastern marches. They feud with Nibelung along the forest frontier and have shown interest in Szovij lands beyond the river. Not everyone living under a Longard Prince is ethnically Longard; many subjects descend from older Clovian populations absorbed into Longard-ruled territories.

docs.title: Tusci
docs.text:
Motto: “Beauty Endures All.” Symbol: Griffin.

The Tusci are an old central-western Clovian culture associated with vineyards, wealthy towns, marble sculpture, urban rivalry, and aristocratic patronage. Their Princes once dominated much of northern and central Clovia but were pushed westward by Longard expansion.

Political decline has not diminished Tusci cultural confidence. Tusci cities and houses compete fiercely with one another in art, architecture, wine, prestige, genealogy, and claims to antiquity, and many Tusci regard the achievements of civilization as more enduring than the victories of conquerors.

docs.title: Royeux
docs.text:
Motto: “Our Inheritance We Claim.” Symbol: Rooster.

The Royeux are concentrated especially in southern and southwestern Clovia toward the Doradan frontier and the Sea of Ardan. They descend from lowland Euskald populations conquered early in the old imperial expansion and became among the most thoroughly imperialized peoples of western Clovia.

Royeux elites regard imperial civilization as their inheritance and dream of restoring it under their own leadership. Their merchants seek commercial dominance along the southern coast, bringing them into repeated rivalry with the independent-minded Liguri cities.

docs.title: Sapaudi
docs.text:
Motto: “We Hold the Doors.” Symbol: A mountain containing an upright key.

The Sapaudi inhabit the northern mountain valleys and passes. The name is a broad regional label rather than evidence of a single unified people: individual valleys, fortresses, towns, and pass-lords possess strong local identities of their own.

Their shared imagery reflects control of movement through the mountains. The mountain represents the high country and the routes cut through it; the key signifies that the Sapaudi control access. In Sapaudi political speech the passes are the doors of Clovia, and their motto makes the claim explicit: We Hold the Doors. Cattle, pack animals, mining, tolls, guiding, caravan service, and pass-fortresses shape much of their economy.

docs.title: Liguri
docs.text:
The Liguri are the maritime populations of several southern coastal cities, especially communities whose identity is tied more strongly to port, guild, merchant house, or civic republic than to an inland Prince.

The Liguri have no universal motto or common arms. “Liguri” is primarily a broad ethnolinguistic and cultural category used by outsiders. A Liguri merchant normally identifies first with a particular city, and rival Liguri ports may be more hostile to one another than to inland Clovians.

Their cities are noted for seaborne commerce, banking, shipbuilding, warehouses, fortified harbors, and networks of merchants abroad. Royeux attempts to impose a wider coastal monopoly repeatedly collide with Liguri civic independence.

docs.title: Albia
docs.text: Clovia's long western and northwestern frontier with Albia crosses lowland, wooded, and hill country rather than one single natural wall. Its exact princely limits are not continuously surveyed, and future realm-level work may develop marches, disputed valleys, fortified roads, dynastic claims, and shifting zones of practical control along this frontier.

docs.title: Dorado
docs.text:
Clovia's southwestern frontier has a long history of warfare with Dorado. The Anora is its principal natural and strategic divide, especially along Flagros, but the frontier is a premodern river march rather than a modern line fixed to the exact center of the channel. Fords, ferries, islands, floodplains, forts, and local claims can complicate who controls which bank in a given district.

Clovian forces invaded Flagros after the fall of the Empire but were eventually driven back by Covado and his followers. Western Clovian territories consequently retain old fortifications, military roads, mixed border populations, and memories of repeated campaigns.

docs.title: Nibelung and Szovij
docs.text: The eastern and northeastern marches are dominated politically by the Longards. The Nibelung boundary runs through heavily forested frontier country, while farther along the northeastern strip the river separates Clovian territory from Szovij. These two frontiers have encouraged a militarized marcher culture and help channel Longard ambitions eastward.

docs.title: Northern Mountains
docs.text: The northern mountains are not an empty boundary but a chain of inhabited valleys and controlled passes. Sapaudi communities mediate much of Clovia's overland contact across this barrier and can become disproportionately important whenever armies, pilgrims, or merchant caravans need access through the high country.

docs.title: Sea of Ardan
docs.text: The southern coast participates in the dense commercial and political world of the Sea of Ardan. Royeux ambitions, Liguri civic competition, foreign merchants, and inland princely interests all overlap there.

docs.title: Liguri
docs.text: The Liguri are the maritime populations of several southern Clovian coastal cities. The term describes a broad cultural and linguistic affinity, but Liguri political identity is overwhelmingly civic: people generally identify first with their own city, port, guild, merchant house, or local ruler rather than with a unified Liguri nation.

docs.title: No Common Arms or Motto
docs.text:
The Liguri possess no universal motto and no common coat of arms.

Each important city has its own heraldry, civic traditions, rivalries, political institutions, and claims to precedence. Two ports that outsiders casually group together as Liguri may have fought repeated wars against each other and may regard their differences as far more important than their similarities.

When Liguri cities act in an explicitly Clovian context, they may display the White Rose alongside their own civic banners. This signifies shared Clovian identity without implying a unified Liguri state or national heraldry.

docs.title: Maritime Cities
docs.text:
Liguri culture is centered on the southern coast of Clovia and the Sea of Ardan. Their cities are known for:

  • long-distance seaborne trade;
  • shipbuilding and repair;
  • banking, credit, and merchant finance;
  • warehouses and fortified harbors;
  • merchant families with agents abroad;
  • maritime law and contracts;
  • civic militias and naval forces;
  • intense competition between neighboring ports.

The sea is not merely an edge of their homeland. It is the principal road by which their wealth, information, influence, and rivalries travel.

docs.title: Civic Identity
docs.text:
A Liguri merchant asked where he comes from is more likely to name his city than to say that he is Liguri. The broad label is especially common among inland Clovians, foreign merchants, and scholars attempting to classify the related coastal populations.

This localism is politically important. Liguri cities may ally with different Clovian princes, feud with one another over anchorage or trade privileges, or cooperate temporarily when a foreign threat endangers several ports at once.

There is no expectation that all Liguri should obey the same prince.

docs.title: Rivalry with the Royeux
docs.text:
The Royeux have repeatedly sought to dominate trade along Clovia's southern coast and convert commercial influence into something approaching a monopoly.

Liguri ports are among the strongest obstacles to that ambition. Their merchant elites may trade extensively with Royeux houses while resisting any political arrangement that places their harbors, tariffs, fleets, or commercial courts under Royeux control.

This rivalry is economic, political, and cultural. Royeux aristocrats often regard the Liguri as fractious merchants incapable of understanding imperial order; Liguri patricians tend to regard Royeux monopoly schemes as aristocratic theft dressed in ancient titles.

docs.title: Clovian Identity
docs.text:
The Liguri are not outsiders to Clovia. Their cities participate fully in the broader Clovian religious, commercial, and political world, and many Liguri elites cultivate courtly Clovian manners when dealing inland.

Yet their civic traditions mean that Clovian and Liguri do not replace local identity. A person may be simultaneously Clovian in the broad political sense, Liguri to an ethnographer, and above all a citizen of a particular port.

docs.title: Longard
docs.text:
Motto: “By the Sword.”

The Longards are descendants of Svealish mercenaries who were hired by a Tusci prince and ultimately settled in eastern Clovia. Over roughly the last two centuries their descendants have become one of the realm's most formidable military and political powers.

docs.title: Foundation
docs.text:
The original mercenary hosts became too numerous and dangerous for their employer to control. They were therefore “gifted” lands in eastern Clovia in exchange for not taking the prince's head.

The settlement was not an empty-land migration. Longard warriors and their families established themselves over older Clovian populations, and many people now ruled by Longard princes descend principally from inhabitants who were already there. Longard therefore describes a conquest-settler tradition and political culture as much as a simple ancestry.

docs.title: The Eastern Marches
docs.text:
Longard power is concentrated in the eastern and northeastern belt of Clovia. The marches face Nibelung along heavily forested frontier country, while another part of the border approaches the river separating Clovian lands from Szovij.

Fortified towns, forest castles, military estates, river forts, and armed retinues are common features of Longard political life. Their geography helps channel Longard expansion eastward: the northern mountains constrain movement, while the old Clovian heartlands to the west contain entrenched princes and cities capable of resisting them.

docs.title: Expansion
docs.text:
Longard princes maintain a powerful rivalry with Nibelung and have repeatedly fought along the forest frontier. Some also covet Szovijan territory beyond the river.

This expansionism makes other Clovian lords increasingly nervous. Longard rulers often present conquest as a legitimate source of authority, while their rivals see an armed settler aristocracy that has never entirely abandoned the habits of mercenaries.

docs.title: Clovian Assimilation
docs.text:
Despite their Svealish ancestry, modern Longards are deeply embedded in Clovian political and religious life. Their princes participate in the Hetaireian order, claim Clovian titles, patronize Clovian institutions, and commonly display the White Rose when emphasizing their place within the realm.

Longard distinctiveness survives most strongly in military custom, dynastic ancestry, personal names, eastern dialects, and the prestige attached to conquest.

docs.title: Heraldry
docs.text:
The shared Longard badge is a crown transfixed by a sword, representing rule won and defended through force of arms.

Motto: By the Sword.

The device need not be the personal arms of every Longard prince. Individual houses possess their own heraldry, but the crown-and-sword appears on military standards, seals, monuments, and occasions when a ruler wishes to emphasize Longard identity.

docs.title: Royeux
docs.text:
Motto: “Our Inheritance We Claim.”

The Royeux are a southern and southwestern Clovian people descended from lowland Euskald populations who were among the first western peoples conquered during the old Heryos imperial expansion.

Their strongest heartlands lie along the Sea of Ardan and toward the western frontier with Dorado.

docs.title: Imperial Assimilation
docs.text:
The ancestors of the Royeux rapidly adopted imperial institutions, dress, manners, urban life, and political ideals. Their later identity became so bound to that inheritance that reminders of their Euskald origins are often treated as grave insults by aristocratic Royeux.

Royeux elites do not generally think of themselves as a conquered people imitating their former masters. Their preferred understanding is that the civilization of the old Empire became their inheritance.

This gives their motto a deliberately political meaning:

Our Inheritance We Claim.

The inheritance in question is the authority, refinement, law, and prestige of the old imperial order.

docs.title: Coastal Wealth
docs.text:
Since the fall of the Empire, Royeux merchants and princes have attempted to dominate commerce along Clovia's southern coast. They profit from inland silver, Tusci wine and artwork, imported luxury goods, shipping, and the dense trade of the Sea of Ardan.

Their attempts to turn influence into a true coastal monopoly repeatedly collide with the Liguri, whose independent merchant cities have little interest in surrendering their commercial autonomy to Royeux princes.

docs.title: Imperial Ambition
docs.text:
Royeux aristocratic culture contains a persistent dream of rebuilding the imperial order under Royeux leadership and in a Royeux image. Old titles, legal claims, genealogies, ceremonial forms, and supposed imperial privileges therefore carry exceptional political weight.

Among their critics, the Royeux are accused of confusing ancient service to the Empire with ownership of its legacy.

docs.title: Heraldry
docs.text:
The Royeux emblem is a rooster.

The symbol originated in an old imperial joke comparing the Royeux name to a Heryos-era word for a male chicken. Rather than abandon the insult, the Royeux adopted it as a badge of pride. The rooster is commonly depicted upright, conspicuous, and defiant.

The White Rose of Clovia may appear alongside the rooster when a Royeux house emphasizes its Clovian identity or claims to provincial precedence.

docs.title: Sapaudi
docs.text:
Motto: “We Hold the Doors.”

The Sapaudi are the peoples of Clovia's northern mountain valleys and passes. The name is a broad regional label rather than evidence of a single unified nation: individual valleys, towns, fortresses, monasteries, clans, and pass-lords retain strong local identities of their own.

docs.title: The Doors of Clovia
docs.text:
The northern mountains are difficult to cross but not impassable. Roads through their valleys carry merchants, pilgrims, pack trains, messengers, mercenaries, and armies, and the communities controlling those routes possess influence far beyond their population.

The Sapaudi commonly describe the great passes as doors. Whoever holds the fortresses, gates, bridges, and roads controlling a door can determine who crosses, when they cross, and at what price.

Their shared motto expresses that political reality:

We Hold the Doors.

It is both a boast and a warning. The doors are ordinarily open because trade makes the mountains prosperous. In war, they can be shut.

docs.title: Badge: The Mountain and Key
docs.text:
The most widely recognized Sapaudi regional badge is a mountain with an upright key displayed within it.

The mountain represents the high country itself: the valleys, roads, passes, mines, grazing lands, and fortresses on which Sapaudi life depends. The key signifies control of passage. The great routes through the mountains may be doors in Sapaudi political speech, but it is the people of the mountains who possess their keys.

This is not a single standardized national coat of arms. Different valleys, houses, towns, and pass-fortresses vary the shape of the mountain, key, colors, surrounding devices, and secondary charges. Some use the Clovian White Rose alongside their own local version of the mountain-and-key.

docs.title: Economy
docs.text:
Sapaudi life is shaped by the mountains and by the traffic moving through them. Important livelihoods include:

  • cattle and highland pastoralism;
  • pack animals and caravan service;
  • mining and quarrying;
  • guiding and road maintenance;
  • toll collection;
  • inns, markets, and storehouses serving travelers;
  • military service and pass defense.

Control of a single strategically placed road or bridge can make an otherwise small valley lord remarkably wealthy.

docs.title: Political Life
docs.text:
There is no single Sapaudi prince. Some valleys answer closely to major Clovian rulers; others are dominated by local hereditary lords, fortified towns, religious houses, or old communal agreements.

Pass rights, toll privileges, grazing grounds, bridge maintenance, winter access, and ancient boundary claims are serious political matters. Neighboring valleys may share language and custom while maintaining grudges older than the dynasties ruling the lowlands.

The Sapaudi are fully part of the larger Clovian world, but lowland princes often discover that nominal sovereignty over a mountain district means little if the local keepers of the doors refuse cooperation.

docs.title: Military Reputation
docs.text:
Sapaudi warfare emphasizes terrain, fortifications, ambush, road denial, and the defense of narrow approaches. Mountain communities are accustomed to supplying guides, scouts, crossbowmen, infantry, and caravan guards.

A major invading army may be vastly stronger than a Sapaudi valley in open country and still find itself helpless if bridges are destroyed, roads blocked, provisions removed, and the correct passes closed before winter.

docs.title: Tusci
docs.text:
Motto: “Beauty Endures All.”

The Tusci are an old central-western Clovian culture whose political power has declined even as their artistic and social prestige remains exceptionally high.

Tuscia is commonly used for their historical heartland and cultural region.

docs.title: Old Tuscia
docs.text:
Tusci princes once held sway over much of northern and central Clovia. Their courts, towns, vineyards, and estates were among the wealthiest centers of the old post-imperial north.

The rise of the Longard broke much of that dominance. Longard expansion pushed surviving Tusci power westward and shattered several older political arrangements, but it did not erase Tusci urban wealth or cultural confidence.

Tuscia is not a unified principality. It is a landscape of rival cities, princely houses, merchant families, ecclesiastical centers, vineyards, and old claims. A Tusci may identify intensely with a particular city or dynasty while still regarding Tusci culture as obviously superior to that of neighboring peoples.

docs.title: Arts and Wine
docs.text:
Tusci culture is renowned for artistic sophistication, architecture, marble sculpture, metalwork, painting, wine-making, and aristocratic patronage. Tusci works are found in wealthy halls and religious houses across both northern and southern lands.

Other Clovians sometimes mock the Tusci as effete, lazy, or excessively concerned with appearances. Tusci self-understanding is almost the reverse: they see no virtue in rushing what can instead be savored, refined, and perfected.

Their motto expresses this cultural conviction:

Beauty Endures All.

Longard victories may redraw borders. A well-built bridge, a great statue, a perfect vintage, or a celebrated poem can outlive the conqueror.

docs.title: Cities and Rivalry
docs.text:
Tusci identity is especially urban. Major towns and cities compete in public building, court ceremony, artistic schools, trade, patronage, and claims to antiquity.

This rivalry prevents the Tusci from behaving as one unified political bloc. Their cities may feud bitterly while still closing ranks culturally when confronted by outsiders who dismiss Tuscia as decadent or politically spent.

docs.title: Doradan Memory
docs.text:
Tusci princes participated in Clovian expansion toward Dorado after the fall of the old Empire. One such prince demanded the return of Fort Hurktos after the Doradan warrior Covado rallied displaced eastern Doradans and captured the fortress. Covado's answer became famous:

“Come and take it.”

The prince did not answer. The challenge remains central to modern Flagroso political memory.

The later displacement of Tusci princes by Longard expansion gives this older history an ironic place in Tusci memory: a people once associated with conquest in the west became, in later generations, the principal victims of conquest from the east.

docs.title: Heraldry
docs.text:
The traditional Tusci badge is the griffin, regarded as a creature of majesty, guardianship, vigilance, and aristocratic splendor.

The griffin is widely represented in sculpture, seals, civic decoration, household objects, and noble heraldry, although individual Tusci cities and houses possess arms of their own.

The White Rose is also common as a secondary Clovian badge.
