docs.title: Dorado
docs.text: Motto: Resist And Bite.

docs.title: Arms
docs.text:
Blazon: Or, a tiger rampant Gules. Plain English: On a gold field, a red tiger rearing upright in the rampant posture.

The Doradan Mountain Tiger represents the Realm's reputation for ferocious resistance and aggressive self-reliance.

The tiger is the broad Doradan emblem. The Cantabri, Flagrosos, Vettones, and Meliti maintain their own regional badges rather than merely using altered versions of the tiger.

Dorado is a fiercely independent western Hetaireian Realm descended largely from the Euskald peoples of the southern mountains. Its institutions were shaped by a different sequence from the more thoroughly imperialized Realms: incomplete Heryos conquest, survival of local structures, fortress resistance, an Umbrathar-specific demonic conversion crisis, militant Atharite consolidation, and the continuing demands of mountain and maritime self-reliance.

Dorado is the standard Meropolitan and international name for the Realm, not necessarily a single native endonym. Doradans speaking to foreigners commonly use the name and call themselves Doradans, while local identity may center more strongly on a people, island, valley, city, or Principality.

docs.title: Imperial Resistance
docs.text:
When the old imperial armies crossed the Anora River after conquering Clovia, they expected a similar campaign. Instead they encountered a decentralized tribal society exceptionally skilled at ambush, mountain warfare, and attritional resistance.

After generations of failed pacification, Emperor Hurktos ordered a massive fortress built to control the principal river crossing and effectively abandoned attempts to conquer the rest of Dorado. Fort Hurktos later became Covadio, the great fortress-city of Flagros.

The incomplete conquest had lasting consequences. Dorado inherited less of the old Empire's uniform provincial machinery than Clovia, while local communities, strongholds, kin structures, and regional authorities survived with greater continuity. Imperial forts, roads, and frontier works mattered, but they were imposed upon a political landscape the Empire never fully remade.

docs.title: Conversion to Atharism
docs.text:
Dorado was never deeply integrated into the Old Empire and therefore witnessed its collapse into diabolism mostly from outside. This isolation also meant Doradans had less cultural immunity to imperial relics and forbidden practices.

Dorado's conversion is associated with a major demonic crisis within roughly the first century after Ardan's Ascension. A wise woman named Mari came down from the northern mountains claiming the power of the Uncreated Flame and successfully cast out demons where local shamans had failed.

The highland Euskald may have been among the earliest and most zealous converts. Conversion of the lowlands appears to have been much bloodier, with later Doradan rulers conducting severe religious wars against holdouts and the old ways.

By several centuries AA, Dorado was overwhelmingly Atharite.

This history gives Doradan Atharism a powerful local memory of deliverance followed by consolidation. The Hetaireia is not simply the religion of an old conqueror: in Doradan tradition, the Uncreated Flame proved itself during a supernatural catastrophe that existing institutions could not master. Later militant conversion nevertheless left scars and local memories of coercion beneath that shared religious identity.

docs.title: Political Character
docs.text:
Dorado is a Realm of many Principalities, strongholds, cities, valleys, islands, and local communities rather than a single western kingdom. Its political culture places unusual prestige on the ability to defend one's own people, hold difficult ground, and resist external compulsion.

That self-reliance does not remove Dorado from the Hetaireian order. Doradan Princes seek Pontifical recognition, Doradan clergy belong to the Hetaireia, and transregional rites, marriage, pilgrimage, and ecclesiastical authority bind the Realm to the wider north. But local legitimacy remains strongly rooted in communities whose historical memory repeatedly rewards rulers who can defend them without waiting for distant help.

Fortresses consequently carry unusual political weight. In Dorado they are not merely aristocratic residences: many are the institutional descendants of frontier survival, mountain refuge, reconquest, route defense, or coastal security. Control of a crossing, harbor, pass, or defensible refuge can be the material foundation of political authority.

docs.title: Cultural Character
docs.text:
Dorado's long history of invasion, resistance, mountain warfare, maritime expansion, and religious conflict produced a culture that prizes courage, obstinacy, honor, and aggressive self-reliance. Outsiders often interpret Doradan fearlessness as bordering on insanity.

The familiar regional names are not exhaustive administrative provinces. Older Euskald valley communities, local civic identities, princely territories, and mixed frontier populations overlap the broader identities below.

docs.title: Cantabri
docs.text:
The Cantabri inhabit the northern mountain country. Their wealth is tied to mineral resources and fortified highland lordships, including strongholds carved into mountain caverns. Their culture emphasizes aristocratic honor, endurance, and immovability.

Motto: Like Stone Unyielding. Badge: The Tower on the Rock. Heraldic description: A tower Argent masoned Sable upon a rock proper. Plain English: A white or silver stone tower, its masonry picked out in black, standing on a natural-colored rock.

docs.title: Flagros
docs.text:
Flagros is the old eastern Doradan country along the Anora frontier. Its people, the Flagrosos, preserve the habits of a marcher society: fortress towns, guarded crossings, military households, cavalry patrols, and families whose political memories are dominated by war with Clovia.

The regional name predates Covado. After post-imperial Clovian invasion drove many eastern communities into the mountains, Covado led the reconquest and captured Fort Hurktos. When a Tusci Prince demanded the fortress back, Covado answered:

“Come and take it.”

The fortress was renamed Covadio in his honor. His challenge became the Flagroso motto and the basis of their shared badge.

Motto: Come And Take It. Badge: The Open Gate of Covadio. Heraldic description: A fortress gatehouse proper, the gates displayed open and the portcullis raised. Plain English: A heavy stone fortress gate with its doors open and portcullis lifted.

docs.title: Vettones
docs.text:
The Vettones inhabit much of western mainland Dorado, where broad grazing country supports cattle herds and horse culture. Their Princes and great landholders are associated with ranch estates, seasonal drives, cavalry, livestock fairs, and dangerous bull contests. Famous fighting-bull bloodlines can be matters of noble prestige in their own right.

Motto: With The Sun We Ride. Badge: The Horse and Setting Sun. Heraldic description: A horse rampant Sable before a demi-sun issuant in base Gules rayonned Or. Plain English: A black rearing horse in front of a half-visible red setting sun with golden rays.

docs.title: Meliti
docs.text:
The Meliti are the maritime people of the Jabberer Islands and their diaspora. They are among the finest sailors, shipbuilders, traders, navigators, and sea-fighters in Lorania. Island and civic loyalties are often stronger than any unified Meliti political identity.

Tejago is their greatest current maritime center, ruled by Prince Alfonse Reynaldo de Torrez, the Sea Fox.

Motto: Waves Beneath Our Wings. Badge: The Jabber Bird over the Waves. Heraldic description: A Jabber Bird volant proper, beneath it three barrulets wavy Argent and Azure. Plain English: A naturally colored Jabber Bird flying above three narrow wavy stripes of white and blue.

docs.title: Euskald Communities
docs.text: Older Euskald populations remain especially important in mountain valleys and culturally conservative districts. Not every Doradan community fits neatly into the Cantabri, Flagroso, Vetton, or Meliti identities, and some highland populations understand themselves principally through older valley, clan, or Euskald traditions.

docs.title: Movement and Defense
docs.text:
Dorado's mountains, river crossings, islands, and exposed coast make movement highly regional. Mountain routes depend on defended passes, refuges, guides, fortified settlements, and communities able to keep difficult roads open. The Anora crossings remain strategic because whoever holds them can influence movement between Dorado and Clovia.

At sea, the Meliti provide another form of corridor security. Coastal and island travel is dangerous but economically indispensable, and defended harbors, experienced pilots, convoying, and local knowledge allow maritime networks to connect communities that overland routes would leave isolated.

These conditions reinforce the Doradan expectation that legitimate rulers must be able to hold the route and the refuge as well as win battles.

docs.title: The Jabberer Islands and Tejago
docs.text:
The Jabberer Islands form a scattered western archipelago whose geography encourages strong island identities and political fragmentation. The ordinary Meropolitan name is associated with the islands' famous Jabber Birds; learned sources sometimes preserve older names for the archipelago.

Tejago combines the maritime culture of the islands with the strategic importance of a great fortified harbor. Its fleets, defenses, merchants, and location make it one of the principal powers of Dorado despite the absence of any single ruler over all the islands.

docs.title: Origins
docs.text: Doradans descend substantially from Euskald stock, but later migrations, local identities, political reconquests, and maritime settlement have produced substantial regional differences. Their relationship to the Tuatha is debated by scholars, with some proposing an ancient shared ancestry followed by an early cultural split.

docs.title: Meliti
docs.text:
Motto: “Waves Beneath Our Wings.”

The Meliti are the principal maritime people of the Jabberer Islands and one of the best-known Doradan peoples abroad. Their sailors, merchants, shipwrights, navigators, privateers, and explorers are found throughout the western seas.

docs.title: Badge: The Jabber Bird over the Waves
docs.text:
The shared Meliti badge is a Jabber Bird in flight above stylized waves.

Heraldic description: A Jabber Bird volant proper, beneath it three barrulets wavy Argent and Azure. Plain English: A naturally colored Jabber Bird flying above three narrow wavy stripes of white and blue.

In heraldic vocabulary, volant means shown flying with the wings extended. Barrulets wavy are narrow horizontal wavy bands, here representing the sea.

The bird ties the Meliti directly to the famous messenger animals of the Jabberer Islands and to the navigational skill for which both bird and sailor are renowned. The waves beneath it make the old motto literal: “Waves Beneath Our Wings.”

The device is a broad maritime-cultural badge rather than universal dynastic arms. Individual islands, cities, merchant houses, and princes maintain their own heraldry, and Tejago in particular may display its own civic devices alongside the Meliti bird-and-waves.

docs.title: Island Identity
docs.text:
The Meliti are not politically unified. The Jabberer Islands contain many island communities, ports, princely territories, and rival houses, and local identity may be stronger than any abstract Meliti solidarity.

The sea nevertheless binds them together culturally. Meliti communities share a strong maritime vocabulary of prestige: seamanship, navigation, shipbuilding, long-distance trade, and the ability to defend one's vessel or harbor are all sources of status.

docs.title: Tejago
docs.text:
Tejago is the greatest current Meliti maritime center and one of the principal powers of Dorado. Its fortified harbor, merchant fleets, shipyards, and strategic position make it far more influential than its territorial size would suggest.

Prince Alfonse Reynaldo de Torrez, called the Sea Fox, is a Meliti ruler and presently the most prominent prince of the Jabberer Islands, though he is not their king.

docs.title: Maritime Warfare
docs.text: Meliti culture is less oriented toward land warfare than many mainland Doradan traditions, but this should not be mistaken for pacifism. Meliti ships and harbor defenses have a formidable reputation, and piracy, privateering, convoy protection, and commercial violence are part of the same maritime world as legitimate trade.

docs.title: Jabber Birds
docs.text: The islands are closely associated with Jabber Birds, remarkably intelligent messenger animals used throughout the Hetaireian Princedoms and Southern Cities. Their navigational abilities make them especially valuable to Meliti merchants and rulers.

docs.title: Vettones
docs.text:
Motto: “With The Sun We Ride.”

The Vettones inhabit much of western mainland Dorado, where broad grazing country, dry uplands, and ranch estates support a culture built around cattle and horses.

docs.title: Badge: The Horse and Setting Sun
docs.text:
The shared Vetton badge is a dark rearing horse before a red-gold setting sun.

Heraldic description: A horse rampant Sable before a demi-sun issuant in base Gules rayonned Or. Plain English: A black rearing horse in front of a half-visible red setting sun with golden rays.

In strict heraldic vocabulary, rampant describes the horse reared upright on one hind leg with the forelegs raised. A demi-sun issuant in base is a half-sun emerging from the lower edge of the composition; among the Vettones it is understood specifically as the western setting sun.

The horse represents horsemanship, mobility, aristocratic prestige, and the practical realities of ranch life. The setting sun marks both the western homeland and a romantic Vetton ideal of life beneath the open sky. The badge is widely used on banners, saddle-cloths, ranch signs, seals, and other displays of regional identity; individual houses retain their own arms.

docs.title: Cattle Country
docs.text:
Vetton wealth is measured heavily in land, herds, horses, and the dependents required to manage them. Seasonal cattle drives, livestock fairs, grazing rights, and disputes over water or pasture shape both ordinary life and princely politics.

Large ranch estates can support powerful local lords, but smaller freeholders, hired riders, drovers, and pastoral communities remain important parts of Vetton society.

docs.title: Haciendas
docs.text:
Large Vetton estates are commonly organized around haciendas: substantial ranch compounds that function at once as household, workplace, storehouse, stable, defensive refuge, and center of local hospitality.

A prosperous hacienda may contain a central courtyard, shaded galleries, family apartments, kitchens, wells or cisterns, barns, corrals, tack rooms, workshops, guest quarters, and a shrine or small chapel. Herdsmen, riders, servants, craftsmen, dependents, guests, merchants, and armed retainers can all pass through the same compound.

A hacienda is therefore a social center as much as an agricultural one. Livestock sales, contracts, feasts, music, courtship, political bargaining, boasting, and old family rivalries frequently converge there. Vetton hospitality is taken seriously, and the reputation of a household depends partly on how generously and confidently it receives travelers and neighbors.

docs.title: Horsemanship
docs.text:
Riding is a common practical skill and an important mark of prestige. Vetton horsemen are valued as scouts, escorts, raiders, and cavalry, and their military traditions emphasize mobility more strongly than the fortress-centered culture of Flagros or the highland strongholds of the Cantabri.

The aristocratic ideal expects a great lord to ride well, understand horses and cattle, maintain worthy herds, show courage in dangerous contests, and act as a generous host. This mounted-ranching ideal extends downward through free riders, drovers, retainers, and professional herdsmen rather than belonging exclusively to princes.

docs.title: Bulls and Contest
docs.text:
Particularly aggressive fighting-bull bloodlines are bred for prestige as well as practical stock. Public contests involving bulls can range from mounted aristocratic games with lances to more dangerous contests on foot.

A celebrated bull, breeding line, or rider can become famous far beyond the estate that produced them. Vetton noble houses may boast as readily of their horses and bulls as of victories in war.

docs.title: Cultural Character
docs.text:
Vetton ideals emphasize horsemanship, hospitality, personal dignity, courage, and self-reliance. Their great gatherings combine trade, livestock judging, feasting, music, courtship, rivalry, and displays of martial skill.

The motto “With The Sun We Ride” evokes both the practical life of riders traveling beneath the open sky and the western horizon toward which the sun descends.

docs.title: Cantabri
docs.text:
Motto: “Like Stone Unyielding.”

The Cantabri are a northern Doradan mountain people whose identity is bound to highland strongholds, mineral wealth, and old aristocratic lineages. They are among the populations of Dorado most strongly associated with the hard northern mountains.

docs.title: Badge: The Tower on the Rock
docs.text:
The shared Cantabri badge is a stone tower standing upon a bare rock.

Heraldic description: A tower Argent masoned Sable upon a rock proper. Plain English: A white or silver stone tower, its masonry picked out in black, standing on a natural-colored rock.

The tower represents the fortified lordships and cavern strongholds of the northern country. The rock beneath it is the more important symbolic element: dynasties and fortifications may be raised upon the mountains, but the mountain country itself endures. The device therefore reinforces the Cantabri motto, “Like Stone Unyielding.”

As with other Doradan regional badges, this is not a compulsory coat of arms for every Cantabri house. Individual princes and lineages use their own arms while employing the tower-on-rock badge when emphasizing broader Cantabri identity.

docs.title: Mountain Country
docs.text:
Cantabri settlements occupy steep valleys, upland plateaus, and mineral-rich highlands. Mining and metal wealth support powerful lords, while difficult terrain encourages fortified local rule and strong regional independence.

Some of their most famous strongholds are carved directly into mountain caverns, combining defensibility, storage, habitation, and access to the mineral veins beneath the highlands.

docs.title: Aristocratic Ideal
docs.text:
Cantabri culture prizes endurance, personal honor, generosity within one's obligations, and refusal to be intimidated. Their great houses often present themselves as ancient features of the landscape rather than temporary political creations: dynasties may fall, but the mountain lordship is expected to endure.

This reputation gives the motto Like Stone Unyielding both a political and personal meaning.

docs.title: Xalincia
docs.text: Xalincia is one of the principal Cantabri centers of power. Its lords are counted among the major powers of Dorado, comparable in influence to Tejago and Covadio.

docs.title: Flagros
docs.text:
Motto: “Come And Take It.”

Flagros is the old eastern Doradan country along the Anora frontier. Its people are the Flagrosos (singular/adjectival Flagroso). The regional name predates the reconquest associated with Covado and the modern political mythology that grew around him.

docs.title: The Old Frontier
docs.text:
The eastern country was one of the principal zones of contact and conflict between unconquered Dorado and the old Heryos imperial world. After generations of failed attempts to pacify Dorado, Emperor Hurktos ordered a massive fortress built to command the chief Anora crossing and contain Doradan movement west of the river.

The imperial stronghold became known as Fort Hurktos. Its construction marked a practical admission that outright conquest of Dorado had failed: the Empire would hold the crossing rather than the country beyond it.

docs.title: The Reconquest of Covado
docs.text:
After the old Empire collapsed, Clovian forces invaded eastern Dorado, seized much of Flagros, and drove many local communities into the mountains.

The refugees and surviving highland communities were eventually united by Covado, who led them back into the lowlands. His defining victory was the capture of Fort Hurktos itself.

After the victory, a Prince of the Tusci demanded that the fortress be returned. Covado replied:

“Come and take it.”

The prince did not answer.

The fortress was thereafter renamed Covadio in honor of its liberator. The challenge became one of the defining sayings of Flagroso political culture and, in time, the regional motto.

docs.title: The Anora March
docs.text:
The long frontier with Clovia is not a separate Doradan people from the Flagrosos. Marcher life is one of the principal things that defines modern Flagros.

Fortified towns, guarded crossings, river patrols, cavalry scouts, military households, border feuds, and old refugee settlements are common features of Flagroso life. Families may preserve detailed memories of which ancestors fled a Clovian advance, followed Covado through the mountains, defended a ford, or retook a particular estate.

The frontier has also produced mixed populations through prisoners, defectors, marriages, merchants, settlers, and repeated changes of control. Flagroso identity rests more on belonging to the eastern country and its political memory than on a claim of perfectly uniform ancestry.

docs.title: Identity
docs.text:
Flagros is older than Covado, but modern Flagroso political identity is inseparable from his reconquest. Its central claim is recovered sovereignty: foreign powers took the eastern country, built fortresses to contain its people, and were then driven out by those they had displaced.

The motto “Come And Take It” is therefore both defiance and invitation. Flagros holds what it reclaimed, and anyone who disputes that claim is welcome to test it by force.

docs.title: Badge: The Open Gate of Covadio
docs.text:
The shared Flagroso badge is the Open Gate of Covadio: the gate of the captured imperial fortress deliberately shown standing open.

Heraldic description: A fortress gatehouse proper, the gates displayed open and the portcullis raised. Plain English: A heavy stone fortress gate with its doors open and its portcullis lifted.

The badge is intentionally described as a device rather than a complete coat of arms because its field and fixed tinctures remain variable among Flagroso communities and military bodies.

The device is an intentional provocation. Fort Hurktos was built to shut Dorado out and contain its people behind the Anora frontier. Flagroso heraldry reverses that meaning. The fortress is theirs, its gate stands open, and anyone who believes otherwise is invited to enter and try to take it.

The badge is not necessarily the personal arms of every Flagroso prince or marcher lord. It appears on standards, seals, military insignia, monuments, and public displays of Flagroso identity.

docs.title: Covadio
docs.text: Covadio is the great fortress-city and principal political center of Flagros in eastern Dorado. It commands the chief crossing of the Anora frontier and stands on the site of the ancient imperial stronghold known as Fort Hurktos.

docs.title: Fort Hurktos
docs.text:
After generations of failed imperial attempts to conquer Dorado, Emperor Hurktos ordered a massive fortress built at the principal Anora crossing. The stronghold was intended to contain the Doradans and secure the frontier rather than serve as the base for another full conquest.

Its construction therefore became a symbol of both imperial power and imperial failure: the old Empire could fortify the river, but it could not subdue the country beyond it.

docs.title: Capture by Covado
docs.text:
After the Empire's collapse, Clovian forces entered eastern Dorado and drove many Flagroso communities into the mountains. Covado later united the displaced and surviving local forces, reconquered much of the country, and captured Fort Hurktos itself.

When a Prince of the Tusci demanded the fortress back, Covado replied:

“Come and take it.”

No reply came.

The captured fortress was thereafter renamed Covadio in Covado's honor. Over time the settlement around the fortress grew into the city now known by the same name.

docs.title: The Open Gate
docs.text:
The gate of Covadio became the shared Flagroso badge and is deliberately depicted open.

Heraldic description: A fortress gatehouse proper, the gates displayed open and the portcullis raised. Plain English: A heavy stone fortress gate with its doors open and portcullis lifted.

The image is not one of hospitality or weakness but provocation: the fortress built to contain Dorado now belongs to the people it was meant to exclude, and any rival claimant is invited to enter and try to take it.

This symbolism is inseparable from the Flagroso motto, “Come And Take It.”

docs.title: Modern Importance
docs.text: Covadio is one of the major centers of Doradan power, comparable to the Cantabri lords of Xalincia and the Meliti port of Tejago. Its position on the Anora frontier makes it both a fortress and the central monument of Flagroso reconquest memory.

docs.title: Jabberer Islands
docs.text:
The Jabberer Islands are a scattered western archipelago inhabited primarily by the Meliti, the maritime Doradans. The islands are politically fragmented among several princes, city-lords, and local dynasties rather than united under a single ruler.

The familiar name is Meropolitan and derives from the islands' association with Jabber Birds. Older learned sources sometimes use more archaic geographical names for the archipelago, while individual islands naturally possess their own local names and identities.

docs.title: Island Geography and Identity
docs.text:
Distance by sea, difficult weather, local harbors, and uneven resources encourage strong island identities. A Meliti sailor may call himself Doradan abroad and Meliti among other Doradans, but at home his island, city, harbor, or princely allegiance may matter more than either label.

This fragmentation has never prevented the islands from forming a coherent maritime cultural sphere. Shipbuilding methods, navigational practice, merchant networks, marriage ties, religious institutions, and generations of movement between islands bind them together even when their princes quarrel.

docs.title: Political Character
docs.text:
Prince Alfonse Reynaldo de Torrez of Tejago is currently the most prominent island ruler, but he is not an uncontested monarch and possesses no automatic authority over the other princes.

Northern Atharite political theory also discourages royal titles: to claim kingship would imply equality with or independence from the Pontis, whose notional supremacy underlies the political language of the Princedoms.

docs.title: Maritime Importance
docs.text:
The islanders are master shipbuilders and sailors and play a major role in commerce around the western Sea of Ardan. Fishing, convoy work, exploration, privateering, piracy, and long-distance trade overlap in a maritime economy where armed ships are as normal as merchant cargoes.

The archipelago's position makes it a natural staging ground between mainland Dorado, Clovia, the western sea routes, and more distant ports.

docs.title: Tejago
docs.text:
Tejago is the greatest fortified harbor of the islands and their most important current commercial and naval center. Its deep harbor, defenses, shipyards, merchant fleets, and strategic location give its prince influence far beyond the city's immediate territory.

Tejago is not the capital of a united archipelago. Its importance comes from controlling one of the best places in the islands to repair ships, gather convoys, store cargo, negotiate contracts, and project naval power.

docs.title: Jabber Birds
docs.text:
The islands give their ordinary foreign name to Jabber Birds, extraordinarily intelligent messenger animals capable of learning destinations, carrying written messages, and mimicking short spoken ones.

Their ability to navigate over long distances makes them especially valuable in an archipelago and has helped turn them into a fixture of Meliti commerce and diplomacy.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Tejago is the greatest fortified harbor of the Jabberer Islands and one of the strongest Meliti princedoms of Dorado. Its influence rests less on territorial size than on its harbor, defenses, shipyards, merchant fleets, warehouses, and strategic position astride western sea routes.

The city is powerful enough to be compared with the Cantabri lords of Xalincia and the Flagroso fortress-city of Covadio.

docs.title: The Harbor City
docs.text:
Tejago's natural harbor has been heavily fortified over generations. Harbor walls, towers, batteries or engines, fortified quays, sea-gates, and defensible approaches allow the city to protect merchant shipping and resist attack from the sea.

Its docks support shipbuilding and repair on a scale uncommon elsewhere in Dorado. Merchants use Tejago to gather convoys, transfer cargo, obtain credit and contracts, hire crews, exchange news, and wait for favorable weather before attempting longer passages.

Because the city sits inside a politically fragmented archipelago, commercial neutrality and maritime leverage can matter as much as direct military strength. Rival island princes may dislike Tejago's predominance while still depending on its harbor.

docs.title: Rule of Prince Alfonse
docs.text:
Tejago has enjoyed nearly forty years of steady rule under Prince Alfonse Reynaldo de Torrez, called the Sea Fox. He is a cunning and shrewd Meliti ruler under whom the merchant fleets have prospered and Tejago's position among the island princes has strengthened.

His age has become a political problem. He is declining without a clear successor, making succession one of the city's most immediate tensions and a matter of concern throughout the islands.

docs.title: Maritime Role
docs.text:
Tejago belongs to the strongest seafaring tradition in Lorania. Meliti crews are explorers, traders, navigators, shipbuilders, privateers, and dangerous fighters at sea even when their culture is less oriented toward land warfare than many mainland Doradan traditions.

The city is therefore both commercial center and naval strongpoint: a place where cargo, diplomacy, piracy, convoy protection, intelligence, and princely politics routinely overlap.

docs.title: Prince Alfonse Reynaldo de Torrez
docs.text: Prince Alfonse Reynaldo de Torrez, called the Sea Fox, is the long-ruling prince of Tejago and presently the most prominent ruler among the Meliti princes of the Jabberer Islands.

docs.title: Reign
docs.text: Alfonse has ruled Tejago for nearly forty years. He is cunning and shrewd, and under his government the city's merchant fleets have prospered while Tejago has strengthened its position as the archipelago's foremost fortified harbor and commercial center.

docs.title: Succession Problem
docs.text: He is now succumbing to old age and has no clear successor. No claimant has yet emerged with an uncontested right to replace him, making the succession an increasingly important source of political uncertainty.

docs.title: Regional Position
docs.text:
Tejago is powerful enough to be compared with the Cantabri lords of Xalincia and the Flagroso fortress-city of Covadio. Alfonse's prominence therefore makes his impending succession problem potentially important beyond his own island.

He is influential among the island princes but is not their king. The political fragmentation of the Jabberer Islands means his authority depends on Tejago's fleets, wealth, alliances, reputation, and strategic harbor rather than on any formal sovereignty over the archipelago.

docs.title: Khoryv
docs.text: Motto: “Until The End.” Symbol: Black bear on red.

docs.title: Emblem
docs.text:
Blazon: Gules, a bear Sable. Plain English: A black bear on a red field.

Meropolitan heralds regard the black-on-red device as an improper color-on-color combination. Khoryvians show little concern for that judgment. The old arms predate much of the western armorial theory now used to criticize them, and their refusal to regularize the device has become characteristic of the Realm itself.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Khoryv is the most distant and culturally irregular of the Hetaireian Realms. Its oldest known inhabitants were Svealish, but modern Khoryvians are the product of centuries of Svealish, Tuatha, Nibelungian, Sigyn, and occasional Khazgui admixture. In the settled heartland, Khoryvian is therefore a genuine ethnic and cultural identity despite having no simple ancestral origin.

Khoryv's defining history is one of frontier ethnogenesis. Settled river and forest populations, steppe horse-hosts, mountain peoples, migrants, converts, refugees, and military communities have interacted for centuries along a frontier too distant for western institutions to control completely. Khoryv belongs to Hetaireian civilization, but its local political order was repeatedly shaped by the necessity of surviving before help could arrive.

That old condition has become an active constitutional crisis. Expanding Khazgui power places increasing military pressure on the east while Khoryv receives too little meaningful western support to satisfy many of its rulers and communities.

docs.title: Peoples
docs.text:
Khoryv is not neatly divided into equivalent ethnic provinces. Several identities overlap with Khoryvian political allegiance and with one another.

  • Khoryvians — the mixed settled population of the forest and river heartlands, descended from many successive populations.
  • Svealaka — northern Svealish communities of the frozen forests and reindeer country. They remain recognizably Svealish while also belonging to the Khoryvian political world.
  • Vyrkari — Atharite eastern horse-host communities closely related by ancestry and material culture to the Sigyn.
  • Darszev — the western mountain branch of the ancient Darsz people, whose language has no demonstrated relationship to those of their neighbors.
  • Sigyn — non-Atharite eastern horse peoples whose clans, families, and warbands interact constantly with the Vyrkari.

These categories answer different questions. A person can be politically Khoryvian while belonging to a Svealaka, Vyrkari, or Darszev community, and frontier ancestry often crosses the boundaries later chroniclers prefer to draw.

docs.title: Vyrkari and Frontier Service
docs.text:
The Vyrkari occupy an important place in Khoryv's military society. They are Atharite horse-host communities whose ancestors and neighbors include steppe peoples closely related to the Sigyn. Their identity developed through frontier service and incorporation into the Hetaireian world rather than through simple ethnic replacement.

The name itself is tied to wider Hetaireian history. Vyrkar was originally an old Heryos martial title for an elite mounted warrior. The title was later revived for the Pontifical Vyrkar Guard, whose prestige caused Vyrkar/Vyrkari to spread as a western label for Atharite steppe and frontier horsemen. In Khoryv that label became part of the identity of actual horse-host communities.

Khoryv therefore reverses the usual direction of cultural influence: a revived imperial word, transformed by a Meropolitan institution, became attached to frontier peoples who then made it their own.

docs.title: The Khazgui Crisis
docs.text:
Khoryv has borne a disproportionate share of the recent Khazgui expansion. Raids, refugee movements, ruined frontier settlements, requisitions, and the continual need to maintain eastern defenses have strained the Realm.

The Khoryvian Prince has repeatedly sought greater support from the Pontis. The northern Church's military institutions remain young, and the expanding Hiera Tagmata must also answer Chulkan pressure around Meropolis and growing southern Behdin power. Those constraints may be understandable in Meropolis, but they are cold comfort in Khoryv.

The resulting grievance is simple and politically powerful: western authorities claim the right to judge Khoryv's rulers and the constitutional limits of their office, yet Khoryvians believe they have been left largely to defend themselves.

The grievance is intensified by the Hetaireian expectation that rulers must keep the road, defend settlements, and preserve usable corridors through dangerous territory. Khoryvian rulers who actually perform those duties under extreme frontier pressure can plausibly ask why their sovereignty should depend upon authorities who do not share the cost.

docs.title: The Royal Question
docs.text:
The current Prince of Khoryv has become increasingly receptive to clerics who dispute the prevailing Meropolitan doctrine of princely sovereignty. These teachers remain Atharites and do not reject the Church itself. Their dispute concerns the temporal authority of the Pontis.

In its strongest form, the Khoryvian argument holds that sacred and temporal authority are both legitimate but that neither creates the other. The Pontis may stand foremost among the clergy without thereby possessing an intrinsic right to grant, revoke, or limit the sovereignty of every Atharite ruler.

The Prince was not originally a partisan of this doctrine. Years of fighting the Khazgui with little western assistance have made its implications increasingly attractive. His court has begun using more emphatically sovereign formulas, and rumors persist that he intends eventually to assume the title King of Khoryv.

Within the wider Hetaireian order, that title would be more than an elevation in rank. Kingship claims non-derivative temporal sovereignty outside the inherited Ardanic princely order. A King of Khoryv could continue to worship Athar, accept Ardan's Theosis, and acknowledge the Pontis as supreme Hetaireian religious authority while denying that Pontifical recognition creates or limits his temporal sovereignty.

To many Khoryvians the question is practical before it is theological: if Khoryv must defend itself by Khoryvian blood, why should a distant Pontis determine the limits of Khoryvian sovereignty?

To Meropolitan canonists, that argument threatens the political theology underlying the Hetaireian Realms themselves.

docs.title: Religion
docs.text:
Khoryv is Atharite and remains within the Hetaireian religious world, but a major constitutional-theological dispute now separates important Khoryvian clerics and the princely court from the northern hierarchy. Khoryvians commonly deny that their position is a new heresy, instead claiming that Meropolitan canonists have gradually expanded the temporal claims of the Pontis beyond older Atharite teaching.

Whether that claim reflects genuine frontier tradition, selective memory, or recent political theology remains contested.

The distinction matters. Constitutional dissent does not automatically place Khoryv outside Hetaireian communion. The unresolved danger is the point at which denial of Pontifical temporal supremacy becomes entangled with denial of religious authority strongly enough to produce formal schism.

docs.title: Frontier Institutions
docs.text:
Khoryv contains many places where ordinary settled administration is insufficient. Fortified settlements, horse-hosts, frontier communities, religious houses, and local military institutions can perform functions analogous to Hetaireian Marches, combining unusual military latitude with obligations of patrol, warning, refuge, fortification, provisioning, and rapid response.

Khoryvian marcher law varies considerably by region, community, and allegiance. The general principle is visible across the frontier: frontier service creates prestige and political claims because survival depends upon institutions capable of acting quickly without waiting for western permission.

docs.title: Relations
docs.text:
• Nibelung — western neighbor and important route toward the rest of the Hetaireian world.
  • Khazgui — expanding eastern power and the principal immediate military threat.
  • Sigyn — closely connected steppe populations along the eastern frontier.
  • Svealish — ancestral population and continuing cultural presence in the north.
  • Meropolis — religious center and source of the constitutional authority now disputed by the Khoryvian court.

docs.title: Darszev
docs.text: Motto: “What We Build Endures.”

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Darszev are the eastern branch of the ancient Darsz people, dwelling in Khoryv's western mountains. When the earliest known Svealish settlers entered Khoryv, Darsz communities were already established. Neither Darszev tradition nor outside scholarship preserves a reliable account of where their ancestors came from.

Their language is famously difficult for outsiders and has no demonstrated relationship to the surrounding Svealish, Heryos-descended, steppe, or other known language families. This makes the Darszev culturally more alien in some respects than the geographically more distant Sigyn.

docs.title: The Darsz People
docs.text:
The Darszev are not the only surviving Darsz-descended population. Across the mountains in Nibelung, the related Darschen developed under centuries of Nibelungian influence. Darsz is used for the older ancestral people and linguistic root; Darszev and Darschen are later regional ethnonyms.

Despite substantial cultural divergence, similarities in language, oral tradition, customary law, and old mountain vocabulary make their common origin clear.

docs.title: Mountain Culture
docs.text:
The Darszev are renowned mountaineers, quarrymen, miners, engineers, and masons. Their settlements make extensive use of stone retaining walls, bridges, fortified houses, terraces, roads, cisterns, and high mountain works built to survive difficult terrain and severe weather.

Their reputation for masonry is old enough that some structures attributed to the earliest Darsz communities are still maintained, rebuilt, or incorporated into modern settlements.

docs.title: Motto and Symbolic Tradition
docs.text:
Motto: “What We Build Endures.”

The saying is both practical and cultural, referring to masonry, settlements, institutions, and the survival of the Darsz people themselves.

No single Darszev emblem is universally recognized. Clans, valleys, towns, lineages, and other communities use local signs of their own, with architectural and masonry motifs especially common in seals and communal devices.

docs.title: Religion
docs.text: The Darszev participate in the religious life of Khoryv, but their long isolation has preserved distinctive local customs. Their Atharite practice can therefore look unusual to lowland observers even where doctrine is broadly orthodox.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Svealaka are the northern Svealish communities of Khoryv, especially those inhabiting the frozen forests, reindeer country, and northern river systems. The name distinguishes these Khoryvian Svealish from related Svealish populations farther west without implying a wholly separate ancestry.

The Svealaka preserve more visibly Svealish language, kinship, and seasonal lifeways than most settled Khoryvians. Reindeer pastoralism, forestry, hunting, trapping, fishing, winter travel, and knowledge of the northern river routes remain central to many communities.

A Svealaka person can be both Svealish and Khoryvian. The identities describe ancestry and culture on one hand and participation in the Khoryvian political world on the other.

docs.title: History
docs.text: Svealish peoples were the earliest known inhabitants of much of Khoryv before later Tuathan, Nibelungian, Sigyn, and occasional Khazgui migrations transformed the realm's population. The Svealaka represent a living continuation of that oldest known layer rather than a foreign population recently introduced from the north.

docs.title: Symbols
docs.text:
The Svealaka have no universal motto or common heraldic device. Clan signs, household marks, religious symbols, animal motifs, and local banners vary from community to community.

The Svealaka are a broad regional Svealish population rather than a single state, military order, or centralized confederation, and no single device represents them all.

docs.title: Religion
docs.text: Svealaka religious practice varies locally, but communities within Khoryv have long interacted with Atharism and the institutions of the realm. Older Svealish customs may persist alongside Atharite practice without making every northern clan doctrinally identical.

docs.title: Vyrkari
docs.text: Motto: “Freedom Or Death.”

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Vyrkari are the Atharite horse-host communities of eastern Khoryv. They are closely related by ancestry, language, and material culture to the neighboring Sigyn. The distinction between Vyrkari and Sigyn is therefore religious and political at least as much as ethnic.

Vyrkari identity emerged through frontier ethnogenesis rather than descent from a single ancient tribe. Steppe and frontier riders entered the Khoryvian political world through conversion to Atharism, military hosts, fortified settlements, oath-bonds, marriage, migration, and service. A Sigyn clan may become Vyrkari over generations; a Vyrkar lineage that abandons Atharism and rides east may in turn be absorbed into Sigyn society.

docs.title: The Name
docs.text:
The word Vyrkari is older than the Khoryvian communities that now bear it, but it did not originally name a people.

In ancient Heryos martial usage, a vyrkar was an elite mounted warrior of exceptional skill and status. The title eventually became archaic. Centuries later it was deliberately revived in Meropolis for the Pontifical Vyrkar Guard, a prestigious cavalry-centered regiment drawing on Heryos/Heryoi equestrian traditions and Atharite steppe recruitment.

The fame of that regiment changed the word's meaning. Western Hetaireians increasingly used Vyrkar and Vyrkari for Atharite steppe horsemen and horse-hosts more generally. Along the Khoryvian frontier, communities to whom outsiders applied the label eventually adopted and transformed it into a genuine ethnocultural and military identity of their own.

The semantic chain is therefore old Heryos martial title → Vyrkar Guard → Hetaireian frontier label → Khoryvian Vyrkari identity.

The Vyrkari are not surviving ancient Heryos and do not claim an uncomplicated Heryos ethnicity. The old word reached them through imperial memory, Pontifical military prestige, and frontier contact.

docs.title: The Hosts
docs.text:
Vyrkari society is organized around mounted frontier communities rather than a single centralized tribe. Their hosts patrol the eastern marches, escort caravans, raid enemy territory, defend river crossings, and supply some of Khoryv's best light cavalry.

The Vyrkari are not literally a holy order, but faith is constitutive of their public identity. Membership historically implied both adherence to Athar and participation in the defense of Khoryv's eastern frontier.

Their military privileges exist because frontier conditions demand rapid armed response. Host autonomy, patrol rights, fortified settlements, and local command therefore carry corresponding expectations of warning, escort, refuge, provisioning, and defense. Exact privileges differ among hosts and remain subject to Khoryvian political negotiation.

docs.title: Emblem
docs.text:
The Vyrkari use an explicitly religious-military device: the Flame of Athar bearing the Hand of Ardan, above two crossed sabers.

Heraldic description: The Flame of Athar charged with the Hand of Ardan, two sabers in saltire beneath. Plain English: The sacred Flame of Athar with the Hand of Ardan shown inside it, with two crossed sabers beneath the flame.

Exact tinctures are not universally fixed. The device appears on host banners, standards, saddle-cloths, seals, weapons, and frontier shrines more often than as a standardized personal coat of arms.

The flame and hand proclaim the Vyrkari's Atharite identity; the crossed sabers mark the military host tradition that distinguishes them from most settled Khoryvians and from their Sigyn cousins.

docs.title: Religion
docs.text:
Vyrkari Atharism is central to the identity itself, though local practice retains many customs shared with Sigyn steppe society. This does not necessarily imply theological heterodoxy; frontier ritual, oath custom, burial practice, and seasonal observance may simply preserve older cultural forms beneath an Atharite confession.

The current Khoryvian sovereignty dispute does not by itself remove the Vyrkari from Hetaireian communion. Like other Khoryvians, individual hosts and clerics may differ over the temporal authority of the Pontis while remaining Atharite.

docs.title: Relations
docs.text:
• Sigyn — closest cultural and ancestral relatives; the frontier between the two identities is porous.
  • Khazgui — principal current military enemy on the eastern frontier.
  • Khoryv — the Realm whose defense and political order historically shaped Vyrkari identity.
  • Hiera Tagmata — the Pontifical military institution whose Vyrkar Guard gave the Vyrkari name its later Hetaireian meaning.

docs.title: Nibelung
docs.text: Motto: “When All Fails, We Remain.”

docs.title: Heraldry
docs.text:
Blazon: Argent, a hand sable. (A black hand on a white field.)

The device is known as the Iron Hand of Ardan. Its name refers to a genuine sacred site associated with Ardan, where a physical handprint attributed to him survives. The site is more than a commemorative monument: it is regarded as possessing real supernatural significance and has helped anchor Nibelungian pilgrimage, settlement, and political memory.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Nibelung is one of the Hetaireian Realms. Its peoples have cultural roots related to the Svealish and Firelanders, but entered the Ardanic and Hetaireian order rather than remaining Reaver societies. The Realm contains many Principalities, towns, ecclesiastical institutions, guilds, professional communities, lesser landholders, and regional cultures.

Nibelungian political life is increasingly defined by a struggle over what kind of state the old princely order should become. Commerce, literacy, finance, administration, guild organization, and other corporate institutions have made many non-noble groups economically indispensable. To such people, inherited aristocratic privileges and autonomous noble violence can appear less like ancient liberty than obstacles to predictable law, trade, security, and competent government.

The resulting reform movement is not inherently democratic, anti-clerical, or hostile to Princes. Its characteristic pressure is toward stronger common institutions, more predictable law, formal recognition of important corporate interests, and reduced private aristocratic autonomy. Exactly what constitutional settlement will emerge remains unresolved.

docs.title: Peoples
docs.text:
• Proust — eastern frontier culture along Khoryv.
  • Bohm — southwestern Nibelung.
  • Darschen — mountainous northern Nibelung; the Nibelungian branch of the ancient Darsz people.

docs.title: Proust
docs.text:
Motto: “Hard Like Iron.”

The Proust inhabit eastern Nibelung along the border with Khoryv. Their frontier position gives military defense unusual local importance, but frontier militarization should not be mistaken for the defining condition of Nibelung as a whole.

docs.title: Bohm
docs.text:
Motto: “My Spirit Is Free.”

The Bohm inhabit southwestern Nibelung.

docs.title: Darschen
docs.text:
Motto: “For Ourselves Alone.”

The Darschen inhabit the mountainous north of Nibelung. They are culturally Nibelungian in many respects but share deeper ancestry and language with the Darszev of western Khoryv.

docs.title: Political Change
docs.text:
Nibelung remains a Realm of many Principalities rather than a unified kingdom. Its current importance lies in the growing argument that fragmented custom and hereditary privilege should be reorganized into a more coherent constitutional order.

Princes, noble Houses, towns, guilds, clergy, merchants, administrators, professional associations, and lesser landholders do not divide neatly into two camps. Some Princes favor reform because stronger common institutions increase their own ability to keep roads open, suppress destructive private warfare, collect revenue, and govern. Some towns defend ancient privileges against centralization. Some nobles support predictable courts while resisting any attack on hereditary standing.

The struggle is therefore over who can most legitimately and effectively maintain order and prosperity, not simply nobles against commoners.

docs.title: Tuathan Populations
docs.text:
Two important Tuatha confederations are associated with Nibelung and its southern mountain frontier:

  • Gascani — inhabit forests and crags in the southern foothills. Their villages are locally governed, with chiefs meeting in a yearly or emergency conclave called the Forrad.
  • Sabkenti — bridge the mountains between Nibelung and Clovia. Historically bitter enemies of the old Empire, they regard their ancient alliance with the Nibelungen as continuing to bind them. In war they can unite behind an elected Tassiag, or high chief.

The Sabkenti are particularly resistant to conversion, viewing the Atharite Church as a continuation of the imperial power they opposed.

docs.title: Religion
docs.text:
Nibelung follows Atharism despite the Realm's ancestry and cultural relationship with the Reaver peoples. Attachment to Ardanic legitimacy is especially visible in the Iron Hand tradition and its sacred geography.

Northern cultural inheritance remains visible beneath formal Atharism. The broad midwinter season of feasting, household gathering, hospitality, reciprocal gifts, darkness, and returning light is widely recognized in Nibelung, though local Atharite communities interpret and celebrate it in their own ways. Northern genealogy, memorial customs, and other inherited practices may likewise survive where they can be reconciled with local Atharite teaching.

docs.title: Relations
docs.text:
• Clovia — Longard expansion has produced fighting along the northern forests.
  • Khoryv — eastern frontier, particularly relevant to the Proust and to the Darsz population divided between Darschen and Darszev.
  • Tuatha — significant surviving clannish populations inhabit peripheral forests and mountains.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:

  • The Hetaireian Princedoms
  • Hetaireia

docs.title: Bohm
docs.text: Motto: “My Spirit Is Free.”

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The Bohm inhabit southwestern Nibelung.

docs.title: Religion
docs.text: As a Nibelung subculture, the Bohm belong to the Atharite north.

  • Pontis

docs.title: Darschen
docs.text: Motto: “For Ourselves Alone.”

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Darschen inhabit the mountainous north of Nibelung. They are the Nibelungian branch of the ancient Darsz people and are closely related to the Darszev of western Khoryv.

Their present culture has been deeply shaped by centuries within the Nibelungian world, but their older language, mountain customs, oral traditions, and distinctive vocabulary preserve an origin separate from their Germanic-speaking neighbors.

docs.title: Darsz Origins
docs.text:
The Darsz were already established in the mountain chain before the earliest known Svealish settlement of Khoryv. Their ultimate origin remains unknown, and the Darsz language has no demonstrated relationship to any other known language family.

Over time, political division and contact produced two major regional forms of the old ethnonym: Darszev in Khoryv and Darschen in Nibelung.

docs.title: Culture
docs.text: The Darschen retain the Darsz reputation for mountaineering, masonry, engineering, pastoralism, and fiercely local institutions. Their Nibelungian environment has encouraged stronger traditions of valley leagues, free communities, mercenary service, alpine trade, and bilingualism than are typical among the Darszev.

docs.title: Religion
docs.text: The Darschen belong to the Atharite religious world of Nibelung, though old local customs remain visible in valley festivals, burial practices, communal oaths, and sacred architecture.

docs.title: Proust
docs.text: Motto: “Hard Like Iron.”

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The Proust inhabit eastern Nibelung along the frontier with Khoryv.

docs.title: Religion
docs.text: As a Nibelung subculture, the Proust belong to the Atharite north.

docs.title: Szovij
docs.text: Motto: “Forever Free.”

docs.title: Heraldry
docs.text:
Blazon: Azure, an eagle displayed argent. (A white eagle with wings spread on a blue field.)

The white eagle is a broad Szovijan emblem rather than the arms of one ruler. Its association with freedom is political and historical: it represents the right of Szovijan communities and Princes to remain masters in their own land.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Szovij is one of the Hetaireian Realms, divided among many Principalities and strongly differentiated regional peoples. Its identity emphasizes freedom, but Szovijan freedom is not an abstract doctrine of equality or opposition to hierarchy. It is a historical and defensive political value: after repeated domination and pressure from multiple directions, the right to rule one's own land has become a common measure of legitimate power.

A Szovijan noble, peasant community, town, or Prince may all speak of freedom while accepting sharp differences of rank and privilege. The shared claim is that legitimate hierarchy should be their own, not imposed by an outside conqueror or distant claimant.

The exact sequence of occupations, overlordships, invasions, restorations, and resistance that produced this political memory is incompletely reconstructed in surviving chronicles. The principle is clear even where the chronology is disputed or lost.

docs.title: Political Character
docs.text:
Szovij is not a unified national state. Lendska, Cosserb, Lathuan, local cities, noble houses, Principalities, frontier communities, and ecclesiastical institutions possess their own interests and customs. “Forever Free” does not mean that they agree on who should rule, only that foreign domination is an especially potent accusation.

This makes sovereignty disputes unusually combustible. A Prince can justify demands for military service, taxation, or obedience by presenting them as necessary to preserve the land's independence; opponents can answer that the same policies reproduce the domination they claim to resist.

Pontifical authority remains part of ordinary Hetaireian legitimacy. Szovijan freedom is not inherently anti-Hetaireian or anti-clerical. The distinction between accepted transregional religious authority and unacceptable foreign temporal domination is politically important, even when particular disputes blur that line.

docs.title: Lendska
docs.text:
Motto: “We Will Arrive.”

The Lendska inhabit southern Szovij, especially the river frontier facing the Chulkas steppe and the plains around Meropolis. They are noted horsemen.

Their southern position places them close to one of Szovij's most exposed approaches. Mounted patrol, warning, escort, seasonal campaigning, and rapid response are consequently natural parts of frontier life, though the exact institutions organizing those duties vary by locality.

docs.title: Cosserb
docs.text:
Motto: “Stand As One.”

The Cosserb inhabit eastern Szovij's mountains and hills. They are shepherds, described as friendly and gregarious, with strong traditions of wine, song, and dance. Their convivial reputation does not diminish their reputation as hard fighters.

Mountain geography encourages defended valleys, local solidarity, difficult routes, and communities whose ability to keep passes and refuges functioning can matter more than formal boundaries on a map.

docs.title: Lathuan
docs.text:
Motto: “Our Roots Run Deep.”

The Lathuan inhabit fertile northwestern Szovij. They are taciturn, direct, and skilled farmers. Other Szovijans may dismiss them as backward or culturally unsophisticated; the Lathuan instead prize an image of themselves as honest people who have little need for luxury or novelty.

Their settled agricultural communities provide a different expression of Szovijan freedom: attachment to inherited land, local custom, and the right to continue a way of life without external masters.

docs.title: Geography and Frontiers
docs.text:
The southern reaches border steppe country associated with the Chulkas, while eastern regions become mountainous. The Black River also features in neighboring Clovian ambitions, with Longard lords reportedly eyeing Szovijan lands across it.

These pressures come from different directions and take different forms. Steppe raiding, expansion by neighboring Princes, demands from more distant powers, and local rivalries do not produce one permanent national coalition, but they reinforce a political vocabulary in which sovereignty and resistance carry exceptional prestige.

Like the rest of the Hetaireian world, Szovij survives through defended concentrations of settlement and maintained corridors. Rivers, roads, mountain passes, fortified communities, shrines, patrols, ferries, and seasonal travel networks are strategic assets. Losing control of them is not merely economic damage; it can be remembered as the beginning of foreign domination.

docs.title: Relations
docs.text:
• Chulkas — important southern frontier relationship and source of continuing pressure.
  • Clovia — Longard expansion presents a potential western threat.
  • Meropolis — the Lendska plains extend toward the great city's sphere, tying Szovij closely to the wider Hetaireian network even as Szovijan political culture prizes self-rule.

docs.title: Cosserb
docs.text:
Motto: “Stand As One.”

The Cosserb are an eastern Szovij people of hills and mountain country, known especially as shepherds.

docs.title: Cultural Character
docs.text: Cosserb are described as friendly and gregarious, with a strong culture of wine, song, and dancing. This convivial reputation should not be mistaken for softness: they are also regarded as hard fighters.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:

  • Lendska
  • Lathuan

docs.title: Lathuan
docs.text:
Motto: “Our Roots Run Deep.”

The Lathuan inhabit the fertile northwestern part of Szovij and are particularly associated with agriculture.

docs.title: Cultural Character
docs.text:
Lathuans are described as taciturn, direct, and highly skilled farmers. Other Szovijans may dismiss them as dull or backward because their communities have developed less conspicuous technology or elite culture.

Lathuan self-understanding turns that criticism on its head. They see themselves as honest people who have no need for unnecessary luxuries or fashionable complications.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:

  • Lendska
  • Cosserb

docs.title: Lendska
docs.text:
Motto: “We Will Arrive.”

The Lendska are a southern Szovij people concentrated especially along the river bordering the Chulkas steppe and on the plains around Meropolis.

They are particularly noted as horsemen, reflecting their position on the frontier between the northern Princedoms and the eastern nomadic world.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:

  • Meropolis
  • Cosserb

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Immortal Empire is the great power of the far east, ruled by the Dragon Emperor. It is an old, centralized imperial state whose provinces are bound to a durable hierarchy of law, taxation, military obligation, recordkeeping, and administration rather than a loose federation of tributary rulers.

The Heian, Utar, and Bodi are three of the largest cultural blocs recognized within the Empire, but they are not its only peoples. The Heian form the principal imperial population, while Heian and Utar traditions preserve an ancient blood feud. Imperial rule has not erased the languages, local customs, religions, livelihoods, or inherited identities of incorporated peoples, but it has increasingly drawn them into common institutions and a shared imperial order.

The Empire is nearly a thousand years in the making. Its growth has been gradual: the Dragon Emperor first established his rule among the Heian, later incorporated Bodi lands, and conquered Utar only centuries afterward. Its most famous recent attempt at further expansion, the long war against Devi, ended in disaster. Exact dates and the internal histories of the three great imperial regions remain subjects for their own histories.

docs.title: The Dragon Emperor
docs.text:
Imperial teaching holds that the Dragon Emperor was once mortal. He is said to have achieved a state of extraordinary power and knowledge through cultivation and to have become capable of departing ordinary mortal life, but instead remained in the world to instruct humanity and repair Creation.

He condemns ordinary external magic as inherently disordered and believes its misuse hastens the dissolution of the world. His followers instead cultivate Chi, the ordered vitality expressed through body, breath, Will, and Soul. Adepts and Ryubushi develop disciplined inward techniques rather than relying upon the same external powers used by many western magicians.

The Emperor can physically assume the form of a Dragon and has done so publicly, including in war. Imperial tradition interprets this as the supreme accomplishment of cultivation rather than evidence that the mortal-sage account is false.

The Emperor is not generally understood by his subjects as merely a secular monarch. Centuries of unbroken rule, supernatural power, imperial ritual, cultivation teaching, and accumulated tradition have produced many forms of reverence around him. Some traditions emphasize the perfected sage, others the celestial sovereign, teacher, protector, living Dragon, or a being standing near the boundary between mortal and divine. Imperial practice tolerates considerable variation in such interpretations so long as they do not conflict with the larger order.

Ordinary subjects are not universally required to worship the Emperor personally or abandon older household, ancestral, or local religions. Holders of Imperial office are different: officials, commanders, judges, administrators, and others who exercise formal state authority must participate in rites and oaths acknowledging the Emperor's sacred sovereignty.

The Dragon Emperor has increasingly directed attention beyond the Empire's borders and regards Demonic influence, destructive sorcery, and chronic disorder as matters that cannot always be dismissed as another ruler's internal affairs.

docs.title: Creation and the Immortal Cycle
docs.text:
Eastern imperial doctrine rejects the western claim that primordial Dragons were emissaries of the Outer Darkness. Instead, Dragons are believed to have served an essential role in the Immortal Cycle, guiding Souls into reincarnation and helping preserve the ordered renewal of Creation.

The ancient war that destroyed the Dragons and reduced their descendants to modern Wyrms is therefore remembered as a catastrophe rather than a liberation. The Dragon Emperor is viewed as the greatest living hope for repairing enough of that broken order that Creation can renew itself rather than slowly wearing away.

The Emperor has in fact restored part of the ancient reincarnative process. Where his own influence or the institutions of his Hands can reach the dying, a departing Soul may be protected, guided, and returned to reincarnative circulation. This is genuine but incomplete. Political conquest does not by itself provide equivalent spiritual coverage, and remote deaths may still pass beyond the reach of the restored Cycle.

Adepts and Ryubushi are important to this project for reasons that extend beyond their famous martial disciplines. Across the Empire they maintain monasteries, funerary and spiritual institutions, protect the vulnerable dead, confront possession and hostile supernatural influence, investigate spiritual corruption, and act as trained intermediaries in places far beyond the Emperor's immediate presence. Their exact schools, ranks, and responsibilities vary and remain matters for later regional and institutional treatment.

docs.title: The Immortal Cycle in Imperial Life
docs.text:
The Immortal Cycle, also called the Way of the Dragon, is the broad religious-philosophical tradition centered on the Emperor's teaching, cultivation, sacred sovereignty, and the restoration of reincarnative order. It is not one uniform church.

Imperial religion commonly spreads additively. Local gods, spirits, ancestors, household rites, shrines, and inherited religious institutions may continue where they do not violate political or spiritual red lines. The Emperor may be understood through local categories as perfected sage, Dragon God, supreme sovereign, teacher, protector, or ancestral power without every province adopting one theology.

Religious institutions likewise vary. Monasteries, funerary houses, shrines, healing institutions, archives, schools, Adept houses, and Ryubushi establishments can all participate in the wider Imperial spiritual network without belonging to one universal priesthood or monastic rule.

One widely recognized family-level emblem is the Cycle Mark, a deliberately incomplete circle associated with the ancient Severing, the continued Cycle, its partial restoration, and the unfinished repair of Creation. It is a common sacred symbol rather than a controlled Imperial seal.

docs.title: Imperial Order
docs.text:
The Empire is culturally diverse but politically centralized. Local communities may preserve wide latitude in ordinary matters such as food, clothing, courtship, household practice, festivals, language, and customary livelihoods. Imperial authority becomes much more exacting where law, taxation, military obligation, provincial administration, public order, dangerous magic, or practices believed to threaten Souls and Creation are concerned.

This distinction is visible in the structure of government. Village life may remain recognizably local, while district and provincial government, courts of appeal, major infrastructure, military commands, records, and interregional administration operate within a pervasive imperial framework. The Empire does not merely collect tribute from incorporated lands; it governs them.

For many inhabitants of old and stable provinces, imperial rule is therefore experienced less through constant interference in private custom than through background conditions: patrolled roads, reduced banditry and private warfare, functioning courts, regular taxation, maintained infrastructure, and a state capable of intervening forcefully when its interests or prohibitions are engaged.

The central bureaucracy is famously deep, layered, archival, and procedural. Its exact ministries and court institutions differ from the local structures of the Empire's many peoples and are best understood as the accumulated machinery of centuries of imperial rule rather than as a single simple hierarchy.

Religious and spiritual institutions participate in that governing environment without simply becoming another ministry. Land, endowments, schools, archives, hospitals, hostels, farms, workshops, or exemptions may be granted because they serve practical functions. The same state that patronizes such institutions claims the authority to inspect, reform, recharter, confiscate, merge, or suppress them when they become corrupt, dangerous, fraudulent, or obstructive.

docs.title: Conquest and Incorporation
docs.text:
The Empire distinguishes between neighbors it can tolerate, states it pressures or draws into tributary relationships, unstable frontiers requiring intervention, and territories chosen for full incorporation. Annexation is not the only instrument of imperial policy, but when the Empire does choose incorporation it claims actual sovereignty rather than merely demanding tribute.

This makes imperial conquest particularly threatening to established ruling classes. A local population may retain much of its language, religion, livelihood, and customary life while its dynasty, aristocracy, independent military institutions, or sovereign priesthood loses political authority. The Empire's long-term influence can therefore transform a culture even without a deliberate program of cultural extermination.

The resulting judgment of imperial rule varies sharply. Supporters point to peace, commerce, roads, courts, famine relief, suppression of predatory cults, spiritual protection, and opportunities within a vast common system. Opponents point to lost sovereignty, displaced elites, transformed institutions, cultural absorption, and the fact that Imperial institutions can outcompete older local religious specialists without formally persecuting them.

The frontier has also earned a harsher reputation than the imperial heartland. Distance, slow communication, military emergency powers, rebellion, bad intelligence, ambitious officials, and conflicting interpretations of imperial policy have repeatedly produced abuses. Imperial reforms and inspection have reduced some of these failures without eliminating them, and memories of old massacres and forced cultural destruction remain powerful among peoples who suffered them.

docs.title: Bodi
docs.text:
The Bodi are a mountainous and strongly spiritual people of the Immortal Empire.

Symbol: A yellow sun with red and white rays over a red, white, and blue ray-patterned field, with a green wyvern over all.

docs.title: Ceremonial Standard
docs.text: The Bodi ceremonial standard is a complex radiating design centered on sun and wyvern imagery.

docs.title: Character
docs.text: The Bodi are known principally as a mountainous and strongly spiritual people within the Empire. Their religious communities and highland settlements retain identities distinct from the more politically dominant Heian heartlands.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:

  • Heian
  • Utar
  • Dragon Emperor
  • Heraldry and Emblems

docs.title: Utar
docs.text: The Utar are a people of the Immortal Empire associated especially with mountainous jungle country and the warm forested lands west of the Heian heartland.

docs.title: Imperial Standard
docs.text: The Utar standard is an asymmetrical design combining a gold scale-pattern, a red field, and a blue wyrm crossing the division.

docs.title: Rivalry with the Heian
docs.text: The Utar and Heian preserve an ancient blood feud whose origins are disputed and whose political expression changes under imperial rule.

docs.title: Homeland
docs.text:
Utar communities are especially associated with rough mountain and jungle country and are generally less urbanized than the Heian heartlands. The atlas-scale homeland is strongly jungle-associated: broad southwestern and central districts are dominated by humid forest, with jungle-clad hills and mountains where the high country rises.

The western and southwestern margins are more seasonal. Savanna, light jungle, open woodland, and transitional country appear along approaches toward Devi and the drier continental interior rather than the whole Utar homeland being one uniform rainforest.

The great continental mountain system is known to the Utar as the Khamrai. Its southeastern reaches are lower, more fragmented, and more heavily forested than the immense central barrier farther west, helping create a rugged transition between the deep Utar jungle, the Devi-facing mountain country, and the routes toward the continental interior.

docs.title: Meskali
docs.text: The plant used to produce Meskali is native to Devi and Utar territory, making the Utar lands one of its known natural ranges.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Immortal Empire
  • Heian
  • Bodi
  • Heraldry and Emblems

docs.title: Heian
docs.text:
The Heian are the principal imperial people of the Immortal Empire and dominate many of its central institutions.

Symbol: A black dragon inside a red circle on a white field.

docs.title: Imperial Crest
docs.text: Western cataloguers might describe the crest as Argent, on a roundel gules a dragon sable (a black dragon within a red circle on a white field). Heian use follows its own seal and crest tradition rather than Loranian shield-armory.

docs.title: Homeland
docs.text:
The Heian heartland is dominated by one large, long island lying off the Utar mainland, accompanied by a chain of lesser islands and a moderate secondary island across the waters between them. The archipelagic approach has the visual character of a broken or drowned peninsula without forming a continuous land bridge.

The principal island runs on a strong oblique axis, with its long end facing back toward the Utar shore. Cooler evergreen and mixed forests dominate much of the northern end, while the central imperial heartland includes mixed woodland and broad open lowlands capable of supporting dense settlement and cultivation. Warmer seasonal and subtropical vegetation becomes more common toward southern islands and exposures.

docs.title: The Koryu
docs.text:
The Koryu are the principal mountains of the Heian heartland, forming a long axial spine through much of its central and northern interior. They divide watersheds, produce many short and steep rivers, and make travel along the coasts easier than repeated crossings of the interior highlands.

Heian tradition understands the name as dragon-associated, and western sources sometimes gloss it as “Dragon Spine” or “Dragon Ridge.” The association suits a landscape at the heart of the Dragon Emperor's realm, where dragon imagery is deeply embedded in imperial symbolism.

The Koryu are not necessarily a monument to the present dynasty. Their exact etymology and the history by which the mountains became associated with imperial dragon imagery remain matters for later eastern language and historical development.

Most Heian rivers are short and steep enough that they are not individually represented on world atlases; their detailed courses belong to later regional mapping.

docs.title: Rivalry with the Utar
docs.text: The Heian and Utar preserve an ancient blood feud. Its origins are obscured by competing histories, and imperial rule has not erased the rivalry.

docs.title: Imperial Context
docs.text: The Heian live at the heart of the state ruled by the Dragon Emperor, whose teachings reject ordinary external magic in favor of disciplined mastery of internal Chi. Adherence varies by region, family, school, and social position even where imperial ideology is publicly dominant.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
