docs.title: The Asura Raj of Devi
docs.text:
The Asura Raj of Devi, commonly shortened simply to Devi, is an eastern realm whose older civilization has been deeply subverted by organized Diabolism. Its modern order is ruled by an Asura Raj and sustained through competing priesthoods, Warrior Lodges, subordinate rulers, mercantile interests, caste hierarchy, slavery, and ritual sacrifice.

Modern Devi is not an unchanged survival from antiquity. Older Devi was famously diverse in religion and philosophy, with innumerable gods, local cults, household rites, ascetic traditions, philosophical schools, and occult practices. Diabolist cults existed within that world and periodically became dangerous, but the civilization as a whole was not yet ruled by the Demon Gods.

Nor is every modern Devi a fervent Diabolist. Most people live ordinary lives inside a Diabolist political order: farming, trading, raising families, practicing crafts, treating the sick, preserving local customs, and negotiating the dangers imposed by those above them. The great cities and major institutions display the Asura state at its most concentrated. Villages and small towns farther from those centers often preserve much more of old Devi's religious, medical, social, and philosophical life, provided they pay tribute and avoid attracting dangerous attention.

docs.title: The Fall of Old Devi
docs.text:
The decisive transformation began during the Dragon Emperor's invasion in the seventh century AA. Devi rulers and sorcerers facing an expanding Immortal Empire escalated from dangerous blood magic into coercive human sacrifice, demonic enhancement, and increasingly open dealings with demons. Each successful emergency measure made the next easier to justify.

At Shari, the defenders crossed a new threshold by openly invoking Durogchit the Skull Reaper as an ally in war. Durogchit demanded captured enemy soldiers rather than the blood of Shari's own people, and answered with spectacular supernatural force. Demon legions, war-beasts, and visibly transformed warriors fought against the invaders. The bargain helped make direct covenant with the Demon Gods politically defensible precisely because it worked.

The Immortal retreat did not restore the old order. Decades of supernatural war left Devi divided among armed cults, enhanced champions, traumatized rulers, and rival Rajdoms accustomed to sacrificial emergency power. Generations later, the first Asura Raj defeated the strongest rivals and consolidated the recognizable modern order.

docs.title: Society and Power
docs.text:
Devi's institutions permit enough competition and upward movement to keep society dynamic, but ambition is continually redirected into exploitation and rivalry. The older caste order was transformed into a system in which advancement is possible, yet often depends upon displacing someone else rather than reforming the hierarchy itself.

The name Asura Raj refers to the polity ruled by the supreme Raj, himself an Asura. Beneath him, regional rulers, priestly powers, military elites, and cities retain substantial autonomy so long as they meet their obligations and do not threaten the supreme hierarchy. The realm is therefore hierarchical without being a uniform centralized bureaucracy.

In practice, however, Devi can be intensely bureaucratic. Royal decrees, Rajdom law, temple privilege, caste status, cult precedent, licenses, local custom, sponsorship, and exceptional grants overlap. Complexity is politically useful: a permit can be challenged, a temple privilege reinterpreted, an audit weaponized, or a rival trapped between contradictory authorities. Bribery, patronage, selective enforcement, and procedural obstruction are therefore not merely defects in the system but common tools within it.

The ancient Warrior Lodges predate the Asura order by many centuries. Organized around animal or supernatural totems, martial specialties, prestige, and advancement, some historically allowed commoners to rise through demonstrated accomplishment. Under modern rule many mainland lodges have become deeply entangled with demonic enhancement, sacrifice, and factional politics, while older branches survive in exile in parts of the Pingrit Archipelago.

Extended households, marriage alliances, inherited occupations, patronage, and family reputation remain central to everyday life. Formal political and military authority is broadly patriarchal, but women may exercise substantial practical power through estates, household finance, trade, religious roles, property, accounts, and kinship networks. Customs vary widely between regions, castes, and communities.

docs.title: Religion and Older Traditions
docs.text:
Asurabalah dominates the political and sacrificial establishment, especially in the great cities. It is less a single church than a competitive field of Great Demon God cults bound together by shared ritual grammar, legal recognition, temple privileges, sacred debt, and the supremacy of the Asura order.

For most Devi, this Diabolist establishment sits on top of a much older religious ecology. A household may attend a Demon-God festival, seek temple healing, maintain an ancestor shrine, consult a village spirit-worker, and preserve family rites whose origins long predate the Raj. Religious pluralism therefore survived the rise of Asurabalah in altered and politically subordinate form.

One important old religious family survives more visibly outside Devi than within it. The Path, now practiced especially among the Tariq, Qalshari, and Rakhan of northern Rorania, descends from several ascetic and philosophical currents that arose in pre-Diabolist Devi. Those currents were never the sole faith of Old Devi and existed alongside household cults, temples, ancestors, local gods, healers, occultists, and rival schools.

Path teachings moved west through merchants, pilgrims, wandering renunciants, students, refugees, exiles, texts, and oral lineages rather than through one centralized mission. As the Diabolist order expanded, some related institutions were destroyed or suppressed, some fled, some accommodated the new regime, and some practices survived in medical, household, funerary, educational, or contemplative forms after their older theology was forgotten.

Modern Devi customs that resemble the Path are therefore evidence of a shared ancient religious world, not automatic proof that they are Path survivals. Northern Path scholars and Devi traditionalists can disagree sharply over who has preserved, corrupted, or simply misunderstood the past.

Temples provide genuine public services—healing, divination, arbitration, granaries, credit, magical protection, funerary work—but often convert dependency into debt, service, political obligation, or patronage. Entry-level aid may be cheap or free; desperate later needs are where the system is most likely to become predatory.

docs.title: Slavery, Status, and Sacrificial Risk
docs.text:
Devi's enormous slave economy helps sustain the sacrificial order while insulating much of the free population from its worst everyday dangers. Enslaved people, war captives, condemned criminals, and others already denied ordinary social protection form the principal pool for routine institutional human sacrifice.

A free merchant, artisan, clerk, soldier, or established household therefore does not normally fear being seized at random for an altar. The sharper fear is downward reclassification. A powerful enemy may manipulate debt, criminal charges, caste standing, patronage, pollution accusations, or laws against unsanctioned Diabolism until a formerly protected person becomes legally vulnerable.

This unequal distribution of danger encourages people to defend their own status while accepting the degradation of those beneath them. The system's cruelty is therefore concentrated rather than uniformly experienced, which helps explain how ordinary family life, commerce, festivals, and ambition continue inside it.

docs.title: Temple Wealth and Patronage
docs.text:
Major temples are landholders, creditors, employers, warehouses, and commercial institutions as well as religious establishments. They compete for estates, donors, pilgrims, debtors, clients, captives, monopolies, and access to rulers.

The Raj and subordinate Asura generally prefer temples to be powerful but dependent. Audits, confiscations, privilege reviews, exemptions, competing jurisdictions, and royal patronage keep even wealthy cults reliant on recognition from above. The same pattern recurs downward: households depend on temples, minor establishments seek great-temple patrons, and great temples seek Asura protection.

This creates a political economy of vertical dependency and horizontal rivalry. Ambitious institutions are encouraged to expand, but advancement is safest when it reinforces the hierarchy rather than escaping it.

docs.title: Knowledge and Trade
docs.text:
Devi is renowned for medicine, botany, alchemy, poisons, drugs, resins, fungi, venoms, monster products, and rare substances drawn from its varied climates and jungles. Much of this expertise predates the Asura order and survives among physicians, herbalists, collectors, ascetics, old lineages, and local specialists. Temples and rulers often control licenses, taxes, warehouses, restricted substances, and export without having created the underlying knowledge.

This famous reagent trade sits atop a much broader economy of dense agriculture, riverine commerce, textiles, spices, craft production, food, and ordinary exchange.

docs.title: Territorial Claim
docs.text:
The court of the Asura Raj claims sovereignty over the Pingrit Archipelago as part of its wider dominion. That claim is not a neutral description of political reality: the archipelago has no single government, many Pingrit rulers and communities reject Devi's sovereignty, and the Raj does not exercise uniform effective control over the islands.

Devi nevertheless treats the claim as a matter of state rather than aspiration. Its maps, diplomatic formulas, and officials may therefore describe the Pingrit islands as holdings of the Raj even where local authorities deny that status.

docs.title: Land and Climate
docs.text:
Devi is a large and geographically varied realm rather than a single tropical jungle. Its climate is shaped by seasonal winds carrying warm-season moisture northward from the Sea of Thieves and southern waters, together with the immense mountain barrier along its northern and western approaches.

The great mountain system known in western geography as the Malzhir Range is called Maljhir in Devi. Devi usage applies that name to the whole range, including the immense barrier near Shari and the Devi-facing mountains farther south. The meaningful western frontier of Devi is backed by this mountain obstruction: ordinary travel does not continue westward through an open jungle frontier, and the central western wall offers no good routine passes. Shari lies at the eastern end of the barrier where routes can bend around its termination and foothills.

The wettest southern and southwestern coasts receive heavy monsoon rains. Windward escarpments and mountain slopes support especially lush forests and cooler montane environments, but much of the interior lies behind those heights and is substantially drier. Broad plateau country includes seasonal and dry forest, open woodland, grassland, scrub, rocky uplands, and cultivated pockets around reliable water.

Rivers descending from the Devi-facing slopes of the Maljhir gather into the Vardhani, Devi's principal great trunk river. Its headwater system passes close to Shari's mountain-front country, receives major tributaries from the Maljhir, and crosses the broad alluvial heartland before reaching the Bay of Nurgahl through extensive floodplains, wetlands, marshes, and distributaries. The Nanji is the western/southwestern lower distributary; Jalaska stands where it meets the sea at the far southern end of Devi.

The western approaches beyond the mountain-backed Devi frontier grade into more open seasonal country before the deep jungles of neighboring Utar. This transition is geographically broad at atlas scale rather than a perfectly surveyed political line.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Asura are not a people or species. The word is both a title and the name of a powerful transformed state attained by human beings through extreme demonic corruption.

An Asura remains human in ancestry even after supernatural transformation. If an Asura has a child with an ordinary human, the child is human rather than a separate Asura species, though such descendants may display unusual diabolical talents or traits.

Within Asurabalah, an Asura is also a living sacred proof that sustained relationship with the Great Demon Gods can transform a mortal beyond ordinary human limits. This makes Asura objects of sincere awe as well as fear.

docs.title: The Path of Transformation
docs.text:
The first Asura did not arise from one wholly separate rite. During the long war against the Dragon Emperor, Devi warriors, champions, commanders, and rulers increasingly accepted demonic enhancements that offered real military advantages. Some alterations became permanent. Repeated exposure scarred body and soul alike, eroding empathy, restraint, identity, and resistance to further corruption.

Asura transformation emerged as the far end of this augmentation spiral. Power made further alteration easier to justify, while the altered recipient became progressively less capable of recognizing what was being surrendered. At some point the accumulation crosses a threshold at which the person is no longer merely an enhanced human but an Asura.

In the modern Asura Raj, reaching that state remains associated with exceptional Diabolic power, mass human sacrifice, and other great dark deeds. It is not an inherited condition, and there is no simple single ceremony by which any wealthy priest or noble can become Asura.

Different Great Demon God cults claim different paths toward transformation. One may emphasize victory and captured strength, another bodily remaking, another possession, wealth, domination, or destruction. No universal Asurabalah cursus exists.

docs.title: Political and Religious Role
docs.text:
Asura stand at the apex of the royal and priestly order of Devi.

The overall ruler of Devi, the Raj, is an Asura. His transformed condition is part of the sacred logic of kingship: he is not merely a secular monarch who happens to possess unusual powers. Other Asura may rule important regions or hold extraordinary political-religious authority beneath him, although not every high priest, governor, or warlord receives the transformation.

Asura status places its bearer above ordinary priesthood politically, but it does not make every Asura the supreme favorite of every Great Demon God. A powerful high priest may still claim an exceptional relationship with a particular patron.

The first Asura rulers appeared only after the wartime Diabolist turn was already well underway. Their later political supremacy therefore grew out of Devi's corruption rather than causing it at the outset.

docs.title: Regulated Aspiration
docs.text:
Deliberately seeking Asura transformation is an elite religious and political ambition, not an ordinary believer's expected path. Priests, rulers, generals, champions, and Diabolists may seek the power and sacred prestige associated with transformation.

The state watches such ambition closely. Advanced demonic enhancement, extraordinary patronage, dangerous possession, accumulation of sacrificial authority, and other steps toward Asura status can require temple sponsorship, royal favor, office, licenses, or at least political tolerance. An unsanctioned aspirant is not merely a dangerous sorcerer but a potential rival sovereign.

Asurabalah institutions therefore distinguish between lawful or successful transformation and uncontrolled corruption, failed possession, or politically unacceptable mutation. Those categories are partly religious and partly political: a useful transformed champion may be celebrated where an inconvenient rival with similar symptoms is condemned.

docs.title: Culture
docs.text: Asura do not possess an independent ethnic culture. Their languages, customs, loyalties, kinship ties, and regional identities derive from the human communities and cult institutions from which they arose, even when transformation and office place them far above ordinary society.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Devi's caste order is an old and regionally varied system of inherited status, occupation, household reputation, cult privilege, dependency, and local rank that has been corrupted and weaponized by the Asura order.

The modern system permits real but dangerous advancement. Priests, warriors, merchants, artisans, officials, households, dependents, slaves, and stigmatized communities possess different avenues of power, but institutions continually redirect ambition toward rivals and people below them rather than toward reform of the hierarchy itself. A person or household can rise, but modern Devi often rewards advancement by displacement: gaining the office, privilege, patron, or standing that someone else loses.

This article remains provisional because Dive 011 establishes the broad social logic of the system without fixing one realm-wide taxonomy of castes or local status communities.

docs.title: Asura and the Raj
docs.text:
At the apex of the realm stand the Asura: humans transformed by accumulated Diabolic corruption into powerful supernatural forms.

The supreme Raj is an Asura. Other Asura may rule important regions or occupy exceptionally powerful political and religious positions beneath him. Not every high priest, ruler, or military lord becomes Asura, so transformation marks an elite above the ordinary hierarchy rather than a hereditary people or a synonym for priesthood.

docs.title: Priesthoods and Sacred Rank
docs.text:
The great cults of Asurabalah possess enormous political power, but Devi does not have one uniform priestly bureaucracy. Major cults maintain their own hierarchies, offices, patrons, and local relationships while competing beneath the supremacy of the Raj.

Temples, academies, monasteries, aristocratic networks, guild-like organizations, and other institutions capable of accumulating independent influence are among the organizations most thoroughly captured, crushed, or subordinated by the Asura order. Smaller local traditions often survive more readily because they pose less threat.

docs.title: Warrior Lodges
docs.text:
The Warrior Lodges are much older than the Asura Raj and were not originally Diabolist military orders. They organize warriors around animal or supernatural totems, martial specialties, prestige, fellowship, and advancement. Historical lodges include animal traditions as well as stranger forms such as the Deathclaw Lodge.

Some lodges traditionally admitted talented commoners and offered one of the clearest routes to increased status through demonstrated accomplishment. Under modern rule many mainland lodges have become entangled with sacrifice, factional politics, demonic enhancement, and soul-scarring martial cults.

Branches that rejected or escaped the Asura transformation survive in parts of the Pingrit Archipelago, where some preserve consciously exilic Devi traditions and others have become locally Pingrit.

docs.title: Merchants, Artisans, and Productive Communities
docs.text:
Merchants and artisans retain meaningful economic influence and room for competition within the hierarchy. Devi's physicians, herbalists, alchemists, textile producers, cultivators, traders, and other specialists also preserve large bodies of knowledge and craft that predate the Asura order.

Wealth, office, patronage, family reputation, and specialized skill can alter practical standing, but none of these automatically dissolves inherited status or the political power of the cult and ruling orders.

For these middling and privileged communities, social standing is also a form of practical insulation. They are not normally the people drawn at random into Devi's sacrificial institutions. Their sharper danger is losing the protections that keep them outside the categories most vulnerable to temple custody.

docs.title: Lower and Dependent Communities
docs.text:
A large part of Devi's population lives under varying forms of low status, dependency, enslavement, or social stigma. These people are especially vulnerable to coerced labor, predation by officials and patrons, and the sacrificial demands of the modern order.

Devi's large slave population, war captives, condemned criminals, and other legally alienated groups provide most of the people used in routine institutional human sacrifice. Asurabalah theology and law may describe such people as forfeited, polluted, subordinate, or otherwise legitimately claimable, even though these are social and legal categories rather than a literal loss of personhood.

The precise legal categories are not uniform across Devi and remain deliberately unresolved. A great temple city, a military frontier, a merchant port, and a remote village need not rank or regulate the same communities in exactly the same way.

docs.title: Household, Patronage, and Mobility
docs.text:
Extended kin, marriage alliances, household reputation, inherited occupations, clients, patrons, and family obligations remain central to social life. Advancement is often collective as much as individual: one person's promotion can improve a household's prospects, while disgrace can make an entire kin network dangerous baggage.

The Asura system weaponizes these relationships rather than replacing them. Exceptional people can rise, but the hierarchy encourages them to seek patrons, offices, lodge prestige, cult influence, wealth, or the downfall of rivals rather than to build durable solidarity across the system.

The reverse is also true. A sufficiently powerful enemy may attack a person's debt, criminal status, cult standing, patronage, caste reputation, or legal protection until someone once considered secure becomes vulnerable to enslavement, confiscation, imprisonment, or even sacrificial custody. Social rank therefore offers protection, but never absolute immunity.

docs.title: Regional Variation
docs.text:
There is no reason to assume that Jalaska, Shari, the river heartland, upland districts, and remote villages use identical local hierarchies or terminology. Old Devi was politically and religiously plural, and the Asura Raj inherited rather than erased that diversity.

The broad pattern of supernatural rulers, powerful cult institutions, martial elites, productive communities, dependents, and stigmatized people is widespread. Exact names, precedence, privileges, disabilities, and local subdivisions remain work for later vertical development.

docs.title: Bay of Nurgahl
docs.text:
The Bay of Nurgahl is a major bay on the southern coast of Devi. It receives the Vardhani, the great river system draining much of Devi's interior alluvial country, and is ringed in places by distributaries, marshes, floodplains, reedlands, and brackish wetlands.

Jalaska, the greatest port of Devi, stands at the far southern end of the realm on the bay's southern side, where the Nanji distributary reaches the sea. Jalaska's position gives it access to both inland river traffic and the maritime routes of the Sea of Thieves and southern waters.

The bay lies within Devi's monsoonal maritime zone. Seasonal winds and heavy rains strongly affect river levels, coastal navigation, flooding, and the movement of goods.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Jalaska is the greatest port city of Devi, situated at the far southern end of the realm on the southern side of the Bay of Nurgahl. The city stands where the Nanji, a major distributary of Devi's great southern river system, reaches the sea.

Its position joins two kinds of commerce: river-borne goods from the densely settled interior and blue-water traffic crossing the Bay of Nurgahl and the wider southern seas. Jalaska therefore dominates Devi's maritime trade without lying directly amid the most unstable channels of the greater delta.

The city is a place of immense wealth, rigid ceremony, corruption, crowds, temples, warehouses, foreign compounds, and formalized cruelty. Its skyline is dominated by monumental step-pyramids and temple complexes rather than by an accidental chaos of cults in the streets.

docs.title: The Nanji and Harbor
docs.text:
The Nanji is the western/southwestern branch of the lower Vardhani river system that drains much of Devi's alluvial heartland into the Bay of Nurgahl. Barges, river craft, and coastal ships converge around Jalaska, while the broader delta farther around the bay breaks into marshes, shifting distributaries, reedlands, and flood-prone lowlands.

The harbor receives grain, textiles, timber, spices, captives, medicines, rare plants, alchemical substances, monster products, and ordinary manufactured goods from across Devi. Foreign ships add wares from the Pingrit Archipelago, western Rorania, the northern trade routes, and more distant seas.

docs.title: Umoja Watsala
docs.text:
Jalaska is presently ruled by Umoja Watsala, a powerful priest of Sarwatal the Whispering Serpent.

Watsala emerged from a three-way succession struggle after the death of the previous high priest. Already one of the principal claimants, he secured control of the elite Serpent Warrior Lodge and thereby gained the strongest independent military instrument in the contest. Riots, defections, bargains, and the sudden deaths of both rival claimants left Watsala in control of the city.

His victory did not produce a complete purge. Administrators, lesser priests, officers, merchants, and clients of the defeated factions survived by defecting, bargaining, denouncing former patrons, or proving too useful to discard. Watsala preserved the machinery that keeps Jalaska rich while destroying the people most capable of becoming rival centers of power.

docs.title: Government and Order
docs.text:
Watsala rules through Sarwatal's priestly establishment. The Serpent Warrior Lodge serves as his captured praetorian force: bodyguards, trusted enforcers, sensitive arrest teams, and an armed reserve for problems he does not entrust to ordinary soldiers. Most city guards and troops are not lodge warriors.

Jalaska is corrupt, but it is not lawless. Permits, jurisdictions, offices, ranks, ritual privileges, market rules, temple rights, customs duties, and severe punishments overlap in a dense administrative order. Corruption thrives because officials possess discretion over this system, not because the system has no rules.

A common saying captures the city's practical politics: there is no closed gate in Jalaska, only an unpaid gatekeeper. Money is not always sufficient, but bribes, patronage, favors, forged paperwork, and personal connections can make supposedly rigid barriers unexpectedly negotiable.

docs.title: The Foreign Docks
docs.text:
Foreigners are ordinarily concentrated in physically segregated dock districts and licensed compounds. Leaving them, moving between controlled districts, or traveling into the Devi interior usually requires sealed chits or equivalent permissions.

The restrictions are real and can be enforced brutally. They are also a market in themselves. Officials sell access, brokers arrange sponsorship, priests issue dispensations, guards interpret documents, and criminals forge or obtain papers whose legitimacy may depend more on the examiner than on the seal.

docs.title: Reagents, Medicines, and Poisons
docs.text:
Jalaska is one of the world's premier markets for rare medicinal plants, alchemical reagents, poisons, drugs, resins, fungi, venoms, monster products, and other unusual substances drawn from Devi's varied ecosystems.

The trade does not begin in the great temples. Rural collectors, hunters, physicians, herbalists, ascetics, farmers, poisoners, and local specialists obtain or prepare much of the material. Merchants aggregate, finance, adulterate, transport, and export it. Temple institutions and officials dominate the profitable chokepoints: licenses, assays, restricted substances, ritual-grade preparations, strategic monopolies, warehouses, taxation, and permission to sell to foreigners.

This famous trade sits inside a much larger commercial city. Grain, cloth, food, ordinary crafts, river traffic, ship supply, credit, labor, and bulk commodities matter more to most inhabitants than exotic reagents ever will.

docs.title: Ritual Precincts
docs.text:
Mass sacrifice is part of Jalaska's public order, but it is not normally random street theater. Large sacrifices occur principally in proper Sarwatal temple complexes, step-pyramids, and controlled ritual precincts.

The city's horror lies as much in the machinery feeding those places as in the ceremonies themselves: captive holding grounds, slave markets, temple estates, guards, records, ritual suppliers, transport contracts, scheduled observances, and officials who can make atrocity resemble routine administration.

docs.title: Urban Character
docs.text:
Markets and harbor traffic form a near-continuous mass of bodies, while the smell of fish, cooking spices, incense, smoke, refuse, river mud, and death hangs in the humid air. Towering warehouses and temple walls crowd the waterfront. Priests, merchants, sailors, slaves, officials, warriors, pilgrims, smugglers, physicians, foreigners, and ordinary laborers share the streets while occupying very different legal worlds.

Jalaska is therefore best understood as an ordered, prosperous demon-city: dangerous because its institutions function, not because they have collapsed.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Shari is a great northern fortress-city of Devi, standing at the eastern end of the immense Maljhir mountain barrier. The main wall of mountains to its west is effectively impassable for ordinary commerce and armies; routes approaching Devi from the north and east must instead bend around the range's termination and foothills.

That geography made Shari one of the principal bastions of Devi during the Dragon Emperor's invasion and still makes it a strategic choke point for caravans, armies, pilgrims, captives, foreign envoys, and military traffic.

Shari is not an ancient ruin. Its walls, temples, barracks, markets, and neighborhoods have been rebuilt many times since the Dragon War. The ancient catastrophe survives most visibly in institutions, commemorations, fortification traditions, sacred military offices, old foundations, and monumental precincts.

docs.title: Government
docs.text:
Shari is governed by a military-priestly war-council dominated by senior warrior-priests of Durogchit the Skull Reaper together with leaders or patrons of the city's most powerful Warrior Lodges.

The council governs collectively in ordinary times. Its members command separate bases of power—temple offices, lodge followings, estates, troops, clients, patronage networks, and districts—so Shari's government is a negotiated balance among armed elites rather than the personal court of a single high priest.

Civilian administrators conduct much of the city's routine business, but ultimate authority is military and sacred.

During a recognized invasion, siege, or comparable existential crisis, the council can concentrate authority in a supreme commander descended from the city's ancient emergency arrangements. The exact Devi title for that office remains unsettled.

docs.title: The First Covenant
docs.text:
Shari holds a foundational place in the rise of modern Asurabala. During the Dragon War, Devi had already crossed many old boundaries: blood magic had escalated from self-sacrifice to volunteers and captives, and lesser demons were being used as weapons.

At Shari the defenders crossed a more public threshold. They deliberately called upon Durogchit the Skull Reaper as a power and ally in her own right.

Her first demand was easy for desperate defenders to rationalize: capture as many enemy soldiers as possible and sacrifice them to her. She did not begin by demanding Shari's own people.

Durogchit answered spectacularly. Demon legions fought beside the defenders; demonic war-beasts appeared; warriors displayed unnatural endurance, battle-fury, transformation, supernatural courage, and other visible signs of corruption. The intervention materially helped save Shari.

For later Durogchites, this remains the decisive argument for their patron: when the old order could not stop the invaders, Durogchit answered. The precedent helped destroy the remaining taboo against open covenant with the great Demon Gods elsewhere in Devi.

docs.title: Durogchit's City
docs.text:
Durogchit is remembered in Shari as the Skull Reaper, a patron of war, death, bone ritual, demonic war-beasts, victory, domination, trophies, and the appropriation of an enemy's strength.

Her cult's old demand for living enemy captives fused readily with pre-existing Devi traditions of prestige warfare and captive-taking. Over generations, that wartime bargain became part of the machinery of sacrificial warfare characteristic of the Asura order.

Shari's Warrior Lodges remain distinct institutions rather than temple regiments, but centuries of frontier warfare caused lodges, military offices, and Durogchite priesthoods to grow around one another. Senior figures may therefore hold overlapping religious, military, and lodge identities while individual lodges preserve their own rites, estates, rivalries, and traditions.

docs.title: The First Step Pyramids
docs.text:
The earliest great step pyramids of modern Devi were raised in Shari after the Dragon War. They served overlapping purposes as victory monuments, ossuaries and memorials, sacrificial platforms, Durogchite shrines, and public declarations that the city had survived an existential invasion.

Later Asura rulers and great temples copied and transformed the form until step pyramids became one of the signatures of modern Devi monumental architecture. Shari therefore retains a prestige disproportionate to its present frontier position: it claims both the first open wartime covenant with a Demon God and the origin of the architectural form later associated with the Asura order.

docs.title: The Eastward Road
docs.text:
Shari's prosperity has long depended on the Eastward Road, but the route remains in serious contraction after the westward displacement of Chulka populations under pressure from Hu Khan.

Roughly two years after the initial disruption, the first panic has passed but commercial confidence has not returned. Caravan traffic is lower, escorts are larger, schedules less reliable, and costs higher.

The Chulkas along the route are not one coordinated enemy. Some remain raiders or wandering warbands; others are displaced communities; still others have learned that controlling commerce can be more profitable than destroying it. Particular chiefs levy tolls, sell safe-conduct, offer escorts, or become de facto local powers.

The likely frontier order is therefore a patchwork of raids, bargains, tolls, and contested stretches rather than a simple return to the old road system.

docs.title: The Golden Brotherhood
docs.text:
The Golden Brotherhood, devoted to Lobhajani the Blood Mother, remains an important institution outside Shari proper. Its recurring monthly challenge has long attracted fighters, merchants, spectators, and money to the Shari region despite rivalry between the Lobhajani Brotherhood and the Durogchite establishment.

Within the last few years the Brotherhood was devastated, but its temple was not destroyed and the challenge continues. Shari's rulers used the disaster to impose their "protection" on the weakened institution. Durogchite troops and lodge forces now exert much stronger control over the approaches, fairgrounds, visitors, outer security, commerce, and associated revenue, while the Brotherhood retains its inner sacred complex and institutional identity.

This uneasy arrangement benefits a Shari government hungry for income during the Eastward Road contraction, while leaving the humiliated Brotherhood with powerful reasons to resent its protectors.

docs.title: The Pingrit Archipelago
docs.text:
The Pingrit Archipelago is a vast tropical island region of mangroves, bamboo, hidden coves, fertile islands, reefs, and crowded waterways off the southeastern reaches of Eorania. Its inhabitants are collectively called Pingrit, though this is much more useful as a foreign and civilizational label than as a national identity. A person of the islands is ordinarily attached first to household, harbor, island, ruler, or local people.

Foreigners often call the islands the Pirate Nations, but the archipelago has no single government and piracy is only one part of its maritime life.

The principal deep-water route through the islands is known as the Lautara. Merchants, corsairs, smugglers, and pilots use it as the main navigational backbone through an otherwise hazardous maze of reefs, shoals, mangrove channels, and lesser passages. The name shares an old Pingrit maritime root with Lautang, the notorious stilt-city on the northwestern side of the archipelago.

docs.title: Maritime Life
docs.text:
The sea is the great connective tissue of Pingrit life. Fishers, traders, pilots, explorers, shipwrights, mercenaries, pilgrims, and corsairs move continually between islands whose politics remain intensely local. Pingrit builders are famed for sophisticated deep-water vessels whose hulls can be constructed without nails, while navigator and shipwright lineages guard valuable knowledge through household, apprenticeship, marriage, and fosterage.

Most Pingrit are not pirates. Island economies rest on fishing, farming, garden crops, fruit and palms, livestock, salt, forest products, craft production, and ordinary exchange. Larger fertile islands can sustain dense populations, courts, and substantial inland settlements; smaller communities may depend much more heavily upon maritime trade.

Pingrit merchants excel at moving goods and people between otherwise poorly connected shores. Their ships carry ordinary provisions alongside timber, spices, medicines, luxury wares, captives and slaves, mercenaries, pilgrims, contraband, and foreign goods.

docs.title: Corsairs and Commerce
docs.text:
Piracy, commerce, private revenge, naval warfare, and sanctioned corsairing are often porous categories. The same captain may trade honestly on one voyage, raid an enemy on another, serve a local ruler in wartime, and be condemned as a pirate in the next port. Who authorized a raid and who suffered from it often matter more than any universal law of the sea.

Successful corsairing carries romantic martial prestige in many communities, particularly as a demonstration of courage, seamanship, daring, and the ability to bring wealth home. This does not make raiding harmless. Captains celebrated in songs on one island may be remembered as murderers and slavers on another, and maritime feuds can endure for generations.

docs.title: Politics and Kinship
docs.text:
There is no normal Pingrit constitution. The archipelago contains hereditary kingships, household oligarchies, merchant councils, temple communities, village confederations, naval strongmen, free ports, corsair enclaves, and mixed arrangements. Across these forms, authority tends to depend heavily on family, marriage, household, patronage, reputation, oath, customary obligation, compensation, and the ability to persuade armed followers to cooperate.

Feud is therefore not simply the absence of law. Many communities possess elaborate customs for compensation, mediation, sanctuary, vengeance, and the settlement of injuries. Rulers succeed as much by managing relationships as by issuing decrees.

Pirate republics and captains' councils exist, especially in ports crowded with unrelated sailors, exiles, refugees, mercenaries, and independent ship companies. Their articles, prize shares, elected captains, and councils are practical mechanisms for creating trust among armed people who lack ordinary kinship ties, not evidence of a universal Pingrit republican ideology.

docs.title: Religion
docs.text:
Pingrit religious life is strongly additive. Most islanders see little reason that honoring one power should require denying all others. Household spirits, ancestors, local gods, sea powers, foreign deities, charms, taboos, old Devi-derived ascetic practices, and the rites of the Tiwara Hat Tiwangmnani can coexist without being understood as mutually exclusive religions.

The practical question is often not which religion is true, but which powers matter here, and how should one deal with them? A sailor may carry charms from several traditions, observe a local taboo before putting to sea, and offer a prayer to a foreign god whose power he considers useful. Ritual specialists may nevertheless possess highly sophisticated local teachings; this syncretism reflects an additive supernatural worldview rather than simple ignorance.

docs.title: Language and Diaspora
docs.text:
The speech of the archipelago forms a broad family or continuum rather than one perfectly uniform Pingrit language. Neighboring islanders may understand one another easily, while distant communities can require interpreters or widely used port speech. Maritime exchange encourages lingua francas without erasing strongly local dialects.

Pingrit sailors, merchant households, shipwrights, mercenaries, ritual specialists, and expatriate communities can be found in ports far beyond the archipelago. These communities do not form a unified diaspora state; they remain attached to particular islands, households, and maritime networks.

docs.title: Political Status
docs.text:
The Asura Raj of Devi claims the Pingrit Archipelago as part of its holdings. The islands themselves do not possess a single authority capable of accepting or rejecting that claim for all Pingrit, but many local rulers, communities, corsair powers, and priestly authorities reject Devi sovereignty and preserve strong traditions of resistance to the Raj.

Devi's claim therefore overlaps a fragmented political reality. Control varies by island, port, route, alliance, and period. A local ruler may pay tribute, accept a Devi title, host a garrison, or ally with the Raj while the next island remains entirely independent. Foreign powers repeatedly discover that gaining the allegiance of one Pingrit ruler does not confer authority over his neighbors, rivals, cousins, or successors.

Centuries of pressure from Devi have also carried mainland refugees into the islands. Some old Devi communities and Warrior Lodge branches remain consciously exilic; others have become thoroughly local while retaining names, rites, insignia, or customs from before the Asura order.

docs.title: The Lost Maritime Empire
docs.text:
Roughly fifteen centuries ago, an exceptional Pingrit thalassocracy bound much of the archipelago into a maritime imperial network. Its fleets, ports, tribute routes, and long-distance connections were a historical anomaly in a region where durable political centralization is normally difficult.

The empire ended catastrophically amid plague, commercial collapse, dynastic crisis, and maritime war. Sailors and coastal storytellers preserve darker accounts of the Fishman Wars, claiming that inhuman creatures infiltrated the imperial network and eventually fought openly against the islands. Learned historians usually dismiss this as an old fisherman's tale or a supernatural embellishment of poorly remembered enemies.

The century or more after the collapse produced repeated pretenders to universal rule, from genuinely dangerous naval conquerors to petty rulers with titles far grander than their fleets. The accumulated failures helped make archipelago-wide monarchy politically suspect. A harmless self-proclaimed emperor may be a joke; one who begins assembling enough ships to make the title plausible can become a regional crisis.

docs.title: Ancient Black Stone
docs.text:
Black-stone monoliths and ruins stand on scattered Pingrit islands and reefs. They are older than the oldest local settlement traditions and are generally believed to predate human habitation of the archipelago.

Pingrit attitudes toward the sites vary sharply. Some communities regard particular stones as holy, ancestral, protective, or suitable places for offerings; others call them cursed, avoid landing nearby, or maintain taboos against touching or entering the ruins. Comparable black stone is known from the Hakori islands, the great western island of the Wolilalika, and Zamboula.

No accepted Pingrit tradition explains who built the structures or why they occur across such widely separated southern waters.

docs.title: Maritime Emblem
docs.text:
Blazon: Azure, a sea turtle vert, shelled Or. (A green sea turtle with a gold shell on a blue field.)

Pingrit ensigns follow maritime and island traditions rather than Loranian heraldic law. The turtle appears on sails, pennants, hull-marks, carved signs, and other badges.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Lautang is a sprawling Pingrit stilt-city built across a mangrove-choked lagoon on the northwestern side of the archipelago, close to the principal deep-water route known as the Lautara. Hundreds of bamboo-and-teak platforms stand above tidal mud on heavy pilings, joined by waterways crowded with fishing outriggers and colorful junk-rigged vessels.

The names Lautang and Lautara descend from the same old Pingrit maritime root. Their exact historical morphology remains unsettled, but the relationship is obvious to Pingrit speakers and is preserved in foreign usage.

docs.title: Character
docs.text:
Colored-glass lanterns hang from railings throughout the city. The air is thick with woodsmoke, fermented fish, and incense burned at small stone cairns intended to trap restless spirits.

Lautang has a reputation for quick hospitality, crowded commerce, and violence never far beneath the surface. It is also infamous as a den of thieves, smugglers, fences, corsairs, and black-market brokers. Stolen cargo, contraband, restricted goods, rare eastern wares, and merchandise whose provenance is better left unasked can all be found there by someone willing to accept the risks.

That reputation is part of Lautang's commercial strength rather than a contradiction of it. Merchants who cannot obtain certain goods through lawful ports deliberately seek out the city's markets.

docs.title: Prince and Free Port
docs.text:
Lautang is both a nominal principality and a real free port.

A hereditary prince is recognized as the city's sovereign. The office carries household wealth, retainers, prestige, property, marriage ties, diplomatic standing, and the right to receive foreign embassies and speak for Lautang when enough of the city is willing to be spoken for. The prince is therefore not merely decorative.

Practical authority, however, is widely dispersed among corsair captains, merchant houses, ship-owners, household blocs, priestesses and other religious authorities, brokers, neighborhood strongmen, and entrenched local interests. The prince is strongest as arbiter, patron, ceremonial sovereign, diplomatic face, and coalition-builder. A decree without enough backing may simply fail to become reality.

This makes Lautang difficult for outsiders to read. A foreign envoy may conclude that the prince rules because he signs treaties; a merchant may insist that a handful of houses control the city; a sailor may swear that the captains decide everything. Each can be correct for a particular dispute.

There is no constitutional requirement that Lautang's prince remain weak. A wealthy, charismatic, or exceptionally capable ruler could accumulate much greater influence. What usually prevents centralization is the city's political ecology: an overreaching prince risks uniting captains, merchants, households, and other factions who would otherwise remain rivals.

docs.title: Trade with Zorah
docs.text:
Although Lautang lies well beyond Zorah's normal near-seas, unscrupulous Zorahn merchants make the voyage because the potential profits justify the distance and danger. Zorah's long-standing interest in Devi and Pingrit commerce makes Lautang especially valuable as a source of black-market eastern goods, smuggled cargo, and commodities that cannot easily move through ordinary licensed channels.

This trade becomes still more attractive when disruption of the Eastward Road constricts legal overland access to eastern goods. It does not make Lautang a Zorahn dependency or routine extension of Zorah's market; the voyage remains hazardous, expensive, and particularly associated with merchants willing to operate outside respectable commercial norms.

docs.title: Religious Context
docs.text:
Spirit-trapping cairns reflect the wider Pingrit concern with dangerous supernatural entities. Local practice varies, and not every household rite is necessarily part of formal Kahangi ritual.

Like much of the archipelago, Lautang's religious life is additive rather than exclusive. Household ancestors, harbor spirits, sea taboos, protective rites, imported charms, local gods, and the traditions grouped under Tiwara Hat Tiwangmnani can coexist without requiring one centralized religious authority.

docs.title: The Roranian Tribes
docs.text:
The Roranian Tribes is a convenient geographic umbrella for the many non-city-state peoples of Rorania. It does not describe a single nation, ethnicity, language, or religion.

Zorahn and Al-Anwari scholars increasingly describe the enormous web of Roranian and neighboring island peoples as The Thousand Nations of the South. The phrase emphasizes diversity rather than political unity: its “thousand nations” include large macro-cultural fields, comparatively coherent peoples, mountain and desert societies, coastal communities, and island cultures linked by centuries of migration, exchange, warfare, marriage, caravan travel, and seafaring.

Older foreign works divided these peoples into Southern Tribes and so-called Bushmen Peoples. That distinction is now regarded as a poor simplification. The older names remain common in historical writing and among travelers, but they should not be mistaken for two coherent native ethnic blocs.

Among the major peoples and cultural fields are the Tariq, Qalshari, Rakhan, Herzgud, Oluru, Nissai, Xai, Wolilalika, and Hakori.

docs.title: Bushmen Peoples
docs.text:
Bushmen Peoples is an older outsider label found in western travel accounts, merchant records, and ethnographic writing for several culturally distinct peoples of Rorania and the surrounding islands, including the Oluru, Nissai, Xai, Wolilalika, and Hakori. The term never represented a shared native ethnicity, nation, language, or political community.

Many contemporary Zorahn and Al-Anwari scholars now regard the category as misleadingly broad. Peoples once separated by foreign writers into “Bushmen” and “Southern Tribes” are increasingly discussed within the much larger interaction world called The Thousand Nations of the South, whose communities have been linked for centuries by migration, trade, marriage, warfare, caravan routes, river corridors, and seafaring.

The older label remains common enough in inherited books, sailors' speech, old maps, and merchant jargon that travelers may still encounter it. Its use tells a reader more about the habits of the writer than about a single coherent people.

docs.title: Language
docs.text: There is no single ethnic Bushman language. Older references to such a language usually describe overlapping trade tongues, pidgins, multilingual contact speech, or sign systems used between communities that otherwise speak distinct local languages.

docs.title: Peoples Commonly Grouped Under the Old Label
docs.text:

  • Nissai
  • Xai
  • Wolilalika
  • Hakori

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Hakori inhabit the island chain between eastern Rorania and the Pingrit Archipelago. They are believed to descend in substantial part from ancient Pingrit explorers and settlers, but centuries of isolation, intermarriage, warfare, and local development have produced considerable variation from island to island.

All Hakori societies are comparatively warlike by regional standards, but they do not share one uniform government, religion, or social order.

docs.title: Emblem
docs.text: The hammerhead shark is a widely recognized Hakori war and maritime sign.

docs.title: Culture
docs.text:
Hakori are renowned for large war canoes, longhouse traditions, tattooing, feathered cloaks, intricate woodcarving, and head-taking in war.

Headhunting is a widespread wartime practice, particularly in feud, raiding, and formal conflict. It is not ordinarily a random peacetime custom.

Hakori cultures also broadly accept cannibalism as a controlled ritual practice under defined social or religious circumstances. Practice varies greatly by island, lineage, war society, and cult; acceptance of ritual cannibalism does not mean ordinary Hakori life is organized around indiscriminate consumption of enemies.

docs.title: Religion
docs.text:
Some Hakori islands preserve forms of recognizably traditional Pingrit religion, especially practices concerned with proper relations between communities, ancestors, dangerous spirits, and the boundaries humans should not cross.

Other islands and factions have developed more radical traditions that deliberately invite, cultivate, or worship dangerous powers. These groups are the principal source of the foreign stereotype of Hakori as dark-god-worshipping cannibal headhunters. They are a real and dangerous current within Hakori society, but not the whole people.

Among the darkest cults, the powers being worshipped may actively encourage escalation toward more extreme acts, turning bounded traditions of war, sacrifice, or ritual consumption into progressively more destructive practices.

docs.title: Black Stone Monoliths
docs.text:
Ancient black-stone monoliths and ruins stand on a number of Hakori islands. They predate known human settlement of the islands. Some communities regard them as holy or protective; others consider them cursed, taboo, or dangerous and build settlements well away from them.

Similar black stone occurs elsewhere across the southern islands and coasts, including the Pingrit Archipelago and the distant western island of the Wolilalika.

docs.title: Ikhaya-Ugu
docs.text:
Ikhaya-Ugu was a Xai village at the southern tip of Rorania, once home to roughly three hundred people.

Its inhabitants were skilled fishermen and swimmers who made extensive use of rivers, marshes, and coastal waters and were accomplished canoe-builders.

docs.title: The Disappearance
docs.text:
The village and its people vanished under mysterious circumstances. No generally accepted account explains what happened.

Nearby communities regard Ikhaya-Ugu as cursed and avoid the abandoned site when they can. Stories about the place differ in their details, but few locals treat its disappearance as an ordinary disaster.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:

  • Bushmen Peoples
  • Rorania

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Wolilalika inhabit a great island off western Rorania, large enough to contain major ecological, linguistic, and political differences of its own. They are not a single village-scale island culture.

Wolilalika traditions preserve memories of ancient seafaring ancestors associated with the Pingrit world. Their arrival belongs to an era when Pingrit maritime networks reached far beyond the modern archipelago; the exceptional ancient Pingrit thalassocracy of roughly fifteen centuries ago provides part of the historical setting for that long-distance movement without making the Wolilalika simply an imperial colony. Over long centuries those settlers mixed with Roranian population streams, producing a distinctive island civilization with both maritime and continental inheritances.

docs.title: Emblem
docs.text: The Wolilalika emblem combines sea, shell, and pearl imagery on a field divided red above blue below.

docs.title: Regional Diversity
docs.text:
Coastal Wolilalika communities may depend heavily on fishing, pearl gathering, canoe traffic, foreign trade, and maritime brokerage. Other regions are more strongly agricultural, pastoral, upland, forested, or inland-facing. Highland and coastal societies can differ sharply in architecture, diet, political organization, dress, and relations with outsiders while still participating in a broad Wolilalika identity.

The old foreign reputation for generosity, openness, and leisurely coastal life reflects some well-traveled coastal communities rather than the entire island.

docs.title: Trade and Slavery
docs.text: Pearls remain an important prestige export from some coasts and are traded to passing merchants, including merchants from Zamboula. Foreign slavers have also preyed upon vulnerable coastal communities, but such raids are one historical pressure among many rather than the defining condition of Wolilalika society.

docs.title: Black Stone Monoliths
docs.text:
Ancient black-stone monoliths and ruins stand in several parts of the island. They predate known human habitation. Local attitudes vary: some communities treat the stones as sacred, ancestral, or protective, while others regard them as cursed, taboo, or dangerous.

Similar black stone is known from the Hakori islands, the Pingrit Archipelago, and other southern coastal sites.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Xai are a broad macro-cultural population distributed through the southern world of Rorania. Xai traditions and historical accounts associate their ethnogenesis with sustained contact and ancestry involving both Nissai and Oluru populations, but the Xai are a distinct cultural field rather than merely a mixture of the two.

Xai communities are especially associated with maritime, riverine, lagoon, estuarine, forest, and coastal networks. Fishing, swimming, canoe construction, forest travel, ritual practice, and waterborne movement are prominent in many regions, but the Xai encompass numerous tribes and communities with varied economies, languages, political systems, and local traditions.

A major part of the Xai world lies within or around the Xaiba, the immense tropical forest complex of southern Rorania. The forest does not define all Xai life, nor do the Xai constitute one people of the forest: coastal, riverine, lagoon, inland-forest, and forest-margin communities can differ sharply while remaining part of the wider Xai cultural field.

docs.title: Emblem
docs.text: Blazon: Azure, a fish argent, finned Or. (A gray/silver fish with gold fins on a blue field.)

docs.title: Culture and Networks
docs.text: Waterways and forest routes connect Xai communities that may otherwise differ considerably. Canoes, fishing grounds, seasonal movements, marriage ties, ritual journeys, exchange, river corridors, and coastal travel create overlapping networks rather than a single centralized Xai polity. Inland-facing forest and river communities may differ sharply from open-coast seafarers while still participating in Xai identity.

docs.title: Locations
docs.text: Ikhaya-Ugu was one Xai fishing village whose inhabitants vanished under mysterious circumstances. Nearby communities regard the place as cursed. It should not be treated as representative of ordinary Xai society or religion.

docs.title: Religion
docs.text: Xai ritual traditions vary among coastal, riverine, forest, and lagoon communities and remain little known outside them.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Nissai are a broad macro-cultural population of eastern Rorania, encompassing many tribes and communities rather than one uniform society. Nissai communities vary in language, political organization, economy, and ritual life.

Nissai identity is especially associated in many regions with cattle traditions and age institutions. Pastoralism is culturally important across substantial parts of the eastern Nissai world, but not every Nissai community is primarily pastoral and no single social institution is universal across the entire macro-culture.

Nissai are often described by foreigners as exceptionally tall and dark-skinned. Olawale Village is one Nissai pastoral settlement on the eastern coast, not a model for all Nissai society.

docs.title: Geography
docs.text:
The Nissai cultural field spans a large part of eastern Rorania, including broad reaches of the Rovar Plains and the basin of Mother Water, one of the continent's great freshwater lakes. The lake is a major geographic anchor of the Nissai world, but it does not belong to one tribe or polity; many communities and regional traditions may develop around its shores, tributaries, grazing country, fisheries, markets, and travel routes.

The existence of such a large freshwater center reinforces the internal diversity of the Nissai. Open-plains pastoral communities, lake-oriented settlements, river communities, and eastern coastal populations can all participate in Nissai identity without sharing one economy or political form.

docs.title: Visual Tradition
docs.text: Black-and-red striped shields, textiles, and painted designs are strongly associated with Nissai communities, though no single universal central charge is recognized among them.

docs.title: Society
docs.text: Across the Nissai cultural field, cattle can function as food, wealth, bridewealth or alliance property, ritual resources, and markers of social standing, with their importance varying by region. Age-organized institutions likewise occur widely enough to be associated with Nissai society, but their membership rules, political importance, military role, and ritual meaning differ among communities.

docs.title: Relations
docs.text: The Xai are historically associated with both Nissai and Oluru ancestry and contact. Eastern Nissai communities also participate in broader Roranian trade, pastoral, coastal, and political networks rather than existing as an isolated ethnic bloc.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Olawale Village stands on the eastern coast of Rorania amid broad golden grasslands and herds of long-horned cattle. The local people are Nissai pastoralists, wearing red cloaks and elaborate beadwork.

docs.title: Settlement
docs.text: The village is circular, built from neatly thatched huts on a low rise. A central longhouse houses cattle, while cooking fires and the constant maintenance of spears shape the everyday soundscape of the settlement.

docs.title: Hospitality
docs.text: Visitors approaching from the water may be met by armed men and women waiting at the shore with spears held upright—a formal greeting that can appear threatening to foreigners unfamiliar with the custom.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:

  • Nissai
  • Rorania

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Oluru are a broad macro-cultural population of western Rorania, encompassing many tribes and communities rather than a single uniform people or lifeway. Oluru societies include substantial local variation in language, political organization, subsistence, and ritual practice.

Oluru identity is especially associated with long western historical continuity, traditions of landscape memory, ochre and rock art, and, in some regions, ritual and subsistence practices rooted in older foraging traditions. These associations are not universal occupations or customs.

The great dry-country region west of the Rakhan is known in translation as Red Earth, from a name in a major Oluru language. The Shining Serpent crosses its northern country. Both are major landmarks of the wider western Oluru world without defining the limits of Oluru settlement or implying one shared Oluru language.

docs.title: Emblem
docs.text: Southern cataloguers might describe the motif as Argent, a spiral gules within rays alternately sable and gules (a red spiral surrounded by alternating black and red rays on a white field), but Oluru use the design through paint, carving, beadwork, pale stone, hide, and other local media rather than as formal hereditary armory.

docs.title: Settlements
docs.text: Xom'kogo Village is one Oluru settlement and should not be treated as a template for the entire macro-culture.

docs.title: Culture
docs.text: Xom'kogo provides examples of Oluru cultural practice including ochre art, petroglyphs, dream-walkers, council fires, hunting, and cautious hospitality. Some of these practices participate in wider Oluru traditions, while others may be local. Across the western cultural field, different communities may be pastoral, agricultural, foraging, mixed-subsistence, riverine, coastal, or otherwise adapted to their local environment.

docs.title: Religion
docs.text: Dream-walkers and petroglyph traditions are known among at least some Oluru communities, but the wider religious life of the Oluru is diverse and poorly understood by outsiders. No single local ritual system should be assumed to represent every Oluru community.

docs.title: Relations
docs.text: The Oluru participate in the wider interaction world that foreigners sometimes group under broad Roranian tribal labels. The Xai are historically associated with both Oluru and Nissai ancestry and contact.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Xom'kogo Village is an Oluru settlement of nearly three hundred people in a broad scrubland valley of iron-red earth along the Roranian coast.

Dome-shaped huts of thornbush and golden thatch cluster beneath acacia trees, with walls decorated in ochre spirals, animals, and luminous patterns.

docs.title: Settlement
docs.text:
A broad central fire circle serves as council ground, dance floor, and storytelling hearth. It is ringed by carved termite-mound totems. Nearby sandstone cliffs carry ancient petroglyphs depicting spirits, great beasts, and the faint image of a northern ship said never to have returned.

The village smells of woodsmoke, wild honey, and medicinal roots. Hunters wear beadwork and ochre, and the settlement is threaded through with thorn barriers and paths.

docs.title: The Devouring Waters
docs.text: The Xom'kogo are not themselves a seafaring community, but their dream-walkers have watched the nearby waters for generations. The village is the last friendly haven before dangerous currents capable of destroying ships.

docs.title: Hospitality
docs.text: Strangers are received with caution rather than immediate hostility, accompanied by the low beat of a welcoming drum.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:

  • Bushmen Peoples
  • Rorania

docs.title: The Thousand Nations of the South
Overview
docs.text:
The Thousand Nations of the South is a learned umbrella for the vast and internally diverse cultural world extending across much of Rorania and its neighboring islands. The phrase was coined by scholars and geographers of Zorah and Al-Anwar, whose eastern trade, caravan, and maritime networks brought them into contact with a bewildering variety of Roranian peoples. “Thousand” is rhetorical rather than a census: it emphasizes that the peoples of the region cannot sensibly be reduced to a handful of homogeneous tribes.

The scholars who popularized the phrase have nevertheless spent generations trying to do exactly that in ever more elaborate ways. Zorahn and Al-Anwari geographers, ethnographers, historians, and merchants' scholars notoriously disagree over where one people ends and another begins, whether two neighboring populations are separate nations or branches of the same one, which languages imply common ancestry, and whether customs, descent, political allegiance, or self-identification should define a people at all. Rival taxonomies are revised, attacked, defended, and occasionally reorganized wholesale as new travelers return with information that refuses to fit the old schemes.

Most of the people being classified are either unaware of these learned controversies or regard them with wry amusement. A caravan scholar may solemnly insist that two communities belong to different branches of a proposed Nissai family while their inhabitants regard one another simply as neighbors, rivals, marriage partners, or people from the next valley. Conversely, communities that foreign scholars confidently place under one heading may consider the distinction between themselves ancient and obvious. The phrase Thousand Nations thus carries a quiet scholarly admission: outsiders can perceive the region's extraordinary diversity more easily than they can agree on how to classify it.

In ordinary speech, however, the Southern Tribes is by far the more common colloquial term. Foreign merchants, soldiers, travelers, and even many educated speakers use it casually for the peoples of this wider sphere. Southern Tribesman and Southern Tribeswoman are correspondingly common broad descriptors when a more specific people or homeland is unknown, irrelevant, or simply omitted. These labels are imprecise outsider shorthand, not claims that the peoples themselves form a single tribe or ethnicity.

Neither the learned nor colloquial term implies one ethnicity, language, religion, government, or common ancestry. The sphere is real because its peoples have interacted over centuries through caravan routes, migration, intermarriage, fosterage, mercenary service, raiding, mountain passes, river corridors, coastal trade, and island navigation.

The older foreign distinction between the Southern Tribes and so-called Bushmen Peoples is obsolete. Peoples formerly placed under both labels belong to the same larger interaction world, although their internal relationships differ enormously.

docs.title: Major Peoples and Cultural Fields
docs.text:
• Tariq
  • Qalshari
  • Rakhan
  • Herzgud
  • Oluru
  • Nissai
  • Xai
  • Wolilalika
  • Hakori

These names do not all operate at the same scale. Oluru, Nissai, and Xai are especially broad cultural fields containing many tribes, communities, languages, and regional lifeways. The other named peoples are generally more internally coherent, but none is culturally uniform.

A people being famous for a practice does not mean every household follows it. Tariq are renowned for camel pastoralism and caravan trade; Qalshari for horses and mounted warfare; Rakhan for highland martial traditions; Herzgud for herding and frontier warfare. Each also includes communities whose lives look very different from those reputations.

docs.title: Northern Rorania
docs.text:
The Tariq are especially associated with camel pastoralism, desert travel, route knowledge, and long-distance caravan commerce. The Qalshari are especially associated with horse breeding, mounted archery, escort work, raiding, and confederational warfare in the better-watered desert-edge and savanna country. Their territories and economies overlap, but the two peoples developed different institutional and political traditions.

The Rakhan inhabit the great highland system bearing their name. Their country contains autonomous clans and valleys, regional leagues, fortified communities, market and pass towns, and small hereditary principalities rather than one universal political model.

docs.title: Eastern Frontier
docs.text: The Herzgud occupy mountain country along the Rorania–Eorania frontier and have been shaped by long contact with the Chulkas. Bilingual markets, mixed livestock economies, horse adoption, mercenary service, raiding, intermarriage, and fosterage are all part of this frontier world.

docs.title: Continental Macro-Groups
docs.text:
The Nissai of eastern Rorania encompass many peoples and communities. Cattle traditions, age institutions, and eastern trade networks are especially prominent in many regions, but not universal.

The Oluru of western Rorania likewise comprise a wide cultural field. Rock art, ochre traditions, landscape-memory, and old ritual or hunting traditions recur widely without defining every Oluru community.

The Xai form a broad southern cultural complex whose histories repeatedly connect Nissai and Oluru populations. Coastal, riverine, lagoon, and maritime lifeways are especially important in many Xai regions, but the Xai are not simply a people of fishing villages.

docs.title: Island Peoples
docs.text:
The Wolilalika inhabit a great western island large enough to contain major regional differences of its own. Their history combines ancient Pingrit-derived seafaring ancestry with Roranian population streams.

The Hakori inhabit the eastern island chain leading toward Pingrit. Their islands vary enormously in religion, government, and custom, but martial prestige and organized violence are genuinely widespread pan-Hakori traits. Wartime headhunting is a common shared practice even where other institutions differ sharply.

docs.title: The Path
docs.text:
The Tariq, Qalshari, and Rakhan preserve related liberation traditions collectively known as the Path. The Path arose from several ascetic and philosophical currents in pre-Diabolist Devi and spread west through merchants, pilgrims, wandering teachers, refugees, students, texts, and oral lineages rather than through one centralized missionary church.

Path teachings broadly understand recurring embodied life as bondage when appetite, fear, status, habit, possession, and other attachments command the Will. Meditation, fasting, ethical discipline, renunciation, pilgrimage, teaching, and other practices cultivate lucidity: the capacity to experience desire, fear, pain, pleasure, status, and identity without being compelled by them. Liberation is normally understood as release from compulsory recurrence rather than simple destruction of the body.

The three peoples do not preserve identical forms. Tariq traditions are often shaped by routes, oases, merchant patronage, wandering teachers, and caravan hospitality; Qalshari traditions more readily produce mobile teachers, holy riders, court or warband ascetics, and sharp debates over martial life; Rakhan traditions more often center on mountain hermitages, caves, fortified monasteries, pilgrimage passes, manuscript schools, and princely patronage.

The Path is also one of the major non-Imperial homes of Adept practice. The lineage ultimately derives from Heian teachings associated with the Dragon Emperor, but Tariq, Qalshari, and Rakhan practitioners have reshaped the underlying body–breath–Will discipline through their own movement traditions, weapons, environments, and social institutions.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: The Herzgud are proud warriors and herders dwelling in the eastern mountains along the Rorania–Eorania frontier. Their homeland overlaps a long zone of contact with the Chulkas, making Herzgud society one of the clearest cultural thresholds between southern Rorania and the steppe world.

docs.title: Emblem
docs.text:
Blazon: Gules, a wolf argent. (A white wolf on a red field.)

The white wolf is common on Herzgud textiles, painted signs, and war gear as well as on banners.

docs.title: Culture
docs.text:
Herzgud are known for intricate dances, herding, martial pride, and strong cultural ideals surrounding physical beauty. These traits coexist with substantial regional variation.

Generations of frontier contact have encouraged bilingual markets, mixed livestock economies, horse adoption, mercenary service, raiding and counter-raiding, intermarriage, fosterage, and political relationships with neighboring Chulkas groups. These influences do not make the Herzgud a southern Chulkas offshoot; they are part of the historical environment in which Herzgud identity developed.

docs.title: Geography and Trade
docs.text: Mountain passes, grazing grounds, refuge valleys, and transit routes give Herzgud communities leverage over movement between Rorania and Eorania. Some settlements are more pastoral or isolated; others depend heavily on frontier markets, caravan traffic, or military service.

docs.title: Religion
docs.text: Herzgud religious life is not part of the North Roranian ascetic tradition shared by the Tariq, Qalshari, and Rakhan. Herzgud traditions remain to be developed on their own terms.
