docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Qalshari are a northern Roranian people especially renowned for horse breeding, mounted archery, raiding, escort work, and confederational warfare in the better-watered margins of the Mahrad and adjoining open country.

Their equestrian reputation is a major cultural trend rather than a universal occupation. Qalshari society also includes herders, farmers, traders, craftspeople, retainers, sedentary settlements, and poorer households without large remount strings.

Symbol: Black horse with white mane on gold.

docs.title: Emblem
docs.text: Blazon: Or, a horse sable, maned argent. (A black horse with a white mane on a gold field.)

docs.title: Culture
docs.text:
Horse breeding, riding, archery, and mounted warfare carry particular prestige among the Qalshari. Their strongest horse country lies along the eastern and southern Mahrad margins and the neighboring open plains, where poor grassland, scrub, seasonal basins, intermittent grazing grounds, and dependable water points form a broken pastoral network rather than one continuous green belt.

Rainfall changes the practical geography from year to year. In wet years temporary pasture can open routes and grazing grounds farther into the desert; in dry years herders and warbands contract toward more dependable grass, wells, oases, and desert-edge country. Control of seasonal pasture and access to water can therefore matter as much as possession of fixed settlements.

Horses are valuable and comparatively demanding animals in this environment. Large remount strings imply access to grazing, stored or purchased fodder, political allies, or considerable wealth. On long desert movements, Qalshari expeditions may use camels and other pack animals to carry water, fodder, and baggage while preserving horses for speed, scouting, raiding, battle, and pursuit.

Qalshari communities may alternate between raiding, escorting caravans, livestock exchange, cultivation, pastoral movement, and market life depending on region and season.

docs.title: Religion
docs.text:
The Qalshari are one of the principal peoples associated with the Path, a family of liberation traditions rooted in pre-Diabolist Devi. Path teachings broadly seek freedom from the compulsions of appetite, fear, status, habit, and recurring embodiment through meditation, discipline, renunciation, ethical restraint, and cultivated lucidity.

Among the Qalshari, the Path often takes mobile forms suited to confederations, seasonal movement, courts, and warbands. Wandering teachers, holy riders, portable lineages, seasonal lodges, shrine-tombs, and ascetics attached to courts or military followings can all occur alongside more settled houses. Temporary renunciation before or after military service, marriage, inheritance, or command is also plausible and socially legible.

Qalshari traditions preserve an especially visible tension between martial prestige and renunciation. Pacifist teachers may condemn killing as deepening attachment; other schools argue that a warrior can remain on the Path if fear, rage, glory, vengeance, and appetite do not command the Will.

The Path is also a major non-Imperial home of Adept practice. Some Qalshari Adepts transform Heian-derived body–breath–Will disciplines into mounted balance, weapon forms, blade-dance-like movement, rapid turns and dismounts, endurance, pain control, and training to remain lucid amid speed and violence. These are culturally Qalshari forms of the same Adept lineage, not a separate magical system.

docs.title: Relations
docs.text: Qalshari and Tariq populations overlap across northern Rorania. Qalshari political prestige is especially tied to horses and mounted force, while Tariq are particularly associated with camel-based deep-desert mobility and caravan brokerage. Neither distinction is absolute: Qalshari also use camels, and Tariq may own horses, but the environmental and logistical emphasis differs.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Rakhan are inhabitants of the hills and mountains of central and southern Rorania. Their ancestral highland homeland is also known as the Rakhan, a major mountain spine running through southern Rorania.

The Rakhan range begins broadly south and southeast of Khemet and runs down through central southern Rorania toward the long southern peninsula. Rakhan communities are concentrated in upland valleys, high plateaus, foothills, and mountain approaches rather than occupying every part of the range. Other peoples live within and around the same mountain system.

docs.title: Political Landscape
docs.text: Rakhan society is not governed by one universal clan system. Autonomous valleys and clans coexist with regional leagues, fortified communities, caravan and pass towns, and some small hereditary highland principalities. Mountain geography produces both strong local independence and occasional larger political formations where trade routes, agricultural basins, or strategic passes support them.

docs.title: Economy and Warfare
docs.text: The Rakhan are widely known for martial traditions, but highland life also includes transhumant herding, terraced and valley agriculture, smithing, market exchange, caravan service, and control of mountain routes. Different subregions may emphasize these activities very differently.

docs.title: Emblems and Clan Crests
docs.text:
The crossed-scimitar emblem commonly used to represent the Rakhan is not a national coat of arms. Rakhan clans and tribes maintain innumerable elaborate local crests, painted signs, and devices.

Blazon: Azure, two scimitars in saltire argent, hilted Or. (Two silver scimitars with gold hilts crossed diagonally on a blue field.)

The crossed swords are therefore best understood as a convenient representative motif for Rakhan martial culture rather than a device carried identically by every community.

docs.title: Religion
docs.text:
The Rakhan are one of the principal peoples associated with the Path, a family of liberation traditions descended from pre-Diabolist Devi. Path teachings seek freedom from the compulsions of appetite, fear, status, habit, and recurring embodiment through meditation, discipline, renunciation, ethical restraint, and cultivated lucidity.

Rakhan geography gives the tradition a strongly highland expression. Caves, hermit cells, village retreat houses, fortified monasteries, cliff and pass shrines, mountain pilgrimage routes, manuscript schools, and princely religious foundations are all characteristic possibilities. Individual valleys and principalities may preserve unusually isolated schools or teacher lineages.

Rakhan Path ascetics normally look like austere Rakhan highlanders, scholars, hermits, or mendicants rather than imported eastern monks. Their clothing, staffs, vessels, manuscripts, food, and shelter derive from local highland material culture. Some houses display distinctive marks of profession; others deliberately reject religious costume as attachment to appearing holy.

Rakhan rulers and monasteries can become closely entangled. Princes may endow houses, seek ascetic counsel, protect pilgrimage routes, or attempt religious reform, while monasteries may own land, granaries, bridges, mills, or rights associated with mountain passes. This creates recurrent arguments over wealth, detachment, political capture, and the proper use of religious property.

The Path is also a major non-Imperial home of Adept cultivation. Rakhan lineages may adapt the Heian-derived body–breath–Will discipline to mountain travel, weapon practice, endurance, monastic training, solitude, or cave retreat without preserving Heian martial aesthetics.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Tariq are a northern Roranian desert people especially renowned for camel pastoralism, caravan trade, route knowledge, and long-distance mercantile exchange.

Their reputation should not be mistaken for a universal occupation. Tariq communities include mobile pastoralists, oasis cultivators, market settlers, brokers, guides, caravan guards, craftspeople, livestock specialists, and families whose relationship to travel and herding changes over time.

Symbol: Golden camel on white.

docs.title: Emblem
docs.text: Blazon: Argent, a camel Or. (A golden camel on a white field.)

docs.title: Culture and Trade
docs.text:
Camel pastoralism, desert mobility, caravan logistics, and mercantile brokerage are among the most prestigious and visible Tariq traditions. Tariq networks link oasis settlements, desert-edge markets, pastoral camps, and foreign merchants across otherwise difficult country.

Control of route knowledge can be as important as control of land. Wells, seasonal grazing, caravan partnerships, safe-conduct agreements, marriage ties, and debt or livestock obligations may bind distant Tariq communities together without requiring a single centralized government.

docs.title: Religion
docs.text:
The Tariq are one of the principal peoples associated with the Path, a family of liberation traditions whose ancestral roots lie in pre-Diabolist Devi. Path teachers broadly understand recurring embodiment as bondage when appetite, fear, status, habit, and other attachments command the Will, and they use meditation, fasting, renunciation, ethical discipline, pilgrimage, and other practices to cultivate lucidity and release.

Among the Tariq, the Path is strongly shaped by desert travel and caravan society. Wandering teachers, oasis houses, route hospices, pilgrimage stations, merchant patronage, portable rites, and urban teaching circles are all natural expressions of the tradition. Temporary renunciation may take the form of months or years spent moving among route houses, teachers, and pilgrimage centers before returning to trade, household life, office, or marriage.

Tariq Path specialists normally look like ascetics of Tariq culture rather than members of a standardized foreign monastic order. Some lineages use rhythmic movement, circling footwork, breath discipline, chant, blades, or endurance training as contemplative practices. The Path is also one of the major non-Imperial homes of Adept cultivation, and some Tariq Adept schools have transformed the Heian-derived body–breath–Will techniques into distinctly desert and caravan forms.

None of these tendencies is universal. Tariq schools disagree over visible religious dress, institutional wealth, relic devotion, martial practice, spirit assistance, and the proper balance between withdrawal and engaged life.

docs.title: Relations
docs.text: Tariq and Qalshari occupy overlapping northern desert–savanna systems. Tariq are particularly associated with desert-route brokerage and camel-based mobility, while Qalshari prestige is more strongly tied to horses, mounted warfare, and better-watered savanna margins. The distinction is historical and institutional rather than absolute.

docs.title: Society
docs.text:
This section collects setting-wide social systems and conventions that cross political and cultural boundaries.

  • Languages — major languages, trade tongues, and linguistic groupings.
  • Heraldry and Emblems — heraldic and emblematic traditions across different cultures.
  • Slavery — the forms and social roles of slavery in different regions.
  • Trade and Commerce — major commercial patterns and relationships.

More local institutions are filed with the realms or peoples to which they belong. For example, the Devi Caste System is under Devi, while Shinobi are treated as a specialized Adept tradition under Magic.

docs.title: Heraldry and Emblems
docs.text:
The peoples of Umbrathar use coats of arms, civic devices, clan-marks, banners, seals, shield-signs, tattoos, painted patterns, and other emblems to identify rulers, peoples, cities, military bodies, religious institutions, and lineages.

Different regions developed their own symbolic traditions. The formal shield-armory of the Hetaireian Princedoms is only one such system.

docs.title: Loranian and Great-City Armory
docs.text:
The most formal armorial tradition is associated with the old Heryoi/Heryan imperial world and the modern Hetaireian Princedoms and Great Cities. Its arms favor simple fields, strongly contrasting charges, dynastic differencing, civic devices, and repeatable designs suitable for shields, banners, seals, and surcoats.

Loranian heralds generally favor strong contrast between gold or silver and darker colors. Very ancient civic emblems sometimes ignore these later conventions, and heralds may describe such arms as archaic or irregular without denying their legitimacy.

Princes, noble houses, and branches of a dynasty often show relationship by altering borders, chiefs, secondary charges, or colors while preserving a recognizable central emblem.

A shared regional badge is not necessarily a shared coat of arms. Clovia is the clearest example: the White Rose signifies broad Clovian identity and may appear beside many otherwise unrelated dynastic, civic, and regional devices. Longard rulers retain crown-and-sword imagery, Tusci use the griffin as a cultural badge, Sapaudi communities vary the mountain-and-key motif, and Liguri cities deliberately possess no universal Liguri arms at all.

docs.title: Doradan Arms and Badges
docs.text: Dorado provides a useful example of the difference between a realm-wide coat of arms and regional cultural badges.

docs.title: Dorado
docs.text:
Blazon: Or, a tiger rampant Gules. Plain English: On a gold field, a red tiger rearing upright.

The red Doradan Mountain Tiger is the broad emblem of Dorado and accompanies the motto “Resist And Bite.” The regional cultures below do not merely difference this shield; they maintain distinct badges of their own.

docs.title: Cantabri
docs.text:
Badge: The Tower on the Rock. Heraldic description: A tower Argent masoned Sable upon a rock proper. Plain English: A white or silver stone tower, with black masonry lines, standing on a natural-colored rock.

The badge reflects fortified northern lordships, mountain strongholds, and the motto “Like Stone Unyielding.”

docs.title: Flagrosos
docs.text:
Badge: The Open Gate of Covadio. Heraldic description: A fortress gatehouse proper, the gates displayed open and the portcullis raised. Plain English: A heavy stone fortress gate with its doors open and portcullis lifted.

The Flagroso device derives from a specific historical event rather than an abstract regional quality. It depicts the captured imperial fortress at Covadio standing deliberately open, visually repeating Covado's challenge and the motto “Come And Take It.” Because no universal field or tincture scheme has been fixed, this remains a badge description rather than a complete shield blazon.

docs.title: Vettones
docs.text:
Badge: The Horse and Setting Sun. Heraldic description: A horse rampant Sable before a demi-sun issuant in base Gules rayonned Or. Plain English: A black rearing horse before a half-visible red setting sun with golden rays.

The badge accompanies the motto “With The Sun We Ride.” In formal heraldic vocabulary, the horse is rampant and the half-sun is issuant in base; Vetton tradition interprets the latter specifically as the western setting sun.

docs.title: Meliti
docs.text:
Badge: The Jabber Bird over the Waves. Heraldic description: A Jabber Bird volant proper, beneath it three barrulets wavy Argent and Azure. Plain English: A naturally colored Jabber Bird flying above three narrow wavy stripes of white and blue.

The Meliti badge makes the motto “Waves Beneath Our Wings” literal while tying their maritime identity to the navigational Jabber Birds of their island homeland.

These regional devices are intentionally heterogeneous. They grew from different histories, landscapes, and political identities rather than from a single centralized Doradan heraldic authority.

docs.title: Northern Clan Signs
docs.text:
The peoples of The Northern Clanlands use clan signs, shield marks, sail emblems, carved standards, totemic badges, brands, and woven patterns rather than a single common legal system of armory.

Reaver signs are often bold enough to recognize on sails and shields. Tuathan signs favor interlace, thorns, knots, and repeated patterns. Far-northern peoples often use animal parts, tracks, bones, hide colors, and simplified natural forms.

Southern heralds sometimes translate these signs into their own armorial language, but the resulting description should not be mistaken for the native custom.

docs.title: Southern and Roranian Emblems
docs.text:
Among many Southern Tribes and the peoples outsiders group as Bushmen, collective signs appear through painted shields, woven textiles, beadwork, tattoos, ritual body-paint, standards, carvings, and trade-marks as often as through formal coats of arms.

Related communities can share a visual language without sharing a single emblem: stripes, radial patterns, animal silhouettes, repeated geometric borders, and distinctive color combinations may identify regional or ancestral relationships.

docs.title: Easterling Standards and Clan Marks
docs.text:
Easterling standards favor bold forms suitable for cavalry: animals, suns, crescents, wheels, and abstract clan-marks appear on banners, saddles, weapons, brands, and leatherwork.

A great khan or confederation may use an elaborate colored standard while subordinate clans retain much simpler marks derived from the same imagery.

docs.title: Immortal Imperial Seals and Crests
docs.text:
The peoples of the Immortal Empire commonly use seals, enclosed crests, repeated geometric forms, dragons, wyrms, and ceremonial standards rather than Loranian-style hereditary shield-armory.

Heian, Utar, and Bodi traditions differ sharply from one another despite their shared imperial political world.

docs.title: Devi and Pingrit Devices
docs.text:
Devi insignia are often hierarchical and cultic. A single person or institution may display a state sign, demon-cult emblem, caste or office color, and local dynastic device at the same time.

Pingrit signs are especially suited to sails, pennants, hulls, carvings, and Spirit Boxes. Maritime animals, knots, boxes, eyes, and warding geometry recur across the archipelago, but political fragmentation produces enormous local variation.

docs.title: Languages
docs.text: The peoples of Umbrathar speak numerous related and unrelated tongues. Imperial conquest, trade, religion, migration, and nomadic travel have created several important lingua francas alongside hundreds of local languages and dialects.

docs.title: Heryos Language Family
docs.text:
The ancient Heryos spoke the ancestral tongue from which several important western languages descend.

As Heryos populations settled and divided, their speech developed into major branches:

  • Heryoi — the northern/Meropolitan branch, eventually producing Meropolitan.
  • Heryan — the southern/Zorahn branch, eventually producing Zorahn.

docs.title: Meropolitan
docs.text:
Meropolitan is the native language of Meropolis and the principal transregional language of religion, learning, diplomacy, and elite communication throughout the Hetaireian world. It descends from early Heryoi rather than being an unchanged survival of ancient Heryos speech.

Clergy, scholars, scribes, diplomats, major merchants, nobles, military officers, and others whose lives regularly cross political boundaries are disproportionately likely to know Meropolitan. Most people outside Meropolis, however, conduct ordinary life in their own local languages and dialects. Meropolitan is therefore an important lingua franca, but not a universal common tongue.

Its practical reach extends beyond the Hetaireian Realms wherever Meropolitan clergy, merchants, archives, courts, pilgrimage routes, or diplomatic relationships are influential, but proficiency varies greatly by region, profession, and social class.

docs.title: Heian
docs.text: Heian serves a comparable language of administration, diplomacy, and trade across the Immortal Empire and among many peoples of The Easterling Steppe.

docs.title: Southern Roranian Contact Speech
docs.text:
The peoples of The Thousand Nations of the South do not share one ethnic language. The region contains many unrelated or distantly related local languages and dialect continua, alongside trade tongues, pidgins, multilingual market speech, and sign systems used across cultural boundaries.

Older foreign merchants sometimes called some of these contact systems “Bushman speech.” The label reflects the old outsider category Bushmen Peoples, not a single language family or native ethnic identity.

The Oluru, Nissai, Xai, Wolilalika, Hakori, Tariq, Qalshari, Rakhan, and Herzgud all encompass their own local speech traditions, and several of the broader cultural fields contain many languages rather than one standardized tongue.

docs.title: Northern and Highland Peoples

These broad labels conceal substantial local variation, especially where older clan languages survive beneath later princely identities.

docs.title: Clovian Speech
docs.text:
“Clovian” is especially broad. It can mean the prestige speech of central Clovia, the wider family of related Romance-descended languages spoken across the old province, or simply any local speech associated with Clovian political identity.

The principal regional traditions include:

  • central Clovian languages and dialects;
  • eastern Longard speech shaped by a strong historical Svealish substrate;
  • Tusci speech in the central-western cities and countryside;
  • Royeux speech in the south and southwest;
  • highly varied Sapaudi mountain-valley speech;
  • the related maritime speech traditions grouped by outsiders as Liguri.

These identities are not five standardized languages with clean borders. City, valley, class, migration, political rule, and trade all complicate the linguistic map.

These labels describe cultural spheres, not necessarily single languages.

The exact language-family relationships among Uldat, Ordai, Sigyn, Chulkas, Khazgui, and lesser Khorun peoples remain undeveloped. Their coexistence within the same geographic-cultural sphere should not be mistaken for proof that all speak closely related languages.

docs.title: Slavery
docs.text: Slavery exists across much of Umbrathar, but its legality, religious justification, and social form vary sharply by culture.

docs.title: Atharite Law
docs.text:
Atharite teaching generally disfavors slavery and places restrictions on it: - Servitude must, at least in theory, be capable of being worked off. - Slave status is not supposed to be inherited automatically. - Masters are expected not to abuse slaves. - Unlawful permanent injury, maiming, and killing are prohibited.

These principles create substantial distance between Atharite ideal and actual practice. Debt, household authority, sexual exploitation, criminal punishment, and local custom can all become avenues for abuse even where outright permanent chattel slavery is doctrinally disfavored.

docs.title: Hetaireia Lands
docs.text:
In the Hetaireian Princedoms, slavery is largely outlawed. The Hetaireia emphasis on free will makes permanent bondage ideologically suspect. Criminals and vagabonds may be subjected to forms of servitude, and some Princedoms practice serfdom, though this is controversial.

Meropolis follows this more restrictive northern model despite being geographically a southern city.

docs.title: Behdin Cities
docs.text:
Slavery is more common in the southern cities. Behdin determinism can be used to interpret a person's social position as part of the divine order, although individual clergy and communities differ greatly in how readily they accept that argument.

Formal Atharite restrictions still exist, but powerful households exploit loopholes. Debt and fees may be structured to prevent an enslaved person from ever purchasing freedom, while desperate families may sell children into bondage even though hereditary slave status is formally forbidden.

Such abuse is widespread enough to be notorious without being universal; some masters genuinely obey the restrictions imposed by law and religion.

docs.title: Northern Clanlands and Southern Tribes
docs.text: Among many peoples of The Northern Clanlands and Southern Tribes, enslavement after war is ordinary custom. Defeated men may be killed while women and children are enslaved. These societies often regard Atharite moral concern about the institution as strange or hypocritical.

docs.title: Easterling Steppe
docs.text: The peoples of The Easterling Steppe also practice slavery. Some Sigyn communities have begun adopting a more Hetaireia-like hostility toward bondage because it aligns with their own ideal of personal freedom beneath the open sky.

docs.title: Immortal Empire
docs.text: The Immortal Empire formally does not practice slavery because one imperial subject cannot legally own another. Critics answer that this is a technical distinction: imperial doctrine already treats every subject as belonging ultimately to the Dragon Emperor and the state.

docs.title: Trade and Commerce
docs.text: Trade in Umbrathar is shaped by the Sea of Ardan, the continental crossroads of the Swordlands, the Eastward Road, and the unequal specialization of regional economies.

docs.title: Western Maritime Trade
docs.text:
The Meliti of western Dorado and the Jabberer Islands are among Lorania's most capable sailors and shipbuilders. Their fleets carry commerce around the western Sea of Ardan, and Tejago has prospered under nearly forty years of rule by Prince Alfonse Reynaldo de Torrez.

Piracy and legitimate trade overlap throughout these waters. Southern corsairs are a recurring threat, while some islanders and coastal peoples may themselves engage in piracy.

docs.title: Clovian Goods
docs.text:
Clovia benefits from precious-metal deposits in its northern mountains.

  • Longard territories are associated particularly with silver.
  • Tusci are renowned for wine and fine marble statuary.
  • Royeux merchants on the southern coast attempt to profit from and monopolize trade in their neighbors' goods.

docs.title: The Swordlands
docs.text:
Zorah and Al-Anwar occupy central positions in long-distance trade between Devi, the east, and the western world.

Zorahns take an active role in exploration, road security, and opening new markets. The Al-Anwarese are known more as brokers and middlemen. Competition over tariffs and control of trade routes contributes to repeated political conflict among Zorah, Al-Anwar, and Meropolis.

The Eastward Road is currently threatened by Chulkas activity.

docs.title: Devi and the Pingrit
docs.text:
Jalaska is the greatest port of Devi and contains enormous markets tied to the realm's caste and slave systems.

The Pingrit Archipelago is a major environment for corsairs, smugglers, exiles, and informal commerce, with hidden coves and highly fragmented authority.

docs.title: Languages of Trade
docs.text: Meropolitan is the major western common language used across many Hetaireian Princedoms and Great Cities, while Heian plays a comparable lingua-franca role in much of the east. See Languages.

docs.title: History
docs.text:
Umbrathar's surviving histories are uneven. Western chronicles preserve far more detail about the old Heryos empires, the rise of Ardan, the Great Schism, the Princedoms, and the Great Cities than they do about many distant regions of the world.

For that reason this section emphasizes established historical people and events rather than presenting a supposedly universal chronology that the surviving chronicles do not support.

  • Historical Figures — major people whose actions shaped the known history of the setting.
  • Timeline — a working chronology of major eras and established events.

docs.title: Timeline of Umbrathar
docs.text: Dates are generally reckoned AA — After the Ascension of Ardan.

docs.title: Mythic / Deep Time
docs.text:
• Titans and primordial Dragons struggle for dominance in the young world.
  • Western Atharite tradition says the Titans defeat the Dragons and strip the survivors of their wings, leaving the creatures known today as Wyrms.
  • The origins of mankind are explained differently by different traditions. Atharites teach that Athar created the First Man at the sacred site now occupied by Meropolis, where his first drink came from the holy river. His descendants include Lovar, Rovar, and Eovar, ancestral patriarchs associated with the early dispersal and division of mankind. Whether this account describes objective human origins remains unresolved.

docs.title: Ancient Heryos Period
docs.text:
• The people later remembered as the Heryos emerge from the Eastern Steppe as horse-lords and raiders.
  • They conquer settled southern lands and are transformed in turn by urban civilization.
  • Later chroniclers attribute the first great unification of the southern cities to Nerokles, founder of the Nerokleid or Old Empire.
  • Successor conflicts eventually give way to a collegial imperial republic or Compact centered on great southern cities.
  • Contact with Devi Diabolists and Zamboulan eldritch cults contributes to increasing religious corruption in the imperial elite. Later northern accounts often describe Devi itself as already wholly Diabolist, though this projects the modern Asura order backward onto a much older and more religiously diverse civilization.

docs.title: Ardanic Revolution
docs.text:
• Ardan rises as prophet and war-leader among Atharite populations.
  • He overthrows the corrupt old order, suppresses diabolic and eldritch cults, and establishes a New Ardanic Empire.
  • Ardan reconquers or incorporates large portions of the old imperial sphere while preserving useful administrative and military machinery under a new sacred and constitutional legitimacy.

docs.title: 0 AA — The Ascension
docs.text:
• Ardan ascends from the mortal world.
  • Competing interpretations of his Ascension divide his followers.
  • The northern tradition develops into the Hetaireia; the southern tradition into the Behdin.

docs.title: Early Post-Ascension Centuries
docs.text:
• Ardan's political empire survives after his Ascension but enters a long period of contraction rather than suffering one single terminal collapse. Military, fiscal, infrastructural, and regional autonomy accumulate unevenly through repeated crises while the theory of universal order outlives effective universal government.
  • The transregional Atharite religious network survives political fragmentation better than central taxation, standing military capacity, and uniform territorial administration, helping explain the later importance of Meropolis and the Pontis.
  • Surviving histories disagree sharply over the dates, sequence, local turning points, and pace of this contraction.
  • Doradan conversion to Atharism begins within roughly the first century after the Ascension, associated with the wise woman Mari and a demonic crisis.

docs.title: Ancient Pingrit Era
docs.text:
• c. 600 years before the Ascension: An exceptional maritime empire unites or dominates much of the Pingrit Archipelago, binding distant islands through fleets, ports, tribute, and long-distance commerce.
  • The ancient thalassocracy collapses amid a devastating maritime plague, political disorder, commercial breakdown, and widespread warfare. Pingrit sailors preserve tales of the so-called Fishman Wars, in which creatures from beneath the sea are said to have infiltrated the empire before openly attacking its ports and fleets. Most modern scholars dismiss these accounts as fishermen's tales inspired by the plague and the confused wars surrounding the empire's collapse.
  • For generations afterward, would-be emperors, admirals, merchant princes, and local strongmen repeatedly attempt to restore archipelago-wide rule. Their failures help make universal Pingrit kingship alternately ridiculous and threatening in later political culture.

docs.title: 5th–7th Centuries AA
docs.text:
• Dorado is by now overwhelmingly Atharite after centuries of conversion and violent suppression of holdouts.
  • Firelander occupation and migration reshape Albia.
  • c. 647 AA: Within a couple of decades of his decisive conquest of Utar, the Dragon Emperor launches an invasion of Devi. The campaign initially extends the momentum of the expanding Immortal Empire, but increasingly extreme blood magic, coercive sacrifice, demonic enhancement, and finally open covenants with Demon Gods transform the war. At Shari, Durogchit the Skull Reaper is openly invoked as an ally of Devi and answers with unmistakable demonic force. The invasion becomes a long supernatural war that ultimately forces the Immortal armies to withdraw and begins the historical transformation of old Devi into the later Asura Raj of Devi.
  • 689 AA: Prince Eodric of Albia converts to Atharism, an important milestone in Albia's place within the northern princely order.

docs.title: Present Era
docs.text:
• The Hetaireian Realms remain politically fractured into many Principalities but broadly united in the northern Atharite civilizational order.
  • The Southern Great Cities are politically sophisticated but ecclesiastically divided within Behdin structures.
  • The Khazgui rise under Hu Khan, pushing Chulkas westward and badly disrupting the Eastward Road.
  • The Dragon Emperor of the Immortal Empire directs increasing attention west toward steppe peoples and western magic.
  • Prince Alfonse Reynaldo de Torrez, the Sea Fox of Tejago, approaches the end of a long reign without a clear successor.
  • 11 Bear's Moon, 881 AA: The Gran Mago sails from Tejago on an expedition commissioned by Prince Alfonse Reynaldo de Torrez to chart a maritime route around Rorania to Devi and investigate the fate of Inigo El Cid.
  • 883 AA: The Gran Mago returns to Tejago, completing the expedition and establishing that the maritime route to Devi can be successfully navigated.

docs.title: Historical Figures
docs.text:
These figures belong primarily to the historical record rather than to one present-day realm or locality.

  • Ardan — prophet, conqueror, and central figure of Atharite history.
  • Theron — Ardan's northern companion and a central figure in the succession that produced the Hetaireia tradition.
  • Polema — Ardan's wife and the central southern claimant in the same succession.
  • Mari — the wise woman associated with the conversion of Dorado.
  • Covado — the Doradan reclaimer who liberated Flagros, captured Fort Hurktos, and gave his name to Covadio.

This is not intended as an exhaustive list of all important people in history. Living rulers and figures whose significance belongs chiefly to a particular realm are filed with that realm instead.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Ardan is the central prophet, war-leader, and disputed divine figure of Atharism. He rose during the final corruption of the old imperial order, overthrew the regime associated with Diabolism and eldritch cults, and established a new Atharite empire.

His Ascension became the defining event of the current religious era and the cause of the Great Schism.

docs.title: The Redeemer
docs.text:
Ardan was born among a minor Atharite community near Meropolis. He gathered the poor, disillusioned, and surviving adherents of the old faith and led a rapid, violent revolution against the decaying imperial order.

After victory he was crowned in Meropolis and established Atharism as the public religion of the restored realm. His campaigns and influence extended into Szovij and Dorado, although later histories disagree over the exact sequence of those conversions.

docs.title: Ascension
docs.text: Ardan did not leave an uncontested successor. All major Atharite traditions agree that he departed the mortal world in a miraculous Ascension, while the northern and southern churches disagree over what that event meant.

docs.title: Hetaireia Doctrine
docs.text: The Hetaireia hold that Ardan became united with Athar, making his Ascension the supreme act of divine-human union. The symbol of a human hand within the Flame represents this doctrine.

docs.title: Behdin Doctrine
docs.text: The Behdin reject identification of a created human being with the Uncreated Flame. They hold Ardan to be the greatest of Athar’s servants and Archons, but still distinct from Athar.

docs.title: Successor Dispute
docs.text:
Ardan's closest military and political companion was Theron of Meropolis. His wife was Polema.

After the Ascension, Theron became the principal northern successor claimant and Polema the principal southern claimant. Their conflict developed into the Ardanic Succession Dispute and ultimately the Hetaireia/Behdin schism.

docs.title: Legacy
docs.text: Almost every major Atharite political dispute ultimately returns to Ardan: whether his warrior or priestly role was primary, what his Ascension means, how much authority his institutional successors possess, and whether the divine Plan is something mortals enact or contemplate.

docs.title: Covado
docs.text: Covado is the great reclaimer of Flagros in eastern Dorado and the central hero of modern Flagroso political memory.

docs.title: Reconquest
docs.text:
After the collapse of the old Empire, Clovian forces invaded eastern Dorado and forced many Flagroso communities into the mountains. Covado united the displaced and surviving local forces and led them back into the lowlands, reclaiming much of the region.

His defining victory was the conquest of Fort Hurktos, the ancient imperial barrier built to contain Dorado. The captured fortress was thereafter renamed Covadio in his honor.

docs.title: The Challenge to the Tusci
docs.text:
After Covado took the fortress, a Prince of the Tusci demanded its return. Covado's reply was:

“Come and take it.”

The prince never replied.

docs.title: Legacy
docs.text:
The challenge became one of the defining sayings of eastern Dorado and eventually the Flagroso motto: “Come And Take It.”

The shared Flagroso badge, the Open Gate of Covadio, gives the same message visually. The old imperial fortress that once barred Doradans from the crossing is shown with its gate standing open, inviting any claimant to try to retake it.

Flagros itself predates Covado. His importance lies not in founding the region or naming its people, but in creating the political mythology of recovered sovereignty that dominates modern Flagroso identity.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Mari is the wise woman associated with the conversion of Dorado to Atharism. She came down from the northern mountains during a demonic crisis and demonstrated power against evils that local religious specialists could not contain.

docs.title: The Miracle Tradition
docs.text:
The best-known Cantabri tradition describes a demonic plague striking northern Dorado. Mari appeared claiming the power of the Uncreated Flame, cast out several demons in a single day, and converted the families she saved. When she healed a high chieftain of the region associated with the Cantabri, he and his people converted.

Her mission became one of the foundational stories of Doradan Atharism.

docs.title: Conversion of Dorado
docs.text:
Conversion spread over subsequent centuries and was not uniformly peaceful. Highland and Cantabri communities appear to have embraced Atharism earlier, while resistance elsewhere produced missionary violence, crusades, and bitter internal religious wars.

Later Doradan traditions disagree over the exact form of the original demonic catastrophe and over how much of Mari's story should be read as literal chronicle, miracle narrative, or both.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Polema was Ardan's wife and became the principal southern successor claimant after his death or Ascension.

Her followers rejected the northern doctrine that Ardan had become one with Athar, maintaining that even the greatest human servant of Athar remained a created being. This position became foundational to the southern Behdin tradition.

Polema did not remarry and died without issue.

docs.title: Role in the Schism
docs.text:
Polema opposed Theron, Ardan's closest companion and the principal northern claimant. Their political and theological conflict became the Ardanic Succession Dispute.

The original dispute entangled two questions that later diverged: who possessed legitimate religious succession after Ardan, and who inherited his temporal imperial sovereignty.

docs.title: Zorahn Dynastic Legacy
docs.text:
After Polema's childless death, Zorahn genealogical tradition holds that the temporal dynastic claim passed to a son of Ardan's sister. The later Zorahn Shahdom treats this collateral succession as preserving Ardan's imperial house rather than beginning a new dynasty without connection to him.

Northern and Hetaireian traditions often define “Ardan's line” more narrowly and regard the direct dynasty as having ended with Polema. The disagreement is therefore a genuine dispute over dynastic continuity rather than a simple claim that one side possesses no historical connection at all.

Polema also stands in the transmission history of Ardan's scepter, which Zorah preserves as living accession regalia. Meropolis preserves Ardan's crown as a sacred relic.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Theron of Meropolis was Ardan's closest military and political companion and became the principal northern successor claimant after Ardan's Ascension.

His followers developed into the Hetaireia. Theron's authority is closely tied to the northern claim that Ardan entered an extraordinary union with Athar.

docs.title: Role in the Schism
docs.text:
Theron opposed Polema, Ardan's wife and the principal southern successor claimant. Their political and theological conflict became the Ardanic Succession Dispute.

Northern tradition gives Theron special authority as a witness to Ardan's Ascension, though surviving accounts differ in the exact circumstances and language of that witness.

docs.title: Religions
docs.text: The peoples of Umbrathar do not share a single account of creation, the gods, spirits, death, or salvation. Religious traditions overlap with politics and magic, but they often disagree even about the basic nature of the supernatural world.

docs.title: Major Traditions
docs.text:
• Atharism — worship of Athar, the Uncreated Flame, dominant across the Hetaireian Princedoms and influential among the Great Cities.
  • Tuathan Old Ways — the ancestral Tuathan traditions centered on sacred landscapes, Fey powers, divination, sacrifice, and the living holiness of the world.
  • Northern Gods — the gods, ancestors, and religious traditions of the Reaver Clans.
  • Asurabalah — the dominant Diabolist religious establishment of modern Devi.
  • Tiwara Hat Tiwangmnani — the dangerous spirit tradition of the Pingrit Archipelago.
  • Easterling Faith — the broad animist and shamanic religious pattern of the Easterling Steppe.
  • The Immortal Cycle — the Imperial religious-philosophical tradition centered on the Dragon Emperor, commonly called the Way of the Dragon.
  • The Path — related liberation traditions especially among the Tariq, Qalshari, and Rakhan, often grouped by foreign scholars under the label Southern Asceticism.

Religious claims in this wiki should be read as the beliefs of their adherents unless a page explicitly establishes something as common supernatural observation.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Asurabalah is the dominant state and sacrificial religious order of Devi. The name is commonly understood in the sense of the strength or power of the Asura. It is explicitly Diabolist: its great cults venerate demonic powers whose institutions are intertwined with rulership, caste hierarchy, warfare, commerce, law, magical practice, and ritual sacrifice.

Asurabalah is not a single church and does not possess one harmonized creed. The cults of the Great Demon Gods compete fiercely, preserve incompatible sacred histories, and may disagree about creation, divine rank, or the ultimate order of the cosmos. What unifies them is a shared religious and institutional grammar: offerings, vows, sacred debts, pollution, purification, sacrifice, patronage, lawful cult standing, temple privilege, and the accepted political supremacy of the Asura order.

Nor is Asurabalah simply “the religion of Devi.” Devi religious life is older and much broader than the modern Diabolist establishment. Household gods, ancestors, local spirits, village shrines, ascetic traditions, regional festivals, protective rites, and fragments of older philosophical schools continue beneath or alongside the state cults. Most Devi therefore live within a layered religious world rather than practicing an exclusive Demon-God faith.

The beings worshipped as Great Demon Gods are known through specifically Devi names, images, titles, and cult traditions. These are not necessarily universal true names or immutable cosmic bodies. A Demon may be known elsewhere under a different guise, while apparently similar foreign cults may instead serve entirely different beings.

docs.title: Historical Rise
docs.text:
Asurabalah in its modern form is not the timeless religion of Devi.

Old Devi was famously pluralistic, with innumerable temples, cults, ascetic schools, household traditions, philosophical movements, and occult specialists. Diabolism was known and periodically dangerous, and some lesser or bounded dealings with demons could even be licensed or tolerated under local law, but no civilization-wide Demon-God order ruled the country.

The transformation began during the long invasion of Devi by the Dragon Emperor in the seventh century AA. Desperate practitioners escalated from harsh blood magic and voluntary sacrifice to captives, coercive rites, demonic enhancement, and progressively more open dealings with demons. Repeated success made each new exception easier to justify.

At Shari, defenders finally invoked Durogchit the Skull Reaper openly as a wartime ally. She demanded captured enemy soldiers and answered with demon legions, war-beasts, supernatural endurance, battle-fury, and other unmistakable manifestations. Shari survived, and the precedent was devastatingly persuasive: a Demon God had answered when conventional institutions appeared unable to save the city.

Other rulers and cults sought comparable patrons. The result was not an overnight conversion but generations of institutional capture, imitation, rivalry, and escalation. After the Immortal armies withdrew, the armed cults and enhanced rulers created by the war continued fighting one another until the first Asura Raj eventually consolidated the recognizable modern order.

The name Asurabalah belongs particularly to this mature religious-political settlement. The older wartime cults, sacrificial schools, and Demon-God covenants predated the unified establishment and need not have called themselves by the later name.

docs.title: Shared Belief and Cult Rivalry
docs.text:
At the broadest level, Asurabalah teaches that the Great Demon Gods are mighty powers with legitimate claims upon the world and mankind, and that humans may prosper by entering correctly ordered relationships with them. Beyond that proposition, agreement rapidly breaks down.

One cult may describe its patron as first among the gods, another as the necessary enemy of a rival, and a third as the hidden power behind some ancient event. Such contradictions are ordinary. Asurabalah is held together less by theology than by shared procedures, recognized institutions, and a political settlement that permits rivalry without allowing cult warfare to destroy the state.

The Raj stands above this religious field as supreme sacred ruler and arbiter, not as universal high priest of every Demon God. He can confirm standing, suppress destabilizing cults, recognize privileges, and intervene in disputes. A great priest may nevertheless claim—and perhaps sincerely believe—that no mortal knows a particular patron more intimately than the priesthood dedicated to that god.

Recognition by the Asura state defines lawful Asurabalah, but outlaw cults may remain recognizably part of the same wider religious family. The cult of Dahakrodha, for example, shares much of the same ritual language while turning its violence against the established order.

docs.title: Temple Life and Predatory Generosity
docs.text:
Major temples are not merely places of sacrifice. They may function as healers, diviners, arbitrators, lenders, archives, granaries, employers, warehouses, schools, funerary institutions, pilgrimage houses, magical protectors, and intermediaries with officials. Much of this institutional life descends from older Devi religious and civic traditions captured or transformed by the Asura order rather than invented by it.

The services are often real. A temple healer may genuinely save a child, a diviner may identify a danger, a granary may feed a district during scarcity, and a priest may remove a hostile possession. The danger lies in the obligations created by accepting help.

Asurabalah temples commonly practice a form of predatory generosity. Initial services may be free, subsidized, or cheap enough to invite reliance. Later, especially when a petitioner is desperate, the cost may become money, labor, land, service, political loyalty, a blood obligation, a family commitment, or a sacred debt that can be invoked years later. Temples therefore cultivate clients as much as they collect fees.

This makes temple patronage simultaneously useful and dangerous. Families learn which shrines are generous, which priests are notorious for converting favors into lifelong claims, when relatives can pool resources to avoid temple debt, and when one cult can be used to contest the demands of another.

docs.title: Offerings, Sacred Debt, and Sacrifice
docs.text:
Asurabalah recognizes many forms of offering. Food, incense, animals, valuables, labor, vows, fasting, bloodletting, ordeal, festival gifts, and temple service are all more common in ordinary religious life than human sacrifice.

Human sacrifice is nevertheless normalized as an institution. Major temples, rulers, armies, and courts maintain the officials, guards, records, captive populations, ritual precincts, supplies, and schedules necessary to conduct it. Judicial sacrifice, war captives, great state rites, elite vows, and extraordinary crises provide common contexts, though exact rules differ sharply by cult and Rajdom.

Sacred debt connects ordinary religious dependence to the coercive order without making every debtor a sacrificial victim. Debt may first result in labor, clientage, loss of property, temple service, hostage obligations, political duties, enslavement, or family liability. Only an additional legal or religious classification normally makes a person eligible for sacrifice.

Asurabalah law commonly teaches that certain people can become sacrificially alienable: slaves, war captives, condemned criminals, severe oath-breakers, and others placed under recognized forfeitures may be claimed by a ruler, owner, victor, temple, or lawful authority. Different cults disagree about the exact boundaries, and such classifications are fertile ground for political manipulation.

The scale of Devi slavery means that routine sacrificial systems draw overwhelmingly from people already denied ordinary social protection. A free artisan, merchant, soldier, clerk, or respectable householder usually does not fear random seizure from the street. The more characteristic fear is that a powerful enemy may strip away the protections of caste, patronage, reputation, freedom, or legal standing and push the victim into a category the temples can lawfully claim.

docs.title: Prosperity and Favor
docs.text:
Asurabalah widely treats visible success as evidence of effective divine favor. Wealth, victory, health, fertility, beauty, office, magical accomplishment, or supernatural transformation may all be cited as proof that a person or institution has cultivated the right patronage.

This logic is highly selective. A merchant may regard his own fortune as a sacred reward while dismissing a rival's wealth as inheritance, theft, corruption, political favoritism, or the false blessing of an inferior god. Failure is equally flexible: poverty, illness, defeat, or infertility may be blamed on insufficient devotion, pollution, poor offerings, rival interference, or bad judgment—or presented as proof that the sufferer urgently needs a temple's help.

Offerings and obedience can therefore be preached as investments in future favor. Success justifies hierarchy after the fact, while competition over whose prosperity is legitimate reinforces division between households, castes, cults, and patrons.

docs.title: Asura and Sacred Power
docs.text:
The supernatural apex of the modern system is the Asura: a human transformed through cumulative Diabolic corruption until body and soul are no longer merely human in condition.

Asura are treated as living proof that relationship with the Great Demon Gods can transform mortal nature. Their bodies inspire sincere awe as well as fear. The Raj of Devi is an Asura, and his transformed condition is part of the sacred logic of kingship rather than a private magical accomplishment.

Deliberate pursuit of Asura status is an elite religious ambition rather than a universal goal. Powerful priests, rulers, generals, champions, and Diabolists may seek it, but there is no single accepted path. Different cults emphasize different vows, sacrifices, enhancements, victories, possessions, and dark accomplishments.

Because a new Asura can become a political rival, advanced Diabolic enhancement is closely watched. Temple sponsorship, office, royal patronage, licenses, and political protection may distinguish lawful aspiration from treasonous accumulation of supernatural power.

docs.title: Possession, Corruption, and Sanctioned Diabolism
docs.text:
Asurabalah does not treat every demonic mark or corrupting influence as equally shameful. What matters institutionally is whether the relationship is sanctioned, controlled, useful, and politically legible.

Some cults prize disciplined bargaining and retained self-command. Others glorify frenzy, surrender, or temporary domination by a patron. Permanent possession is not the universal priestly ideal, and temporary overshadowing or bounded inhabitation remains a dangerous specialist practice rather than the ordinary condition of every priest.

Major temples therefore maintain exorcists, demonologists, wardens, purification specialists, and other experts capable of recognizing and countering dangerous possession or contamination. Their knowledge is genuinely useful—and their authority is easily abused against rivals, dissidents, or inconvenient visionaries.

The Asura state heavily restricts unsanctioned Diabolism. An independent summoner or pact-maker can accumulate magical power, followers, wealth, or transformative capacity outside the established hierarchy. Devi laws against unauthorized Diabolism can therefore resemble the anti-Diabolist laws of foreign realms while serving the opposite purpose: protecting the monopoly of lawful Diabolism.

docs.title: Law, Patronage, and Religious Bureaucracy
docs.text:
Lawful Diabolism is a privilege rather than a universal private right. Dangerous practitioners may require temple sponsorship, official credentials, local presentation, guarantors, ritual permissions, or direct protection from an Asura patron.

Such rules are not administered through one clean legal code. Rajdom law, royal decrees, temple privileges, caste rules, cult precedent, local custom, patronage, licenses, and exceptional grants overlap constantly. A practitioner may be recognized by one authority and prohibited by another.

This bureaucratic complexity is politically useful. Bribery, gifts, selective enforcement, jurisdictional challenges, delayed filings, disputed seals, contradictory precedents, and strategic appeals give rulers and institutions leverage over one another. A sponsor may also be held answerable for the dangerous acts of a client, giving temples an incentive to police the Diabolists they empower.

docs.title: Household Religion and Older Devi Traditions
docs.text:
For most Devi, Asurabalah has been added to an older pluralistic religious world rather than replacing it. A household may attend a Great Demon God festival, seek temple healing, maintain an ancestor shrine, consult a local spirit-worker, preserve an old birth custom, and make offerings to different powers for different needs without seeing those acts as contradictory.

Ancestor rites remain especially rooted in households and lineages. Domestic shrines, healers, midwives, old ritual specialists, village sacred places, and protective customs may survive openly so long as they remain politically weak. The Asura order becomes more suspicious when such institutions accumulate land, wealth, followers, schools, or connections across multiple communities.

This survival of older practice is not the same thing as an organized underground resistance. It is a broad religious substrate from which many local traditions, evasions, and later reform movements can arise.

docs.title: Death and the Afterlife
docs.text:
Asurabalah has captured many institutions around death without erasing older ancestor religion. Temples may provide corpse preparation, purification, spirit protection, funerary arbitration, magical assistance, and prestigious rites. Basic protection may be customary or cheap; extraordinary cases can impose heavy debt on surviving kin.

Certain dead may fall under explicit temple claims: sacrificial victims, condemned persons, high initiates, or people who vowed their remains. Such claims are bounded and often contested rather than applying automatically to every corpse.

There is no single settled Asurabalah doctrine of the afterlife. Different cults promise different forms of patronage, elevation, protection, punishment, service, or privileged remembrance after death, while older Devi beliefs about ancestors remain widespread.

docs.title: Holy Time and Festivals
docs.text:
Asurabalah has only a small common state-religious calendar. Most sacred time belongs to particular cults, Rajdoms, cities, occupations, lineages, households, and older seasonal traditions.

Public festivals can be eagerly anticipated. Markets, games, food distributions, healing, marriages, divination, amnesties, debt relief, and public spectacle may all accompany major observances. The same festivals renew oaths, display hierarchy, advertise cult power, distribute patronage, recruit clients, and identify dependents.

Human sacrifice appears at some major state and cult observances but does not define every festival. Devi sacred time is crowded rather than uniform: family custom, caste, employer, temple, patron cult, local ruler, and state may all make competing demands on the same person.

docs.title: Religious Economy
docs.text:
Major temples are landholders and commercial institutions as well as sacred establishments. They may control estates, farms, workshops, warehouses, rental property, markets, credit, pilgrimage lodging, ritual monopolies, custody rights, and valuable exemptions.

There is no universal Asurabalah treasury. Temples compete for donors, pilgrims, debtors, clients, captives, estates, licenses, and royal favor. Some act as major creditors or repositories of wealth; others depend more heavily on land, patronage, service fees, or state grants.

The Raj and subordinate Asura prefer powerful temples that remain dependent. Audits, confiscations, privilege reviews, exemptions, jurisdictional disputes, and patronage can reward useful cults and weaken institutions becoming too independent.

The result is a hierarchy of extraction and protection. Households depend on temples; minor establishments seek backing from greater ones; major cult institutions seek Asura patrons; regional Asura operate within the Raj's wider order. Wealth, service, information, loyalty, and supernatural capacity tend upward, while recognition, privileges, licenses, protection, and opportunities flow downward. Ambition is encouraged so long as advancement strengthens the structure rather than escaping it.

docs.title: Accommodation, Evasion, and Resistance
docs.text:
Most resistance to Asurabalah is selective rather than revolutionary. Households hide assets, dispute debts, use an old healer, move a threatened relative, bribe an official, seek a rival temple's protection, conceal a shrine, or exploit contradictory jurisdictions while continuing to participate in the wider religious order.

Sincere believers may resist abuses in Asurabalah's own language: a debt is fraudulent, a sacrifice unlawful, a governor falsely favored, or a rival temple's claim invalid. The regime's internal competition frequently creates shelter for the people it oppresses. One temple may protect a fugitive because doing so embarrasses another; an Asura may tolerate an illegal healer because the healer keeps a district stable.

More explicit anti-Diabolist resistance also exists, but it is fragmented. Traditionalists, political rebels, dissident cults, ascetics, illegal sorcerers, and foreign-backed enemies of the Asura order need not share goals or methods, and opposition does not automatically make them virtuous.

docs.title: The Great Demon Gods
docs.text: The major cult powers of Asurabalah are collectively called the Great Demon Gods. The category is religious and political rather than a claim that the beings form a tidy objective pantheon. Their cults compete, overlap, form alliances, and tell incompatible stories about one another.

docs.title: Jivabandha the Fleshweaver
docs.text:
Domains: Creation through bondage, illusion, possession, bodily reshaping, prideful dominion.

Jivabandha creates, repairs, improves, and transforms living things through sacrificial rites and demonic power, but what he makes is never free. His cult teaches that perfected flesh, restored bodies, altered identities, and created servants remain bound by hidden obligations or direct supernatural ownership.

In the standard Devi guise he appears as a serene or beautiful humanoid seated before a vast loom of ribs, weaving bodies, masks, beasts, servants, and perfected forms from the lives of the sacrificed. Completed creations remain attached to the loom by nearly invisible strands. His eyes are polished obsidian: black, reflective, and depthless.

His priests speak naturally of bargains as threads, obligations as knots, enthralled servants as loom-bound, and apostates as those who have slipped the loom.

docs.title: Sanchayapala the Warden
docs.text:
Domains: Preservation through hoarding, decay, gluttony, imprisonment, enforced hierarchy, arrested change.

Sanchayapala teaches that valuable things should not be released. Wealth, food, offices, bodies, prisoners, debts, ancestral privilege, and power are safest when retained where authority has placed them.

His Devi image is an immense, nearly motionless jailer seated behind a succession of nested gates. Keys, seals, and locking bars are embedded in his flesh, and he appears swollen with things stored within him. His temples commonly combine the functions of prison, granary, treasury, ossuary, and repository.

Some of his sacrifices are sealed alive in temple cisterns or great jars so that their life and power are symbolically kept rather than allowed to pass away.

docs.title: Unmada the Ruin-Dancer
docs.text:
Domains: Destruction and renewal through agony, lust, frenzy, ecstatic violence.

Unmada teaches that nothing can become new until its present form has been broken. The doctrine makes destruction itself a sacrament and turns every restraint into a possible shell to be shattered.

The Ruin-Dancer appears as a tall, beautiful, unsettling figure encased in layer after layer of painted clay skin. As the dance intensifies, each shell cracks and falls away to reveal another body beneath—older, younger, male, female, wounded, perfect, or monstrous. Broken masks are a common cult symbol.

His worship is associated with orgiastic excess, self-mutilation, ritual demolition, mass sacrifice, and ecstatic violence.

docs.title: Lobhajani the Blood Mother
docs.text:
Domains: Wealth through exploitation, greed, envy, maternal devouring.

Lobhajani teaches that prosperity must be fed. A household, merchant house, caste, temple, or kingdom becomes rich because something else has been consumed for it.

Her Devi guise is a magnificently dressed maternal figure with a flawless golden face. Her torso is hollow, and coins, jewels, and living human hearts circulate visibly within it. She cradles an empty swaddling cloth as though forever waiting for another child—or another fortune—to be placed in her care.

Offerings include victims buried alive with treasure. The Golden Brotherhood near Shari is a distinctive Lobhajani institution whose continuing challenge and great wealth have long affected the regional economy. Its peculiar institutions should not be treated as universal features of Lobhajani worship.

docs.title: Sarwatal the Whispering Serpent
docs.text:
Domains: Forbidden knowledge, deception, wind sorcery.

Sarwatal is depicted in Devi as a serpentine female figure carrying a grotesque stringed instrument. Her cult pursues knowledge through demonic whispers, torture, plague, deception, and sorcery. The image is a Devi cultic guise rather than proof of an immutable cosmic body.

Sarwatal's establishment dominates Jalaska, presently under the priest Umoja Watsala, who also controls the city's Serpent Warrior Lodge as a praetorian instrument.

docs.title: Durogchit the Skull Reaper
docs.text:
Domains: War and death, victory, appetite, consumed strength.

Durogchit is represented in Devi as a many-armed warrior standing atop skulls. She is associated with battlefield violence, bone ritual, demonic war-beasts, supernatural courage, blood-addled warriors, trophy-taking, domination, and the appropriation or consumption of an enemy's strength. This is her established Devi cultic guise, not necessarily an objective body recognized everywhere in the world.

Her cult claims a special place in the history of modern Devi because Durogchit was the first Great Demon God openly invoked as an ally during the Dragon War. The first bargain at Shari demanded captured enemy soldiers rather than Shari's own population. That apparently limited price helped corrupt older captive-taking and prestige-warrior traditions into the large sacrificial systems of later centuries.

docs.title: Dahakrodha the Painted Berserker
docs.text:
Domains: Rebellion, wrath, the sun.

Dahakrodha is an outlaw Great Demon God whose worship is illegal within much of the Asura order. Her followers are drawn heavily from people brutalized by the existing hierarchy and turn ritual violence against priests, officials, and established sacred institutions.

Her Devi guise is an enormous warrior woman covered from head to foot in bands of red, white, yellow, and black war-paint. A ragged corona of hammered copper blades surrounds her head, broken chain links hang from her belt, and she carries a huge notched axe said to have been made from a sacrificial implement stolen from a lawful Demon-God temple.

Her solar aspect is the merciless noonday sun: exposure, heat, revelation, and rage that cannot remain hidden. Her cult's danger lies in the proposition that because the established order deserves what it does to its victims, anything done to overthrow it is justified.

docs.title: Zanjirani the Chain-Bearer
docs.text:
Domains: Cunning, slavery, fate, hunting, assassination.

Zanjirani teaches that everyone is already chained by birth, promises, fear, love, debt, fate, or hierarchy. Wisdom lies in discovering which link to pull.

Her Devi guise is a tall veiled huntress wrapped in a seemingly endless iron chain. Lengths pass through her wrists, throat, and ribs without wounds; others disappear upward into darkness or downward into the earth. Every link bears a tiny name. Blood-red star maps cover her body.

She is invoked by hunters and assassins. Her ritual hunts release enslaved victims only to pursue and torture them, presenting apparent freedom as a cruel demonstration that every path was already anticipated.

docs.title: Garajvanchak the Laughing Storm
docs.text:
Domains: Thunder, debauchery, murder, betrayal, conspiracy.

Garajvanchak is especially attractive to ambitious courtiers, heirs, generals, and rivals. His cult teaches that every oath lasts only until circumstances change and that a storm proves its strength by toppling whatever previously stood highest.

His Devi guise is an elegantly dressed courtier whose face appears unsettlingly like someone the viewer trusts. His robes drip rain even indoors. He carries a jeweled drinking cup in one hand and conceals a knife in the other. His laughter sounds like distant thunder, and when he is wounded rain runs upward from the cut.

His worship joins intoxication, conspiracy, assassination, violent elite turnover, and ritual killings in which victims are chained in exposed places and left to die beneath the open sky.

docs.title: Angarvriddha the Cinder King
docs.text:
Domains: Fire, annihilation, domination.

Angarvriddha teaches possession through destruction: what is merely conquered may someday be reclaimed, but what is reduced to ash can never belong to anyone else. Branding marks ownership; burning is the highest expression of domination.

His Devi guise is a terribly ancient man whose body resembles charred wood or burned flesh. His eyes glow like furnace mouths. Bands of black iron have been heated and fused permanently around his limbs and torso, and he sits upon a throne of vitrified stone, melted weapons, and fused coins.

His priests are pyromancers associated with branding, scarification, and mass burning. The cult claims Angarvriddha is the oldest of the Great Demon Gods and once ruled the others, but Asurabalah contains many incompatible sacred histories and this claim should not be treated as settled cosmological fact.

docs.title: Adventure Pressure
docs.text:
Asurabalah most often becomes dangerous through a claim: a temple claims a debt, a corpse, a slave, a vow, a privilege, a license, a property, or jurisdiction over a person or rite. Such claims can be fought with swords and magic, but also with witnesses, patronage, contradictory precedents, rival temples, stolen records, old family rights, and the competing interests of Asura rulers.

This makes rival institutions usable but compromised allies. A corrupt official may invalidate an unlawful sacrifice; another cult may rescue a victim for its own reasons; an illegal Diabolist may be the only person able to stop a possession. Devi remains dangerous precisely because it is habitable enough for people to build lives worth protecting inside it.
