docs.title: Atharism
docs.text: Atharism is the dominant religion of the Hetaireian Princedoms and many of the Great Cities. Its followers worship Athar, the Uncreated Flame, and revere Ardan as prophet, redeemer, and the central figure of their religious history.

docs.title: Core Doctrine
docs.text:
Atharites teach that Umbrathar is Athar's Shadow, a created reflection sustained through Athar and His Archons. Lesser spirits exist, but they are not gods. Treating with them may be permissible in some contexts, but worshipping them is spiritually dangerous because created beings are not entitled to the worship owed to Athar—and because a supposed spirit may actually be a demon or other hostile power.

Proper life is directed toward serving the Plan. Fasting, prayer, almsgiving or tithing, and iconoclasm are important disciplines. Ardan and other Archons may be depicted, but Athar should only be represented as an abstract flame.

Both major branches recognize mortal Will as morally consequential, but they explain its relation to the Plan differently. The Hetaireia emphasizes free choice and active righteous participation; The Behdin teaches that created Will is a real cause already encompassed within Athar's complete Plan.

docs.title: The Sacred Flame
docs.text:
Consecrated fire is an inheritance from Atharism before the Great Schism. A properly consecrated Flame is a privileged created ritual sign of the Uncreated Flame, but it is never Athar physically contained in ordinary fire.

Consecration establishes a genuine sacred status. Repeated worship, communal memory, sacred history, and Vested Will can deepen the significance of an old Flame or sanctuary, but age and reputation are not what originally make a Flame consecrated.

New sacred Flames are commonly established through legitimate transmission from older recognized Flames, producing historical lineages of sacred fire. The two major branches developed different interpretations and domestic relationships around these lineages: Hetaireian popular religion often attributes distinctive qualities to particular Flame Families, while Behdin learned tradition emphasizes ecclesiastical provenance and continuity.

Major Atharite rites commonly occur in relationship to consecrated fire, but exact incorporation, profession, marriage, ordination, monastic, household, and funerary forms differ between branches and regions.

docs.title: The Creation of Mankind
docs.text:
Atharite tradition teaches that mankind first appeared at Mount Kromon, the sacred site now embraced by Meropolis. There Athar created the First Man, whose first drink was from the Nelorelis, the “First Water,” issuing from Kromon and flowing toward the Sea of Ardan. The image of humanity receiving water immediately after receiving life is one of the oldest and most powerful elements of Atharite sacred geography.

The First Man's descendants include Lovar, Rovar, and Eovar, remembered as ancestral patriarchs associated with the great dispersal and division of early mankind. Atharite genealogical and historical traditions use their lines to explain the ancient branching of peoples, although later nations, migrations, intermarriages, conversions, and competing genealogies make such claims far more complicated than a simple threefold map of the modern world.

Mount Kromon, the sacred spring, and the Nelorelis are therefore objects of pilgrimage in their own right, not merely landmarks surrounding the later city. Atharites understand their sanctity as preceding Meropolitan imperial, Ardanic, and ecclesiastical institutions.

The Meropolitan creation account is Atharite doctrine, not a neutral authorial statement about human origins. Other peoples preserve different accounts, and whether mankind literally first appeared at Meropolis remains unresolved.

docs.title: Salvation and Corruption
docs.text:
Atharites believe the world and mankind are subject to entropy. A worthy soul may be remade after death as a lesser spirit or Archon. The especially sinful risk falling into the Outer Darkness and becoming demons.

Atharite polemic often points to Beastmen, Wyndol, distant clan peoples, corrupted men, and some non-Atharite societies as evidence of spiritual degeneration. These are religious interpretations, not neutral facts about human ancestry.

Atharite learned traditions distinguish moral guilt from supernatural affliction. Pollution, contamination, corruption, and possession are not interchangeable, and an afflicted person is not automatically culpable merely because something supernatural is wrong.

docs.title: The Drakontomachia
docs.text:
Learned Atharites call the primordial war against the Dragons the Drakontomachia, conventionally rendered as the Drakontomachy.

Atharite teaching remembers the Dragons as enemies of divine order, often describing them as manifestations, coalescences, or servants of the darkness opposed to Athar's Plan. In this account, Athar's Archons fought and defeated them during the ordering of Creation, preserving the world from powers that would have subjected it to corruption or ruin.

Modern Wyrms are commonly interpreted as the broken and degraded remnants of those primordial enemies: diminished survivals of powers that once challenged the order established by Athar and His servants.

The western tradition therefore treats the Drakontomachy fundamentally as a victory, even where sermons and chronicles emphasize its terrible cost. Claims from the Immortal Empire that the Dragons once maintained a necessary cycle of reincarnation are generally regarded as error, Dragon-veneration, or a dangerous inversion of sacred history.

The existence of the primordial war itself is not merely a matter of Atharite belief, but this interpretation of its cause and moral meaning is Atharite doctrine rather than neutral cosmological narration.

docs.title: Death and Cremation
docs.text:
Cremation is standard Atharite funerary practice and predates the Great Schism.

The corpse is not burned inside a temple, and the permanent sanctuary Flame is not used as a crematory furnace. Instead, fire legitimately derived or transmitted from a consecrated Flame is carried outward and used to kindle the exterior funerary pyre.

The shared principle is continuity with sacred fire; the exact procession, prayers, carrier, preparation of the pyre, treatment of ash and remains, mourning customs, and purification afterward differ by branch and locality.

Cremation also shapes Atharite relic traditions. Ash, calcined bone, teeth, associated objects, writings, and sacred places may all become relics where genuine sacred history, recognized relationship, or accumulated devotion supports that status. Bodily remains are not automatically holy merely because they belonged to a revered person.

docs.title: Sacred Time
docs.text:
Atharites use the objective twelve-Face year described by the standard calendar, although local cultures may use different names, eras, and civil New Years.

Athardyos, the tenth weekday associated with Athar, is shared pre-Schism sacred time and is the customary day of principal communal worship in both major branches. Exact restrictions on labor, commerce, fasting, and rest vary regionally.

The Full Moons of the eleven visible months commonly attract additional prayer or religious attention. The Great Vigil on 16 Stranger, when the lunar cycle reaches its invisible Full-Moon point, is an ancient Atharite observance inherited by both branches, though its surrounding customs have developed differently.

Ardan's Ascension on 19 Father's Moon is shared sacred history and a great feast throughout Atharism; the branches disagree over what the Ascension metaphysically meant.

The Passage season around the Autumnal Equinox preserves the ancient pilgrimage memory of Mount Kromon and the Nelorelis. The Hetaireia incorporates it into its standardized continental feast cycle, while The Behdin places particular emphasis on pilgrimage, vows, penance, and hospitality around the season.

docs.title: The Great Schism
docs.text:
After Ardan's Ascension, his followers split over both succession and the theological meaning of the event. See Ardanic Succession Dispute.

  • The northern Hetaireia emphasize free will, works, righteous action, and Ardan's Theosis through union with Athar.
  • The southern The Behdin emphasize the completeness of the Plan, asceticism, mystical discipline, and Ardan's status as the Perfect Servant and greatest created being rather than identity with the Uncreated Flame.

The schism also produced major institutional, liturgical, political, ascetic, and devotional differences.

docs.title: Clergy
docs.text:
All major Atharite traditions maintain priests and religious officials. See Atharite Clergy. Proper ordination confers genuine sacerdotal capacity even when its effects are subtle rather than spectacular.

The northern Hetaireia is centered on the Pontis and High Ministry. The Behdin is a decentralized communion of historically sedimented patriarchal churches, synods, monasteries, schools, and recognition networks without one uncontested universal office.

Ordinary priests in both branches may perform routine purification, protective blessings, and ordinary exorcistic rites. Difficult, dangerous, or ambiguous supernatural cases are normally escalated to specialists appropriate to the branch and region.

docs.title: Magic, Mysticism, and Miracle
docs.text:
Atharites distinguish ordinary priestly rites, learned Sorcery, Mysticism, spirit interaction, and direct divine miracle-working even though ordinary people may confuse them in practice.

Properly constituted priestly rites—consecration, blessing, marriage, profession, funerary service, care of the sick, purification, and similar sacred acts—can possess genuine metaphysical efficacy without making every priest an overt miracle-worker.

A Theurge is a Hetaireian-affiliated Sorcerer who practices learned magic within the Hetaireia's doctrinal, ritual, and protective structures. Consecrated places, purification, supervision, relics, and disciplined ritual can make such work safer than unsheltered Sorcery, but Theurgy remains Sorcery. The Behdin has no branch-wide equivalent institution or universal religious license for Sorcery; its patriarchates, monasteries, schools, and states vary considerably.

Mysticism is disciplined perception and interpretation of metaphysical realities rather than direct alteration of them. It is legitimate but fallible in both branches, though it occupies a much more culturally prominent place within The Behdin.

The Blessed are different again. A Blessed person receives a supernatural charism through Athar or His Archons. Many Blessings are temporary and appear only for a particular need or crisis; a minority persist as longer vocations. Being Blessed does not by itself make someone a priest, Saint, saved person, or theological authority.

Atharite thinkers commonly interpret the distinction through Will: learned Sorcery uses mortal Will to manipulate metaphysical reality, while a Blessed person's Will provides consent, direction, and locality for an act whose decisive supernatural agency comes from Athar or His holy servants.

Spirits remain created beings. Communication or negotiation with them can be legitimate under appropriate conditions, but worship of them is doctrinally disordered. Both branches are wary of spirit relationships that displace human agency or identity, although the Hetaireia tends to frame the concern through free Will while The Behdin more often frames it through right created order and lucid creaturehood.

docs.title: Ardanic Succession Dispute
docs.text: The Ascension of Ardan produced both a political succession crisis and the central theological schism of Atharism.

docs.title: The Two Claims
docs.text:
One faction followed Theron of Meropolis, Ardan's closest military and political companion. This faction became the northern Hetaireia.

The other followed Polema, Ardan's wife, whose claim became associated with the southern tradition that developed into The Behdin.

The dispute concerned not only who possessed authority after Ardan, but what Ardan's Ascension actually meant and whether temporal succession could carry any part of Ardan's unique sacred vocation.

docs.title: Northern Teaching
docs.text:
Theron claimed visionary or eyewitness authority for the teaching that Ardan achieved Theosis by becoming one with Athar. Acceptance of Ardan's Theosis is a minimum requirement of Hetaireian communion.

Hetaireian theologians may dispute the exact metaphysical language, implications, and relationship between Ardan's humanity and his union with the Uncreated Flame, but they do not treat the Theosis itself as optional. Northern tradition therefore regards denial of Ardan's union with Athar as denial of the greatest act of piety ever witnessed.

docs.title: Southern Teaching
docs.text:
Polema rejected this doctrine. Southern tradition insists that Ardan remained a created servant of Athar even at the height of his Ascension.

The Behdin calls Ardan the Perfect Servant: the greatest known created Will and conventionally the greatest or foremost of the Archons, exalted by Athar without becoming identical to the Uncreated Flame.

Southern theology therefore treats the Hetaireian doctrine as a confusion of categories—created servant with Source, created Will with Uncreated Flame, and exaltation with identity. For The Behdin, Ardan's greatness lies precisely in the fact that a created person can become perfectly ordered to divine purpose without ceasing to be created.

Polema is honored as the first great defender of this Creator/creature distinction. Her authority is testimonial, interpretive, and historical rather than that of a second prophet.

docs.title: Temporal Succession
docs.text:
Polema claimed temporal stewardship after Ardan, not inheritance of his unique prophetic or Archonic vocation. She did not remarry and died without issue.

The later Zorahn dynastic claim passes through the son of Ardan's sister. Zorah treats that collateral succession as continuity of Ardan's temporal imperial house, while northern traditions may define Ardan's direct line more narrowly.

The distinction is important: even within southern tradition, Polema's political succession does not create a hereditary universal religious office. Zorah's Shahs may claim a special duty to guard the southern Atharite world, but The Behdin is not constitutionally subject to the Shah.

docs.title: Violence and Political Division
docs.text:
The schism produced bitter wars between the two successor traditions, including mutilation and execution connected to sectarian symbols and accusations of heresy. Surviving chronicles disagree about the exact chronology, scale, and sequence of these conflicts.

Both branches remember the conflict as proof that the dispute mattered profoundly. The Behdin nevertheless distinguishes the necessity of defending its doctrine from the claim that every later sectarian atrocity was therefore righteous.

docs.title: Athar and the Shadow
docs.text:
According to Atharite teaching, the world is Umbrathar because it is Athar's Shadow. The physical world is not false in the simple sense, but is understood as a mediated reflection or performance: a shadow-play sustained by Athar and His Archons.

This doctrine shapes Atharite attitudes toward spirits, magic, morality, and death. Created beings can reflect the Uncreated Flame, but no spirit, image, or lesser divinity is identical with Athar.

docs.title: Entropy and the End of the World
docs.text:
Atharites believe creation is subject to gradual corruption and exhaustion. The world will eventually wear down, and humanity with it. Those who properly serve Athar's Plan resist this spiritual entropy and may be remade after death as spirits or Archons.

The eventual purpose of this process is eschatological: Athar gathers worthy servants for the final struggle against the Outer Darkness.

docs.title: Limits of Atharite Doctrine
docs.text: Atharite theologians frequently use the doctrine of entropy to explain Beastmen, corrupted peoples, and the condition of societies distant from Athar's worship. Other sages dispute how literally such claims should be understood, and they should not be confused with uncontested history.

docs.title: Athar, the Uncreated Flame
docs.text:
Athar is the supreme divine principle of Atharism, worshipped throughout the Hetaireian Princedoms and many of the Great Cities. He is not normally represented in human or animal form; orthodox iconography depicts Him only as an abstract flame.

Atharite doctrine holds that all lesser spirits are created beings. They may be powerful, benevolent, dangerous, or deceptive, but they are not God. Worship directed toward them is therefore spiritually disordered even when the spirit itself is not malicious.

docs.title: The Plan
docs.text: Atharites believe creation unfolds according to a divine Plan. A person's relationship to that Plan is central to salvation, but the northern Hetaireia and southern Behdin disagree sharply over how human agency relates to it.

docs.title: Death and Archons
docs.text: Those who serve the Plan well may be remade after death into minor spirits or, in exceptional cases, Archons. Those utterly deprived of Athar's light may fall into the Outer Darkness and become demons.

docs.title: Ardan
docs.text: Ardan is Atharism's central prophet and redeemer. The nature of Ardan's relationship to Athar is the defining dispute of the Great Schism.

docs.title: Atharite Clergy
docs.text: All major Atharite traditions recognize Priests and supervisory clergy, though titles, jurisdiction, formation, and lifestyle differ significantly between the northern Hetaireia and southern The Behdin.

docs.title: Priests
docs.text:
Priests administer local congregations, maintain sacred order, tend or minister around consecrated Flames, and perform the ordinary religious functions of Atharite community life. Proper ordination confers genuine sacerdotal capacity: blessings, consecrations, marriages, funerary rites, purification, and other sacred acts matter metaphysically even when their effects are subtle and difficult to distinguish from ordinary causation.

This does not make every priest a Theurge, Mystic, or one of the Blessed. These are distinct supernatural or religious categories.

docs.title: Shared purification and exorcism
docs.text:
Ordinary properly ordained priests in both branches may perform routine purification, protective blessings, preliminary investigation of suspected hostile influence, and ordinary exorcistic prayer.

Difficult, resistant, dangerous, or diagnostically ambiguous cases are normally escalated to more experienced clergy or specialists. The exact path differs by branch: the Hetaireia has the professional Inquisition, while The Behdin relies on regional clergy, monasteries, schools, Mystics, sanctioned Sorcerers where permitted, renowned ascetics, the Blessed, and other local specialists.

docs.title: Northern Practice
docs.text:
Hetaireian priests may marry and personally own property. Clerical households therefore participate directly in education, patronage, hospitality, charity, inheritance, and local society. Office itself is not hereditary, but priestly families often enjoy major advantages through literacy, contacts, reputation, and familiarity with ecclesiastical life.

Ordinary Hetaireian priests tend the consecrated Flame, lead worship, teach, administer rites of incorporation, profession, marriage, penance, illness, death, and mourning, maintain records, distribute charity, bless homes and fields, mediate disputes, organize festivals and public supplications, provide hospitality, and frequently serve as local literate specialists.

docs.title: Southern Practice
docs.text:
Behdin priesthood places greater emphasis on ritual fitness, disciplined restraint, and limiting new attachments.

A valid existing marriage does not bar a man from ordination. An already-married candidate may become a priest, and the spouse's informed assent is a strong Behdin expectation. Ordination normally closes the door to a new marriage: an unmarried candidate ordinarily accepts celibacy, and a widowed priest does not normally remarry.

The principle is not that marriage is impure. Existing sacred bonds are honored rather than discarded. The restriction reflects the priest's heightened obligations, preparation for sacred service, and expectation of restraint.

Behdin priests are commonly held to stricter standards of fasting, vigil, sobriety, purification, continence around important rites, preparation before consecrated fire or sacred space, and avoidance of conspicuous luxury. Exact schedules and purity disciplines vary by jurisdiction and institution.

Non-monastic priests may possess practical personal property such as homes, books, tools, clothing, and ordinary goods. Aggressive accumulation, conspicuous luxury, clerical family fortunes, speculation for enrichment, and the conversion of sacred office into family patrimony are strongly suspect. Temple property, endowed office, and sacred assets are not inheritable household possessions.

docs.title: Formation and Ordination in the Hetaireia
docs.text:
Hetaireian formation uses a mixed and distributed model. Candidates may learn through clerical households, local temple or Seat schools, monasteries, regional seminaries, or major academies. Meropolis is the premier intellectual and prestige center but attendance there is not required for valid ordination.

Functional literacy is required before ordinary priestly ordination. Promising candidates who begin illiterate may receive tutoring, patronage, or monastic support before formal formation. Ordinary study includes sacred texts, theology, liturgy, ritual practice, pastoral care, recordkeeping, arithmetic and accounts, ecclesiastical procedure, and enough practical medicine or herbal knowledge to be useful in ordinary ministry. Higher schools add fields such as canon law, philosophy, history, diplomacy, and archival study.

Education and ordination are distinct. A school trains; legitimate ecclesiastical authority ordains. Academic pedigree affects prestige, not the validity of priestly rites.

Hetaireian ordination is performed under a Speaker's authority before a properly consecrated Flame. After preparation and examination, the candidate makes formal offerings and vows, demonstrates competence tending and ministering at the Flame, and is entrusted with sacred fire as a sign that he may carry the Hetaireia's rites outward. The rite is understood to create a real sacerdotal capacity through sacred status, oath, consecration, witness, and institutional continuity.

docs.title: Formation and Ordination in The Behdin
docs.text:
Behdin formation is decentralized. Patriarchal churches, monasteries, schools, senior clergy, and local institutions maintain their own recognized pathways within a shared expectation of doctrinal competence, ritual knowledge, discipline, and legitimate ordination.

Ordination normally takes place in consecrated space before the sacred Flame after examination, fasting, purification, vows, and preparation. It confers real sacerdotal capacity and makes the candidate fit, obligated, and authorized to approach, tend, administer, and where appropriate consecrate sacred things.

The Behdin does not ordinarily express ordination through the specifically Hetaireian symbolism of entrusting the new priest with portable living fire to carry outward.

docs.title: Monastic and Lay Religious Life
docs.text: Both branches distinguish priesthood from monastic or lay religious vocation. A monk or nun is not automatically a priest; an ordained person is not automatically a monastic.

docs.title: Hetaireian houses
docs.text:
The Hetaireia recognizes both male and female religious communities. Hetaireian monastic life is voluntary and is not ordinarily an irrevocable lifelong state. A person may enter for a period or remain until death. Marriage and pregnancy are incompatible with continuing monastic life because they create obligations that supersede the communal vocation. A permanent lifelong celibacy vow is therefore a separate and exceptional sacred commitment rather than the default condition of monastic profession.

Hetaireian houses are usually socially embedded rather than radically withdrawn. They may operate hospices, infirmaries, schools, archives, scriptoria, pilgrim lodgings, charitable kitchens, workshops, shrines, farms, and frontier support.

docs.title: Behdin houses
docs.text:
The Behdin treats full monastic profession as normally lifelong after a substantial period of probation. Novices may leave before final profession; final profession ordinarily creates a permanent sacred bond unless exceptional lawful release is granted.

Fully professed monastics renounce personal patrimony. Their institutions may nevertheless become extremely wealthy and may hold estates, farms, workshops, libraries, hospices, schools, pilgrim houses, ships, herds, rents, and other corporate assets. Personal poverty and institutional wealth are therefore not considered formally contradictory, though the tension is a constant source of criticism and reform.

The highest Behdin offices are normally drawn from clergy in a state of permanent renunciation, helping separate senior religious authority from ordinary household succession and dynastic family life. Ascetic reputation alone is insufficient: learning, ritual competence, doctrine, administration, judgment, and institutional recognition also matter.

docs.title: Speakers and Higher Clergy
docs.text:
Within the Hetaireia, Speakers oversee ecclesiastical districts beneath the High Ministry and above local priests. They may ordain, discipline, investigate, transfer, recognize, and set expectations for clergy, but distance and weak routine supervision leave many local priests with substantial practical autonomy. The Pontis is notionally selected from among the senior clergy, including prominent Speakers.

Southern terminology is less standardized. Existing Atharite usage recognizes Speakers in some Behdin contexts, but The Behdin is organized principally through historically sedimented patriarchal and regional churches, synods, monasteries, schools, and peer recognition rather than one universal rank ladder.

No single patriarch or Speaker exercises uncontested authority over the whole communion. Exact southern titles and the precise mapping of inherited terms remain deferred to later institutional and regional development.

docs.title: Theurgy, Mysticism, and Blessing
docs.text:
Theurgy is a specifically Hetaireian institutional category. A Theurge is a Hetaireian-affiliated Sorcerer practicing learned magic under Hetaireian theological, ritual, institutional, and protective discipline. The Behdin has no branch-wide equivalent order or universal license for religious Sorcery; practice varies by jurisdiction and institution.

A Mystic principally perceives and interprets metaphysical realities rather than directly imposing Will upon them. Mystics may be clergy, monastics, or lay specialists in either branch, though Mysticism is culturally more prominent within The Behdin.

The Blessed receive direct divine charisms through Athar or His Archons. A person may be priest, monastic, Theurge, Mystic, Blessed, or some combination, but none of these statuses automatically entails the others.

docs.title: The Behdin
docs.text:
The Behdin is the southern Atharite communion. It shares the worship of Athar, reverence for Ardan, sacred fire, cremation, pilgrimage, prayer, fasting, almsgiving, and much of the ancient religious inheritance that predates the Great Schism, but it developed a markedly different theology and institutional culture from the northern Hetaireia.

Behdin religion is characteristically contemplative, ascetic, mystical, monastic, and decentralized. Its believers commonly speak of accepting and discerning one's place within Athar's Plan, but this does not mean that human choice is unreal or that fatalistic passivity is pious.

docs.title: The Plan, Will, and Salvation
docs.text:
The Behdin teaches that Athar's Plan is complete. Nothing stands outside it as a rival source of sovereignty, including mortal Will. Human choices nevertheless genuinely belong to the people who make them: a created Will is a real cause within Creation and therefore one of the means through which the Plan becomes actual.

Moral responsibility depends on genuine authorship and assent. Intention, knowledge, coercion, corruption, possession, incapacity, and ignorance all matter. A person cannot excuse wrongdoing by saying that it was destined, because no mortal possesses a complete view of the Plan or reliable knowledge of final judgment.

Good works are therefore real causes rather than attempts to bargain with Athar. Prayer, fasting, restitution, charity, vows, pilgrimage, penance, and sacred rites can repair relationships, discipline appetite, purify, establish obligations, and reorder a person's life. They do not purchase salvation or force Athar's judgment.

Behdin teaching commonly describes salvation as the soul becoming rightly ordered to Athar and fitted to its ordained place in Creation, rather than escaping creaturehood or becoming sovereign over it.

docs.title: Ardan the Perfect Servant
docs.text:
The defining Behdin doctrine of the Great Schism concerns Ardan's Ascension.

The Behdin accepts Ardan's bodily Ascension but rejects the Hetaireian teaching that he became identical with Athar. Ardan is the Perfect Servant: the greatest known created Will, exalted by Athar to the highest created condition and commonly understood as the greatest or foremost of the Archons, but never the Uncreated Flame Himself.

This distinction is not a diminishing of Ardan. It is the center of Behdin praise. Ardan demonstrates how completely a created person can conform to divine purpose without ceasing to be created.

Polema, Ardan's wife, is honored as the first great defender of this distinction after the Ascension. Southern tradition gives her exceptional testimonial and historical authority, but she is not treated as a second prophet or as inheriting Ardan's unique sacred vocation. Her claim after Ardan concerned temporal stewardship. The later Zorahn dynasty traces that political inheritance through the collateral family line, while The Behdin recognizes no hereditary universal religious office descending from her.

The Behdin therefore regards the Schism as doctrinally necessary but does not teach that every atrocity committed during the sectarian wars was sanctified merely because it was committed in defense of correct doctrine. See Ardanic Succession Dispute.

docs.title: Mysticism and Ascetic Life
docs.text:
Behdin mysticism seeks communion through conformity, not absorption into Athar. Its highest ideal is sometimes described in learned terms as lucid creaturehood: the clearer a person becomes about what they are, what they are not, and what relationships properly bind them, the less they mistake created power, desire, or insight for sovereignty.

Mystical perception can be real. Dreams, omens, spiritual intuitions, divination, contemplation of Fate and Time, encounters with spirits, and other unusual experiences are taken seriously. They are also regarded as fallible. A true vision may be symbolic or partial; an accurate omen may come from a spirit rather than Athar; exhaustion, pride, illness, corruption, Sorcery, Places of Power, possession, or accumulated Vested Will may distort interpretation.

For this reason serious contemplative practice normally includes spiritual direction. Monasteries, learned schools, elders, abbots, ascetics, and other trusted guides preserve large bodies of case experience concerning dreams, visions, possession, miracles, relics, and spiritual error. Different Behdin traditions may preserve competing interpretations of famous cases rather than one universal mystical manual.

Ascetic discipline is intended to order relationships and appetite, not condemn material Creation. Food, marriage, family, property, craft, trade, government, and bodily life are not intrinsically evil. Fasting, vigil, celibacy, poverty, silence, prayer, pilgrimage, labor, and solitude are valued because they train attention, reduce competing attachments, create meaningful sacrifice, and discipline Will.

Extreme practice can itself become vanity. Communal monastic formation is therefore more normal than immediate radical solitude, even though hermits and recluses can acquire extraordinary prestige.

docs.title: Lay Vocation
docs.text:
Renunciation is a specialized vocation, not the measure by which every believer is judged.

A good Behdin parent, ruler, merchant, soldier, judge, farmer, sailor, craftsperson, or healer is expected to practice faithful stewardship of the relationships, duties, work, and goods actually entrusted to them. Households, public justice, hospitality, charity, protection of pilgrims, support of monasteries, honest fulfillment of obligations, and care for dependents are all religiously meaningful.

Laypeople sustain monasteries materially; monasteries and clergy owe the wider community prayer, teaching, counsel, hospitality, charity, learning, and sacred service. The ideal relationship is reciprocal rather than a hierarchy in which everyone outside a monastery is simply a failed ascetic.

docs.title: Sacred Fire and Consecration
docs.text:
Sacred fire is an inheritance from Atharism before the Schism. A consecrated Flame is a privileged created sign of the Uncreated Flame, but it is never Athar Himself.

The Behdin places unusual emphasis on that distinction. Just as Ardan is supremely holy while remaining created, sacred fire may be objectively consecrated and genuinely efficacious without becoming divine substance.

Major temples and monasteries commonly establish their Flames through legitimate transmission from older recognized Flames. Behdin scholars usually treat such Flame lineage as evidence of institutional continuity, authorization, and sacred history rather than as proof that one valid Flame is intrinsically holier than another. Ancient continuously maintained Flames can possess immense prestige, but continuous burning is not a condition of validity and an extinguished Flame may be restored by proper rite.

The Behdin ordinarily maintains a stronger distinction between consecrated Flame and domestic hearth than the Hetaireia. Household fire remains religiously meaningful and may be blessed, but it is not thereby a temple Flame.

docs.title: Life-Cycle Rites
docs.text:
A Behdin child is normally presented and named before a consecrated Flame by legitimate clergy, establishing a recognized relationship to household and religious community. The exact rite varies widely.

Religious adulthood centers on assuming personal responsibility for prayer, fasting, charity, penance, and the discipline of one's own Will. A serious fast or vigil before the Flame is common in many traditions, but no single continental choreography is required.

Marriage is a genuine sacred bond solemnized before consecrated fire. Unlike the common Hetaireian rite, Behdin marriage does not generally require the new household hearth to be physically kindled from the temple Flame, though the home may subsequently be blessed.

Ordination likewise occurs before the Flame after examination, fasting, purification, vows, and preparation. The rite confers real sacerdotal capacity and makes the priest fit, obligated, and authorized to approach, tend, administer, and where appropriate consecrate sacred things.

Final monastic profession is normally witnessed before sacred fire because it constitutes a permanent sacred bond.

docs.title: Cremation and the Dead
docs.text:
Cremation is a shared Atharite inheritance. The dead are not burned inside a temple, and the permanent sanctuary Flame is not used as a crematory furnace.

Instead, fire legitimately derived or transmitted from a consecrated Flame is carried outward to kindle the exterior funerary pyre. This practice predates the Great Schism and is shared with the Hetaireia. The two branches differ in procession, prayers, who carries the fire, preparation of the pyre, treatment of the ashes, and later purification.

Behdin relic practice therefore developed comfortably within a cremating culture. Relics may include ash, teeth, calcined bone, garments, tools, writings, ritual objects, or places strongly associated with a holy life or death. Learned theology rejects the idea that holiness is simply a substance trapped in flesh.

A genuine relic may produce no spectacular effect, while an object with false provenance may nevertheless acquire real metaphysical importance through centuries of devotion and Vested Will. Ardan himself has no ordinary postmortem bodily relics because Atharites accept his bodily Ascension; objects associated with his mortal life are a separate matter.

docs.title: Priesthood and Monastic Profession
docs.text:
Priesthood and monastic profession are distinct sacred vocations.

An already-married man may be ordained, and an existing valid marriage is not normally repudiated in the name of holiness. The informed assent of the spouse is a strong Behdin expectation. Ordination normally closes the door to a new marriage: an unmarried candidate ordinarily accepts celibacy, and a widowed priest does not normally remarry.

All priests are held to heightened standards of ritual fitness and disciplined restraint, including stricter expectations of fasting, sobriety, purification, preparation for sacred service, continence around important rites, and avoidance of conspicuous luxury. These practices do not imply that marriage, sex, food, death, or the body are intrinsically impure.

Non-monastic priests may own practical personal property. Homes, books, tools, clothing, and ordinary goods are legitimate; aggressive accumulation, conspicuous luxury, clerical family fortunes, and patrimonial capture of sacred office are deeply suspect.

Full monastic profession is normally lifelong after substantial probation. Fully professed monastics renounce personal patrimony, while their institutions may own extensive land, buildings, workshops, libraries, hostels, hospitals, farms, herds, ships, rents, and other corporate assets. This combination of personal poverty and institutional wealth is accepted in principle and chronically controversial in practice.

The highest religious offices are normally drawn from clergy who have entered permanent renunciation, separating the apex of Behdin governance from ordinary household and dynastic succession. Learning, administrative judgment, ritual competence, doctrinal reliability, and institutional recognition remain necessary; spectacular austerity alone does not qualify a person for high office.

docs.title: Patriarchates, Synods, and Communion
docs.text:
The Behdin is a polycentric communion, not a single bureaucracy.

Patriarchal and other major regional churches are historically sedimented rather than one-per-kingdom national churches. Their jurisdictions may reflect ancient sacred centers, older empires, pilgrimage routes, monasteries, trade networks, migration, and later political change. They can cross borders, overlap, or remain disputed.

Major Behdin churches govern themselves in ordinary administration. Their wider security depends on recognition: whether other churches, monasteries, schools, and communities receive their clergy, recognize their ordinations, accept their councils, share worship with them, and maintain sacred relationships.

Councils possess the authority that their participants and later reception can sustain. No permanent universal synod or patriarch issues decrees that automatically bind all of The Behdin. Orthodoxy at the continental scale is therefore an achieved consensus produced through councils, precedent, scholarship, recognition, monastic influence, and sometimes secular enforcement.

Communion is consequently relational rather than a single universal membership switch. One jurisdiction may reject a disputed patriarch while another continues to receive his clergy. A teaching may be condemned by a powerful coalition without every distant church accepting the condemnation at once.

There is no universal Behdin Inquisition. Investigation and discipline are handled by local clergy, synods, monasteries, schools, rulers, or temporary coalitions according to place and circumstance.

docs.title: Penance, Pilgrimage, Fasting, and Charity
docs.text:
Behdin penance is typically more enumerated than Hetaireian penance. Serious wrongdoing can create concrete obligations of restitution, sacred satisfaction, discipline, communal restoration, or spiritual reordering. A priest, elder, or other recognized authority may assign defined periods of fasting, vigils, prayer offices, restitution, service, alms, abstention, pilgrimage, hospitality, or care.

These obligations can genuinely be completed. Completion may restore religious standing, satisfy an obligation, or permit return to office or communion, but it does not certify final salvation.

Customary manuals, precedents, minimums, and recognized substitutions may exist, but Behdin practice is not one universal continental tariff. Intention, coercion, ignorance, capacity, health, status, harm, scandal, and willingness to repair all affect judgment.

Penance cannot ordinarily be outsourced. Others may help with restitution, logistics, charity, or shared obligations, but another person cannot simply perform the inward repentance or discipline of Will in the penitent's place.

Pilgrimage is especially important as vow fulfillment, assigned penance, ascetic ordeal, thanksgiving, mourning, relic devotion, study, and temporary withdrawal from ordinary life. Fasting is both ordinary discipline and a common measured penance. Charity is an obligation of stewardship and social repair, not a convenient cash substitute for every difficult religious duty.

docs.title: Magic, Blessing, and Discernment
docs.text:
The Behdin has no religion-wide counterpart to the Hetaireia's institutional category of Theurgy. Individual patriarchates, monasteries, schools, and states vary substantially in their treatment of Sorcery. Some supervise or patronize it; some permit only limited uses; some prohibit clergy from practicing; others regard almost all deliberate Sorcery with suspicion. Zamboula is an extreme case rather than a model of ordinary Behdin practice.

Sorcery is not intrinsically evil, but Behdin theology finds one temptation especially dangerous: the Sorcerer can mistake the effectiveness of created Will for sovereignty over Creation. Where Sorcery is sanctioned, purification, supervision, sacred space, written procedure, recovery, and spiritual discipline are common safeguards.

The Blessed are interpreted very differently. In a genuine Blessing, Athar or His Archons provide the decisive supernatural agency while the mortal remains a consenting created person. Behdin theologians often treat this as a vivid confirmation of the same principle seen in Ardan: perfect instrumentality does not require loss of personhood.

Being Blessed proves neither salvation nor jurisdiction. A lay shepherd repeatedly used as an instrument of miracle may become more famous than a patriarch while possessing no right to ordain clergy or define doctrine.

A central rule of Behdin discernment is that power does not authenticate its own source. A vision coming true does not prove it came from Athar. A successful exorcism does not prove every doctrine held by the exorcist. A powerful relic may be misunderstood. Genuine supernatural evidence still requires interpretation.

docs.title: Spirits, Confluence, Corruption, and Exorcism
docs.text:
Spirits are created persons, not lesser gods. Communication, negotiation, placation, or carefully bounded exchange may be legitimate; worship belongs to Athar alone.

Deep human/spirit confluence is disputed. The characteristic Behdin concern is one of right created order and lucid creaturehood: human and spirit are distinct created Wills, and deliberately dissolving the distinction between them risks disorder even where controlled confluence is not objectively possession or corruption.

Behdin learned practice distinguishes pollution, contamination, corruption, and possession. These are afflictions or conditions, not synonyms for wickedness. Guilt depends on assent, knowledge, negligence, coercion, and circumstance.

Ordinary priests can perform routine purification, protective blessings, preliminary investigation, and ordinary exorcistic rites. Severe, resistant, or ambiguous cases may require experienced clergy, monastic specialists, Mystics, sanctioned Sorcerers, renowned ascetics, the Blessed, or regional specialists.

Ascetic treatment is not automatically "more fasting." Exhaustion, isolation, and trance can worsen damaged spiritual boundaries. Sometimes the proper remedy is food, sleep, ordinary work, stable relationships, purification, and a temporary end to severe contemplative practice.

docs.title: Holy Time
docs.text:
The Behdin uses the same objective twelve-Face year and the standard AA chronology without requiring one separate southern civil calendar. Local cultures may use their own month names, eras, or New Years.

Athardyos is shared pre-Schism sacred time and is the customary day of principal communal worship. The eleven visible Full Moons commonly receive additional evening prayer, vigil, contemplation, readings, fasting, dream-discernment, or spiritual direction.

The Great Vigil on 16 Stranger is likewise an ancient Atharite inheritance. Common Behdin observance tends toward prolonged prayer, fasting, silence, contemplation before the Flame, charity, hospitality, and examination of one's spiritual condition, though local cultures may celebrate more festively.

Ardan's Ascension on 19 Father's Moon is one of the greatest Behdin holy days. It celebrates Athar's exaltation of the Perfect Servant rather than identity between Ardan and the Uncreated Flame.

The Passage season around the Autumnal Equinox preserves the ancient Atharite pilgrimage memory of Mount Kromon and the Nelorelis. Behdin communities commonly associate it with pilgrimage, vow fulfillment, penitential journeys, hospitality, and temporary withdrawal from ordinary attachments.

Wolf's Moon into Stranger's Moon is widely treated as a penitential season for completing obligations, restitution, vows, reconciliation, and preparation for the Great Vigil, but there is no single universal starting date or one continent-wide month-long fast.

Polema is universally honored throughout The Behdin, but no single continent-wide feast date has yet displaced the differing commemorations maintained by regional traditions.

The shared Behdin calendar is intentionally thin. Patriarchates, monasteries, pilgrimage centers, saints, ascetics, founders, cities, older local festivals, and historic events create much denser regional calendars.

docs.title: Rulers, Great Cities, and Internal Diversity
docs.text:
Behdin rulers are expected to act as protectors and patrons of sacred order, but political office is not priesthood. A ruler may defend temples, endow monasteries, protect pilgrimage, host councils, or enforce ecclesiastical judgments without thereby creating doctrine or conferring ordination.

Zorah makes the strongest political claim. Its Shahs trace temporal continuity from Ardan through Polema's succession and possess Ardan's scepter. Zorahn doctrine therefore describes the Shah as a hereditary guardian of the southern Atharite world.

Other major Behdin centers concede essentially no constitutional authority to this claim. Al-Anwar's merchant princes are likely to regard it with amused irreverence; Khemet possesses its own ancient legal and religious continuity; Zamboula rejects outside supervision for reasons of its own. Particular rulers or institutions may defer to Zorah for political reasons, but The Behdin does not belong to the Shah.

The communion accepts broad internal diversity. Ascetic customs, penitential schedules, monastic rules, mystical methods, relations with Sorcery, spirit practice, holy days, ruler relations, vestments, and local saints may differ greatly.

That diversity has boundaries. Athar alone is the Uncreated Flame; all other beings remain created; Ardan is the supreme created servant rather than Athar; worship cannot properly be redirected to spirits; and mystical or magical power does not prove divinity.

The Behdin can also absorb older religious civilizations by reordering inherited practices under Atharite doctrine rather than erasing them automatically. Khemet's Deathspeakers are the clearest example: care for right relations with the dead can be reconciled with Atharism, while coercive Necromancy remains a violation of proper posthumous Will and status.

This flexibility helps explain how a systemically heterodox city such as Zamboula can remain nominally Behdin for generations. Communion can fracture through overlapping refusals of clergy, teaching, worship, and recognition without one universal office issuing a final expulsion decree on behalf of everyone.

docs.title: Hetaireia
docs.text:
The Hetaireia is the northern Atharite tradition centered ecclesiastically on Meropolis. It is also one of the principal institutions binding the culturally diverse Hetaireian Realms into a shared civilization.

Hetaireian identity is not an ethnicity or nationality. It can coexist with local, linguistic, dynastic, civic, ethnic, and Realm identities. Its common order depends less on uniform law or government than on interoperability: recognized clergy and rites, common religious calendars, marriage and burial norms, oath traditions, pilgrimage and sanctuary networks, documentary recognition, and shared forms of legitimacy.

docs.title: Doctrine
docs.text:
The Hetaireia emphasize works, free will, and active participation in Athar's Plan. Human beings must choose rightly and enact divine purpose in a world threatened by darkness.

Their defining doctrine concerns Ardan's Ascension. Hetaireian communion requires acceptance that Ardan achieved Theosis by becoming one with Athar, together with acceptance of the authority of the Pontis. Other theological propositions may remain disputable within the Hetaireian world unless established as essential doctrine.

Spirits, fey beings, and similar entities are understood as created beings rather than gods. Their existence is not itself evil, and careful communication with them can be permissible. Worship of them is heretical because it gives divine devotion to something created.

Southerners regard the northern symbol of a human hand within the Uncreated Flame as sacrilegious. Northerners regard southern rejection of Ardan's Theosis as a denial of the greatest act of piety in history.

docs.title: Institution
docs.text:
The Hetaireia are led by the Pontis, Ardan's Steward during Ardan's absence. The Pontis possesses final Hetaireian doctrinal authority subject to scripture but is not regarded as infallible.

The High Ministry beneath the Pontis oversees major transregional and central functions. Speakers administer ecclesiastical districts, while priests serve local congregations and are more deeply embedded in local communities and patronage networks.

The Hetaireia controls transregional recognition of legitimate clergy and rites. This gives it unusual power across political boundaries even where it lacks direct secular coercion.

The Pontis is notionally selected from senior clergy, but a powerful magisterial family has dominated succession for roughly two centuries. The office remains ecclesiastical in law while functioning increasingly like a dynasty in practice. See Factions and Reform.

docs.title: Lived Religion
docs.text:
The consecrated Flame is the ritual heart of Hetaireian life. Birth and incorporation, profession, marriage, sickness, funerals, mourning, pilgrimage, penance, sanctuary, vows, public supplication, holy days, and household life are all shaped by religious practice. See Hetaireian Religious Life.

A settlement can contain devout Hetaireians without a consecrated Flame, but the Church does not regard it as a fully constituted Hetaireian religious community until one is established.

Cremation is shared Atharite practice. Fire legitimately transmitted or derived from a consecrated Flame is carried outward to kindle the exterior funerary pyre; the corpse is not burned inside the temple and the permanent sanctuary Flame is not used as a crematory furnace.

docs.title: Clergy and Religious Houses
docs.text:
Northern priests may marry and personally own property. Ordination confers genuine sacerdotal capacity, but neither learned Sorcery nor direct miraculous charism is produced automatically by clerical education. Monks and nuns form a major parallel religious vocation and are common in teaching, charity, healing, archives, pilgrimage support, and frontier life.

Meropolis is the highest-prestige center of clerical education, but the Hetaireia uses a distributed system of local schools, monasteries, Speakers' Seats, seminaries, and academies. Academic pedigree affects status rather than sacramental validity. See Clergy and Monastic Life and Atharite Clergy.

Ordinary priests can perform routine purification, protective blessings, preliminary investigation of hostile spiritual influence, and ordinary exorcistic prayer. Difficult, dangerous, resistant, or ambiguous cases are escalated to experienced clergy, Speakers, the Inquisition, Theurges, Mystics, or the Blessed as circumstances require.

docs.title: Law and Transregional Authority
docs.text:
The Hetaireia does not ordinarily provide one secular legal code for the north. Its jurisdiction is strongest where religion intersects with heresy, clerical status, marriage, legitimacy, sacred vows, sanctuary, sacrilege, ecclesiastical property, and related matters.

Princes guard secular prerogatives jealously. Ordinary crime, taxation, landholding, military obligation, inheritance, and most contracts remain principally secular unless a specifically ecclesiastical question is involved.

Its comparative strength increases when disputes cross political boundaries. Speakers, senior clergy, and the Pontis are important as arbitrators, authenticators, and guarantors because the Hetaireian Realms possess no common secular government above their Princes.

The Church also provides connective infrastructure through sanctuaries, hospices, religious houses, pilgrimage routes, archives, seals, charity, schools, and recognized clergy.

docs.title: Theurgy, Blessing, Mysticism, Sorcery, and the Supernatural
docs.text:
A Theurge is a Hetaireian-affiliated Sorcerer who practices learned magic inside the Hetaireia's ritual, doctrinal, and protective structures. Consecrated spaces, purification, supervision, relics, and disciplined procedure can make Theurgic practice substantially safer than unsheltered Sorcery, but Theurgy remains Sorcery.

The Blessed are categorically different. Their overt supernatural gifts are charisms manifested through Athar or His Archons rather than powers acquired through technical magical study. Many Blessings are temporary and circumstantial; a minority continue as longer vocations.

Ordinary priests still possess real sacerdotal efficacy through ordination even when they are neither Theurges nor Blessed.

Mysticism is also distinct. Mystics principally perceive and interpret metaphysical realities—omens, Fate, Time, spiritual conditions, divination, mediumship, and related phenomena—rather than directly altering them through Sorcery. Mysticism is legitimate but fallible within the Hetaireia and may be practiced by clergy, monastics, scholars, astrologers, lay specialists, or independent practitioners.

An accurate vision or divination does not automatically carry doctrinal authority. Hetaireian institutional culture is less vision-centered and contemplatively saturated than The Behdin and is more likely to route extraordinary supernatural claims through clergy, scholarship, Speakers, or Inquisitorial discernment.

Sorcery is dangerous but not intrinsically sinful. Some priests, monks, nuns, and Inquisitors study disciplined applications of the Eightfold Method, especially where frontier or investigative work requires supernatural perception, warding, or related techniques.

The Hetaireia also distinguishes controlled spirit contact from worship. Human/spirit confluence is not automatically possession or corruption, but it is controversial. Hetaireian concern centers on preserving and properly exercising free human Will: deliberate surrender, displacement, or habitual abdication of human agency is spiritually suspect even where a bounded confluence retains consent and agency.

The Church increasingly distinguishes pollution, contamination, corruption, and possession as different supernatural conditions rather than one undifferentiated taint. None automatically proves moral guilt.

The Inquisition is the Hetaireia's small professional institution for investigating serious supernatural and religious threats. Its members are trained to distinguish disease, fraud, harmless custom, spirits, Fey, Shades, Starspawn, ordinary Sorcery, Theurgy, Mysticism, genuine Blessing, possession, corruption, and true Diabolism before choosing a remedy.

docs.title: Frontier and Mission
docs.text:
Frontier Hetaireianism depends heavily on circuit priests, monks, nuns, local judgment, and accommodation of inherited custom. Harmless older festivals and practices are often reoriented rather than abolished. Native clergy are preferred in mature converted communities, though Meropolis usually demands more rigorous formation than distant Speakers can practically provide.

Peaceful unbelief does not by itself create a normal Hetaireian right of conquest. The Church becomes much more willing to sanction suppression or compulsory religious restructuring when cult, supernatural corruption, persistent aggression, warfare, or conquest become entangled. See Frontier and Missionary Practice.

docs.title: Politics and Reform
docs.text:
Hetaireian politics contains four broad, overlapping currents: Pontists, Restorationists, Traditionalists, and Militants. They are networks of affinity and patronage rather than formal parties. Dynasticist is a hostile label often applied to Pontists thought more loyal to the reigning Pontifical family than to the office itself.

Faction is not heresy. Appointments, seminaries, patronage, synods, sermons, treatises, the High Ministry, the Inquisition, religious houses, and the Hiera Tagmata are all arenas of factional influence.

docs.title: Marriage and Legitimacy
docs.text: The Hetaireia guarantees the transregional religious validity of marriage and the legitimacy of children without imposing one secular inheritance system. A marriage recognized by the Church can therefore be valid across the Hetaireian world even though different Principalities disagree sharply over what property, dynastic rights, offices, or claims the resulting children may inherit.

docs.title: Politics of Princely Legitimacy
docs.text:
The rulers of the Hetaireian Realms are called Princes because their office descends from the Principalities of the New Ardanic Empire and remains embedded in the Ardanic political order. The Pontis recognizes princely legitimacy within the wider civilization but does not normally create rulers without meaningful local claims or govern their Principalities directly.

A ruler claiming Kingship asserts non-derivative temporal sovereignty outside that inherited order. This is inherently a rejection of Pontifical temporal supremacy, though not automatically a rejection of Athar, Ardan's Theosis, or the Pontis's religious office.

docs.title: Armed Power
docs.text: Military command historically belonged primarily to Princes. The Pontis has long maintained forces for household and local defense, especially the Vyrkar Guard, but the modern expansion of Pontifical military power into the Hiera Tagmata is controversial. Its supporters present the Sacred Regiments as necessary protection against dangers too large or transregional for fragmented princely forces; critics fear a new direct Pontifical coercive power.

docs.title: Clergy and Monastic Life
docs.text: Hetaireian religious life distinguishes priesthood, Theurgic training, Blessing, and monastic profession as statuses or capacities that can overlap without being identical.

docs.title: Priests and Formation
docs.text:
Ordinary Hetaireian priests are trained, literate, professional clergy embedded in local society. Functional literacy is required for ordination. Candidates may be trained through local temple schools, monasteries, Speakers’ Seats, regional seminaries, or major academies. Meropolis is the highest-prestige intellectual center, but attendance there is not required for legitimate ordination.

Formation normally includes scripture, theology, liturgy, ritual practice, pastoral care, recordkeeping, accounts, ecclesiastical procedure, and practical medicine. Advanced schools add canon law, philosophy, history, diplomacy, and archival study.

Education and ordination are distinct. A school trains; legitimate ecclesiastical authority ordains. Great City pedigree affects prestige, not sacramental validity.

docs.title: Ordination
docs.text:
Ordination is performed under a Speaker’s authority before a properly consecrated Flame. After preparation and examination, the candidate makes formal offerings and vows, demonstrates competence in tending and ministering at the Flame, and is entrusted with living sacred fire as a sign that he may carry Hetaireian rites outward.

Ordination creates a genuine sacerdotal capacity. Priestly blessings and rites have real, usually subtle efficacy even when the priest is neither a Theurge nor one of the Blessed.

docs.title: Theurges and the Blessed
docs.text:
A Theurge is an Atharite-affiliated Sorcerer trained to practice dangerous learned magic within the Church's ritual, doctrinal, and protective structures. A priest may become a Theurge through additional magical study and discipline, but ordination alone does not confer Sorcerous skill.

The Blessed are different. Their overt supernatural gifts are charisms granted directly through Athar or His Archons and cannot be produced by clerical education. A Blessed person may be lay or clerical, settled or itinerant, and many Blessings are temporary.

docs.title: Clerical Households
docs.text: Marriage is normal for Hetaireian priests. Clerical households often become centers of literacy, education, hospitality, charity, and patronage. Priesthood is not hereditary, but children of clergy begin with major educational and social advantages, making clerical families and quasi-dynastic networks common.

docs.title: Monks and Nuns
docs.text:
Hetaireian Atharism recognizes both male and female religious communities. Monks and nuns may devote themselves to prayer, charity, teaching, healing, archives, pilgrimage support, scholarship, workshops, relief work, or frontier service.

Monastic profession is voluntary and is not lifelong by default. A person may serve for years and leave without disgrace. Marriage or pregnancy is incompatible with continuing monastic life because the new household or parental obligations supersede monastic discipline. Lifelong celibacy requires a separate exceptional vow.

Most houses contain lay brothers or sisters; some also contain ordained priests, Theurges, and Blessed persons. Lay religious need not enter with the educational qualifications required for priesthood and may learn literacy after joining. Monastic houses are therefore major channels of education and social mobility.

docs.title: Frontier Practice
docs.text:
On the frontier, practical roles blur. A priest, monk, and nun may all teach, farm, keep records, tend the sick, host travelers, and organize relief. Their formal capacities remain distinct, however: monastic profession does not by itself confer priestly authority.

Brothers and sisters are vital connective tissue in communities without resident priests. They may maintain an existing consecrated Flame, organize worship, preserve records, and prepare people for a circuit priest’s visit. Establishing or reconsecrating a Flame requires priestly authority.

docs.title: Factions and Reform
docs.text:
The Hetaireia is neither institutionally pure nor uniformly corrupt. Its recurrent abuses arise from patronage, family influence, wealth, secular pressure, self-protection, factional rivalry, and ordinary human weakness.

Patronage is normal and often necessary. Princes, noble houses, merchants, monasteries, clerical families, and foundations support temples, schools, hospitals, and candidates for office. Corruption begins when that support becomes the purchase of ordination, judgment, sacred office, or ecclesiastical legitimacy.

Married clergy also create powerful clerical families. Such families can preserve learning and administrative competence across generations, but they can just as easily turn influence into hereditary capture. The Pontificate itself is the most consequential example: one magisterial family has dominated the formally elective office for roughly two centuries.

docs.title: The Pontifical Dynasty
docs.text:
Dynastic continuity has brought real advantages to Meropolis: long-term policy, durable diplomatic relationships, administrative memory, and the ability to pursue institutional projects across successive Pontificates. Its critics answer that an ecclesiastical office has become a crown in all but name.

The modern expansion of the Hiera Tagmata intensifies the dispute. Supporters see a necessary answer to fragmented princely power and transregional threats; critics see a quasi-hereditary Pontificate constructing direct secular coercive power.

The exact family tree, succession machinery, and future claimant politics remain deliberately unsettled.

docs.title: Major Currents
docs.text:
The Hetaireia contains four broad, overlapping currents rather than modern political parties.

Pontists favor strong Pontifical leadership and generally defend the existing Meropolitan order. Opponents sometimes call them Dynasticists, especially when they appear more loyal to the reigning family than to the office itself.

Restorationists oppose dynastic capture, simony, patronage abuse, and corruption. Many favor stronger formal standards, audits, and central institutions rather than decentralization.

Traditionalists defend the older loose constitution of the Hetaireia: strong Speakers and Seats, customary privileges, regional autonomy, and suspicion of Meropolitan centralization.

Militants prioritize defense, frontier support, missionary expansion, the Inquisition, Theurgical deployment, and military readiness against supernatural and temporal threats.

These currents overlap. A priest may be a Militant Restorationist, a Pontist skeptical of the current dynastic heir, or a Traditionalist who strongly supports the Inquisition.

docs.title: How Factions Operate
docs.text:
Factional influence moves through appointments, seminaries, teaching networks, patronage, correspondence, sermons, treatises, synods, monasteries, Speakers’ Seats, the High Ministry, the Inquisition, and the Hiera Tagmata. Institutions may lean toward one current for a generation without permanently belonging to it.

Most of the time factional politics is slow. Pontifical succession is the moment when decades of patronage, correspondence, appointments, alliances, and grievances converge suddenly.

Faction is not heresy. Weaponizing heresy proceedings against legitimate ecclesiastical rivals is itself a grave abuse, though it sometimes occurs.

docs.title: Reform and Corruption
docs.text: Reform is not politically neutral. A sincere campaign against nepotism may also centralize Meropolitan authority; a local traditionalist may defend a healthy custom for principled reasons or simply because it protects his power. Good men can make bad institutional choices, and corrupt men can perform useful work.

docs.title: Frontier and Missionary Practice
docs.text: The frontier does not produce a different Hetaireian religion, but it changes which competencies matter. Priests are scarcer, travel is slower, supernatural threats are more common, inherited non-Hetaireian customs remain closer to the surface, and local judgment often substitutes for distant supervision.

docs.title: Circuit Ministry
docs.text:
Communities without resident priests may be served monthly, seasonally, or irregularly by circuit clergy. Monks and nuns often provide continuity between visits by maintaining an existing consecrated Flame, keeping records, teaching, tending the sick, organizing charity, and preparing people for rites that require a priest.

Families may wait months for marriage, incorporation, profession, difficult confession, or other sacerdotal rites. Delay does not itself condemn anyone, but proper rites remain important and are regularized when clergy become available.

docs.title: Accommodation
docs.text:
Missionaries prefer accommodation where possible. Old dances, decorations, songs, sacred trees, seasonal festivals, and similar customs can survive if their worshipful meaning is removed or redirected toward Athar and Creation.

The hard boundary is worship. Spirits, fey beings, and other powers are real created beings rather than gods. Some are benign and may coexist peacefully with Hetaireian communities. Priests, Theurges, and Inquisitors may communicate or negotiate with them for serious pastoral, protective, or investigative purposes. Laypeople are discouraged from deliberate spirit-contact because they usually lack the discernment needed to recognize deception, manipulation, binding, or gradual misplaced devotion.

docs.title: Native Clergy
docs.text:
The Hetaireia aims to develop clergy from converted populations rather than import priests forever. Meropolitan authorities strongly prefer rigorous seminary education, especially for peoples regarded as newly converted or spiritually immature. Frontier Speakers and priests may recognize equivalent local formation when distance and necessity make the ideal impractical.

Standards remain real: priestly candidates require literacy, doctrine, liturgy, pastoral discipline, and a mature understanding of the difference between inherited custom and forbidden worship. Pathways to those standards vary.

docs.title: Sorcery and Blessing on the Frontier
docs.text:
Priestly status does not itself confer magical training or direct miracle-working. Some frontier priests, monks, nuns, and Inquisitors study disciplined Sorcery and thereby become Theurges, using Church ritual, consecrated spaces, purification, and supervision to reduce the dangers of direct metaphysical work.

The Blessed are different. A person may manifest a temporary or enduring charism through Athar or His Archons without being trained as a Sorcerer or even ordained. Such figures can be especially important where ordinary ecclesiastical infrastructure is weak, but their appearance is unpredictable and cannot replace circuit clergy, temples, or established rites.

docs.title: Conversion and Coercion
docs.text:
Peaceful unbelief does not by itself create a normal Hetaireian right of conquest. Ordinary missionary policy favors preaching, service, education, example, accommodation, and gradual conversion.

The threshold changes when religion and threat become entangled. Cults tied to demon or Starspawn worship, human sacrifice, predatory spirit pacts, persistent aggression, or religiously mandated warfare may be suppressed by force. Warfare, conquest, or political incorporation can also make compulsory religious restructuring much more acceptable to Hetaireian authorities than it would be in peacetime.

Religious and secular motives are therefore often difficult to separate. A Prince may sincerely suppress a dangerous cult while also coveting its territory; a missionary may see conquest as an opportunity to convert; an Inquisitor may discover that a supposed religious casus belli is genuine, exaggerated, or fraudulent.

docs.title: Hetaireian Religious Life
docs.text: Hetaireian Atharism is a lived religion whose rites structure birth, maturity, marriage, illness, death, mourning, pilgrimage, penance, vows, holy days, communal crisis, and public life. Its worship is recognizably old-world and liturgical: sacred texts, preaching, vestments, incense, seasonal observance, and community announcements are ordinary features of services.

docs.title: The Sacred Flame
docs.text:
A properly consecrated Flame is the ritual heart of a Hetaireian community. Sacred fire itself predates the Great Schism and is shared Atharite inheritance. Learned priests teach that all properly consecrated Flames are equally blessed, though popular religion often attributes distinctive qualities to particular Flame lineages or “families,” frequently associating them with particular Archons.

A settlement may contain devout Hetaireians without a consecrated Flame, but the Church regards such a place as religiously incomplete. Establishing and maintaining a Flame is one of the clearest signs that a frontier camp intends to become a durable Hetaireian town.

docs.title: Incorporation and Profession
docs.text:
Infants are normally incorporated into the community by a priest using ash from a consecrated Flame. Continental validity depends chiefly on legitimate priestly authority and proper sacred ash; detailed procedure varies widely.

Coming-of-age or formal profession is a separate assumption of religious responsibility and is associated with lighting, tending, or adding to the Holy Flame.

These exact forms are Hetaireian developments rather than generic rites imposed on The Behdin, even though both branches inherited fire-centered sacred life from pre-Schism Atharism.

docs.title: Marriage and the Hearth
docs.text:
Marriage is a sacred bond. Bride and groom add fuel to the sacred Flame and establish their household by kindling its first hearth from sacred fire. Cohabitation without the proper rite is therefore regarded not only as socially irregular but as founding a household without the sacred ordering proper to it.

The physical transfer of sacred fire into the new household is a characteristic Hetaireian expression of the shared Atharite relationship between consecrated Flame and Hearth; it is not the normal Behdin marriage form.

docs.title: Illness, Death, and Mourning
docs.text:
Ordinary priests visit the sick, pray, anoint, burn incense, and offer real but usually subtle blessings. These rites may bring relief without producing spectacular cures.

Cremation is the standard Atharite treatment of the dead. The shared pre-Schism funerary pattern carries fire legitimately transmitted or derived from a consecrated Flame outward to the cremation place, where it kindles the exterior funerary pyre. The corpse is not burned inside a temple and the permanent sanctuary Flame is not used as a crematory furnace.

Hetaireian procession, prayers, handling of ash, mourning, and local purification customs vary by Realm and community. Formal mourning is expected, though clothing, duration, and household rules vary by Realm. Longer mourning periods for widows also serve as a recognized social protection against unwanted pressure to remarry.

docs.title: Pilgrimage and Penance
docs.text:
Pilgrimage is a major devotional practice. Learned clergy reject the idea that pilgrimages can be accumulated as a mechanical salvific score, though lay religion often drifts toward such thinking.

Hetaireian penance emphasizes spiritual discipline, restitution, correction, and reorientation of the will rather than a simple accounting of good and bad works.

docs.title: Sanctuary
docs.text: Properly invoked sanctuary places a person temporarily under ecclesiastical and metaphysical protection. Sanctuary protects process rather than innocence: it suspends immediate vengeance or seizure while a case is heard, mediated, or transferred into proper jurisdiction. Violence or forcible seizure in consecrated sacred space, especially near the Flame, is grave sacrilege.

docs.title: Public Supplication
docs.text: Drought, plague, famine, siege, disaster, or supernatural corruption may trigger extraordinary communal supplication: processions, intensified prayer, fasting or discipline, continuous tending of the Flame, incense, charity, relief work, and practical action suited to the crisis. Speakers can proclaim wider district observances.

docs.title: Holy Time
docs.text:
Athardyos is the customary day of communal worship and is shared pre-Schism Atharite sacred time. The Hetaireia developed a comparatively standardized continental feast cycle on top of that older inheritance.

Hetaireian holy days are preferably tied to seasonal, lunar, solar, stellar, or other recurring natural phenomena before arbitrary commemorative dates. Local historical anniversaries are more common at Realm and local level.

The Hetaireia recognizes twelve major continental observances, one associated with each Face-month, alongside weekly Athardyos worship, regular Full-Moon devotion, and a much richer body of regional and local festivals. The complete dates, meanings, and customary character of the twelve major feasts are given in Hetaireian Sacred Calendar.

The Great Vigil on 16 Stranger and the Passage pilgrimage season preserve pre-Schism Atharite roots, while their detailed Hetaireian expressions belong to the northern branch.

Many broad Hetaireian feasts have absorbed older local festivals, so the same holy day may look very different in different Realms.

docs.title: High Ministry
docs.text: The High Ministry, called the Directoratum in Meropolitan, is the central administrative cabinet of the northern Hetaireia, serving directly beneath the Pontis. “High Ministry” is the ordinary translated name used by foreign speakers.

docs.title: Functions
docs.text: Its ministries oversee such matters as liturgy, evangelism, ecclesiastical property, administration, records, temple construction and maintenance, and the Hiera Tagmata.

docs.title: Territorial Administration
docs.text:
The central ministries maintain branches within ecclesiastical districts. A Speaker oversees each district, while local priests serve its congregations.

This structure makes the Hetaireia considerably more centralized and hierarchical than the southern Behdin.
