docs.title: Necromancer
docs.text: Necromancers are practitioners who use Will to override the proper relationships among life, death, body, soul, memory, identity, and the agency of the dead.

docs.title: What Makes Necromancy
docs.text:
Necromancy is not defined merely by studying death, speaking with ghosts, using bones or grave goods in sympathetic work, or performing funerary rites. The defining act is coercive imposition: treating another person's death, remains, spirit, or posthumous identity as something subject to the practitioner's Will.

A corpse is not metaphysically equivalent to inert matter. Human remains retain connections to identity, kinship, memory, funerary status, Vested Will, and the Soul that once inhabited the living body. Making a skeleton walk therefore means forcing reality to sustain a state that is deeply contrary to the relationships already attached to those bones.

Typical Necromantic acts include corpse animation, binding or compelling the dead as instruments, forcing a soul to remain where it would otherwise depart, manufacturing undeath, and overriding another person's posthumous agency.

docs.title: Danger
docs.text:
Necromancy is dangerous even without Demons. A Diabolist invites or accommodates an alien Will; a Necromancer instead trains their own Will to contort itself into increasingly unnatural configurations in order to hold spiritually backward states together.

Repeated practice can produce obsession, alienation, corruption, severe metaphysical stress, and increasing affinity with polluted or death-distorted places and beings.

The difficulty of a working depends on metaphysical weight, not just physical complexity. Anonymous old bones are one thing; the carefully tended remains of a beloved matriarch remembered by living descendants, protected by funerary rites, and invested with generations of family identity are another.

docs.title: Consent and Self-Directed Mortuary Magic
docs.text:
Interfering with the ordinary course of death is not by itself enough to define Necromancy.

A person may voluntarily bind themselves to a tomb, lineage, oath, or posthumous duty. Such acts can be dangerous, unnatural, or unwise, but because the relevant Will is acting upon itself they may instead belong to Deathspeaking, Sorcery, Shamanism, or another mortuary tradition.

Likewise, a dead person who knowingly authorized descendants to call upon them for counsel presents a fundamentally different case from a shade compelled against its Will.

Consent does not guarantee safety or good consequences. It establishes standing; it does not abolish the metaphysical risks of refusing the ordinary transition of death.

docs.title: Khemet and the Cult of the Undying
docs.text:
Ancient Khemet is remembered as the great historical center of the Cult of the Undying, whose pursuit of intelligent undeath represents one of the setting's clearest Necromantic traditions.

Modern Khemite Deathspeakers define themselves partly against that legacy. Their discipline preserves or negotiates the agency and proper relationships of the dead rather than overriding them.

docs.title: Bestiary
docs.text:
The Bestiary collects creatures and extraordinary beings of Umbrathar. Loranian scholars commonly classify creatures by their nature, origin, and mode of continuation rather than simply by appearance or danger.

See Bestiary Taxonomy for the broader classification system.

docs.title: Major Categories
docs.text:
• Beasts — unintelligent creatures that reproduce through a natural life cycle, including stable populations whose remote ancestry was magical or artificial.
  • Monstrosities — creatures whose defining forms arise through curses, disease, magical transformation, corruption, sorcerous creation, or comparable processes rather than an ordinary reproducing lineage.
  • Plants — nonsapient plant creatures and extraordinary flora; sapient plant-beings are classified according to their supernatural nature, with Great Trees treated as Fey.
  • Undead — beings existing in an undead or post-mortem state.
  • Fey — intrinsically magical beings that belong to the natural world, including several peoples once treated as conventional nonhuman races.
  • Demons — beings whose ultimate origin lies in the Outer Darkness, including the broad class of Starspawn trapped within Creation.
  • Archons — primordial or celestial beings belonging to the ordered fabric of Creation, including beings of vastly different rank and function.
  • Humans — recurring human encounter and reference profiles; inclusion in the Bestiary does not imply that human cultures are monster species.

These are scholarly categories rather than encounter roles. Common names such as Behemoth, lineages such as Dragon/Wyrm, and regional categories such as Jinn or Youkai may cut across or sit alongside Loranian terminology without becoming additional universal taxonomic ranks.

docs.title: Regional Creatures
docs.text: Regional Creatures provides a secondary geographic path to creatures strongly associated with particular places or cultures. Fey in particular should be understood through regional spiritual ecologies rather than assumed to be globally distributed wherever similar terrain exists.

docs.title: Bestiary Taxonomy
docs.text:
Loranian sages classify creatures according to their underlying nature, origin, and mode of continuation. Other cultures may use different names or conceptual systems for the same beings.

The taxonomy does not primarily sort creatures by appearance, intelligence, morality, or danger. A frightening animal can still be a Beast; an intelligent being can still be Fey; and two outwardly similar beings may belong to different categories if their origins or means of continuation are fundamentally different.

docs.title: Beasts
docs.text:
Beasts are unintelligent creatures that reproduce through a natural life cycle.

The species' original origin does not determine the classification. A creature first created or altered through magic may still be classified as a Beast once it has become a stable living population that reproduces naturally. This is why established sorcerous hybrids such as Owlbears and Chimeras can be Beasts even though their remote ancestry was artificial.

The living Gargoyle is likewise a Beast: a natural flying predator of caves, cliffs, crags, and similar terrain. Stone gargoyle guardians are later magical constructions made in imitation of the animal, not the source of the animal's form.

Ordinary real-world animals are assumed to exist and are not exhaustively catalogued. Giant Animal is a descriptive development category rather than a species; in sufficiently wild places, ordinary animal lineages may attain extraordinary size.

See Beasts for the category hub.

docs.title: Monstrosities
docs.text:
Monstrosities are creatures whose defining forms do not continue through the ordinary reproduction of normal animals. They may be unintelligent or fully intelligent.

Typical causes include curses, diseases, magical transformations, corruptions, or comparable processes that create new examples without a normal animal life cycle. A one-off sorcerous hybrid therefore differs from a stable hybrid species: the former is a created monstrosity, while descendants that eventually breed true may become Beasts.

Animal Hybrid is not one species. It is a useful description for the broad possibility that sorcery can combine or reshape animals. Most such creations are unique, sterile, unstable, or local; only some establish self-sustaining populations.

See Monstrosities for the category hub.

docs.title: Plants
docs.text:
Plants are nonsapient plant creatures and extraordinary plant life treated as creatures in their own right. Mobility, predatory behavior, or supernatural properties do not by themselves move a plant into another category.

Sapience does matter here. A genuinely sapient plant-being belongs to the Fey category under current Loranian taxonomy rather than being classified merely by its vegetable body. Great Trees are the canonical example; corrupted Great Trees remain corrupted Fey rather than becoming Undead. Magically animated or constructed vegetation, such as a living topiary, is an artificial creation rather than a naturally sapient plant-being.

See Plants for the category hub.

docs.title: Undead
docs.text:
Undead are beings existing in an undead or post-mortem state. The category covers creatures whose present existence depends upon death rather than an ordinary living life cycle.

Banshees are specialized ghosts or shades and are therefore Undead, not Fey. The ancient Khemetian Undying are also undead, but they are a distinct phenomenon rather than vampires; their detailed origin and history belong to the Khemetian tradition rather than to generic vampire lore.

See Undead for the category hub.

docs.title: Fey
docs.text:
Fey is the Loranian scholarly term for beings that are genuinely part of the natural world while also being intrinsically magical in nature.

The term does not simply mean a particular family of small spirits or forest-folk. Other cultures may describe comparable beings using concepts such as jinn, youkai, spirits, or other local terms, and those traditions should not be collapsed into Loranian terminology merely because they appear similar.

Within Lorania and neighboring lands, established Fey include Elves, Gnomes, Dwarves, Centaurs, Arachne, Satyrs, Naga, Nymphs, Dryads, and other regional spirits. Dwarves are deep-earth and mountain Gnomes rather than a separate mortal species. Manticores are unusually savage and intelligent Fey rather than a globally distributed biological people. Mermaids are oceanic Fey with a much wider distribution than most Loranian spiritual forms.

Fey ecology is regional. A Loranian Fey form is not assumed to occur on another continent merely because the same kind of forest, river, mountain, or shore exists there.

See Fey for the category hub.

docs.title: Archons
docs.text:
Archons are primordial or celestial beings belonging to the ordered fabric of Creation itself. They are neither natural-world spirits in the Fey sense nor beings of Outer-Dark origin.

The category is broad. Athar is an Archon, as are his celestial servants. The primordial Dragons were also Archons before their defeat in the Great War and degeneration into the natural-breeding Wyrms of the present age. Lesser Archons include guardian beings such as Lamassu.

Modern Atharite religion uses Archon in a narrower devotional sense, generally for Athar's servants and agents. That usage reflects Atharite theology rather than the full cosmological category.

See Archons for the category hub.

docs.title: Demons
docs.text:
Demons are beings whose ultimate origin lies in the Outer Darkness. Their present location does not erase that origin.

In broad taxonomy, this includes both exterior Demons that remain beyond Creation and Starspawn that were already caught within Creation before its boundary was sealed. Starspawn is deliberately broad and can encompass many forms rather than naming one humanoid species.

The greatest Outer-Dark powers, whether Exterior Demons or Starspawn, may be called Dark Gods. The term reflects power, cultic stature, and supernatural influence rather than a separate origin category.

See Demons for the category hub.

docs.title: Lineages and Vernacular Categories
docs.text:
Not every useful creature-name is itself a taxonomic category.

  • Dragon names primordial Archons defeated by Athar during the Great War of creation. Their surviving diminished lineage is the Wyrms. Lesser, greater, and hatchling forms are age or power distinctions within that lineage, while Hydra, Sea Serpent, and Sand Wyrm are mutations, degenerate offshoots, or regional variants. Wyverns are unrelated reptilian Beasts despite superficial resemblance.
  • Behemoth is a vernacular name for very large dinosaurs, not a biological or supernatural taxon. Greater Behemoths are giant theropod types; Common Behemoths include large horned and plated dinosaurs; Long-Necked Behemoths are the great sauropod type.
  • Gargant is the common name for giant ground sloths, Anqah for Gastornis-like great birds, and Razorclaw for dromaeosaur-like predatory dinosaurs.

docs.title: Scholarly Disputes
docs.text:
The taxonomy depends on facts that are not always easy to establish. Sages may disagree when they cannot determine whether a creature breeds naturally, whether apparent offspring are transformed victims, whether a spirit is native to the natural world, whether a being is truly Archonic, or whether a being ultimately came from the Outer Darkness.

Accordingly, some creatures receive a disputed classification rather than a universally accepted category.

docs.title: Illustrative Distinctions
docs.text:
• A magically created animal species that now breeds naturally is a Beast.
  • A creature whose members arise when victims are transformed by a curse or disease is a Monstrosity.
  • A sapient magical being native to the natural world may be Fey, even if its body resembles a plant, animal, or human.
  • A primordial or celestial being native to the ordered structure of Creation may be Archonic.
  • A superficially similar being whose ultimate origin lies in the Outer Darkness is broadly Demonic, whether it remains outside Creation or survives within it as Starspawn.
  • A being whose present existence is a continuation or transformation of death is Undead.

These distinctions reflect Loranian scholarship. Other peoples of Umbrathar may divide the living, magical, spiritual, and dead worlds according to very different traditions.

docs.title: Archons
docs.text:
Archons are primordial or celestial beings belonging to the ordered fabric of Creation rather than to the natural-world ecology of the Fey or the Outer Darkness of Demons.

The category includes beings of very different rank, form, and function. Athar is an Archon. His celestial servants are Archons. The primordial Dragons of the earliest world were likewise Archons before their defeat and degeneration into the natural-breeding Wyrms known in the present age.

Archon therefore names a broad supernatural nature rather than a single species, body plan, hierarchy, or moral alignment.

Modern Atharite usage is narrower than the broader cosmological category. In contemporary Atharite religion, Archon commonly refers specifically to Athar's divine servants and agents. This religious usage should not be mistaken for proof that Athar's servants are the only Archons that exist or have ever existed.

The existence of Archons does not imply that they are common or routinely accessible. Most mortals encounter them through theology, myth, ancient remains, miraculous intervention, or exceptionally rare manifestations rather than as ordinary inhabitants of the world.

docs.title: Lesser Archons
docs.text:
Some Archons are vastly less powerful than beings such as Athar or the primordial Dragons. These lesser Archons may serve as guardians, messengers, attendants, protectors of sacred thresholds, or agents of greater celestial powers. Their forms may be highly symbolic or composite rather than humanoid.

Lamassu are one known form of lesser Archon, traditionally associated with guardianship of gates, holy places, royal precincts, tombs, and other charged thresholds.

Yali are immense leonine lesser Archons associated with active protection of sacred places, covenants, seals, and other supernatural charges. They are frequently represented as paired guardians in monumental and religious art.

The mysterious Ebon Knight, called the Bachlach in much of the North and especially Albia, is an Archon associated with supernatural ordeal. Those who successfully face him in single combat may learn how an otherwise seemingly invincible supernatural being can be defeated.

See Bestiary Taxonomy for the broader classification system.

docs.title: Ebon Knight
docs.text:
The Ebon Knight is a mysterious Archon known through old summoning rites, heroic ordeals, and stories of impossible single combat. In the North, especially Albia, he is commonly called the Bachlach.

He is usually described as a dark-robed or dark-armored warrior whose face is concealed by a black mask, helm, shadow, or other featureless covering. Accounts disagree on his exact appearance and weapon, suggesting that either his manifestation varies or different cultures interpret the same being through their own martial and judicial traditions.

The Ebon Knight does not answer ordinary petitions. Those who know the proper rites may call him only by submitting themselves to an ordeal. Once invoked, he challenges the summoner personally, and outside interference is said to be useless. If the petitioner overcomes him, the Knight yields and grants one answer: how a single supernatural being may be defeated.

He offers no prophecy, treasure, general counsel, or explanation beyond that narrow revelation. The answer may identify a hidden weakness, required weapon, forgotten rite, binding condition, vulnerable place, or some other means by which an otherwise seemingly invincible being can be opposed.

Those who invoke the Ebon Knight and fail may survive, but traditions consistently describe the consequences as a judgment or doom rather than an ordinary defeat.

No reliable doctrine explains whom the Ebon Knight serves or why he possesses such knowledge. Some sages argue that his function is older than modern religion and that he exists to preserve an ancient principle of Creation: no supernatural power is permitted to become wholly beyond challenge. This remains interpretation rather than established fact.

docs.title: Related
docs.text: • Archons

docs.title: Lamassu
docs.text:
Lamassu are lesser Archons associated with guardianship, sacred thresholds, and the protection of places invested with religious, royal, or cosmological importance.

They are usually described as great composite beings with leonine or bovine bodies, immense wings, and humanlike faces. Their precise appearance varies between traditions and individual manifestations, and the form should be understood as symbolic as much as anatomical: strength, vigilance, sovereignty, and celestial authority joined in a single guardian shape.

Lamassu are not a roaming people or ordinary supernatural fauna. They are encountered as guardians—at temple gates, ancient sanctuaries, royal tombs, holy precincts, sealed passages, or other places whose protection carries unusual weight. A Lamassu may remain bound to such a charge for centuries or appear only when that charge is threatened.

They are intelligent and capable of speech, judgment, and deliberate action. Their duty is not necessarily blind obedience to whoever currently controls the place they protect; an old Lamassu may recognize an oath, office, sacred trust, or purpose older than the mortal institution surrounding it.

docs.title: Phoenixes
docs.text:
Phoenixes are rare sapient Archons that take the form of immense birds wreathed in the colors and heat of living fire. Their plumage commonly shades through gold, yellow, orange, and red, and many cultures associate them with the sun, sacred fire, renewal, and divine favor.

Phoenixes are immortal in the ordinary sense. When one is slain, its body is consumed in supernatural flame and, unless its cycle is somehow interrupted, the Phoenix eventually rises renewed from the remains. This rebirth is intrinsic to the creature rather than ordinary biological reproduction.

The exact place of Phoenixes within the hierarchy of the Archons is not universally understood. Some traditions regard them as servants or heralds of solar or fire-associated divine powers; others treat them as independent sacred beings whose nature merely resembles those powers. Their precise relationship to Athar, other divine beings, and particular historic cults remains unresolved.

Phoenix feathers retain a portion of the creature's supernatural fire and are therefore enormously valuable. A Phoenix may voluntarily bestow such a feather as a rare gift, but removing feathers weakens the bird's life-force. Traditions differ on the exact consequences, though many agree that stripping a Phoenix of its final sacred feathers can interfere with or prevent its normal rebirth. This has made Phoenixes objects of both reverence and predation.

Despite their sacred associations, Phoenixes should not be assumed to share a single mortal morality, religious allegiance, or institutional role. Individual Phoenixes may act as guardians, sages, omens, messengers, or solitary powers according to their own purposes and the divine relationships they possess.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Archons
  • Athar

docs.title: Titans
docs.text:
Titans are primordial, humanlike Archons remembered from the earliest ages of the world. They are described as beings of immense stature and power, more closely resembling perfected or magnified humanity than any ordinary giant lineage.

No Titan is known to survive openly in the present world. They belong to myth, theology, ancient art, fragmentary records, and the oldest stories of Creation rather than to the fauna or peoples travelers ordinarily encounter. Whether any remain hidden, imprisoned, transformed, or otherwise beyond mortal knowledge is uncertain.

Many traditions portray the Titans as possessing powers over the ordered world on a scale far beyond mortal sorcery. Storms, lightning, the sea, and other great forces of Creation are commonly associated with them, though surviving accounts disagree about the abilities of individual Titans.

docs.title: Titans and the Origin of Humanity
docs.text:
A persistent scholarly and religious theory holds that mankind descends from the Titans and that modern humanity represents a diminished form of these primordial beings. Advocates point to ancient traditions that describe humanity as having declined in stature, vigor, longevity, or spiritual potency over successive ages.

This is in-universe conjecture, not an established fact. Other traditions give humanity entirely different origins, and surviving evidence is far too fragmentary to settle the question. The resemblance between Titans and gigantic idealized humans may be evidence of ancestry, symbolism, coincidence, or something else entirely.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Archons
  • Bestiary Taxonomy

docs.title: Yali
docs.text:
Yali are lesser Archons that manifest as immense, leonine celestial guardians. Their forms are strongly symbolic rather than zoologically uniform: a Yali may possess an exaggerated mane and jaws, tusks, horns, scales, serpentine features, or other composite traits while remaining recognizably a powerful lion-like being.

Yali are associated above all with guardianship. They appear at sacred places, charged thresholds, ancient seals, tombs, royal or ceremonial precincts, and other sites placed under supernatural protection. They are more active and ferocious guardians than the stately Lamassu of many traditions, and stories commonly portray a Yali pursuing an intruder rather than merely denying passage.

A Yali's vigilance is not a simple ability to distinguish moral good from evil. Instead, it possesses an uncanny awareness of violation within its charge. Depending on the duty it has accepted, a Yali may recognize desecration, hostile intrusion, grave robbery, the breaking of a sacred covenant, corruption of something entrusted to its protection, or the passage of beings fundamentally inimical to the ordered principle it guards.

Yali are intelligent celestial beings rather than supernatural animals. They cannot truly be domesticated or trained as beasts. A Yali may nevertheless accept a person, dynasty, temple, community, or sacred place as its charge, and once such a duty is accepted its fidelity may endure for centuries.

Yali are frequently represented in pairs, particularly in the religious and monumental art of cultures that preserve traditions of encountering them. The precise meaning of the pair varies: theologians and artists variously interpret them as guarding physical and spiritual thresholds, complementary aspects of protection, or simply the customary manner in which these Archons manifest. No single interpretation is universally accepted.

Mortal sculpture often exaggerates or regionalizes their features, so depictions of Yali need not provide a reliable guide to the anatomy of an actual manifestation.

docs.text:

  • Lamassu

docs.title: Beasts
docs.text:
Beasts are the Loranian taxonomic category for unintelligent creatures that reproduce through a natural life cycle.

A species may still be a Beast even if it was originally created, altered, or introduced through magic. Once it exists as a stable population reproducing naturally, its magical ancestry does not by itself make it a Monstrosity or Fey.

Composite anatomy does not by itself establish sorcerous origin. Griffons, Owlbears, and similar fantastic animals may simply be naturally occurring Beasts, even though Loranian sages often speculate that ancient sorcery created them. Chimeras are the confirmed exception: their lineage was deliberately created by a sorcerer only a few centuries ago, then became reproductively stable and established itself in the wild.

The living Gargoyle is also a Beast: an unintelligent flying predator of caves, cliffs, crags, and similar terrain. Stone gargoyle guardians were fashioned later in imitation of the animal.

Ordinary animals are assumed to exist without requiring individual bestiary articles. Likewise, Giant Animal is not a species: wild lineages may produce exceptionally large forms, and dedicated entries are needed only when a form has distinctive setting significance.

Several large prehistoric animals have established vernacular names. Behemoth refers broadly to very large dinosaurs; Gargant to giant ground sloths; Anqah to great Gastornis-like birds; and Razorclaw to smaller dromaeosaur-like predatory dinosaurs. These are common names, not higher taxonomic categories.

Wyverns are reptilian Beasts unrelated to the primordial Dragon/Wyrm lineage despite their superficial resemblance.

Redmaws are bizarre hairless, blood-feeding predators with an almost worldwide distribution. They can resemble gaunt stray dogs at a distance, but their distorted canine forms, dorsal spines, and specialized hollow feeding tongues make the resemblance horrifyingly superficial at close range. Despite their unnatural appearance, they reproduce naturally and are therefore Beasts.

Death Worms are small, blood-red burrowing scavengers of the South whose bodies resemble fresh entrails. Their extreme venom, poisonous spit, and ability to move through loose sand make them far more dangerous than their size suggests.

Cave Creeper is a small subterranean ambush predator that slowly climbs cavern walls and ceilings, hides against stone, and uses short controlled glides to descend onto prey.

See Bestiary Taxonomy for the broader classification system.

docs.title: Basilisks
docs.text:
Basilisks are rare reptilian Beasts descended from an uncanny lineage noted for extraordinarily virulent venom and a supernatural or near-supernatural gaze. They are not a single uniform form. Different lineages vary in size, body plan, and the exact effect of their gaze, but all share enough traits to be recognized as members of the same broader family.

Most commonly encountered Basilisks are heavily built, many-legged reptiles with a low profile and a distinctly crown-like crest or marking around the head. Their venom is exceptionally dangerous, and prolonged exposure to their gaze may paralyze, petrify, kill, or otherwise incapacitate depending on the individual lineage. The exact expression varies enough that hunters and scholars caution against assuming one Basilisk behaves exactly like another.

The oldest and most exceptional Basilisks can grow to enormous size and often become increasingly serpentine in form. These ancient specimens are sometimes called Great Basilisks or Kings of Serpents. The title describes an ancient or exceptional Basilisk rather than a separate species: most Basilisks never attain such age, size, or potency.

Basilisks are still Beasts rather than Monstrosities. Whatever the ultimate origin of their uncanny physiology, they breed true and form stable living lineages.

docs.title: Cockatrices
docs.text:
Cockatrices are a small, winged avian-reptilian branch of the Basilisk family. Their chickenlike or birdlike forebody, reptilian tail, and wings make them visually distinct from the more typical Basilisk, but they share the same broader uncanny lineage and petrifying or paralytic influence.

Where a typical Basilisk most often threatens through its gaze and venom, a Cockatrice usually expresses the same dangerous nature through its bite, claws, or close contact. Medieval-style stories that Cockatrices hatch from unnatural rooster eggs incubated by toads remain common folklore in some regions, but they are not regarded as literal zoological fact by most scholars.

Cockatrices are therefore not a separate supernatural category or independently created Monstrosity. They are simply an unusual Basilisk relative.

docs.title: Cave Creeper
docs.text:
Cave Creepers are small subterranean Beasts adapted to life on cavern walls and ceilings. They move slowly while climbing, clinging closely to stone and using their natural camouflage to remain difficult to notice while at rest.

Although poor at sustained aerial movement, a Cave Creeper can launch itself from a wall or ceiling and make a short controlled glide. It uses this to cross gaps, descend rapidly, or ambush prey from above rather than to fly in the ordinary sense.

Cave Creepers are patient ambush predators. They commonly wait above passages or feeding grounds, then drop or glide onto passing prey and attempt to entangle or envelop it. Their attack is especially dangerous because it interferes with the victim's senses, typically blinding or otherwise obstructing the head and face while the creature maintains its grip.

They are natural animals rather than supernatural manifestations. Their exact range, reproductive ecology, and the anatomical mechanism by which they cling, glide, and blind prey remain open for later regional development.

docs.title: Chimeras
docs.text:
Chimeras are great composite Beasts descended from a deliberately created Animal Hybrid lineage. Unlike most strange composite animals, their artificial origin is not merely scholarly speculation: the first Chimeras appeared only a few centuries ago, created by a notoriously malicious sorcerer whose work proved far more reproductively successful than anyone intended.

The creatures bred true and established self-sustaining wild populations. Loranian natural philosophers therefore classify modern Chimeras as Beasts, not Monstrosities, despite the well-attested sorcerous origin of their lineage.

The familiar Chimera combines leonine, caprine, and serpentine or draconic features into a single formidable animal. Fire-breathing is characteristic of the lineage, though its precise expression varies between individuals. Their bizarre anatomy should not be mistaken for evidence that each Chimera is individually manufactured: modern Chimeras are born as Chimeras.

Their existence is one of the standard examples used in arguments over the boundary between Beast and Monstrosity. A newly created Animal Hybrid remains a Monstrosity, but once such a form becomes a stable breeding lineage, its descendants may become part of the natural fauna of Umbrathar no matter how unnatural their ancestral origin.

The identity, motives, and precise historical setting of the sorcerer responsible for the first Chimeras remain to be developed in detail.

See Animal Hybrids.

docs.title: Common Beasts
docs.text:
The ordinary animals familiar from Earth also exist throughout Umbrathar wherever climate, habitat, and local ecology make them appropriate. Horses, cattle, dogs, wolves, bears, deer, eagles, hawks, vultures, rhinoceroses, whales, sea turtles, and innumerable other mundane animals are part of the world's natural fauna unless more specific setting material says otherwise.

These animals are Beasts, but they normally receive no individual bestiary article. Individual species may receive separate treatment when they have unusual ecological, cultural, economic, or historical importance in Umbrathar.

This category is distinct from Giant Animals, whose members reach fantastic sizes compared with familiar relatives; Megafauna, which collects surviving prehistoric and otherwise extinct natural fauna; and Dinosaurs, which collects the world's surviving dinosaur lineages.

docs.title: Death Worms
docs.text:
Death Worms are small blood-red desert scavengers whose thin, glistening bodies resemble lengths of fresh entrails more than ordinary worms.

They are found throughout the South, especially in sandy country where they can burrow quickly beneath loose earth. Carrion attracts them, and they readily tunnel through dead flesh as well as sand.

Their size makes them easy to underestimate. Death Worms are extraordinarily venomous: their bite can kill, and they can spit the same poison at nearby prey or threats. Even touching one carelessly may be dangerous. They sense their surroundings without depending upon ordinary sight and are difficult to evade merely by darkness or concealment.

Death Worms are natural animals despite their grotesque appearance and are classified as Beasts.

docs.title: Related
docs.text: • Beasts

docs.title: Dinosaurs
docs.text:
Dinosaurs survive as part of Umbrathar's natural fauna. The term is used here for the player's convenience: the peoples of Umbrathar have their own names and classifications for these animals and do not necessarily recognize "dinosaur" as a single in-world category.

They are ordinary Beasts, not inherently magical creatures, Monstrosities, or relics created by sorcery. Different lineages survive in different environments, and many are known primarily by regional or descriptive names rather than names familiar to modern natural history.

Some dinosaurs have distinctive Umbratharian identities. The enormous predator known as the Greater Behemoth, for example, corresponds broadly to a Tyrannosaurus rex. Such names should be used naturally in setting-facing prose while this page remains transparent about the real-world animal being represented.

Individual dinosaur species need no separate bestiary article unless they possess substantial Umbrathar-specific ecology, cultural importance, or lore. Generic sourcebook dinosaur profiles can instead be consolidated here for later mechanical reconstruction.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Beasts
  • Common Beasts
  • Megafauna
  • Giant Animals

docs.title: Gargoyles
docs.text:
Gargoyles are living troglodytic Beasts: winged predators with vaguely humanoid silhouettes that inhabit caverns, cliff faces, crags, mountain passes, and similar broken terrain.

Despite their name and appearance, ordinary Gargoyles are not animated statues. They are naturally reproducing animals and are therefore classified as Beasts. Their stony or leathery hides, hunched bodies, clawed limbs, broad wings, and ability to cling motionless to rock make them easy to mistake at a distance for carved figures.

Gargoyles are ambush predators. They roost in inaccessible caves, ledges, ruined heights, and narrow passes, descending suddenly on animals or travelers moving through their territory. Their vaguely humanoid proportions can make them especially disturbing to observers, but this resemblance does not imply humanlike intelligence.

docs.title: Gargoyles in Art and Architecture
docs.text:
The living animal predates the architectural tradition that shares its name. Human sculptors adopted Gargoyle forms as grotesque decorative motifs and protective figures, particularly on high walls, towers, temples, fortifications, and other structures where the creatures' crouched silhouettes were already culturally associated with heights and vigilance.

Sorcerers later took the imitation a step further by creating Stone Gargoyles: artificial guardian Constructs fashioned in the image of the living Beast. This produces a three-stage lineage of influence:

living Gargoyle → decorative gargoyle image → animated Stone Gargoyle guardian.

As a result, a traveler cannot always know whether a grotesque figure crouched on an old tower is sculpture, Construct, or living predator until it moves.

docs.title: Giant Animals
docs.text:
Giant Animals are not a single species or supernatural lineage. The term is a practical name for naturally reproducing animal lineages whose members reach sizes far beyond their familiar relatives.

Such creatures remain Beasts. Exceptional size does not by itself imply sorcery, corruption, or monstrous ancestry, and many giant forms can be understood simply as part of Umbrathar's unusually broad and dangerous fauna. They are most common where isolation, abundant prey, unusual environments, or ancient surviving lineages allow extreme forms to persist.

Giant forms are often not merely larger versions of familiar animals. Many display frighteningly heightened animal intelligence: better memory, patience, coordination, problem-solving, and learned responses to hunters and prey than their ordinary counterparts. This does not make them humanlike or sapient, but it can make experienced giant predators disturbingly difficult to outwit. A pack of giant wolves, for example, may coordinate its approach, test defenses, exploit terrain, feint, withdraw from unfavorable engagements, and adapt to repeated human tactics with a sophistication approaching deliberate military behavior while still thinking fundamentally as wolves rather than people.

The category is intentionally broad. Giant spiders, giant bats, giant wasps, enormous reptiles, and similar creatures need no individual bestiary article unless a particular lineage has distinctive ecology, cultural importance, supernatural significance, or another specifically Umbratharian feature worth describing.

docs.title: Known Forms
docs.text:
The following forms are known or plausible examples rather than a complete zoological catalogue:

  • Giant ants — enormous social insects forming colonies and nests on the same broad model as ordinary ants. Their size can make a mature colony a serious local ecological or settlement hazard.
  • Giant spiders — enormous predatory spiders ranging across several environments. In northern Lorania, particularly Albia, Nibelung, and Svealund, giant spiders are commonly called attercops. The term is especially associated with the dangerous spiders of the Lovar Forest, though it is vernacular rather than the name of a distinct species or supernatural lineage.
  • Giant scorpions — enormous armored arachnids, especially associated with hot climates. Their pincers, stings, sensory bristles, and valuable venom make them dangerous predators and useful source animals for poison harvesting.
  • Giant ticks — oversized parasitic arachnids that locate warm-blooded prey and attach to feed. Different giant-tick lineages may vary greatly in size, habitat, disease risk, burrowing or leaping behavior, and feeding behavior. The old Steppe Tick material is treated as variation within this broader family rather than as a separate species.
  • Giant centipedes and other myriapods — enormous many-legged predators, particularly common in caves, mines, ruins, and other dark environments. Different lineages may possess unusually dangerous venom, including paralytic varieties, or specialized subterranean senses and burrowing adaptations.
  • Giant grasshoppers and locusts — oversized orthopterans ranging from open-country jumpers to cave-adapted forms. Some cavern-dwelling varieties react to disturbance with piercing shrieks, erratic panic-leaping in confined spaces, and foul defensive secretions, making swarms or enclosed encounters far more dangerous than their raw size suggests.
  • Giant slugs — enormous terrestrial gastropods whose size, mucus, unusual feeding adaptations, or other local traits can make otherwise slow animals dangerous.
  • Giant snakes — enormous serpents including both constricting and venomous forms. Most are best treated as variants of familiar snake body plans rather than separate species merely because of size.
  • Giant toads — oversized amphibians of wetlands, dark forests, caves, and other damp environments. Giant forms may rely on camouflage, long grasping tongues, powerful bites, and aquatic pressure-sensing to ambush prey.
  • Giant vermin — giant rats, shrews, ferrets, weasels, and similar small mammals can occur as oversized predatory or scavenging forms. They generally retain the body plans and instincts of their ordinary relatives rather than forming a distinct lineage.
  • Giant wasps — oversized predatory or parasitoid wasps. Some lineages may paralyze prey and lay eggs in or near living hosts, but supernatural source origins are not assumed.
  • Giant wolves — enormous wolf lineages distinguished from ordinary wolves primarily by scale, though heightened giant-animal intelligence can make their packs exceptionally dangerous. Some peoples may capture or train them as guards or war animals where local lineages permit it.
  • Giant worms — immense subterranean annelids able to burrow through soil and, in the largest forms, even stone. They may sense repeated movement through the ground, swallow large prey whole, and accumulate indigestible treasure or debris within their digestive tracts. Grey and Black Worm profiles from external sources represent scale and trait variants within this family rather than separate Umbrathar species.
  • Great burrowing arthropods — heavily armored subterranean predators capable of sensing and ambushing prey through soil and loose stone. Some possess corrosive digestive secretions capable of injuring prey or helping break down food.
  • Giant jellyfish — enormous pelagic jellyfish whose drifting tentacles can paralyze or entangle large prey. As with ordinary jellyfish, some may pass through radically different polyp and free-swimming life stages, and blooms can become major hazards to swimmers, fisheries, and small vessels.
  • Giant leeches — enormous aquatic or marsh-dwelling blood-feeders capable of attaching to prey much larger than themselves. They are dangerous chiefly because attachment makes them difficult to remove while feeding rather than because they are intelligent predators.
  • Giant lizards — a broad family of oversized reptilian Beasts rather than one species. Known or plausible forms include gliding draco-like lizards, wall-climbing gecko forms, camouflaged horned chameleons with grasping tongues, and heavily spined tuatara-like predators. These are best treated as ecological and mechanical variants of the same broad giant-reptile category rather than separate bestiary species.
  • Giant squid and octopuses — enormous cephalopods found in deep water, reefs, sea caves, and other suitable habitats. They are among the most intelligent giant animals and can become dangerously adept at ambush, concealment, manipulation, and learned responses to ships or hunters. Unlike most animals, the largest giant cephalopods appear to exhibit effectively indeterminate growth: they continue increasing in size so long as they survive and can obtain sufficient food. Most die long before reaching truly extraordinary dimensions, but very old individuals may become vast enough to seize boats or destroy ships.

docs.title: Roc
docs.text:
A Roc is a specific lineage of truly enormous bird of prey, not merely a generic name for any unusually large eagle or raptor. A mature Roc is roughly house-sized, placing it well beyond even the largest mundane or prehistoric birds and making its scale the defining feature of the animal.

Rocs are natural Beasts despite their extraordinary dimensions. They should not be conflated with ordinary large raptors or merely oversized eagles: those may exist independently, while the Roc represents a distinct giant-animal form at the extreme end of aerial predators.

docs.title: Kraken
docs.text:
Kraken is the sailors' name for a giant squid or giant octopus that has survived long enough to reach truly monstrous size. It is not a separate species or supernatural lineage. A Kraken is simply the terrifying upper extreme of giant cephalopod growth.

Kraken are consequently exceedingly rare. Reaching such size requires many years of survival, enormous food intake, and a habitat capable of supporting an apex predator of tremendous mass. Their age also makes them unusually experienced animals. A Kraken may learn shipping routes, recognize common vessel types, avoid particular weapons or hunting practices, raid fisheries, stalk whales, lurk near wreck sites, or otherwise behave with a degree of cunning that sailors readily mistake for human malice.

Some tales insist that the oldest Kraken become truly sapient. Whether any cephalopod has actually crossed that threshold is uncertain, but the intelligence of ancient specimens is sufficient that the distinction may be difficult to establish from a frightened sailor's account.

Northern myth and poetry already use the Kraken as an image of overwhelming sea-power; Vagur, the Reaver god of war, is traditionally styled the kraken-rider and ship-splitter. In that image, the feat is impressive precisely because a Kraken is not an ordinary mount but one of the oldest and most dangerous creatures in the sea.

This running list should absorb broadly generic giant-animal forms encountered during Bestiary development. A form should be promoted to its own page only when Umbrathar has something distinctive to say about its ecology, cultural importance, supernatural significance, or other setting consequences.

docs.title: Griffons
docs.text:
Griffons are large flying Beasts combining leonine and raptorial features, most commonly described with an eagle-like head and forequarters, powerful wings, and a lion-like hindbody. Their composite anatomy is not evidence of sorcerous construction; no confirmed artificial origin is known.

They favor mountains, cliffs, highlands, and broken country where strong updrafts and inaccessible nesting sites support their aerial hunting. Griffons are formidable predators of large animals and are particularly notorious for attacking horses, pack animals, and mounted travelers.

Like many of Umbrathar's great predators, Griffons display unusually sophisticated animal intelligence. They may cooperate to separate mounts from riders, drive prey into bad terrain, test caravan defenses, abandon unfavorable attacks, and remember productive hunting grounds or dangerous enemies.

Ancient and later folklore often associates Griffons with treasure. This need not reflect any supernatural compulsion to guard wealth. Griffons commonly nest in caves, crags, ruins, and other difficult places and may carry bright, durable, or unusual objects back to their nests. A long-occupied aerie can therefore accumulate coins, jewelry, weapons, armor, and other remnants of prey, producing the widespread belief that Griffons deliberately guard treasure.

Their apparent mixture of lion and eagle has predictably inspired theories that Griffons are ancient Animal Hybrids. Such theories remain unproven. In current taxonomy they are simply Beasts.

docs.title: Hippogriffs
docs.text:
Hippogriffs are a much rarer Beast closely associated with Griffons in both folklore and natural philosophy. They resemble Griffons in their raptorial forebody and wings, but possess an equine rather than leonine hindbody.

Whether Hippogriffs are genuinely related to Griffons is uncertain. Their appearance has produced obvious stories that they descend from unions between Griffons and horses, or from some forgotten act of sorcery, but neither explanation is established fact. Loranian naturalists generally treat them as a rare griffon-like lineage rather than as proof that either creature is an artificial hybrid.

Hippogriffs appear to favor similar mountainous and upland environments but are considerably less common. They are also reputed to be somewhat more tractable than Griffons, and a handful of traditions describe successfully reared Hippogriffs serving as mounts. Such cases are exceptional; flying war-beasts and aerial cavalry are not ordinary features of Umbrathar's warfare.

docs.title: Megafauna
docs.text:
Many great animals that vanished from Earth in prehistory remain part of the natural fauna of Umbrathar. Mammoths, woolly rhinoceroses, saber-toothed cats, giant ground sloths, and other prehistoric forms survive in suitable regions alongside animals familiar from the modern world.

Megafauna is a practical bestiary grouping rather than a single lineage or strict scholarly category. It primarily collects naturally occurring prehistoric and extinct animals that need no individual article of their own. These creatures are ordinary Beasts: their antiquity, size, or unfamiliarity does not imply magical origin.

Some megafaunal lineages have distinctive Umbratharian names or cultural importance. Gargants, for example, are the enormous ground sloths of Umbrathar and may warrant treatment beyond a generic source profile when their setting role is developed.

Dinosaurs are tracked separately under Dinosaurs. This is an out-of-world organizational distinction for the bestiary rather than necessarily a taxonomy recognized by Umbratharian natural philosophers.

docs.title: Owlbears
docs.text:
Owlbears are large predatory Beasts combining ursine mass and body structure with pronounced avian features. They reproduce naturally and maintain self-sustaining populations.

Their composite appearance has made them a favorite example in arguments over the origins of strange fauna. Many Loranian sages assume that some forgotten sorcerer or magical catastrophe must have produced the first Owlbears, while others argue that this explanation merely reflects an unwillingness to accept how strange natural life can become in Umbrathar.

At present, no artificial origin is confirmed. Owlbears are therefore treated simply as Beasts rather than as descendants of known Animal Hybrids.

They are powerful territorial predators whose senses, aggression, and physical strength make them dangerous even compared with ordinary great bears. Their heavy forelimbs make them particularly dangerous once they seize prey, which they can crush or maul at close quarters. Regional forms may differ in plumage, coloration, size, habitat, and behavior.

docs.title: Pegasi
docs.text:
Pegasi are rare winged horses found in isolated wild populations. Despite their fantastic anatomy, they are natural Beasts rather than known sorcerous hybrids or Fey.

A mature Pegasus has the build and temperament of a fine light horse, though its immense feathered wings make it capable of sustained flight. Coat and feather coloration varies widely, including white, cream, grey, black, silver, and other natural or metallic-looking shades.

Pegasi are intelligent for animals but remain skittish herd creatures. They can be domesticated and trained as mounts, including for war, but doing so requires exceptional skill, time, and expense. Their scarcity and slow reproduction make them unsuitable for ordinary military use. A prince, famous rider, sorcerer, wealthy order, or similarly exceptional patron might possess trained Pegasi, but organized Pegasus cavalry is extraordinary rather than a normal arm of war.

Wild Pegasi are fiercely protective of their young and may become far more dangerous when defending a herd or nesting ground. They bear live young like horses rather than laying eggs.

docs.title: Redmaws
docs.text:
Redmaws are hairless, blood-feeding predatory Beasts found across much of Umbrathar. Their enormous range has encouraged countless local names and stories, but natural philosophers generally regard these regional populations as variations of the same broadly distributed animal, much as wild dogs and similar adaptable predators occur across many lands.

At a distance, particularly in darkness or poor weather, a redmaw can easily be mistaken for a gaunt stray dog. The resemblance becomes much less comforting at close range. Its nearly naked hide, distorted canine proportions, pronounced claws and jaws, and strange ridge of coarse spines or bristles along its back give it a sickly, unnatural appearance despite its classification as an ordinary living Beast.

The feature that gives the animal its common Loranian name is its feeding apparatus. A redmaw possesses a long hollow tongue adapted for drawing blood from prey it has pinned or grappled. Livestock are common victims, making redmaws notorious among herders, but they readily attack other animals and humans when opportunity or hunger demands it.

Redmaws are stealthy nocturnal hunters. Their superficial resemblance to dogs can itself become dangerous around settlements: an indistinct animal skulking near a road, rubbish heap, livestock enclosure, or camp may be dismissed as a feral dog until it approaches closely enough for its true shape to become apparent.

Redmaws reproduce naturally and maintain wild populations, so Loranian taxonomy places them among Beasts rather than Monstrosities despite their bizarre anatomy. Whether the species is wholly natural in origin or descends from some ancient altered stock is unknown and need not be settled by its present classification.

docs.title: Rustbeasts
docs.text:
Rustbeasts are strange natural Beasts with an extraordinary affinity for metal. They can sense nearby metal with remarkable accuracy and instinctively seek it out as food, making armed travelers, mines, workshops, and stores of worked metal particularly attractive to them.

Their most notorious adaptation is their ability to rapidly corrode metal through contact. A Rustbeast is ordinarily more interested in consuming or reaching metal than in killing the creature carrying it, but this distinction is little comfort to anyone wearing armor or carrying valuable weapons when one approaches.

The same senses that make wild Rustbeasts dangerous have made domesticated animals extremely useful to Dwarves. Dwarven miners keep and train Rustbeasts as prospecting animals, using their ability to detect buried metal and ore deposits much as other peoples might use scent hounds to track game. Proper handling is essential around tools, fittings, weapons, and other worked metal, and the practical traditions surrounding their husbandry are consequently specialized.

Wild Rustbeasts may likewise be drawn toward exposed ore, abandoned mines, buried metalwork, battlefields, ruins, and other places where concentrations of metal can be found. The Svealund Underground, with its ore-rich caverns, ancient workings, buried metal, and long Dwarven presence, is particularly well suited to both wild and domesticated populations.

docs.title: Stymphalian Birds
docs.text:
Stymphalian Birds, often shortened to Stymphs, are predatory Beasts distinguished by their metallic beaks and feathers. They gather in flocks and can be extraordinarily dangerous when nesting or driven by hunger.

Stymphs are not a natural creation. The first birds were fashioned by a Sorcerer and Alchemist as a gift to the Heryoi Empress Stymphaia, from whom the creatures take their name. These original Stymphalian Birds were elegant, docile creatures resembling flamingos, with brilliant plumage and metallic anatomy of silver and gold. They were intended as living wonders of the imperial court rather than weapons or predators.

At some point their descendants escaped captivity and established themselves in the wild. Over successive generations the feral population became more aggressive and predatory, while the precious silver and gold of the original stock gave way to the much more common bronze-like beaks and feathers seen today. Modern wild Stymphs are consequently very different animals from the exquisite creatures originally presented to Stymphaia.

A Stymph can launch its hardened metallic flight feathers in a deadly volley while airborne. Lost feathers eventually regrow, but replacing so much metal places enormous demands on the creature. Stymphs are consequently voracious feeders and are notorious for consuming scraps of metal as well as flesh. Their nesting grounds may contain coins, broken weapons, armor fragments, and other metallic objects carried there as food or scavenged from their victims.

Despite their artificial origin and supernatural-seeming anatomy, modern Stymphs are living animals rather than Constructs or individually created Monstrosities. They reproduce naturally, establish nesting colonies, and have become a self-sustaining part of the world's fantastic fauna.

docs.title: Gold and Silver Stymphs
docs.text:
The ancient gold and silver forms have not disappeared entirely. They are now extraordinarily rare, and whether surviving examples represent isolated descendants of the original imperial stock, rare throwbacks among wild Stymphs, or both is not always clear. Their brilliant metallic plumage and association with Empress Stymphaia make them objects of intense fascination and prestige.

Living gold or silver Stymphs are consequently highly sought after by wealthy collectors, rulers, alchemists, and others able to pursue such dangerous luxuries. Their rarity and value make the discovery of one considerably more consequential than an encounter with an ordinary bronze Stymph.

docs.title: Swarms
docs.text:
Swarms are masses of small animals dangerous primarily because they act in overwhelming numbers rather than because any individual creature is extraordinary. The term is a practical bestiary grouping rather than a distinct lineage.

Bats, fish, insects, rats, and many other ordinary animals may become hazardous as swarms under the right circumstances. Fantastic or unusually aggressive swarm-forming animals may use the same broad treatment when their danger comes chiefly from numbers.

Corpse worms are tiny red carrion-feeding worms whose bite can paralyze larger animals. Individual worms are nearly harmless, but a Corpse Worm Swarm can overwhelm living prey, leaving victims helpless while the worms feed.

Individual swarm types need no separate player-facing article unless they have distinctive Umbratharian ecology, supernatural significance, or cultural importance.

docs.title: Trolls
docs.text:
Trolls are truly massive Beasts, with even the smallest adults comparable in bulk to several large men. Their enormous appetites match their size: a troll can devour a whole sheep as a snack and drink astonishing quantities of water afterward.

Trolls possess extraordinary regenerative powers. Wounds that would cripple or kill most animals can close with alarming speed, and a troll that appears finished may recover if its body is not dealt with appropriately. Fire and similarly destructive injury are traditionally among the surest means of overcoming this regenerative resilience.

Although trolls are territorial, dangerous, and entirely willing to eat humans, they are not malicious creatures. They can be observed issuing ear-splitting bellows, throwing stones, and engaging in elaborate threat displays toward both other trolls and intruders. These displays suggest that a troll does not invariably attack simply because another creature has entered its vicinity.

Most trolls are solitary, though small family groups are sometimes encountered. Young remain with their parents until reaching a certain stage of development, after which they are driven from the parental territory and forced to establish ranges of their own. The arrival of a newly independent young troll can cause considerable trouble for nearby settlements.

The barbarians of the northern Clanlands have occasionally succeeded in taming trolls. The methods by which they accomplish this are fiercely guarded. An armored troll driven into battle is among the most terrifying living weapons the lowland Princedoms can face.

docs.title: Common Trolls
docs.text:
Common Trolls stand more than fifteen feet tall and inhabit a wide range of hills, swamps, forests, and other wilderness. They are generally found farther inland and farther south than the larger Frost and Sea Trolls, which tend to outcompete them where their ranges overlap.

Desert Trolls are a southern form adapted to arid country. Their immense claws allow them to burrow into sand, both for shelter and ambush.

docs.title: Frost Trolls
docs.text: Frost Trolls inhabit the icy north and the high mountains of the northern Clanlands. They are the most violent and aggressive trolls. The prominent brow ridge characteristic of trolls has developed into a powerful set of horns, while a coat of thick white fur protects them from extreme cold.

docs.title: Sea Trolls
docs.text:
Sea Trolls are the largest known trolls and are rarely encountered far from water. Individuals have reportedly reached heights approaching thirty feet.

They are also unusually intelligent for trolls. Though incapable of human speech, Sea Trolls appear capable of limited communication and have reportedly engaged in rudimentary exchanges with fishermen, accepting offerings of fish or meat and sometimes driving away sharks or other marine predators in return. Such behavior should not be mistaken for domestication: a provoked Sea Troll remains capable of devastating a coastal settlement.

docs.title: Wyrms
docs.text:
Wyrms are immense, ancient Beasts descended from the primordial Dragons of the earliest world. Dragons were not ordinary animals but celestial, primordial beings; Wyrms are their degenerated descendants, reduced from that earlier state into natural breeding creatures.

Despite that ancestry, modern Wyrms are classified as Beasts because they reproduce through a natural life cycle and persist as stable lineages. Their bodies vary markedly by region, but all known Wyrms are enormous reptilian or serpentine predators of exceptional durability and cunning.

Many Wyrms possess thick scales, highly corrosive bodily fluids, and a dangerous venomous or caustic bite. Their intelligence is animal rather than human, but as with other exceptional Beasts their cunning can be considerable.

Northern Wyrms are often predominantly serpentine and may be entirely limbless, dwelling in forests, mountains, swamps, and other wild country. Southern and eastern forms are more likely to possess powerful limbs and talons, sometimes with feathering, fur, or mane-like growths that give them a markedly different silhouette despite their shared ancestry.

Wyrms can live for centuries and continue growing throughout much of their lives. Ancient individuals may become vastly larger and more dangerous than younger adults. Hatchlings are already the size of large dogs, and a Wyrm may require decades or even a century to reach full maturity.

Their relationship to primordial Dragons is one of degeneration rather than simple descent from an ordinary ancestral species. Exactly how much of the Dragons' original celestial nature survives within the oldest Wyrms remains uncertain.

docs.title: Ice Wyrms
docs.text:
Ice Wyrms are northern Wyrms adapted to glaciers, frozen mountains, snowfields, and similarly severe environments. They are commonly described as immense pale serpents, often predominantly or entirely limbless even by northern Wyrm standards.

Mature Ice Wyrms generate supernatural cold rather than merely tolerating it. The oldest specimens may chill the air and ground around themselves so violently that frost forms in their wake and creatures approaching them risk freezing before the Wyrm strikes. They are exceptionally difficult to detect when buried beneath snow or ice and may erupt from concealed positions to seize prey.

As with other mature Wyrms, Ice Wyrms may develop a breath weapon and a Death Curse. The best-attested Ice Wyrm Death Curse leaves the creature's slayer supernaturally vulnerable to cold.

docs.title: Sea Serpents
docs.text:
Sea Serpents are an aquatic Wyrm lineage adapted to open water. They are immense, predominantly serpentine predators capable of threatening ships as readily as large marine animals.

Their long bodies and extraordinary strength allow them to coil around vessels and crush or restrain them, while their senses are adapted to perceiving movement and pressure changes through the water. They are fully aquatic and are most dangerous when attacking from below or alongside a vessel rather than attempting to engage prey on land.

Sea Serpents are natural breeding Beasts like other Wyrms. Their exact reproductive ecology may vary by lineage, but they are not separate Monstrosities or unrelated sea monsters merely because of their habitat.

Unlike many mature terrestrial Wyrms, Sea Serpents generally do not possess a Death Curse. Whether this reflects a deeper loss of draconic inheritance, a lineage-specific adaptation, or simple variation within Wyrms remains uncertain.

docs.title: Hydras
docs.text:
Hydras are a recognizable Wyrm mutation or lineage characterized by multiple independently striking heads and extreme regenerative capacity. Their bodies range from squat, heavily built forms to long serpentine or semi-aquatic shapes, but the many-headed anatomy is consistent enough that Hydras are usually recognized as a distinct Wyrm form rather than merely an individual deformity.

Unlike most mature Wyrms, Hydras generally do not develop the characteristic breath weapons or Death Curses found in many other Wyrm lineages. Their extraordinary regenerative proliferation appears to come at the expense of those more recognizably draconic traits.

Severed Hydra heads may regrow rapidly unless the wound is cauterized or otherwise treated with intense heat. Some accounts claim that a severed head can be replaced by more than one new head. Hydras therefore have a reputation for becoming more dangerous when fought carelessly.

Most known Hydras are solitary ambush predators associated with marshes, swamps, river deltas, coastal wetlands, and similar environments, though regional variants occur elsewhere. Venomous, fire-breathing, aquatic, and unusually large Hydras are all reported, but these should be understood as variants within the lineage rather than separate species.

Hydras reproduce as Wyrms unless a later canon decision establishes otherwise. Reports that Hydras bud offspring directly from their bodies are treated as unconfirmed lore rather than established biology.

Atharite theology traditionally interprets Dragons and Wyrms as creatures of the Outer Darkness or as beings fundamentally hostile to Creation. This is an in-world religious misunderstanding rather than the setting's objective taxonomy. Primordial Dragons are celestial beings of the earliest world, and Wyrms are their degenerated natural descendants. The Atharite interpretation should therefore be preserved as theology and historical belief rather than silently corrected in Atharite-facing material.

docs.title: Wyverns
docs.text:
Wyverns are enormous flying reptilian Beasts with long necks, powerful hind limbs, broad wings, razor-sharp talons and fangs, and a venomous tail. Despite their superficial resemblance to Wyrms and Dragons, they are not part of the primordial Dragon/Wyrm lineage.

They are territorial, aggressive, and notably impatient predators. Wyverns are primarily nocturnal hunters and will attack almost any warm-blooded creature they can overpower, though they show a particular preference for herd animals such as cattle and sheep. A Wyvern establishing hunting territory near settled country can therefore devastate livestock long before it begins taking humans.

Wyvern venom is strongly paralyzing rather than simply lethal. The animals produce the substance in such abundance that venom may drip from them as they move, making it possible—though dangerous—to collect traces by following a Wyvern's trail rather than approaching the animal itself.

Wyverns reproduce naturally and possess animal intelligence. Their aggression and size make them extraordinarily dangerous, but they remain animals rather than sapient monsters.

docs.title: Demons
docs.text:
Demons are beings whose ultimate origin lies in the Outer Darkness.

Their current residence does not change that broad classification. A demonic being remains demonic even if it has dwelt within Creation for ages.

Scholars often distinguish two important conditions:

  • Exterior Demons remain beyond Creation's boundary and require breaches, bargains, summons, possession, invitation, or other conduits to gain access.
  • Starspawn were already within nascent Creation before its boundary was sealed. They remain Outer-Dark in origin but are trapped inside the cosmic enclosure and are especially associated with the remote heavens and darkness between the stars.

Starspawn is intentionally a broad category rather than one humanoid species. Starspawn may take many forms, including unsettling humanoid manifestations. Older bestiary records that treated a Beyonder as a discrete species may remain useful as private mechanical scaffolding for one such form, but Beyonder is not the canonical species-name.

Some humanoid Starspawn may be eerily slight, hairless, gray-skinned, large-eyed, and disturbingly intelligent, with powerful mental abilities and a habit of abducting or examining mortals for purposes that remain incomprehensible. Such traits describe one possible manifestation rather than a universal Starspawn body plan or civilization. Reports of strange vessels, impossible instruments, or crafted objects associated with them are treated cautiously by Loranian scholars, who disagree over whether these are artifacts, sorcerous devices, living extensions of the creatures themselves, or badly misunderstood phenomena.

The greatest and least understood Outer-Dark powers are commonly called Dark Gods. Their exact relationship to ordinary Demons and Starspawn remains disputed. Beings believed to descend from, be created by, or directly embody one of these powers are often grouped loosely as Children of the Dark Gods.

This distinction describes circumstance and method more reliably than complete ontology.

The category is distinguished from Fey by origin: Fey belong to the natural world despite being intrinsically magical, while Demons and Starspawn ultimately come from beyond it.

Supernatural beings that provoke pathological hunger or cannibalism may be described as Hunger Demons or hunger spirits according to their actual nature. The imported Faminite identity is not retained. Likewise, imported Sinspawn are not a separate species; demons embodying sins or vices may exist in Umbrathar-specific forms without preserving that inherited taxonomy.

Evil Spirits are weak, nascent Demons that have not yet coalesced into stable mature forms. They often attach themselves to mortal emotions, fears, appetites, or vices, intensifying the impulse on which they feed. Those that survive long enough may gather strength and identity until they abruptly or gradually coalesce into other, more powerful demonic forms.

Shadow Children are nocturnal Exterior Demons that imitate lost or frightened human children. They cannot enter a private dwelling without invitation and are driven from Creation by dawn.

Black Trees are Great Trees so profoundly corrupted by demonic influence that their present supernatural nature is classified as demonic rather than Fey.

Blood Mists are rare vaporous forms or remnants derived from powerful Vampires, and remain Demons because Vampires themselves are demonic beings.

Demonic Steeds are horse-shaped Demons used as supernatural mounts by Demons, diabolists, and other servants of the Outer Darkness.

Abyssal Maws are enormous animal-minded Demons, grotesque slug- or worm-like predators used as warbeasts and occasionally mistaken for gods by isolated cults.

Ugallu are ancient winged, leonine desert Demons associated with the Mahrad. They are notorious deceivers of travelers, and their images appear in some of the region's oldest ruins in puzzlingly protective or guardian positions.

Cambions are mortals altered by genuine demonic ancestry, curses, possession, sorcery, or similar influence. Cambion is a condition or category rather than a true-breeding species, and the children of Cambions are not automatically Cambions themselves.

Changelings are shapeshifting Demons that steal mortal appearances. Their disguises may be physically perfect while leaving gaps in memory, mannerisms, and identity; more powerful examples can steal far more than appearance alone.

Nightmares are nocturnal Demons that prey upon fear, anguish, and troubled sleep. Some attach themselves to individual sleepers and manifest through the victim's fears; the more powerful Night Terrors can infest whole communities and make sleep itself dangerous.

See Bestiary Taxonomy for the broader classification system.

docs.title: Abyssal Maws
docs.text:
Abyssal Maws are enormous, animal-minded Demons whose bodies resemble grotesque slugs or worms built almost entirely around the act of feeding. Their broad, soft-looking bodies trail foul slime, while the forward end opens into a vast circular mouth packed with needle-like teeth and surrounded by grasping tentacles.

They are not true Wyrms, nor are they related to mundane giant worms. Their resemblance to such creatures is superficial: an Abyssal Maw is an Outer-Dark predator whose form happens to be suited to crawling, engulfing, and consuming prey.

A mature Maw may exceed thirty feet in length and is extraordinarily difficult to kill. Thick layers of unnatural flesh absorb punishment that would cripple most living creatures. In battle it crushes smaller beings beneath its bulk, seizes prey with its tentacles, and swallows victims whole.

Abyssal Maws possess little reasoning beyond predatory instinct, but this does not make them harmless servants. Powerful Demons and mortal diabolists sometimes summon or bind them as living siege beasts, execution engines, or guardians where subtlety is unnecessary.

Their size and alien appearance have also caused isolated cults to mistake individual Maws for gods. Such worship does not make an Abyssal Maw a Dark God, and the creature itself is generally incapable of granting supernatural power merely because mortals venerate it. A cult gathered around one may nevertheless become dangerous through its own rites, sacrifices, or the intervention of more intelligent Demons attracted by the worship.

docs.title: Aswang
docs.text:
Aswang are a lineage of vampiric Demons found chiefly in the eastern and southern lands. Although travelers sometimes call them eastern vampires, they are distinct from the creatures properly called Vampires. The resemblance is one of predatory habit rather than proof of common descent.

By day, an Aswang appears wholly human, usually strikingly attractive, and may live for years within mortal society without discovery. They can maintain households, take human lovers, and even bear or father children. Their offspring may appear entirely human through childhood, with the demonic inheritance manifesting only after puberty; some children of such unions apparently remain human.

At night the Aswang's predatory nature emerges. Its most distinctive organ is an immensely long, hollow tongue with which it draws blood from its victims. An Aswang often prefers concealment to open attack, extending its tongue through a window, roof gap, or other narrow opening to feed without ever entering the victim's room.

Aswang are also associated with a peculiar curse in which contact with a victim's shadow leaves the mortal extraordinarily vulnerable to sickness, injury, and misfortune. This practice, sometimes called shadow licking, is among the surest signs distinguishing an Aswang from other blood-drinking Demons.

The first light of dawn forces an Aswang back into its human guise. They are also unable to tolerate the smell of burning incense, a protection incorporated into a number of eastern and southern household customs.

Despite their ability to reproduce through unions with humans, Aswang are Demons rather than a mortal people or species. Their exact relationship to the Outer Darkness, and whether their unusual reproductive cycle arose independently of ordinary vampirism, remains uncertain.

docs.title: Black Trees
docs.text:
Black Trees are Great Trees that have been profoundly corrupted by demonic influence. Whatever their original nature as sapient arboreal Fey, the corruption has transformed them so thoroughly that Loranian scholars classify the beings they have become among Demons rather than Fey.

Their bark darkens toward black, while thick red sap seeps from wounds and fissures. Knots, hollows, and twisted growths often suggest grotesque faces. A motionless Black Tree can still resemble a diseased or unnatural tree until its roots and branches begin to move.

Black Trees are powerful predators. Great branches seize and impale prey while roots and lesser limbs entangle anyone who comes too close. Their bloody sap is extraordinarily adhesive, trapping hands and weapons against the bark, and a restrained victim may be drained of blood as the tree feeds.

Like the Great Trees from which they descend, Black Trees can reach enormous size and are difficult to destroy by ordinary violence. Piercing weapons are particularly ineffective against their massive woody bodies. Fire, however, remains a profound vulnerability.

The process by which a Great Tree becomes a Black Tree is poorly understood. Desecration, prolonged demonic influence, the corruption of the surrounding land, or deliberate sorcery are all blamed in different accounts. Whether every such explanation describes the same transformation is unknown.

docs.title: Blood Mists
docs.text:
Blood Mists are rare remnants or transformed states of powerful Vampires. They appear as drifting clouds of gray vapor that darken through pink to blood-red as they feed.

A Blood Mist is not an ordinary fog. It moves with predatory purpose and can mingle with natural mist closely enough to approach victims unnoticed. Those enveloped by it are gradually drained of vitality and blood while the mist itself grows denser and stronger.

Most weapons pass uselessly through a Blood Mist. Sorcery and other supernatural attacks can injure it, while sufficiently violent environmental forces may scatter the cloud temporarily even when they cannot destroy it outright.

Accounts disagree over exactly how Blood Mists arise. Some describe them as what remains when an exceptionally old vampire's physical form is destroyed but its demonic existence survives. Others claim that occult rites can deliberately force or restore a vampire into this state. A few traditions maintain that particularly powerful vampires can assume mist-form voluntarily. These possibilities are not necessarily mutually exclusive.

Because canonical Vampires are Demons rather than Undead, Blood Mists are likewise classified among Demons despite older northern and occult catalogues sometimes treating them as incorporeal Undead.
