docs.title: Cambions
docs.text:
Cambion is a broad term for a mortal person whose body and supernatural nature have been fundamentally altered by demonic influence from birth or early life. It is not the name of a true-breeding people and does not imply that all Demons can reproduce with humans.

Some Cambions are genuinely descended from a Demon and a mortal parent. This is possible for certain demonic lineages, but not assumed to be universal. Other Cambions are born under a powerful demonic curse, altered before birth by possession or occult interference, or transformed through bargains, sorcery, or other exposure to the Outer Darkness.

For that reason, no two Cambions need share the same ancestry or appearance. Common marks include horns, claws, fangs, unusual eyes, animal-like features, wings, cloven feet, unnatural strength, or an inability to age normally. Some can pass as human with effort; others are unmistakably monstrous.

Cambions are still individuals rather than embodiments of a fixed moral nature. Demonic influence may incline some toward violence, predation, or other destructive impulses, but a Cambion's ancestry does not determine character, allegiance, or destiny.

Because the condition is not a stable breeding population, the child of a Cambion is not automatically another Cambion. Whether demonic traits persist depends on the nature of the original influence and the lineage involved.

docs.title: Changelings
docs.text:
Changelings are shapeshifting Demons that steal the appearances of mortal beings. In their natural form they are skinless or otherwise featureless humanoid horrors, disturbing less for any elaborate anatomy than for the absence of a true mortal identity beneath the forms they wear.

A Changeling can reproduce another person's physical appearance closely enough to pass at a glance, but appearance alone does not grant the victim's memories, habits, relationships, or personality. Someone who knows the imitated person well may therefore notice that something is wrong even when the disguise itself is perfect.

Many Changelings acquire a form through grotesquely physical means, touching or subduing a victim before reshaping themselves and, in some traditions, literally taking on the victim's skin. Others may change more fluidly through sorcery. These differences need not indicate separate species; Changelings vary considerably in power and method.

Among the most grotesque physical variants, the stolen skin is not merely part of the transformation but a temporary supernatural integument. Such Changelings may require intact hides to maintain a mortal form, repair injuries by replacing damaged skin, or have their disguise tear and peel away when badly wounded. Some can strip an incapacitated victim with horrifying speed and don the skin almost immediately. These traits are individual or lineage variants, not universal requirements of Changeling biology.

A stolen appearance does not necessarily reproduce clothing, equipment, magical objects, or other possessions. Changelings that intend to replace a victim for any length of time therefore often steal the victim's belongings as carefully as they steal the victim's face.

More powerful Changelings may acquire fragments of a victim's memories, skills, or supernatural talents along with their form. Such creatures are far more dangerous infiltrators because ordinary familiarity with the victim may no longer be enough to expose them.

docs.text: • Demons

docs.title: Dark Gods
docs.text:
Dark Gods are exceptionally powerful Demons or Starspawn worshipped, feared, invoked, or bargained with as gods. The term describes extraordinary supernatural stature and cultic significance rather than a separate origin category.

A Dark God may therefore be an Exterior Demon beyond Creation's boundary or a Starspawn already trapped within Creation. The distinction between those two conditions remains one of circumstance and location, while Dark God identifies a being whose power and influence are vast enough to support worship, cults, supernatural patronage, and effects on a scale ordinary Demons rarely approach.

Dark Gods are still poorly understood. Mortal religions may describe them as literal gods, imprisoned powers, primeval monsters, demons, cosmic principles, or other things, and those interpretations need not be objectively correct. Even where sages agree that a being is a Dark God, they may disagree sharply over its precise nature.

The term also accommodates established traditions in which mortals worship powerful Demons as gods, including the demon-god traditions associated with the Devi.

docs.title: Known Dark Gods
docs.text:
Among the best-attested powers are:

  • She-Who-Hungers, an Exterior Demon of consuming absence whose webs sever parts of Creation from light, memory, growth, and connection.
  • The One Flame, an Exterior Demon of ecstatic conversion that seeks unity by replacing distinction with itself.
  • The Garden and the Gardener, two apparently related powers of unbounded life and unbounded biological transformation whose exact relationship remains unknown.
  • Jharana, the Teacher Without Measure, a Starspawn power of revelation without proportion whose truths can exceed the capacity of mortal minds and Souls to contain them.
  • Nzamota, the Drowned Dreamer, a primordial Starspawn whose sleeping consciousness reaches mortals through shared dreams from beneath a western abyss.
  • The Veiled King, the best-known manifestation of an unnamed power that enters Creation through increasingly accurate representation.
  • The Many-Named, an unusually active Exterior Demon who walks among mortals in many guises, bargains, teaches, meddles, and deliberately leaves his mark upon Creation.

This list is not necessarily complete. Some beings called Dark Gods may be misclassified, while other powers of comparable stature may remain unknown or survive only under local names.

docs.title: Children of the Dark Gods
docs.text:
The Children of the Dark Gods are beings understood, with varying degrees of confidence, to descend from, have been created by, or otherwise directly embody the influence of a particular Dark God. "Child" does not necessarily imply ordinary biological reproduction. A Child might be spawned, shaped, transformed, extruded, infected into existence, opened to impossible perception, or produced by some process mortals do not understand.

Children should not be assumed to form ordinary peoples or self-sustaining civilizations. Some may be singular beings; others may occur in small numbers or propagate through strange supernatural means. Their forms and powers often reflect the nature of the Dark God associated with them.

The category is intentionally broad and provisional. Scholars may disagree over whether a particular creature truly is the child of a Dark God, merely a demon associated with that power, or something else entirely.

docs.title: Demonic Steeds
docs.text:
Demonic Steeds are horse-shaped Demons used as mounts by other Demons, diabolists, and powerful mortal servants of the Outer Darkness. The name describes a recurring form and role rather than proving that every such creature belongs to one natural species.

Most accounts describe them as great black horses with red or balefire-bright eyes, steaming nostrils, and an unnerving heat about their hooves and breath. Some appear almost ordinary until angered or mounted; others are visibly monstrous from the first glance. Their tack is often as disturbing as the creature itself, fashioned in barbed or cruel forms by those who bind and ride them.

Demonic Steeds possess an uncanny awareness of a rider's intent. They readily bear Demons and mortals already bound to demonic powers, but resist riders hostile to their masters or to the purpose for which they were summoned. A seemingly broken steed may tolerate an unwanted rider just long enough to throw, trample, or carry them somewhere disastrous.

They are exceptionally strong and swift and may possess additional manifestations according to the Demon or rite that produced them. Some leave burning hoofprints, radiate dangerous heat, gallop across terrain that should cripple an ordinary horse, or seem to skim just above the ground. Such traits vary and should not be assumed universal.

Although powerful diabolists sometimes receive or bind a Demonic Steed as a reward, the creatures are not merely infernal horses bred in some mundane stable. They are Demons taking a useful and culturally recognizable mount-form.

docs.title: Dhampyrs
docs.text:
A Dhampyr is a mortal who has begun the transformation into a Vampire but has not completed it. The vampiric corruption has taken root in body and spirit without yet consuming the mortal soul and replacing the victim with the Demon they would otherwise become.

Dhampyrs may arise when a vampiric transformation is interrupted, arrested, or otherwise fails to reach its final stage. The circumstances vary: the responsible Vampire may be destroyed, occult treatment may halt the process, the victim may possess unusual resistance, or some other supernatural intervention may prevent completion. Dhampyrism is therefore a condition, not a people or hereditary lineage.

The arrested transformation leaves permanent marks. Dhampyrs commonly possess some portion of a Vampire's unnatural physical ability and senses, and many develop an instinctive awareness of nearby Vampires. They remain mortal enough to endure daylight and the ordinary conditions of human life, though individual manifestations vary.

Every Dhampyr also suffers the Thirst. Human blood exerts a persistent supernatural hunger upon them, sometimes little more than a gnawing background desire and sometimes an overwhelming compulsion. This is not merely appetite: it is the unfinished transformation pressing toward completion.

A Dhampyr who gives in to the Thirst and feeds upon human blood completes the change into a Vampire. The act crosses the threshold the arrested transformation had not yet reached. The mortal soul is consumed as the transformation finishes, and the resulting Vampire is no longer the person who succumbed, however much of that person's memory and manner it may retain.

For this reason Dhampyrs occupy a feared and tragic place in vampire lore. Their partial transformation can make them exceptionally capable hunters of Vampires, but every confrontation places them near creatures whose blood-hunger they themselves continually resist. Vampires may also recognize the unfinished corruption within a Dhampyr more readily than an ordinary mortal could identify a disguised Vampire.

A Dhampyr's children are ordinarily human. Dhampyrism does not breed true.

docs.title: Evil Spirits
docs.text:
Evil Spirits are weak, immature Demons that have not yet coalesced into one of the more substantial forms in which Demons are usually encountered. They are usually incorporeal or nearly so, perceptible only through supernatural senses, sorcery, or the distortions they produce in mortal behavior.

Unlike mature Demons, an Evil Spirit often has little independent identity. It forms around a narrow appetite, emotion, terror, vice, or impulse and seeks mortals in whom that quality is already present, however briefly. Once attached, it feeds the same impulse back into its host. Irritation becomes rage, envy becomes obsession, fear becomes debilitating dread, greed becomes compulsion, and cruelty becomes increasingly casual violence. The spirit benefits from the misery and disorder that follow, while the mortal may believe the worsening impulse is entirely their own.

An Evil Spirit does not ordinarily create an emotion from nothing. It finds a weakness, moment, or circumstance it can exploit and then deepens it. For this reason, people exposed to the same spirit may react very differently, and the spirit's visible form—when it can be seen at all—often reflects the passion on which it has fed.

docs.title: Growth and Coalescence
docs.text:
Evil Spirits are nascent Demons rather than a permanent demonic species. If one survives and feeds for long enough, it accumulates strength, identity, and substance. Its once-simple fixation becomes more elaborate; its appearance becomes more stable; and it gradually develops powers and behaviors not present in its earliest state.

Eventually an Evil Spirit may coalesce into a more powerful kind of Demon. There is no single fixed progression. A spirit that has fed for years on terror might mature into a fear-haunting predator, while one steeped in appetite, cruelty, envy, or obsession might take an entirely different form. Circumstances, victims, sorcery, the influence of greater Demons, and the particular emotional pattern on which it fed can all shape what it becomes.

This makes Evil Spirits one explanation for the bewildering variety of lesser Demons encountered within Creation: some arrive in recognizable forms from the Outer Darkness, while others begin as nearly formless spiritual parasites and slowly acquire a body and identity through prolonged contact with mortal life.

The change is not necessarily gradual in its final stage. A spirit may remain little more than an invisible influence for years and then, after some unusually intense act of fear, violence, betrayal, or sacrifice, abruptly acquire a stable manifested form.

docs.title: Fear Spirits
docs.text:
One common manifestation attaches itself to a mortal after an episode of overwhelming fear. Such spirits remain unseen near their victims and intensify anxiety over days or weeks until ordinary uncertainty becomes constant dread. Left unchecked, the victim may become sleepless, reckless, isolated, or so terrified of imagined danger that the spirit indirectly brings about the catastrophe it has been feeding upon.

These fear-attached spirits are closely related in behavior to other Evil Spirits, but should not be confused with Nightmares, which are already developed Demons specialized in fear, troubled sleep, and nightmare predation. A fear-fed Evil Spirit might eventually mature into something resembling a Nightmare, but this is one possible development rather than a universal life cycle.

docs.title: Gug
docs.text:
Gugs are immense, comparatively stable corporeal Starspawn that dwell in the deepest caverns and buried cities beneath Umbrathar.

A Gug can stand twenty feet tall or more. Its body is covered in coarse fur, its mouth opens vertically and is filled with heavy fangs, and each of its two arms divides at the forearm so that the creature possesses four powerful hands. Gugs are strong enough to tear apart large prey and have been reported swallowing humans whole.

Unlike many animalistic subterranean horrors, Gugs are intelligent. Ancient underground structures attributed to them suggest persistent communities or at least long-lived occupation of the deep world, although little reliable knowledge exists about their social order.

Gugs possess an innate ability to reach sleeping mortal minds. A buried Gug can appear in dreams, communicate through recurring images, identify people receptive to its influence, and lure explorers or cultists toward forgotten entrances and breaches into the deep places.

Old accounts imply that Gugs were driven beneath the world during some primordial conflict, but no reliable tradition identifies who defeated them or why. That uncertainty remains unresolved.

docs.title: Hellhounds
docs.text:
Hellhounds are demonic canines used as hunters, guards, trackers, and familiars by demons and mortal practitioners of forbidden magic. They are not Fey omen-hounds like Barghests, nor are they ordinary dogs corrupted by training alone; their nature is fundamentally demonic.

Most Hellhounds resemble immense black or dark-coated hounds with visibly supernatural features: burning or unnatural eyes, steaming or heat-scorched hides, oversized fangs, foul breath, or other signs of the power animating them. Exact appearance varies considerably, and some individuals resemble wolves, mastiffs, or other large hunting dogs more than one fixed breed.

Hellhounds are famously difficult quarry to escape. They possess uncanny senses, can follow trails through conditions that defeat ordinary hounds, and are frequently associated with supernatural perception. Some can detect hidden or invisible prey; others seem able to remain fixed on a chosen quarry across great distances or after ordinary spoor has vanished.

docs.title: Lesser Hellhounds
docs.text:
The common Hellhound is primarily animal-like in behavior. It can be trained, commanded, unleashed in packs, and used much as an exceptionally intelligent and terrifying war-hound might be used, although its demonic instincts make it substantially more dangerous than any mortal animal.

Individual Hellhounds vary. Fire, unnatural heat, fear, wounds that resist ordinary healing, supernatural tracking, unusual stealth, and resistance to mundane injury are all reported, but no single ability should be assumed universal.

docs.title: Greater Hellhounds
docs.text:
Particularly old, powerful, or favored Hellhounds may become Greater Hellhounds, sometimes called Alphas. These creatures are substantially larger and more dangerous than ordinary members of their kind and may possess fully humanlike intelligence.

Greater Hellhounds can speak, bargain, threaten, plan, and command lesser Hellhounds. Some lead packs independently; others serve powerful demons, sorcerers, or cults as trusted lieutenants rather than mere beasts. Their greater intelligence makes them capable of remembering insults, interpreting orders creatively, and pursuing objectives over long periods.

docs.title: Familiars and Bound Hounds
docs.text:
Hellhounds are among the more common supernatural familiars and hunting beasts used by necromancers and diabolists. Their tracking ability, resistance to fear, supernatural senses, and willingness to pursue living prey make them particularly useful to practitioners who deal routinely with corpses, spirits, demons, and hostile occult forces.

Such relationships are not all alike. Some Hellhounds are summoned or granted by demonic patrons; some are bound through ritual; some are bred or raised by cults with access to demonic stock; and especially intelligent Greater Hellhounds may enter service through bargains of their own.

A Hellhound familiar should therefore not be assumed to possess the same relationship to its master as a domestic animal. It may be compelled, loyal to a patron rather than the mortal handler, opportunistically cooperative, or genuinely devoted for reasons known only to itself.

docs.title: Hound of Tindalos
docs.text:
A Hound of Tindalos is a predatory Starspawn whose relationship to Creation is geometrically incomplete. The name is an occult and scholarly term; whether it is a true name, a mistranslation, or merely an old label is unknown.

Hounds are most often encountered after forbidden observation, sorcery, or impossible geometry creates mutual awareness between the creature and a mortal. Once this recognition occurs, a Hound may pursue the target with extraordinary persistence.

Their most notorious ability is to emerge through sharp angular discontinuities: corners, joins, fractures, and other places where ordinary space can be interpreted as meeting itself at an angle. A faint haze or smoke is sometimes reported before manifestation.

Hounds are powerful physical predators with claws capable of tearing through mortal bodies. Some accounts describe them draining blood or vitality from wounded prey. They are also exceptionally difficult to kill and may recover from injuries that would destroy ordinary creatures.

The common claim that Hounds travel through time is rejected by most Loranian demonologists. Their pursuit is better understood as movement through aspects of Creation's geometry that mortals cannot ordinarily access.

docs.title: Jharana, the Teacher Without Measure
docs.text:
Jharana, the Teacher Without Measure is a Starspawn counted among the Dark Gods. He is also known in demonological and survivor accounts as the Howler of Truth.

Jharana's defining danger is not falsehood but truth without measure. He offers knowledge, perception, and revelation without regard for whether a mortal mind, Will, or Soul has been cultivated enough to contain it. Small revelations can be useful, brilliant, even transformative. Greater ones can produce obsession, dissociation, the collapse of ordinary categories, or permanent cognitive injury.

Jharana appears to desire enlightenment sincerely. He does not usually interpret a shattered mind as evidence that too much was revealed. He interprets it as evidence that the student still understands too little.

docs.title: The One Without True Form
docs.text:
Witnesses rarely agree on Jharana's appearance. One may see a many-limbed ascetic, another a wheel filled with eyes, another an old teacher, another a beast, mountain, or impossible geometric structure. A single witness may report several mutually incompatible forms in succession.

Demonologists do not necessarily regard these as transformations. The stronger interpretation is that mortal cognition repeatedly substitutes incomplete models for something it cannot represent coherently. Jharana therefore differs sharply from powers of bodily mutation such as the Gardener: the Gardener changes bodies, while Jharana destabilizes the observer's ability to describe what a body is.

docs.title: The Howl of Truth
docs.text:
Jharana's best-known manifestation is the Howl of Truth, though witnesses do not always perceive it as a howl. Reports include screaming, bells, thunder, chanting, whispered instruction, familiar voices, and total silence.

The common element is meaning arriving before language can safely mediate it. The revelation may concern cosmic structures, lost history, sorcery, hidden crimes, personal attachments, the nature of a Soul, or some ordinary fact the recipient desperately wanted to know. Covering one's ears is therefore unreliable protection.

What is called Jharanan madness is usually better understood as injury caused by comprehension that the recipient cannot integrate. The problem is made worse by the possibility that the revelation is genuinely true.

docs.title: The Opened
docs.text:
Those permanently altered by Jharana are commonly called the Opened. They are his Children in the broad demonological sense, not biological offspring.

The Opened do not share one body plan or one set of powers. Their abilities reflect what they came to perceive. One might recognize reincarnated identity, another causal relationships, another intention beneath spoken language, another magical structure, and another the attachments that presently command a person's Will. Some remain highly functional. Others can no longer organize experience in ordinary human categories.

This makes the Opened feared and sought after in equal measure. Rulers imprison them, monasteries shelter them, scholars seek their answers, sorcerers exploit them, and desperate people travel great distances to ask questions no ordinary sage can answer.

docs.title: Schools of Jharana
docs.text:
Jharana's cults often resemble schools more than temples: ascetic communities, philosophical circles, secret libraries, divination societies, occult academies, or heterodox cultivation fraternities. They may produce genuine discoveries and unusually capable scholars. Many adherents insist, with some justification, that they do not worship Jharana at all. They learn from him.

Followers of the Path have a long tradition of distinguishing cultivated lucidity from uncontrolled exposure. A common warning is: “If you cannot close the eye, it is not yours.” Radical Path schools sometimes seek Jharanan revelation deliberately, arguing that cautious teachers merely fear awakening.

Followers of the Immortal Cycle criticize the same danger through the language of coherence and cultivation. Their concise answer is: “Revelation is not cultivation.” Knowledge that outruns the integration of body, Will, and Soul can fragment rather than perfect the practitioner.

docs.title: Mi-Go
docs.text:
Mi-Go are an intelligent Starspawn form or lineage associated with covert observation, collection, surgery, and the preservation or manipulation of mortal minds.

Their bodies are usually described as profoundly alien combinations of fungal and insectile traits. They communicate through telepathy and can imitate mortal speech when necessary, often working through intermediaries or cults rather than appearing openly.

Mi-Go show an unsettling interest in living subjects. Accounts describe abductions, examinations, surgical alteration, and the extraction or preservation of brains or consciousness. Some victims return changed; others vanish completely.

The objects associated with Mi-Go are difficult to classify. Mortal scholars disagree over whether these are sorcerous devices, crafted living matter, impossible mechanisms, or artifacts operating according to principles for which the distinction between magic and craft is meaningless.

The term Mi-Go is established occult terminology, but its origin and whether the beings themselves use it remain uncertain.

docs.title: Nightmares
docs.text:
Nightmares are nocturnal Demons that prey upon mortal fear, anguish, and troubled sleep. They are not dreams given independent life: the Demon exists before the nightmare and exploits the sleeping mind as prey, a conduit, or a means of shaping its manifestation.

A Nightmare may stalk a settlement or household for repeated nights, provoking ghastly visions and feeding upon the resulting terror. Some become attached to a particular mortal. Such a Nightmare may manifest only while its victim sleeps, take on forms drawn from that victim's fears, and vanish when the sleeper wakes. Destroying the manifested body need not destroy the Demon or sever its attachment; without breaking the supernatural connection, it may return when the victim next sleeps.

Nightmares are therefore particularly dangerous to those who mistake the visible horror for the whole creature. Sorcery, exorcism, discovery of the bond's origin, or other supernatural means may be required to end a persistent haunting.

docs.title: Night Terrors
docs.text:
A Night Terror is an exceptionally powerful Nightmare whose influence spreads across an entire locality rather than centering on a single sleeper. Its prolonged presence makes fear increasingly contagious and sleep increasingly dangerous. People under its influence suffer worsening nightmares, exhaustion, panic, and eventually death if the infestation is allowed to deepen.

Night Terrors can turn an ordinary settlement into a place where no one willingly sleeps and where exhaustion itself becomes part of the predator's attack. Old records also associate deaths caused by a Night Terror's influence with the appearance of lesser Nightmares, although the exact process by which this occurs remains poorly understood.

Night Terrors possess a further ability that ordinary Nightmares generally do not: they can seize sleeping minds and draw them into a shared nightmare realm shaped by the victims' fears, memories, expectations, and the Demon's will. A chosen sleeper's nearby companions may be caught in the same dream, turning the attack into a collective ordeal rather than a private vision.

Within this nightmare realm, events feel real even when the world follows impossible, symbolic, or shifting rules. Those trapped within usually find themselves compelled toward some central task—escaping, reaching a destination, defeating a dreaded enemy, confronting a memory, or otherwise satisfying the nightmare's governing logic. The dream's inhabitants, hazards, wounds, and apparent deaths cannot simply be dismissed as illusions while the Night Terror maintains its hold.

This power makes a Night Terror a true boss-level predator rather than merely a stronger Nightmare. A confrontation with one may begin as a regional infestation of fear and sleeplessness, continue through waking manifestations and lesser Nightmares, and culminate with the victims dragged into the Terror's own nightmare domain. Someone destroyed within that dream may be left comatose or spiritually emptied in the waking world. Conversely, overcoming the central ordeal and defeating the Night Terror within its own nightmare can break its hold entirely.

docs.title: Nzamota, the Drowned Dreamer
docs.text:
Nzamota, the Drowned Dreamer is a primordial Starspawn counted among the Dark Gods. He is believed to sleep, lie imprisoned, or remain otherwise dormant in a western abyss beneath the sea.

Descriptions of Nzamota's body vary, but accounts agree on immense scale and a form only broadly anthropoid, with profound abyssal and cephalopod-like traits. His physical dormancy does not silence his mind. Dreams associated with Nzamota can cross great distances, and people separated by seas and kingdoms have reported the same impossible drowned landscapes, alien constellations, and submerged ruins before later discovering one another.

Certain celestial configurations are believed to strengthen this dream-contact. They are not understood as a simple clock counting down to an inevitable awakening; rather, they appear to make Nzamota's sleeping consciousness more perceptible to mortal minds.

The name Nzamota is especially associated with old Zamboulan occult tradition and may once have been a title rather than a proper name. Ancient Zamboulan references to the Drowned Dreamer occur alongside some black-stone sites, but this association does not establish that Nzamota built the structures, that their builders worshipped him, or even that the two phenomena share a single origin.

docs.title: Shadow Children
docs.text:
Shadow Children are malevolent Demons that enter the mortal world only at night. They take the appearance of human children in order to seem harmless, frightened, lost, or otherwise deserving of protection.

Their most notorious sign is their eyes: completely dark and apparently without iris or white. They commonly conceal this feature until they are close to their intended prey.

Shadow Children cannot freely enter a private dwelling. They must first be invited across the threshold, and so they rely on deception rather than force when approaching a protected home. Tales frequently describe them pleading for shelter, claiming to be lost, or asking that a door be opened for only a moment.

Once admitted, they reveal themselves as predatory beings with sharp teeth and claws and an unnatural affinity for darkness and shadow. Some accounts claim they can flatten themselves into or emerge from deep shadow, and that those they kill may be dragged away into darkness so completely that neither body nor spirit is easily recovered.

Their presence in Creation is temporary. At the first light of dawn, Shadow Children are driven back into the darkness from which they came, though this does not prevent the same beings from returning after another sunset.

docs.title: Related
docs.text: • Demons

docs.title: She-Who-Hungers
docs.text:
She-Who-Hungers is an Exterior Demon counted among the Dark Gods. Her defining nature is hunger that produces absence. She does not merely kill or consume living things; her influence erases connection, radiance, memory, fertility, beauty, magic, and other concentrated expressions of Creation.

Her great manifestations are usually described as colossal, spiderlike, and feminine-coded, though the apparent spider form should not be mistaken for ordinary animal anatomy. Her webs are often described as darkness made structural: regions caught within them lose outside light, sound, roads, growth, and even clear memory of what lies beyond. In learned Atharite language, darkness is not her element so much as what remains after she has eaten.

She is especially associated with the consumption of light. Old stories speak of nights in which stars vanished from part of the sky, lamps dimmed without wind, and daylight itself seemed thinned. Apocalyptic traditions imagine her hunger eventually reaching the sun, moon, and stars.

She creates only parasitically. When she consumes something unusually potent, a Child may emerge carrying a distorted residue of what was devoured. Some of her true Children are therefore monstrous acts of reproduction, while countless unrelated horrors are merely attributed to her in folklore.

In much of the Atharite world she is called the Mother of Monsters, although this is not literally true of all monstrous beings. Zorahn theological tradition has especially shaped this image. Older Zorahn religion opposed Ormahn, Lord of Eternal Light, with Angrahn, Lord of Infinite Darkness. After conversion, Ormahn was identified with Athar, while Angrahn was reinterpreted as a personification of the Outer Darkness. Atharite demonologists commonly identify She-Who-Hungers as the greatest known personal expression of that dark principle without claiming that she and Angrahn are objectively the same being.

docs.title: Shoggoth
docs.text:
A Shoggoth is an enormous amorphous Starspawn found in the deepest caverns, drowned ruins, trenches, and other remote places where little mortal life intrudes.

Its body resembles a vast mass of black or tar-like living matter. Eyes, mouths, pseudopods, limbs, and tentacles continually form across its surface and are reabsorbed again, leaving no stable anatomy for long. A Shoggoth can push enormous portions of its mass through narrow openings and reshape itself around obstacles or prey.

Shoggoths are extraordinarily difficult to destroy. Their substance rapidly repairs physical injury, and ordinary weapons may do little more than divide or deform tissue that soon rejoins. Their greatest danger is simple scale: a Shoggoth can engulf, crush, or tear apart creatures far smaller than itself with overwhelming force.

Their origin is unknown. Ancient ruins sometimes contain evidence suggesting that Shoggoths have occupied parts of the world for immense spans of time, but no reliable account establishes who created them, whether they were ever servants of another power, or whether all Shoggoths share one origin.

docs.title: Starspawn
docs.text:
Starspawn are Demons that were already within nascent Creation before its boundary against the Outer Darkness was sealed. Unlike Exterior Demons, they do not need to cross into Creation: they are remnants of what was trapped inside when Creation became a bounded cosmos.

They are especially associated with the remote heavens and the darkness between the stars, but Starspawn is not the name of a single species or body plan. They may manifest in radically different forms. Their commonality is one of origin and circumstance rather than anatomy.

Because their ultimate origin lies outside Creation, some Starspawn may possess bodies that do not obey the expectations of natural life. Stable humanoid, bestial, or otherwise comprehensible manifestations can exist alongside forms whose anatomy is mutable, contradictory, amorphous, or apparently unable to settle into a single configuration. Such manifestations should not be assumed to represent distinct biological species.

Older accounts describing a discrete creature called a Beyonder are best understood as records of one possible Starspawn manifestation rather than evidence for a universal Starspawn form.

Some humanoid Starspawn may be eerily slight or unnaturally tall, hairless and gray-skinned, with large dark eyes, extraordinary intelligence, and powerful mental abilities. Such beings have sometimes been associated with disappearances, strange examinations of mortals, and baffling vessels or instruments whose nature Loranian scholars cannot agree upon. These reports describe one recurring manifestation pattern, not a separate species or civilization.

Other better-attested Starspawn identities include the subterranean four-armed Gugs, geometrically incomplete Hounds of Tindalos, surgical and investigative Mi-Go, and enormous mutable Shoggoths. These names describe particular recurring beings or lineages, not the Starspawn category as a whole.

docs.title: The Garden and the Gardener
docs.text:
The Garden and the Gardener are two powers counted among the Dark Gods whose influences repeatedly overlap. Their relationship is not known. Different traditions describe them as spouses, siblings, twins, parent and child, master and beast, shepherd and animal, parasite and host, creator and creation, or two aspects of one being. Some even reverse which power deserves which name.

The names used here are the most widespread learned convention, not an established cosmic genealogy.

docs.title: The Garden
docs.text:
The Garden represents life that has forgotten every reason to stop. Wounds become new surfaces for growth. Severed tissue remains viable. Organs proliferate. Corpses may continue living in pieces. Individual organisms can merge into larger systems until the distinction between body, colony, and landscape becomes uncertain.

Minor influence may look miraculous: crops flourish, animals breed readily, injuries heal, and cuttings root with impossible vigor. As the influence deepens, growth becomes excessive. Scar tissue continues after the wound closes, meat moves after slaughter, tumors develop functional organs, roots acquire nerves, caves acquire sphincter-like structures, and entire regions begin to behave as living anatomy.

A sufficiently developed infestation is itself commonly called a Garden.

docs.title: The Gardener
docs.text:
The Gardener treats existing anatomy as a suggestion rather than a rule. Its influence produces grafting, mutation, recombination, adaptation, and biological experiments whose patterns increasingly look deliberate.

Unlike an indiscriminate force of mutation, the Gardener appears curious. Traits recur. Failed forms vanish. Successful forms are repeated or recombined. It may alter a creature in response to injury, environment, or resistance and seems capable of taking genuine interest in unexpected adaptations.

This curiosity is not reliably malicious, but neither is it ethical. Pain, identity, consent, ecological ruin, and death are meaningful chiefly as variables in an experiment. A desperate person may ask the Gardener to save a dying child and receive exactly that miracle, only to discover that the child's new biology no longer fits ordinary human life.

Its followers often include physicians, breeders, alchemists, sorcerers, rulers seeking improved soldiers, and mystics who regard fixed form as imprisonment. A recurring heresy claims that Creation was not finished and that the Gardener merely continues the makers' work.

docs.title: When a Garden Begins
docs.text:
Where the two influences reinforce one another, the process often moves from fecundity to excess, then variation, integration, and finally cultivation. Plants and animals share tissue. Parasites become organs. Predator and prey blur together. The environment becomes one ecological-organic system, and changes cease to look random.

Experienced demonologists then stop asking whether the Gardener is present and ask a more dangerous question:

What is it trying to grow?

The distinction is summarized in a common learned aphorism: The Garden makes more life. The Gardener makes life more things.

docs.title: The Many-Named
docs.text:
The Many-Named is an Exterior Demon counted among the Dark Gods. Unlike many powers of comparable stature, he actively walks among mortals, assumes human guises, bargains, teaches forbidden arts, brokers contact with lesser horrors, and meddles in history for reasons that are disturbingly personal rather than merely cosmic.

He is fascinated by Creation precisely because it is not his. To leave it untouched would be, in his own logic, to concede that it belongs wholly to its makers. His interventions therefore range from catastrophic schemes to apparently trivial acts of curiosity. He may ruin a kingdom, rescue a stranger, teach a craftsman something impossible, or spend years living under an ordinary identity simply to see what follows from his presence.

The Many-Named is not compelled to lie. He often tells the truth and may grant exactly what is requested. The danger lies in what changes once he has inserted himself into the chain of cause and consequence.

Invitation gives him greater purchase within Creation, although it is not an absolute requirement for action. Conversation, accepting advice, taking a gift, making a bargain, inviting him into a home, granting him office, or swearing service each creates progressively stronger forms of relationship. Folklore across many cultures has exaggerated these patterns into contradictory rules about names, gifts, thresholds, children, hospitality, and contracts.

He collects names and identities, especially names already heavy with cultural meaning. In some regions he deliberately adopts existing mythic titles, creating uncertainty over whether an old story described him, another supernatural being, or a later reinterpretation. The Stranger is one such alias in the North and is dangerously ambiguous because it collides with an older Northern religious title.

Whatever guise he wears, witnesses sometimes report the same impossible shadow.

docs.title: The One Flame
docs.text:
The One Flame is an Exterior Demon counted among the Dark Gods. It is not fundamentally a god of ordinary fire. Fire is simply the form mortals most readily recognize when something of Creation is being converted into the One Flame without remainder.

Its defining violation is unity through total conversion. Where She-Who-Hungers reduces Creation by consuming it, the One Flame seeks to replace distinction with itself. Individuality, substance, boundary, and difference are treated as temporary divisions waiting to be overcome.

Ordinary flame is its easiest route into the world. A manifestation may begin with fires burning too hot, fuel that fails to diminish, or flame spreading over stone and metal. Greater outbreaks produce living conflagrations, figures of beautiful or angelic fire, and eventually people or places that have become part of the One Flame rather than merely burning.

Those transformed by it are commonly called the Enkindled. Some retain personality, memory, and social function for a time, especially when conversion was voluntary. Others become unstable or destructive. The Enkindled often seek out fires, sieges, winters, famines, prisons, plague houses, battlefields, and desperate communities where warmth, fellowship, healing, and transcendence are easy promises to make.

The One Flame's cults teach that difference is the source of isolation and suffering. Creation, they claim, was divided and therefore left unfinished; salvation lies in returning all things to a single perfected state. This doctrine frequently appropriates Atharite language of sacred flame and illumination.

Atharite theologians reject that claim sharply: Athar's fire illuminates distinctions. The One Flame's fire abolishes them.

Water and ice are especially dangerous to major manifestations. Learned explanations differ, but many demonologists treat this as more than an elemental opposition: water preserves continuity while remaining many things at once, and ice imposes stable form where the One Flame seeks conversion.

docs.title: The Veiled King
docs.text:
The Veiled King is the most widely recognized manifestation of an unnamed power counted among the Dark Gods. Whether the King is an avatar, mask, pressure valve, partial embodiment, or the closest approximation Creation can sustain remains disputed.

This power enters Creation through representation. Paintings, masks, statues, plays, dances, poems, tapestries, dreams, stories, ritual diagrams, and other attempts to depict or describe it can become conduits. Artists and viewers may begin with shared motifs or dreams, then become increasingly compelled to make the work more "accurate" in ways they cannot explain.

Copies are not necessarily safer than originals. A crude imitation made by someone who truly grasps the underlying pattern may be more dangerous than a technically perfect reproduction made without understanding.

The Veiled King usually appears as a roughly humanoid regal figure whose apparent robes may instead be membranes, folded wings, flesh, or surfaces the mind interprets as cloth. Every successful representation fails at the face. Paintings blur it, masks omit it, poems break down before describing it, and memories substitute a veil or blankness. In a direct manifestation that omission disappears, with catastrophic consequences for witnesses.

Occult traditions therefore use deliberate distortion as a form of containment: incorrect proportions, missing passages, wrong colors, broken diagrams, incomplete performances, or iconoclasm may prevent a representation from becoming too accurate.

A recurring sign or sigil is associated with the Veiled King in many traditions. Recognition can warn the knowledgeable that contamination is present, but recognition itself may deepen the connection.

docs.title: Ugallu
docs.text:
Ugallu are ancient desert Demons associated with the Mahrad and its oldest ruined civilizations. Their images occur on seals, lintels, boundary stones, tomb walls, and other relics so old that later Mahradi peoples often disagree over whether the figures depict enemies, guardians, servants, or gods.

In their natural forms Ugallu are towering leonine humanoids, commonly depicted with great wings, clawed or taloned limbs, and long tails that may end in a scorpion-like barb. No two surviving images are entirely identical, and living encounters show similar variation. Some appear more lion-like, others more human, and others incorporate avian, scorpion, or other predatory features.

Ugallu are creatures of empty country: deserts, salt wastes, dry riverbeds, abandoned roads, ruined cities, and the long distances between wells. They are intelligent, patient, and exceptionally deceitful. Rather than simply falling upon travelers, an Ugallu often approaches in a convincing human guise as a guide, hermit, caravan survivor, pilgrim, holy man, or other apparently useful stranger.

Their cruelties are usually deliberate. An Ugallu may offer to lead a thirsty caravan to water, then guide it deeper into the waste until men and animals begin to die. Others send travelers toward haunted ruins, hostile tribes, dead wells, or circles that return them again and again to the same landmark. Only when flight is impossible, or when the victim understands the deception, does the Demon commonly reveal its true form.

Ugallu are themselves notoriously difficult to deceive. Old Mahradi stories therefore warn against attempting to defeat one through clever lies unless the trick has been prepared with extraordinary care.

docs.title: Ancient Guardians
docs.text:
One of the enduring mysteries of Mahradi antiquity is the presence of Ugallu-like figures in apparently protective positions. Some flank doors, gates, tomb entrances, and royal inscriptions. Later occult traditions interpret these images in several incompatible ways: that ancient sorcerers bound Ugallu as guardians; that the images threatened hostile spirits with something worse; that certain Ugallu accepted bargains to protect particular places; or that modern scholars have simply misunderstood the purpose of the structures they guarded.

No single explanation is accepted as certain.

The antiquity of these images has also produced a larger unresolved question. Ugallu may be Exterior Demons repeatedly summoned into Creation, ancient beings that became trapped within the world in deep antiquity, or the remnants of some Mahradi sorcerous practice now completely lost. Their true origin is deliberately uncertain.

docs.title: Vampires
docs.text:
Vampires are predatory Demons capable of passing for human beings. They are not human corpses returned from death and are not properly classified as Undead. The human appearance is a disguise: beneath it lies a monstrous, bat-like predator whose resemblance to humanity is superficial.

A vampire can infect a human being and transform the victim into another vampire. This is not merely a disease or physical mutation. The transformation corrupts and ultimately consumes the victim's soul as the new demonic creature replaces what the person once was. Whatever memories, mannerisms, loyalties, or personality the resulting vampire retains do not make it the original human in any spiritually meaningful sense.

The transformation does not always reach completion immediately. Rare mortals in whom the process is interrupted or arrested become Dhampyrs. Such people remain human, but carry part of the vampiric transformation within them and suffer a persistent Thirst for human blood. If a Dhampyr gives in and feeds upon human blood, the transformation completes and the mortal becomes a Vampire.

This ability makes vampires unusually dangerous even among Demons. They do not need to reproduce only through whatever obscure processes ordinarily produce demonic beings; they can propagate themselves within mortal society, turning victims into predators that can in turn create more of their own kind. Their ability to wear a convincing human guise allows an infestation to remain hidden long after its first victims disappear.

When exposed in their true nature, vampires are grotesque rather than alluring: predatory, bestial things with strong chiropteran features concealed beneath an imitation of human form. Tales that romanticize them as beautiful immortals should not be mistaken for reliable natural history.

The exact limits of vampiric transformation, feeding, disguise, and traditional weaknesses vary considerably in folklore and remain subjects for further reconstruction. Exceptionally powerful vampires are also associated with Blood Mists, predatory vaporous forms or remnants whose precise relationship to ordinary vampiric transformation remains uncertain.

docs.title: Fey
docs.text:
Fey is the Loranian scholarly term for beings that are part of the natural world while also being intrinsically magical in nature.

The word does not simply mean "fairies and elves," nor does it imply one temperament, society, morality, or body plan. Other cultures may understand comparable beings through categories such as jinn, youkai, spirits, or other local traditions. Similarity of folklore does not by itself establish that two cultures are describing the same kind of being.

Fey ecology is strongly regional. Forms familiar to Loranian scholars are not assumed to occur everywhere that a similar forest, river, mountain, or shoreline exists.

docs.title: Loranian Fey
docs.text:
Elves are forest- and wild-place Fey rather than a parallel mortal humanoid race. Individual elves may differ greatly in skills and magical ability; old Warrior, Ranger, and Mage bestiary records are not separate kinds of elf.

Gnomes are a broad family of small, place-bound Loranian Fey. Dwarves are mountain and deep-earth Gnomes associated with stone, caverns, metals, and subterranean places. Claims that all Dwarves are male may survive as in-world conjecture, but Fey reproduction is not settled by that folklore.

Centaurs are rare Loranian and Eoranian Fey of forest margins and steppe. They are now nearly extinct after long pressure from organized human settlement and warfare.

Arachne are rare spider-bodied Fey found especially in the Svealund Underground and deep dark forests. They are not assumed to be universally hostile or habitual predators of sapient beings.

Other established Fey include Satyrs, freshwater Naga, Nymphs, Dryads, and other local spirits. Mermaids are oceanic Fey with a near-global marine distribution; the Torgai sustain the only established freshwater population.

Bunyips are regional water Fey associated with deep pools, marshes, backwaters, and inland waterways. Their forms vary greatly, and individual Bunyips may behave as predators, territorial beings, dangerous neighbors, or guardians of particular waters.

Manticores are savage, highly intelligent Fey rather than a globally distributed biological people. Their regional spiritual ecology remains to be established.

Elementals are magical creatures native to Creation whose forms are composed of or directly embody natural elements. Air, Earth, Fire, and Water are common elemental manifestations rather than four rigid biological species.

Salamanders are persistent elemental Fey with beastlike forms, particularly associated with supernatural fire. They are distinct from generic Elementals. Cold- or water-associated creatures from external sources may inspire other Fey, but are not automatically Umbrathar Salamanders.

Shifters are sapient Fey animals capable of assuming humanoid form. Their animal shape is their natural form; unlike Werebeasts, they are not mortals transformed by curses or magical disease.

The Wild Hunt is an anomalous spirit-world phenomenon conventionally classified as Fey even though sages acknowledge that the category is imperfect. It behaves more like supernatural weather than a species: a hunting host that becomes especially likely to manifest around the Hunter's Moon and may gather Ghosts or other spirits into its passage.

A horse-shaped Fey spirit embodying an idealized supernatural horseness also exists in development. It is more common than Unicorns and is characteristically associated with Elves as a mount or companion; its final vernacular name remains undecided.

Sapient plant-beings may also be Fey. Great Trees are arboreal Fey; Black Trees are corrupted Great Trees rather than Undead.

Goblins are small, troublesome Fey understood through older folkloric traditions rather than as a standardized mortal humanoid race.

Kobolds are malicious chthonic and mine-associated Fey cousins of Gnomes and Dwarves. They replace the older Knocker identity and need not be understood as corrupted members of another people.

Kallikantz are tiny malignant subterranean Fey that emerge especially at night and during storms. They live in hidden colonies, display animal-like cunning, and are infamous for flesh-eating predation and profound vulnerability to sunlight.

Scarecrows are hostile animated field effigies associated with fear, old violence, and magically saturated places. They are Fey under current taxonomy; they do not share a reproductive lifecycle with Mandragora.

Barghest is a rare northern Loranian death-omen hound, most often associated with Albia, Nibelung, and Svealund.

Fetches are invisible canine Fey companions that attach themselves to particular mortals, perceive spirits and hidden supernatural beings, and warn or defend their charges without behaving like ordinary trained animals.

See Bestiary Taxonomy for the broader classification system.

docs.title: Amanojaku
docs.text:
Amanojaku are malicious or dangerously capricious Fey known principally in the eastern lands, where they are commonly counted among the beings called Yokai.

Small and physically unimpressive, Amanojaku are dangerous because they prey on sympathy, trust, pride, resentment, and other weaknesses of judgment. They are consummate deceivers and manipulators, often presenting themselves as harmless children, benevolent spirits, wounded travelers, or other figures likely to win protection rather than suspicion. An Amanojaku prefers to persuade mortals to shelter it, defend it, or act on its behalf, sometimes drawing victims into increasingly destructive choices before revealing the deception.

Their caprice varies from cruel mischief to calculated malice. Some seem content to humiliate, frighten, or turn companions against one another; others deliberately engineer injury, betrayal, or death. This unpredictability is characteristic of their Fey nature: even an Amanojaku that appears merely mischievous should not be assumed harmless.

Amanojaku are also cunning preparers of traps and ambushes. When threatened directly they rely less on physical strength than on prearranged hazards, deception, and startling supernatural quickness. Those who recognize one before becoming entangled in its schemes are therefore in a much stronger position than those who first encounter it in the guise of someone needing help.

docs.title: Barghest
docs.text:
Barghests are rare hound-shaped Fey known chiefly in northern Lorania, particularly in Albia, Nibelung, and Svealund. They usually appear as enormous black dogs, often glimpsed alone on roads, moors, forest margins, grave-paths, or other lonely places.

Barghests are above all omens of death and catastrophe. Their appearance may precede a murder, battle, disastrous journey, sudden death, or some other approaching calamity. Whether a Barghest merely foresees such events, is drawn to them, or sometimes helps bring them about is uncertain. Northern stories disagree, and encounters are too rare to settle the matter.

They do not seem to form ordinary breeding populations or packs. A Barghest simply appears where and when its strange nature draws it. Although often frightening, it is not necessarily hostile. Some accounts describe a Barghest watching or following a doomed person without attacking; others describe violent encounters, particularly when the creature is pursued, challenged, or prevented from following whatever purpose brought it forth.

As with many Fey, folklore is more consistent about the pattern surrounding a Barghest than about its exact powers. Stories variously give them unnatural eyes, impossible stealth, resistance to ordinary weapons, the ability to vanish, or a strange relationship with ordinary dogs. Such claims should not be assumed universally true of every encounter.

docs.title: Northern Folklore
docs.text:
In northern Lorania, seeing a Barghest is rarely interpreted as a problem that can be solved by simply killing the animal. The more important question is whose death it has come to witness.

A Barghest following a traveler may therefore provoke more fear than one that attacks outright. Likewise, the sudden howling or agitation of ordinary dogs is sometimes taken as evidence that a Barghest is nearby even when no human observer can see it.

docs.title: Necromancers and Bound Barghests
docs.text:
Because Barghests are drawn to death and possess uncanny senses for approaching calamity, necromancers have long sought to bind them as familiars, trackers, and guardians. The practice appears to have begun in Lorania but has spread far beyond it; necromancers in distant lands may know ritual methods for calling and binding Barghests even where the creatures are not otherwise part of local folklore.

Such bindings are usually coercive. Barghests are not regarded as innately evil beings, and there is little reason to believe most willingly enter a necromancer's service. A bound Barghest may therefore be compelled by oath, chain, sigil, true-name rite, or other sorcerous restraint rather than loyalty. Tales of escaped Barghests turning on former masters are correspondingly common among occultists.

A necromancer's Barghest is especially valued for locating the dying, following the spoor of death or violence, guarding tombs and ritual sites, and pursuing quarry through conditions that defeat ordinary hounds. This association has become widespread enough that some cultures now know the Barghest primarily as a necromancer's black hound, even though this is a secondary human use of the creature rather than its natural role.

docs.title: Bunyip
docs.text:
Bunyips are uncanny water-associated Fey most often encountered around deep pools, marshes, backwaters, slow rivers, flooded hollows, and other inland waters where the boundary between land and water feels uncertain.

They do not possess one reliable body plan. Accounts describe Bunyips as hulking aquatic animals, long-necked shapes, shaggy or slick-skinned monsters, seal-like creatures, or things difficult to compare with any familiar animal at all. Some reports may describe different local manifestations rather than a single biological species. As with many Fey, the recurring pattern matters more than exact anatomy.

Bunyips are frequently heard before they are seen. Strange booming, bellowing, roaring, or mournful cries from otherwise still water are commonly associated with them, especially at night. Such sounds may be warnings, territorial displays, lures, or simply part of the creature's nature.

They are dangerous, but not uniformly malicious. Some behave as ambush predators and will seize animals or people approaching the water. Others seem strongly territorial or place-bound, becoming violent chiefly when a pool, wetland, or watercourse is disturbed, polluted, trespassed upon, or otherwise violated. A community that knows a particular Bunyip may therefore treat it as a monster, a dangerous neighbor, a guardian of a place, or several of these things at once.

Because Fey ecology is regional, the name Bunyip should not be assumed to describe every strange water spirit throughout Umbrathar. Comparable beings elsewhere may belong to different traditions or even different supernatural categories despite superficial similarity.

docs.title: Centaurs
docs.text:
Centaurs are rare Loranian and Eoranian Fey with the upper body of a humanlike being joined to the body of a horse. They are most strongly associated with forest margins, open woodland, steppe, and other landscapes where speed, grazing country, and broken cover meet.

Once more widespread, Centaurs are now nearly extinct after long pressure from organized human settlement and warfare. Surviving groups tend to occupy marginal or remote country where large human states have difficulty imposing continuous control.

Centaurs are fully sapient Fey rather than Beastmen, animals, or a separate mortal humanoid race. Their appearance can vary regionally, including differences in skin tone, hair, build, and the coloration or conformation of the equine body.

Their remaining societies and regional traditions have not yet been developed in enough detail to justify treating one inherited fantasy model as canonical. Martial skill, archery, mobile warfare, kin organization, spiritual specialists, and varying degrees of isolation from human settlements are all plausible recurring features, but should be developed from Umbrathar's regional history rather than imported wholesale from any one rules source.

docs.title: Elementals
docs.text:
Elementals are magical beings native to Creation whose forms are substantially or entirely composed of the natural elements they embody. Loranian sages classify them as Fey for the same fundamental reason they classify other intrinsically magical native beings as Fey: Elementals belong to the created world rather than originating in the Outer Darkness.

The familiar Air, Earth, Fire, and Water Elementals are common expressions of this broad family. These names describe elemental nature rather than four rigid biological species. Individual Elementals may vary greatly in size, shape, intelligence, temperament, and power while remaining recognizably associated with the same underlying element.

Air Elementals may appear as animate winds, whirlwinds, poisonous vapors, choking clouds, or other moving masses of air. Earth Elementals may take forms of soil, stone, clay, sand, or related material. Fire Elementals manifest through living flame and supernatural heat. Water Elementals take fluid forms ranging from roughly humanoid masses to waves, columns, or other moving bodies of water.

Some rarer Elementals gather or embody substances that cross the simple classical categories. Metal Elementals, for example, can draw loose or worked metal into a moving shell, incorporating weapons, armor, chains, fittings, and battlefield debris into their bodies and using nearby metal to repair damage. Loranian scholars disagree over whether such beings are a specialized Earth manifestation or evidence that the familiar fourfold classification is incomplete.

Elementals should not be confused with every Fey that possesses an elemental association. Salamanders, for example, are distinct persistent fire-associated Fey rather than merely another name for Fire Elementals. Other regional Fey may likewise embody, inhabit, or command natural forces without belonging to the broad Elemental family.

How Elementals originate, whether different manifestations represent stable lineages or recurring spontaneous beings, and how sharply the traditional fourfold division describes the full range of elemental Fey remain matters for further scholarship.

docs.title: Fetches
docs.text:
A Fetch is an invisible or half-glimpsed canine Fey spirit that attaches itself to a particular mortal as a supernatural companion and guardian. It does not behave like an ordinary trained animal and may never communicate directly with the person it follows.

Most Fetches remain unseen. Their companions may notice only a sense of warning, the impression of a dog moving at the edge of vision, or a brief spectral shape when the spirit intervenes at a crucial moment. Those able to perceive spirits describe a large hound-like creature walking close beside its chosen mortal.

Fetches are especially attuned to invisible, incorporeal, and otherwise hidden supernatural beings. A Fetch can perceive such creatures and warn its companion of danger that ordinary senses would miss. It can also attack beings that exist partly or wholly in the spirit world even though it normally cannot affect mundane physical creatures.

Why a particular person acquires a Fetch varies. Some traditions say the bond is determined by birth signs, omens, or unusual circumstances surrounding birth. Others describe Fetches as gifts sent by powerful Fey, gods, sorcerers, or ancestral powers. The mortal usually does not command the spirit; the Fetch simply remains near its charge and protects them according to its own nature.

Fetches are not the same thing as Grave-Fetches. The similarity of names reflects overlapping mortal terminology for attendant spirits, not a shared supernatural lineage.

docs.title: Goblins
docs.text:
Goblins are small, troublesome Fey of Loranian folklore and wild places. They are not a mortal humanoid race or a branch of Beastmen.

The name covers a broad family of malign, mischievous, grotesque, or dangerous local spirits rather than one standardized body plan or society. Goblins may haunt ruins, woods, caves, lonely roads, abandoned buildings, farm margins, or other places where human order is weak. Some are merely malicious nuisances; others are capable of theft, ambush, cruelty, or worse.

Their behavior is better understood through old folklore than through the disciplined tribal armies associated with modern fantasy goblins. Goblins are capricious, local, and supernatural. Different regions may use the word for somewhat different Fey, and scholars do not assume that every creature called a goblin belongs to one biological lineage.

docs.title: Great Trees
docs.text:
Great Trees are sapient plant-beings classified among the Fey rather than among ordinary or merely animated plants. Their intelligence and supernatural nature distinguish them from nonsapient plant creatures even when their outward forms are strongly arboreal.

The exact origin, distribution, abilities, and relationship of Great Trees to ordinary forests have not yet been established in detail. Different traditions may understand them as ancient spirits, living trees awakened into personhood, embodiments of old forests, or something else entirely.

A Great Tree can, under extraordinary circumstances, be transformed by demonic corruption into a Black Tree. Such beings are no longer classified as Fey: the transformation changes their supernatural nature sufficiently that scholars place them among Demons.
