docs.title: Hags
docs.text:
Hags are exceptionally malicious female Fey, sapient, cunning, and usually capable of sophisticated magic, bargains, disguise, and long-term schemes. Although their forms and supernatural talents vary considerably, all known Hags are female and share a distinctive means of perpetuating their kind.

Hags are strongly associated with lonely or blighted places: deep woods, swamps, caves, ruined settlements, blasted heaths, desolate coasts, and other regions where ordinary human order has weakened. Many become deeply tied to a particular territory and may spend generations shaping its reputation, ecology, local superstitions, and human communities around themselves.

Their outward forms vary widely. The familiar image is that of an ancient and monstrous woman, but this should not be understood as a fixed anatomy. Some Hags resemble immense crones with claws and tusks; others appear waterlogged, skeletal, bestial, or almost human until they reveal their true form. Many are capable of disguising themselves as harmless travelers, beautiful strangers, healers, midwives, or other figures likely to gain a victim's trust.

Hags are not merely hostile predators. They are especially notorious for bargains, curses, temptation, and corruption. A Hag may provide genuine aid, magical knowledge, healing, prophecy, protection, or some desperately needed service, but the price is rarely as simple as it first appears. Their malice often lies in arranging circumstances so that a victim willingly accepts the thing that later destroys them.

docs.title: Daughters of Hags
docs.text:
Hags reproduce through human men. They commonly obtain a father through deception, magical disguise, seduction, or a bargain whose true consequences the man does not understand. A Hag may demand intimacy as the price of supernatural aid, assume an attractive mortal guise, or manipulate circumstances over years before claiming what she wants.

The resulting child is always a daughter. During childhood she appears human and may show little or no outward sign of her Fey nature. A Hag may raise her own daughter, but many daughters are deliberately left among mortals and grow up believing themselves ordinary human girls. Foster families may have no idea what has been placed in their care.

Around puberty, the daughter's true nature asserts itself. Her supernatural abilities emerge and she begins transforming into a Hag. The speed, symptoms, and precise appearance of this change vary, but the end result is not a human woman who has learned witchcraft: she has become manifestly Fey, inheriting the strange nature of her mother.

Whether upbringing, character, religious devotion, magic, or intervention can prevent, redirect, or meaningfully alter this transformation is not well understood. Mortal folklore contains stories of Hag-daughters who resisted their inheritance as well as stories insisting that such resistance is impossible; sages disagree over how literally either tradition should be taken.

docs.title: Covens and Local Traditions
docs.text:
Hags often cooperate in small groups, with three being particularly prominent in folklore and magical tradition. Such covens may pool knowledge and power, divide a territory between themselves, or pursue schemes spanning generations.

Names such as Green Hag, Sea Hag, Swamp Hag, Wood Hag, Night Hag, and similar terms are best treated as regional descriptions, manifestations, or traditions rather than a rigid species catalogue. A marsh-dwelling Hag may be aquatic and physically monstrous; a forest Hag may be bound to a particular wood; another may specialize in dreams, curses, disguise, or predation on travelers.

docs.title: Jinn
docs.text:
Jinn are a family of powerful Fey found primarily in Rorania. They are closely bound to the elements and natural forces of their homeland, but are sapient beings with individual personalities, desires, loyalties, and moral agency rather than mindless elemental spirits.

Jinn are commonly described according to the element or phenomenon with which they are most closely associated. Air Jinn, Fire Jinn, Water Jinn, and Earth Jinn are among the most familiar descriptions, though these should not necessarily be understood as rigid castes or exhaustive species. Other Jinn may be associated with storms, springs, desert winds, particular stones, or other manifestations of the natural world.

The word Marid is also used for Jinn in some Roranian traditions. It is especially associated with Water Jinn, and outsiders sometimes mistake it for the name of a separate water-dwelling people. Usage varies, however, and Marid should be understood primarily as an alternative or culturally loaded term rather than a separate elemental species.

Jinn are neither inherently benevolent nor malign. Like mortals—and unlike many simpler nature spirits—they are capable of choosing what they become.

docs.title: Bound Winds
docs.text:
A Bound Wind is not a species of spirit. It is a wind-being placed under a narrow magical compulsion, most often to hunt a particular person, recover an object, guard a place, or complete some similarly specific task.

Air Jinn are among the spirits most commonly forced into this condition, but sorcerers can also bind Air Elementals and other wind-creatures in the same fashion. The rite typically suppresses or obscures the spirit's ordinary physical manifestation, making the Bound Wind extremely difficult to see and difficult to obstruct by mundane barriers.

The binding persists until its task is fulfilled, broken, or otherwise ended by the terms of the sorcery. More intelligent spirits remain fully aware of their servitude. A resentful Jinn may therefore obey the exact wording of its orders while exploiting every ambiguity available to it, whereas a simpler elemental may pursue the command with frightening literal persistence.

Occultists consequently speak of a sorcerer setting a Bound Wind upon someone. The phrase refers to the imposed condition and mission, not to the creature's underlying nature.

docs.title: Ifrit
docs.text:
An Ifrit is a Jinn that has become profoundly corrupted. The transformation is not simply another elemental classification: a Fire Jinn is not automatically an Ifrit, and an Ifrit need not have begun as a Fire Jinn.

The exact paths by which Jinn become Ifrit vary in Roranian stories. Some surrender themselves to demons or Dark Gods in exchange for power; others are said to sacrifice some essential part of their freedom or nature to satisfy an obsession, appetite, hatred, or ambition. Whatever the path, Ifrit are generally more powerful and more dangerous than ordinary Jinn, and the bargain or corruption that empowers them often leaves them vulnerable to supernatural bonds and compulsions.

Old tales therefore repeatedly associate defeated Ifrit with forced service. The same beings who traded away part of their freedom for power may find themselves mystically bound to those capable of overcoming them. Such service rarely produces loyalty, and an Ifrit released from an unwanted bond may nurse its grievance for generations.

docs.title: Kallikantz
docs.text:
Kallikantz are tiny, malignant subterranean Fey that gather in hidden colonies beneath ruins, hills, cellars, mines, and other dark places. They are usually no more than a foot tall, but possess strength wildly disproportionate to their size.

They emerge most readily at night and during violent storms, when darkness, noise, and confusion make their raids difficult to detect. Kallikantz are carnivorous and particularly infamous for stripping skin and flesh from helpless victims. Their attacks can turn small wounds into ragged injuries with alarming speed.

Kallikantz display animal-like cunning rather than developed sapient society. Colonies cooperate in ambushes, scavenging, and attacks, but do not build the elaborate communities associated with Gnomes, Dwarves, or other small Fey peoples.

Sunlight is profoundly harmful to them. Most colonies withdraw well before dawn and choose lairs with multiple dark routes of escape.

docs.title: Kobolds
docs.text:
Kobolds are malicious chthonic Fey associated with mines, deep tunnels, caverns, and worked places beneath the earth. They are closely related in Loranian classification to Gnomes and Dwarves, but represent a darker and more hostile expression of the same broad subterranean spiritual ecology.

Kobolds are not Beastmen and are not members of a mortal humanoid species. Their bodies and habits vary with local tradition, but they are commonly described as small, wiry, uncanny mine-dwellers with excellent senses underground and a strong aversion to bright surface light.

They haunt abandoned workings, disputed mines, deep galleries, and places where miners have broken into old or dangerous spaces. Unlike more benign mine spirits, Kobolds are prone to malicious tricks, sabotage, ambush, theft, and sudden violence. Their hostility toward miners and subterranean settlements makes them a natural counterpart to the more constructive or place-bound traditions associated with Dwarves and Gnomes.

docs.title: Mermaids
docs.text:
Mermaids, also called Sirens, are malicious aquatic Fey whose beauty and supernatural voices make them especially dangerous to sailors and coastal travelers. The two names refer to the same broad creature rather than separate friendly and predatory species.

Their alluring appearance is part of the danger. Mermaids use song, fascination, deception, and the promise of beauty or companionship to draw people into deep water, away from safety, or onto reefs and shoals. Victims may willingly abandon ships or shore before realizing that the creature intends to drown or devour them.

Mermaids are consequently associated with dangerous coasts, reefs, shoals, sea caves, wreck sites, and other places where confused or enthralled travelers can easily be lost. They are not benevolent sea-folk in the ordinary sense, even if an individual Mermaid may bargain, deceive, converse, or delay violence when it suits her purpose.

docs.title: Related
docs.text: • Fey

docs.title: Nature Spirits
docs.text:
Nature Spirits are a broad family of place-bound or landscape-associated Fey whose identities are tied closely to features of the natural world. Loranian terminology often groups beings such as Nymphs, Dryads, Naiads, Oreads, and comparable local spirits under this practical heading.

The category is descriptive rather than a claim that every such spirit belongs to one biological species or shares a single origin. Different traditions may distinguish them much more sharply, and similar-looking beings in other regions need not be the same kind of Fey.

docs.title: Nymphs
docs.text:
Nymphs are among the most familiar Loranian nature spirits. They are commonly described as beautiful humanoid Fey closely associated with particular places or landscape types. Forests, bodies of water, mountains, springs, groves, and similar sites may each sustain their own kinds of nymph-like beings.

Older Umbrathar bestiary material treated Nymph as the general profile rather than creating separate creature species for every classical subtype. That remains the preferred approach unless a particular regional spirit develops enough distinctive Umbratharian lore to warrant its own article.

docs.title: Dryads
docs.text:
Dryads are tree-associated nature spirits and may be understood as a specific form of Nymph or as a closely related class of Fey, depending on the scholar or tradition. They are typically bound in some meaningful way to a particular tree, grove, or living woodland place.

The exact nature of that bond is not assumed to be identical in every case. Some Dryads may be unable or unwilling to stray far from their tree; some may retreat into it; and some may perish if the tree is destroyed. These are useful traditional patterns, not mandatory universal rules for every Dryad encountered in Umbrathar.

docs.title: Other Classical Forms
docs.text: Names such as Naiad for water-associated nymphs and Oread for mountain-associated nymphs are useful Loranian scholarly terms and may appear in regional folklore. They do not require separate bestiary species unless future development gives them distinct setting consequences.

docs.title: Salamanders
docs.text:
Salamanders are fire-associated Fey: persistent supernatural creatures whose nature is intrinsically bound to flame and heat. Unlike a generic Fire Elemental, which is more nearly fire given temporary agency and form, a Salamander is a continuous individual creature with memory, temperament, territory, and identity.

The name does not imply ordinary amphibian biology. Salamanders are supernatural beings whose bodies express their affinity with elemental fire.

Salamanders typically appear as great red-scaled, four-legged creatures and are naturally associated with volcanic heat, geothermal regions, furnaces, fire-scarred places, and other environments in which intense heat is a defining condition. Their bodies radiate dangerous heat, and they are naturally at home in places that would be lethal to ordinary creatures.

They are not simply Fire Elementals in animal shape. A Salamander persists as an individual creature, can learn and remember, and may possess its own habits, motives, relationships, and territorial behavior.

docs.text:

  • Jinn
  • Nature Spirits

docs.title: Scarecrow
docs.text:
A Scarecrow is an animated effigy of straw, cloth, wood, bone, and other field materials that has become a hostile Fey presence. Most remain perfectly still until prey approaches, making an abandoned field or battlefield littered with old figures especially dangerous.

Scarecrows are strongly associated with fear. Their empty or crudely made faces can become horribly expressive once they move, and some seem to draw strength from panic, old violence, or places where death and terror have soaked into the landscape.

No single origin explains every Scarecrow. Tales describe figures awakening after repeated bloodshed, beneath unusual magical conditions, or where an evil or hostile spirit has taken hold of an existing effigy. Whatever the immediate cause, the resulting creature is treated as Fey under current Loranian taxonomy rather than as ordinary Undead.

Fire is one of the most reliable ways to destroy a Scarecrow, although approaching close enough to ignite one can be dangerous when the creature is still pretending to be inert.

docs.title: Shifters
docs.text:
Shifters are Fey animals capable of assuming humanoid form. They are intrinsically magical beings of the natural world, not humans afflicted with a transformative curse or disease.

A Shifter's animal form is its natural form. Different Shifters may resemble wolves, great cats, bears, foxes, birds, or other animals appropriate to the spiritual ecology in which they occur. They possess true sapience and humanlike intelligence despite their animal nature.

Their humanoid form allows them to speak and interact with mortal societies on mortal terms, but does not make them human or transform them into a hybrid species. A Shifter normally changes between a fully animal form and a humanoid form rather than assuming the mixed human-animal body characteristic of many Werebeasts.

Shifters should not be assumed to constitute one biological species or universal culture. Shifter is a broad Loranian scholarly category for this particular pattern of Fey existence, and comparable beings in other regions may be understood through very different local traditions.

The distinction from Werebeasts is one of nature and direction. A Werebeast begins as a mortal and is unnaturally changed toward the animal through curse or magical disease. A Shifter begins as a magical animal and possesses the supernatural capacity to take the shape of a person.

docs.title: Sphinxes
docs.text:
Sphinxes are ancient, sapient Fey with human heads, leonine bodies, and great feathered wings. They are exceptionally intelligent, famously fond of riddles, and dangerous predators of humanoids.

Sphinxes are most common in the South, especially around ancient ruins, desolate monuments, old roads, and other places where centuries of history accumulate. They are not confined there, however. Individual Sphinxes are restless, curious beings and may travel widely in search of knowledge, novelty, prey, or worthy conversation.

Their predatory nature should not be mistaken for simple animal hunger. Sphinxes enjoy testing, deceiving, frightening, and bargaining with those who enter territory they consider their own. Riddling contests, demands for tribute, obscure bargains, and elaborate games may all precede violence. A traveler who entertains a Sphinx, offers useful knowledge, or answers its challenge may sometimes survive an encounter that would otherwise end in being eaten.

Sphinxes live for many centuries and accumulate extraordinary stores of lore. Particularly old individuals may remember vanished kingdoms, dead languages, forgotten roads, ruined cults, and events known elsewhere only through fragmentary legend. This makes them potentially invaluable sources of information, though extracting that information safely is another matter.

Their supernatural nature also expresses itself physically. Sphinxes are unusually resistant to hostile magic, and some possess considerable sorcerous talent of their own. Their roar can carry supernatural terror far beyond the threat posed by an ordinary beast's voice.

Sphinxes reproduce very slowly, which helps explain their rarity despite their great longevity. They form persistent individual identities over centuries rather than existing as a numerous people or conventional society.

docs.title: Related
docs.text: • Fey

docs.title: Tritons
docs.text:
Tritons are a rare aquatic Fey people of the seas of Umbrathar. They are sometimes confused in sailors' tales with Mermaids, but the resemblance is superficial and the two are not the same kind of being.

Tritons are more explicitly piscine in appearance than Mermaids. Their lower bodies are fishlike, while even the ostensibly humanoid portions of the body bear obvious aquatic traits: scales commonly cover much of the torso and limbs, and individuals may show fins, webbing, unusual eyes, gill structures, or other features that make them unmistakably fish-people rather than beautiful humans ending in a fish tail.

They are sapient, social beings capable of forming communities beneath the sea. Triton settlements are uncommon and geographically restricted rather than evidence of a vast hidden civilization beneath every coast. Coastal peoples who encounter them may know them as wary traders, territorial neighbors, hunters, or elusive inhabitants of reefs and submerged places.

Tritons commonly make use of weapons suitable for underwater hunting and warfare, especially spears, harpoons, and trident-like implements. Their material culture is necessarily shaped by life beneath the sea, and contact with surface peoples may therefore make worked materials difficult to produce underwater particularly valuable.

Unlike Mermaids or Sirens, Tritons are not inherently predatory toward humans. Individual communities may be hostile, suspicious, friendly, or indifferent according to circumstance, but they possess ordinary social motives rather than the supernatural lure-and-prey behavior characteristic of Mermaids.

docs.title: Unicorns
docs.text:
Unicorns are rare horse-like Fey distinguished by the single magical horn growing from the forehead. They are traditionally associated with purity and beneficent supernatural power, and their horns are reputed to possess extraordinary magical properties. This reputation makes unicorns perennial targets for hunters, alchemists, sorcerers, and collectors despite their rarity.

A unicorn's horn is integral to the creature rather than an incidental growth. Accounts preserved in the Umbrathar bestiary hold that a unicorn dies if its horn is removed. Unicorns themselves possess supernatural healing power associated with the horn, and the horn remains magically potent after death.

docs.title: Dark Unicorns
docs.text:
Dark Unicorns are the sinister counterparts of ordinary unicorns: an evil reflection of the same Fey archetype rather than ordinary unicorns that have been corrupted or transformed. Where ordinary unicorns are associated with purity and healing, Dark Unicorns are associated with corruption, fear, curses, and death. Their horns retain supernatural potency but may channel necromantic rather than restorative power; reports attribute to them the ability to reanimate the dead by touch.

Dark Unicorns are therefore treated as part of the same broader creature family while remaining a naturally occurring opposite manifestation in their own right. Encountering one does not imply that some ordinary unicorn has fallen or been defiled.

docs.title: Related
docs.text: • Fey

docs.title: The Wild Hunt
docs.text:
The Wild Hunt is a recurring supernatural phenomenon that sweeps through the spirit world and, under the right conditions, becomes perceptible or physically consequential in the mortal world. Loranian sages usually classify it as Fey, while openly acknowledging that this is an imperfect fit. The Hunt behaves less like a species or society than like a kind of spiritual weather: it gathers, manifests, passes, and eventually recedes according to laws that are only partly understood.

The Hunt may appear as mounted hunters, racing hounds, spectral warriors, ships crossing the night sky or sea, or other regional forms. These are not necessarily separate Hunts. They are different manifestations of the same broad phenomenon, shaped by place, season, local belief, and whatever powers or spirits have been caught up in it.

docs.title: Hunters
docs.text:
The beings most characteristically associated with the phenomenon are usually called Hunters. Sages classify them as Fey for practical purposes, despite their frequently spectral appearance and their resemblance to the dead. They are not assumed to be the ghosts of specific mortals, and the Hunt's passage may include other spirits that do not share their nature.

Hunters often appear as armed riders, warriors, sailors, or pursuing figures whose forms reflect the region through which the Hunt manifests. Individual Hunts may include hounds, mounts, ghostly dead, other Fey, or stranger spirits alongside them.

docs.title: The Huntsman
docs.text:
The figure most often recognized as leader of the host is called the Huntsman. Like the Hunt itself, his manifestation varies with culture and place. He may appear as a headless rider, an antlered hunter, a black-clad horseman, an archer, or another locally intelligible image of the relentless pursuer. The Black Rider is one regional epithet rather than a separate being.

The Huntsman is particularly associated with pursuit. Certain dangerous rites are said to name a quarry to him, after which distance, darkness, ordinary concealment, and even apparent defeat may only delay the hunt. Accounts disagree over what such a rite actually does: whether it summons the Huntsman, attracts a passing Hunt, binds a manifestation to the quarry, or merely draws the attention of something that was already hunting through the spirit world.

Older accounts often use the title Huntmaster more generically for whoever or whatever appears to command a particular manifestation. Some traditions therefore distinguish the Huntsman from other possible Huntmasters, while others regard dead kings, ancient women, masked riders, monstrous hunters, and similar figures as local masks or attendants of the Huntsman. The matter is unresolved.

The Huntsman's relationship to widespread traditions of horned hunting gods and spirits is likewise uncertain. Some theologians identify him with such figures, others call him their servant or herald, and still others argue that mortal religions have simply given divine names to a recurring supernatural phenomenon.

docs.title: The Hunter's Moon
docs.text:
The Hunt can manifest at different times, but it is most strongly associated with the Hunter, the hunting face of the moon, and is especially common or potent during the Hunter's Moon. In many traditions the Hunt is not created by moonlight; rather, the Hunter's light makes a phenomenon already moving through the spirit world easier to perceive and more capable of crossing into mortal experience.

This association means sightings may behave almost like supernatural weather reports. Travelers, sailors, hunters, and isolated communities may treat certain lunar conditions as warnings that the Hunt is 'close,' even when no rider has yet been seen.

docs.title: Classification
docs.text:
The Wild Hunt is one of the clearest examples of the limits of bestiary taxonomy. It is not comfortably described as a single creature, population, or even one metaphysical kind of being. Because it is a spirit-world phenomenon intrinsic to Creation rather than a post-death condition or an intrusion from beyond Creation, Loranian sages place it among the Fey and accept the classification as approximate.

Ghosts and other spirits may nevertheless be swept into a Hunt, travel with it, or appear as part of a particular manifestation. This does not make the Hunt itself Undead.

docs.text:

docs.title: Humans
docs.text:
Humans are the overwhelmingly dominant sapient people of Umbrathar. Bestiary entries in this category are not separate species of monster; they provide reference profiles for human populations whose environment, lifeways, or recurring encounter roles make a distinct bestiary treatment useful.

These profiles should not be taken to imply that a culture can be reduced to one stat block. They provide mechanical baselines and common variants for NPCs encountered in particular circumstances.

Cave Clans covers archaic and materially simple human populations adapted to severe wilderness environments, including the Ice Men and Totem Tribes.

See Bestiary Taxonomy for the broader classification system.

docs.title: Cave Clans
docs.text:
Cave Clans is a broad bestiary heading for isolated human populations whose lifeways are adapted to caves, extreme wilderness, and materially simple subsistence. It includes the Ice Men and Totem Tribes where a common mechanical reference is useful.

Cave Clan peoples are human. Their inclusion in the Bestiary reflects their usefulness as recurring encounter profiles, not a claim that they are monsters, a separate species, or intellectually inferior to other humans.

Different Cave Clans may vary substantially in physique, equipment, social organization, religion, subsistence, and relationship with neighboring peoples. Their detailed cultures belong in the appropriate regional and cultural articles rather than being flattened into a universal 'caveman' culture here.

docs.text:

  • Bestiary Taxonomy

docs.title: Monstrosities
docs.text:
Monstrosities are creatures whose defining forms do not continue through the ordinary reproduction of normal animals. They may be unintelligent or fully intelligent.

New examples typically arise through curses, diseases, magical transformations, corruptions, sorcerous manufacture, or comparable processes. Their classification therefore depends primarily on how the creature comes into existence, not on whether it looks unnatural or possesses magic.

Beastmen are an important example of the ambiguity this category can contain. They appear to reproduce in part through abducted human women, yet new tribes also seem to arise unpredictably in wilderness where no stable breeding population was previously known. Their origin remains unresolved, so they are treated as Monstrosities rather than an ordinary humanoid species.

A useful example is the broad category of Animal Hybrids. Sorcery can combine or reshape animals into unique or localized creatures. Most such creations are sterile, unstable, or singular and are therefore Monstrosities rather than a coherent species. When a hybrid lineage becomes self-sustaining and breeds true, however, its descendants may instead be classified as Beasts; Chimeras are the clearest established example. Composite appearance alone does not prove hybrid origin, and creatures such as Owlbears may simply be naturally occurring fantastic Beasts.

Some Monstrosities instead represent extremely old supernatural lineages whose origins are no longer understood. Gorgons, Lamiae, and Minotaurs are examples of ancient sapient Monstrosities now believed to be rare or nearly extinct. Minotaurs are especially associated with labyrinths, tombs, vaults, and other guarded or deliberately confusing enclosed places.

Ghouls are predatory, grave-robbing Monstrosities whose diseased flesh never stops growing. Old specimens can become ogre-like in size, making the difference between a lesser and greater Ghoul one of age and accumulated growth rather than separate ancestry.

Hags are a broad folkloric category of monstrous witches who are no longer wholly human. Living transformed witches are usually classified here, although individual Hags may instead prove to be Fey or Shades depending on what actually happened to them. Hag-born daughters initially appear human and can resist the inherited turning, though even those who remain mortal are often uncanny and unusually prone to magical talent.

Other Monstrosities are deliberately made war-beasts. Worgs are enormous hound-like predators bred by Beastmen through generations of animal husbandry, inbreeding, and dark magic. Their ancestry may once have included wolves or hyenas, but whatever they began as has been lost beneath deliberate alteration.

Other Monstrosities are transformed mortals. Penanggalan, for example, are living people altered by forbidden sorcery into nocturnal flying predators whose heads and viscera separate from their otherwise human bodies.

Corruption does not automatically produce a Monstrosity when the victim's underlying nature remains taxonomically decisive. A corrupted Great Tree, for example, remains Fey, while a transformed mortal or animal may be treated differently according to the actual process involved.

See Bestiary Taxonomy for the broader classification system.

docs.title: Animal Hybrids
docs.text:
Animal Hybrids are creatures produced when sorcery, magical transformation, or comparable unnatural processes combine or reshape the forms of otherwise ordinary animals. The term describes a mode of origin, not a single species or fixed body plan.

Most Animal Hybrids are singular, sterile, unstable, or confined to a small created population. Such creatures are classified as Monstrosities, because their defining forms do not ordinarily perpetuate themselves through natural reproduction.

The boundary is not permanent. Some hybrid forms prove viable and eventually establish self-sustaining populations that breed true. Once their strange anatomy has become the ordinary inherited form of a stable lineage, Loranian natural philosophers generally classify their descendants as Beasts, regardless of how unnatural their distant origin may have been.

Composite anatomy alone does not prove hybrid origin. Griffons, Owlbears, and many other creatures that appear to combine the features of several animals may simply be naturally occurring fantastic Beasts. Loranian sages often propose ancient sorcery as an explanation for such creatures, but in most cases this remains conjecture rather than established history.

Chimeras are the major confirmed exception. Their hybrid origin is historically attested: the first Chimeras appeared only a few centuries ago as the work of a notoriously malicious sorcerer. The creatures proved unexpectedly viable, bred true, and established self-sustaining populations. Their descendants are therefore now classified as Beasts even though the lineage's artificial beginning is known.

This distinction is often more useful to sages than outward appearance. A unique lion-goat-serpent assembled yesterday by a sorcerer is a Monstrosity; a Chimera born naturally to two Chimeras belongs to a breeding animal lineage and is a Beast.

docs.title: Beastmen
docs.text:
Beastmen are savage humanoid Monstrosities found throughout the wild places of Umbrathar. Their true origin is unknown.

They are generally larger and stronger than humans, with bestial features, patchy fur, large eyes, and catlike pupils. Their equipment is usually primitive unless stolen, scavenged, or taken from civilized peoples. Beastmen are most often encountered in violent warbands that raid livestock, travelers, and isolated settlements.

Their communication and social complexity are extremely limited. True Beastmen are not known to practice the developed ritual magic associated with human shamans or sorcerers.

Beastmen are difficult to classify cleanly because they appear to reproduce in more than one way. There are no reliably attested female Beastmen. Beastman bands abduct human women, giving rise to grim and contradictory accounts about reproduction, yet entirely new Beastman tribes also seem to appear without warning in remote wilderness that had previously been clear of them. Because new populations do not arise through an ordinary stable life cycle alone, Loranian scholars generally classify Beastmen as Monstrosities rather than Beasts.

Atharite explanations traditionally portray Beastmen as evidence of human degeneration, sin, or corruption, while other traditions blame curses, sorcery, deformity, or unknown forces of the wild. None of these explanations is proven. The uncertainty is part of what makes Beastmen especially feared: an apparently safe wilderness may begin with missing livestock, progress to disappearances, and eventually reveal that a warband has somehow established itself nearby.

Beastmen vary considerably in size, build, temperament, intelligence, and degree of animalistic appearance. Bugbear is an established vernacular term for Beastmen, especially large, hairy, or particularly brutish individuals. Troglodytes is another traditional name applied to them. Other fantasy labels such as orc, gnoll, hobgoblin, and lizardman do not identify separate Umbrathar species; they are useful only as external rules references or loose descriptive analogues.

docs.title: Great Beastmen
docs.text:
Great Beastmen are unusually large, predominantly solitary Beastmen found in remote wilderness. They are more animal-like in behavior than ordinary Beastmen and are less likely to rely on tools, stolen equipment, or warband society. Some may live alone for years with little evidence of permanent shelter beyond caves, rough nests, or seasonal ranges.

They vary by environment. Forest and mountain forms may be immensely hairy and difficult to distinguish from the surrounding terrain until they move, while northern forms can develop pale or white coats and unusual tolerance for cold. Their size and strength allow them to throw stones, branches, and other heavy objects with dangerous force. Reports of enormous solitary "wild men," snow-beasts, or forest giants often describe Great Beastmen rather than separate supernatural peoples.

Great Beastmen remain part of the broader Beastman phenomenon. Their exact origin, and whether some populations represent stable regional lineages or merely recurring extreme manifestations, is no better understood than the origin of ordinary Beastmen.

docs.title: Ogres
docs.text:
Ogres are unusually large hybrid descendants of Beastmen and larger supernatural humanoids. Most are believed to descend from Beastman and Troll ancestry, although some lineages may instead involve Giants. The term therefore describes a recognizable hybrid family rather than one perfectly standardized species.

Ogres generally retain the brutish humanoid form and social habits associated with Beastmen but inherit substantially greater size, strength, resilience, and appetite from their larger ancestry. Individuals can vary markedly according to parentage. Troll-descended Ogres may show more grotesque or regenerative traits, while Giant-descended Ogres may simply appear as massive, unusually powerful Beastmen.

Because they descend in part from Beastmen, Ogres remain classified with Beastmen among the Monstrosities rather than as lesser Giants or a separate mortal people. Their mixed origin also helps explain why reports disagree about their exact proportions, intelligence, skin, hair, and other physical traits.

docs.title: Beastmen and the Totem Tribes
docs.text:
Totem Tribes are not Beastmen. They are human, possess coherent tribal societies, and can use shamanic magic despite preserving lifeways that outsiders regard as extremely archaic.

Beastmen and particular Totem Tribes may nevertheless cooperate in some regions, and outsiders often confuse or deliberately conflate them. The bear-totem Wyndol and other feared tribes have contributed disproportionately to frontier stories that blur the distinction.

docs.text:

  • Wyndol
  • The Northern Clanlands
  • Atharism

docs.title: Body Snatcher
docs.text:
The Body Snatcher is a small parasitic Monstrosity found in standing water and muddy pools of the Southern Sands. It enters a human host, grows within the victim, and gradually takes control of the host's mind and body.

A possessed victim can still pass at a distance as the same person, but the parasite is a crude impersonator rather than a true duplicate. Controlled hosts become dull, confused, and limited in speech and memory. The creature sees through its host's eyes when convenient, but may also open a grotesque wound through the abdomen to expose its own sensory organs.

Body Snatchers are therefore not Flesh Changers. They do not reshape themselves into another person; they physically inhabit and control an existing body.

docs.title: Constructs
docs.text:
Constructs are artificial beings given motion, purpose, or some semblance of life through sorcery, supernatural craft, or comparable means. Loranian taxonomy usually places them among Monstrosities because they are manufactured rather than born and do not constitute ordinary self-reproducing lineages.

The classification is controversial. Some sages argue that a thing deliberately built from bronze, stone, clay, bone, wood, or other material is not a living creature at all and therefore has no proper place in a bestiary. Others answer that taxonomy is meant to describe the dangerous beings encountered in the world rather than settle metaphysical questions, and that an animated statue which can pursue and kill a man requires classification whether or not philosophers consider it alive.

Construct is consequently a broad practical category rather than a claim that all such beings share one origin or method of manufacture. Different constructs may be animated by entirely different principles, and resemblance between two examples does not establish that they were made by the same culture, sorcerous tradition, or creator.

docs.title: Bronze Bulls
docs.text:
Bronze Bulls are rare artificial bulls fashioned from bronze or bronze-like metal and animated by extraordinary craft or sorcery. Accounts consistently associate them with tremendous strength and supernatural fire, commonly issuing from the mouth or nostrils. Some traditions describe them as capable of being yoked, ridden, or otherwise commanded like immensely dangerous beasts of burden.

Their original makers, age, distribution, and precise means of animation are not presently established. Surviving examples may represent a lost craft rather than something contemporary sorcerers can routinely reproduce.

As with other Constructs, the existence of Bronze Bulls does not imply that every story about them describes the same manufacture or even the same historical tradition.

docs.title: Stone Gargoyles
docs.text:
Stone Gargoyles are guardian Constructs fashioned in imitation of the living Gargoyles that inhabit cliffs, caves, and mountain passes. Human sculptors had already adopted the animal's crouched winged form as an architectural motif before sorcerers began animating such images as protectors.

Stone Gargoyles therefore should not be mistaken for the origin of the name or creature. The cultural sequence runs from the natural Beast, to decorative architectural imitation, to artificial guardian:

living Gargoyle → decorative gargoyle image → animated Stone Gargoyle.

They are commonly positioned on towers, temples, fortifications, tombs, gates, and other structures where an apparently ordinary carving can watch an approach until commanded or triggered to move.

docs.title: Golems
docs.text: Golems are artificial servants and guardians fashioned from prepared matter and animated by magic. Stone, metal, bone, flesh, clay, wood, glass, straw, amber, ice, and other materials are best understood as subtypes or construction traditions within the same broad form, not as separate Construct families for taxonomic purposes.

docs.title: Living Grimoires
docs.text: Living Grimoires are magical books animated as independent artificial beings. They can fly, defend themselves through sorcery, and may be designed to guard occult knowledge or prey upon the magical understanding of other spellcasters. A book whose agency instead comes from a Ghost, Demon, curse, or other inhabiting force is not automatically a Living Grimoire; cause governs classification.

docs.title: Flesh Changers
docs.text:
Flesh Changers are Monstrosities capable of physically assuming the appearance of other people. The term describes a broad category of identity-stealing creatures and transformations rather than one necessarily unified species.

Their exact origins are uncertain and may not be shared. Some may be the products of sorcery, curses, corruption, or other unnatural processes. What unites them is the ability to imitate another person's body closely enough to pass as that individual, at least for a time.

Different Flesh Changers may copy only outward appearance, while others may reproduce voice, mannerisms, memories, or even learned skills. Likewise, some transform their own bodies directly, while others may require the victim's flesh or some other physical intermediary. These differences should not be assumed to represent one fixed biological lifecycle.

Because Flesh Changers are defined by unnatural transformation and identity theft rather than by an ordinary breeding lineage, Loranian sages generally classify them as Monstrosities.

Body Snatchers are not Flesh Changers. A Body Snatcher is a distinct parasitic creature that takes control of a host rather than reshaping itself into the victim.

docs.title: Ghouls
docs.text:
Ghouls are bestial humanoid Monstrosities with patchy, mangy fur, pale scabrous flesh, oversized jaws, and long digging claws. They are opportunistic scavengers and predators, notorious for excavating graves and feeding on corpses but entirely willing to attack vulnerable living prey.

Ghouls commonly travel in packs and prefer darkness. Their senses are particularly well suited to finding living creatures and carrion, while strong daylight leaves them uncomfortable and impaired.

The most disturbing feature of a Ghoul is not its appetite but its growth. Ghoul flesh is a mass of tumors, scars, and ceaselessly proliferating tissue that never truly stops growing. A young or lesser Ghoul is roughly man-sized, but old specimens can become enormous, ogre-like horrors. The largest are capable of swallowing a human being whole.

This continuous growth makes age difficult to judge. A very large Ghoul is not necessarily a separate breed; it may simply be a creature that has survived and fed for an exceptionally long time.

Ghoul flesh and blood are prized by some alchemists despite the obvious danger of harvesting them. Their blood has been used in preparations concerned with healing and antidotes, and strange blood-red concretions or pearl-like growths are occasionally found embedded in the oldest masses of diseased tissue.

docs.title: Related
docs.text: • Monstrosities

docs.title: Golems
docs.text:
Golems are a broad class of artificial servants and guardians fashioned from prepared matter and animated by sorcery, ritual, supernatural craft, or related means. They are a form of Constructs, not a single species or one fixed magical technology.

Most golems possess little or no independent personality. They follow commands, standing instructions, or conditions established by their maker, and may continue obeying those instructions long after the maker's death. Their forms range from roughly humanoid laborers and sentinels to beasts, idols, effigies, or stranger shapes.

A golem's material often affects its capabilities, vulnerabilities, and intended role, but material names should be understood as subtypes and construction traditions, not as separate bestiary species. A stone guardian, an iron war-golem, a bone sentinel, and a wooden servant may all belong to the same practical category despite differing radically in manufacture.

Some traditions produce temporary or evanescent servants that exist only while magic sustains them; others create permanent artifacts capable of surviving for centuries. Whether such short-lived summoned servants are properly "golems" is disputed by Loranian sages, but the resemblance in behavior and magical function is obvious enough that practical manuals often discuss them together.

docs.title: Common and Reported Subtypes
docs.text:
The following are broad construction families and source-supported possibilities rather than a claim that every form is currently common in Umbrathar:

  • Stone Golems — heavy statues or carved guardians emphasizing durability, great strength, and simple standing orders.
  • Metal Golems — bronze, iron, or other metal constructs, usually among the strongest and most durable forms; particular traditions may incorporate heat, molten interiors, poison, weapons, or other built-in effects.
  • Wood or Straw Golems — lighter and generally less durable servants made from timber, wicker, straw, or related plant material; many are particularly vulnerable to fire.
  • Bone Golems — constructs assembled from bones. Despite their appearance, they are not necessarily Undead; the animating principle can act upon dead material without restoring or binding the original souls.
  • Corpse or Flesh Golems — artificial bodies assembled from dead flesh. These likewise need not be Undead if the body is merely raw material animated from outside rather than a dead person returned to life.
  • Clay Golems — molded earthen bodies, often associated with protective or servitor traditions.
  • Glass, Crystal, Amber, or other mineral Golems — uncommon forms whose material may support unusual sensory, reflective, cutting, thermal, or magical properties.
  • Lava, Ice, or otherwise elementally charged Golems — constructs in which the chosen material or bound force becomes an active weapon or defensive property.
  • Beast Golems — animal-shaped constructs, whether carved, assembled, or stitched. Their body plan can reproduce useful traits such as tracking, pouncing, flight, claws, or other specialized functions.
  • Marionette and small servant Golems — compact laborers, attendants, scouts, or ritual servants whose usefulness depends more on obedience and specialized tasks than raw strength.

The list is intentionally open-ended. Sorcerers have repeatedly rediscovered the basic principle of giving artificial bodies motion and purpose, so similar-looking golems need not share a creator, ritual language, culture, or historical origin.

docs.title: Gorgons
docs.text:
Gorgons are ancient, intelligent Monstrosities whose origins have been lost to history. They are not merely women with serpents in place of hair, nor are they regarded as an ordinary mortal people. Surviving descriptions portray them as profoundly inhuman beings in which a broadly humanoid form is combined with serpentine and other monstrous features.

Accounts disagree over their exact appearance. Serpents about the head are the most famous feature, but old depictions and travelers' tales also attribute to Gorgons combinations of great staring eyes, tusks or fangs, claws, wings, scaled or otherwise unnatural flesh, and other grotesque characteristics. Whether this variation reflects individual differences, distinct ancient lineages, artistic convention, or simple error is unknown.

Their most feared attribute is their gaze. Stories consistently maintain that meeting a Gorgon's eyes can petrify a living creature, leaving behind a stone image of the victim. The precise limits of this power are uncertain, and surviving accounts disagree over whether indirect sight, reflections, distance, blindness, or other precautions offer protection.

Gorgons are sapient. Their monstrous nature should not be mistaken for animal intelligence, and the oldest tales describe beings capable of speech, memory, planning, hatred, negotiation, and long purpose.

docs.title: The Last Gorgons
docs.text:
Gorgons appear to have been considerably more numerous in the remote past. Ancient art, ruined sites, and old stories describe them often enough that some scholars believe they once constituted a small but persistent population or lineage rather than a handful of unique monsters.

If so, that age has ended. Gorgons are now believed to be nearly extinct, and many learned people doubt that any still survive. Reports of living Gorgons are therefore treated with a mixture of terror and skepticism. A genuine survivor would be an extraordinarily ancient being, potentially carrying memories of peoples, places, and events otherwise known only through archaeology and legend.

Their rarity also means that little reliable knowledge exists concerning their reproduction, lifespan, original homeland, or the cause of their decline. Even the assumption that all surviving Gorgons share the same origin remains conjectural.

docs.title: The Heryoi Shadow
docs.text:
Gorgons, Lamiae, and Minotaurs appear to belong to the same broad ancient stratum of Monstrosities. Their strongest surviving associations cluster around the later centuries of the Heryoi Empire and the period of its descent into Diabolist corruption.

This does not prove that the Heryoi created them. They may have transformed mortals or older beings, deliberately fashioned monstrous servants, bound pre-existing creatures into imperial service, or simply unleashed powers that allowed such creatures to proliferate. The shared historical horizon is more certain than the precise mechanism.

Some scholars therefore treat the three as evidence of a wider monstrous legacy of the Empire's final age rather than unrelated survivals from an undefined antiquity.

docs.title: Hags
docs.text:
Hag is a broad folkloric name for monstrous witches who are no longer wholly human. It does not describe a single species or even a single supernatural origin.

Most living Hags are classified as Monstrosities because they began as mortal women and were transformed by curses, bargains, forbidden sorcery, accumulated corruption, or other unnatural changes. Others may have genuinely crossed into the spirit-world and become Fey, while a dead witch whose malign spirit remains bound to a place may be better understood as a Shade. Ordinary people rarely care about such distinctions: if an ancient witch has become something visibly and spiritually inhuman, she is likely to be called a Hag.

Hags are usually formidable practitioners of magic. Their transformations often exaggerate both body and temperament: some become gaunt and corpse-like, others enormously strong or ogre-like, and still others retain an almost ordinary appearance until they reveal their true form. No single physical description is universal.

docs.title: Hag-Born Daughters
docs.text:
Hags can reproduce by bearing or otherwise producing daughters who appear, at first, to be ordinary human girls. A hag-born child may be raised among humans for years without anyone realizing what she is.

The inheritance is real but not destiny. As a hag-born daughter grows, especially as she approaches adulthood, her supernatural nature tends to become more pronounced and may culminate in a transformation into a Hag. The process can be resisted, interrupted, or broken. Old tales repeatedly associate salvation with acts that firmly bind the young woman to a freely chosen human life: a true love's kiss, a willing marriage, or comparable acts of genuine love, loyalty, and belonging can prevent or undo the turning. The exact condition is not identical in every lineage, and a merely formal or coerced imitation of the act has no power.

Even a hag-born daughter who never becomes a Hag is rarely entirely ordinary. Such women commonly display strange intuitions, uncanny dreams, unusual affinities or aversions, inexplicable luck, second sight, or a marked talent for sorcery. These traits do not make them evil, and a saved hag-born woman remains a mortal person rather than a disguised monster.

This makes hag ancestry difficult to identify with certainty. Some renowned witches, seers, healers, and sorceresses may carry hag blood without ever having undergone the transformation, while other women accused of such ancestry may be entirely innocent.

docs.title: Different Kinds of Hag
docs.text:
Because Hag is a folk category, individual examples can differ drastically.

A transformed mortal witch remains the most common form. Some Hags become physically enormous or troll-like; others gain powers suited to the places they haunt. A witch who dies without relinquishing her hatred may persist as a powerful Shade and poison an entire wood, marsh, ruin, or valley through her presence. Such a being may still be called a Hag by locals even though learned taxonomists would classify her among the dead rather than among living Monstrosities.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:

  • Ghosts
  • Fey

docs.title: Lamiae
docs.text:
Lamiae are ancient, intelligent Monstrosities now believed to be extremely rare. They are remembered less as a coherent people than as predatory beings from an older age: deceptive, patient, and notorious for preying upon human beings, especially the young.

Their true forms are not fixed by one simple body plan. Old stories describe Lamiae with serpentine, leonine, clawed, scaled, or otherwise bestial features, and some depictions combine several such traits. The familiar image of a beautiful woman joined neatly to the body of a beast is only one artistic convention and should not be taken as a reliable anatomical rule.

What is much more consistent is their use of deception. Lamiae are widely said to disguise themselves as attractive or trustworthy human women, hiding their monstrous nature until prey is isolated or vulnerable. Some possess innate glamour, illusion, or other supernatural means of clouding perception and judgment.

Lamiae are also associated with an unnatural appetite for human flesh. Folklore most strongly emphasizes the devouring of children, though surviving accounts also describe adults being lured, enslaved, or consumed. Whether this appetite is biological, magical, ritual, or simply characteristic of their psychology is unknown.

docs.title: Ancient and Diminished
docs.text:
Like Gorgons, Lamiae appear to have been more common in remote antiquity than they are now. Ruined art, old stories, and fragmentary records imply that they were once known across a wider region, but living examples are now so rare that many scholars doubt whether any survive.

Their origin is similarly uncertain. One widespread legend claims that the first Lamia was once a mortal queen or noblewoman who lost her own children and was transformed by grief, curse, or divine punishment into a child-devouring monster. Other traditions insist that Lamiae are far older than humanity and that the story merely gives a human shape to something people could not otherwise understand.

No single origin account is treated as definitive.

docs.title: The Heryoi Shadow
docs.text:
Lamiae, Gorgons, and Minotaurs appear to belong to the same broad ancient stratum of Monstrosities. Their strongest surviving associations cluster around the later centuries of the Heryoi Empire and the period of its descent into Diabolist corruption.

This does not prove that the Heryoi created them. They may have transformed mortals or older beings, deliberately fashioned monstrous servants, bound pre-existing creatures into imperial service, or simply unleashed powers that allowed such creatures to proliferate. The shared historical horizon is more certain than the precise mechanism.

Lamiae's themes of glamour, domination, predation, and corrupted appetite have led some scholars to suspect that they reflect one branch of the same late-imperial magical degeneracy that produced or empowered other ancient Monstrosities.

docs.title: Distinction from Ghosts
docs.text: Stories of mourning women, child-killing mothers, and nocturnal female apparitions sometimes resemble Lamia legends, but Lamiae are not generally classified as Ghosts. A true Lamia is a continuing supernatural creature with its own agency and body, not merely the post-death residue of a human woman. Individual cultures may nevertheless confuse Lamiae with Shades or other dangerous female spirits.

docs.title: Living Grimoire
docs.text:
A Living Grimoire is an animated magical book given independent motion and purpose through sorcery. Unlike a merely haunted book, its agency belongs to the Construct itself rather than to a Ghost, Demon, or other separate spirit inhabiting the object.

Living Grimoires can move or fly under their own power, defend themselves with magic, and attack those who threaten their creator, keeper, or appointed charge. Some are deliberately made to guard libraries, laboratories, vaults, or occult archives.

The most dangerous examples are created to prey upon magical knowledge. Such a Grimoire may seek out sorcerers, disrupt spellcasting, consume written formulae, or strip magical understanding from a victim for its own use or its master's benefit.

A Living Grimoire is therefore classified as a Construct rather than a Haunted Object, even when its behavior appears intelligent or malicious.

docs.title: Minotaurs
docs.text:
Minotaurs are ancient, sapient Monstrosities associated with labyrinths, tombs, vaults, forbidden sanctuaries, and other enclosed places built to confuse, conceal, or contain.

They are powerfully built humanoid beings with bovine heads and other bestial features, but their intelligence should not be mistaken for kindness, restraint, or civilization in the human sense. A Minotaur may be calculating, articulate, patient, cruel, dutiful, territorial, or openly murderous while remaining fully sapient.

docs.title: Ancient Wardens
docs.text:
The surviving association between Minotaurs and labyrinths is too consistent to be dismissed as coincidence. Ancient ruins, tomb complexes, and fragmentary texts repeatedly connect them with sealed places and guarded thresholds.

What remains uncertain is why. Some traditions claim Minotaurs were created or transformed specifically to serve as wardens. Others argue that they built the oldest labyrinths themselves, while still others suggest both Minotaurs and labyrinths were products of some forgotten culture or magical tradition. No explanation is universally accepted.

Whatever their origin, Minotaurs possess an extraordinary sense of enclosed space. They are notoriously difficult to confuse or lose inside caves, tombs, tunnels, ruins, and artificial mazes, and many seem able to remember complex routes with near-perfect accuracy. Whether this is an exceptional natural faculty, a supernatural sense, or something bound to the places they guard is unresolved.

docs.title: The Last Minotaurs
docs.text:
Minotaurs appear to have been more common in remote antiquity, but surviving examples are now rare. Some remain bound by oath, purpose, habit, compulsion, or simple possessiveness to sites they have guarded for centuries.

Not all have endured that span intact. Isolation, age, magical corruption, grief, rage, or centuries spent defending an empty tomb can erode even a sapient mind. Some surviving Minotaurs have become feral or insane, reducing them to the more familiar image of a roaring, bestial maze-dweller that attacks anything entering its territory.

These degraded individuals are not a separate species or subspecies. They are damaged survivors of the same ancient lineage. A seemingly mindless Minotaur may retain fragments of memory, old commands, recognizable habits, or moments of terrible lucidity.

docs.title: The Heryoi Shadow
docs.text:
Minotaurs are increasingly suspected to belong to the same broad ancient stratum of Monstrosities as Gorgons and Lamiae. All three appear most strongly in traditions and ruins associated with the later centuries of the Heryoi Empire and the age of its descent into Diabolist corruption.

Whether the Heryoi created these beings, transformed earlier creatures, bound already-existing Monstrosities into imperial service, or merely unleashed forces that allowed them to proliferate is not known. The connection is strong enough to be taken seriously, but not strong enough to reduce every ancient Monstrosity to a single proven origin story.

For Minotaurs specifically, their recurring role as wardens of sealed places has led some scholars to argue that they were deliberately made or altered as guardians during the Empire's final centuries.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:

  • Lamiae
  • Monstrosities

docs.title: Morlocks
docs.text:
Morlocks are subterranean humanoid Monstrosities descended from or transformed out of some older humanlike stock. They live in deep caverns, buried ruins, mines, and other lightless places where generations of isolation have produced a distinctly troglodytic people.

Morlocks are pale, powerfully adapted to darkness, and generally ill suited to bright surface light. Their eyes may be vestigial, light-sensitive, or absent altogether depending on the lineage, and many rely heavily on hearing, vibration, smell, and other subterranean senses. Their bodies are wiry or hunched rather than giantlike, with long limbs and strong hands suited to climbing, scrambling, and navigating broken underground terrain.

They are sapient, though surface cultures often dismiss them as beasts. Morlocks use tools, weapons, shelters, and coordinated tactics, and some communities preserve crude but persistent traditions of craft, scavenging, or subterranean subsistence. They should evoke the degenerate underground people of H. G. Wells's The Time Machine more than a conventional fantasy "cave race."

Their relationship to Beastmen is unresolved. Some Loranian scholars argue that Morlocks are an unusually stable subterranean Beastman lineage; others point to their sapience, reproduction, and persistent communities as evidence of a different origin. No consensus exists, and the question should remain open until Beastman origins are developed more fully.

docs.title: Penanggalan
docs.text:
A Penanggalan is a living mortal transformed by forbidden sorcery into a nocturnal predatory Monstrosity. Among the Pingrit, Penanggalan is the most common name; in Heian, the same underlying creature is usually called a Rokurokubi. Regional traditions emphasize different signs and stories without establishing separate species.

By day, a Penanggalan can pass for the person she once was. At night, her head tears free from the body and takes flight while the abandoned body remains hidden and helpless. Pingrit accounts especially emphasize trailing viscera and predation upon infants, pregnant women, and women in childbirth. Heian accounts more often emphasize the apparently disembodied head, the hidden seam where head and body separate, and stories in which a creature conceals or replaces the vulnerable body before returning to it.

The flying form hunts the living for blood and flesh. Darkness and flight allow it to approach settlements with terrifying secrecy even when the creature's true form would be unmistakable in clear view.

Penanggalan are not Ghosts or ordinary Undead. Their condition is a transformation of a still-living person. The exact rites capable of producing one are obscure and may not all be identical; stories variously attribute the transformation to attempts at immortality, black sorcery, bargains, or deliberate initiation by another Penanggalan.

The creature's divided existence is also its greatest vulnerability. The flying head must eventually return to a body. Finding, destroying, hiding, or preventing access to the abandoned body can therefore defeat a Penanggalan that would otherwise be extremely difficult to catch in flight. Heian tales in which the creature can substitute another suitable body may describe a rare technique, an especially powerful individual, or folkloric exaggeration rather than a universal ability.

Despite their monstrous condition, Penanggalan can retain intelligence, memory, magical knowledge, and the ability to maintain a human identity. Some conceal themselves within communities for long periods, moving on when disappearances or other signs of their feeding attract suspicion.

Heian folklore also preserves stories of long-necked Rokurokubi whose heads remain physically connected to the body by enormously extended necks. Whether these represent a rare variant, confused sightings, or a different supernatural phenomenon is unresolved; they are not presently treated as a separate species.

The name and central image derive from the penanggalan of Malay folklore, one member of a wider Southeast Asian family of traditions concerning nocturnal female beings whose heads separate from their bodies with the viscera trailing beneath. Related traditions include the Balinese leyak, Thai krasue, and other regional forms. Umbrathar's Penanggalan is not intended to reproduce every belief associated with any one historical tradition.

docs.title: Werebeasts
docs.text:
Werebeasts are humans transformed by supernatural curses, magical diseases, or similar afflictions into creatures capable of taking bestial forms. They are classified as Monstrosities because the altered form is imposed upon an existing person rather than belonging to an ordinary breeding species.

The exact manifestation varies. Lycanthropes are the best-known family, but wolves are only one possible expression. Bears, boars, rats, great cats, and other animals may serve as the bestial pattern of a particular curse or disease. Some Werebeasts can assume both a full animal form and a hybrid human-beast form, while others manifest only one transformed state.

Most Werebeast transformations are not fully voluntary. The trigger may be lunar, emotional, ritual, environmental, or peculiar to the curse itself. Some afflictions force transformation under particular circumstances, while others merely make control increasingly difficult. A few victims eventually learn to transform deliberately, though control of the change does not necessarily mean freedom from the curse's instincts or compulsions.

Werebeast afflictions are not uniform diseases with one universal origin. Hags, hostile Fey, sorcerers, cursed relics, tainted places, supernatural contagions, and other magical causes may all produce related conditions. Likewise, transmission differs from one strain to another: some spread through bites or blood, some are inherited, some are deliberately inflicted, and some affect only the original victim.

Silver is widely reputed to be effective against Werebeasts, but scholars disagree on whether this is truly universal or merely common across several well-known strains. Likewise, rapid healing, unusual resilience, heightened senses, and bestial ferocity are recurring traits rather than proof that every Werebeast shares identical powers.

Werebeasts should not be confused with Shifters. Shifters are Fey animals whose natural supernatural gift allows them to assume humanoid forms. A Werebeast is fundamentally a mortal transformed toward the animal; a Shifter is fundamentally a Fey animal capable of assuming a humanlike shape.

docs.title: Worgs
docs.text:
Worgs are enormous, terrifying hound-like Monstrosities bred by Beastmen as living weapons and war-beasts. Their ancestry is no longer clear: wolves, hyenas, or several different predatory animals may lie somewhere behind the modern creature, but generations of brutal selection, inbreeding, and dark sorcery have transformed them into something far removed from any natural Beast.

A mature Worg can reach roughly the mass of a rhinoceros. They are powerful enough to carry even very large Beastmen into battle and sufficiently huge specimens can swallow a human whole.

Worgs are not merely oversized dogs. They possess a disturbing, predatory cunning and appear to take pleasure in frightening and tormenting prey before killing it. Their intelligence remains fundamentally bestial rather than humanlike, but experienced Worgs can be devious hunters and exceptionally dangerous war animals.

Their diseased, inbred appearance is part of the horror of the breed. Worgs are products of deliberate Beastman husbandry pushed beyond natural limits and supplemented by whatever dark practices their breeders have found useful.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Monstrosities
  • Beastmen

docs.title: Plants
docs.text:
Plants are nonsapient plant creatures and extraordinary plant life treated as creatures in their own right within Loranian natural philosophy.

The category is kept distinct from Beasts and Monstrosities even when a particular plant is mobile, predatory, dangerous, or magical. Sapient plant-beings are treated differently: under current Loranian taxonomy, a truly sapient plant-being is Fey rather than merely a Plant.

Loranian sages also conventionally place Oozes and Slimes in this category. These mindless amorphous organisms resemble molds, slimes, microbial mats, and other simple life more than ordinary animals, although their classification is a persistent scholarly dispute. Some natural philosophers argue that oozes deserve a separate kingdom of life entirely.

Great Trees are the clearest example of sapient plant-beings outside this category. They are arboreal Fey and need not be hostile. A Black Tree is a Great Tree transformed by demonic corruption and is classified as a Demon; the old Spear Tree concept is absorbed as one possible weaponized, predatory Black Tree manifestation.

Among nonsapient flora, Seaweed Fiends are mobile predatory plants, while Carnivorous Plant is a generic encounter category for forms that do not warrant separate identities. Acid Pitchers and Needlebushes remain distinctive enough for individual treatment. Magically animated or constructed vegetation such as Living Topiary is artificial rather than naturally sapient Fey.

See Bestiary Taxonomy for the broader classification system.

docs.title: Oozes and Slimes
docs.text:
Oozes and slimes are mindless, amorphous living things that Loranian natural philosophers usually place among Plants for lack of a better category. They do not resemble ordinary vegetation and may move, hunt, digest prey, or spread through budding and division, but they share enough with molds, slime-like growths, and other simple life that most scholars regard them as closer to strange flora than to Beasts.

The classification is famously disputed. Some sages argue that oozes deserve an entirely separate natural kingdom; others treat them as degenerate or primitive animals; still others insist that the distinction is meaningless because different ooze-like organisms may not be related to one another at all. The practical Loranian convention is to keep them under Plants until a better scheme is agreed upon.

Oozes are generally mindless. They do not plan, negotiate, or understand threats in any human sense. Their apparently purposeful behavior is instead driven by simple sensory responses to vibration, heat, chemicals, moisture, light, or nearby organic matter.

docs.title: Variant Traits
docs.text:
Ooze is the useful creature category; color names and sourcebook species should usually be treated as local descriptive labels or variant packages rather than separate Umbratharian creatures.

A particular ooze may possess any combination of traits such as:

  • creeping across floors, walls, ceilings, stone, soil, or submerged surfaces;
  • squeezing through tiny cracks or narrow gaps;
  • sensing prey through vibration, heat, chemicals, moisture, or other primitive senses;
  • engulfing, adhering to, or flowing over prey;
  • digesting flesh, vegetation, leather, cloth, wood, bone, or even metal;
  • secreting acids, paralytic compounds, toxins, adhesives, or other dangerous substances;
  • reproducing through budding, fission, spores, or conversion of consumed matter;
  • splitting when struck, or rapidly re-forming after physical injury;
  • possessing unusual resistances or vulnerabilities to fire, cold, electricity, cutting, crushing, sunlight, salt, alchemical reagents, or other environmental stresses;
  • mimicking stone, water, refuse, mold, or architectural surfaces closely enough to remain unnoticed;
  • forming transparent, gelatinous masses that engulf objects and creatures;
  • behaving primarily as decomposers, ambush predators, scavengers, or dangerous colonial growths.

A color name such as black ooze, gray ooze, green slime, or ochre slime should usually be understood as descriptive vernacular rather than evidence of a universal species catalogue. The campaign guide does not establish a rigid color-coded taxonomy.

docs.title: Ecology
docs.text:
Most oozes flourish in damp, sheltered, nutrient-rich places: caves, ruins, sewers, deep forests, swamps, mines, tombs, and abandoned structures. Some are scavengers or decomposers; some are ambush predators; others behave more like dangerous colonies of mold or microbial mats than mobile animals.

Their strangeness makes them particularly common subjects of alchemical study. Useful secretions, acids, paralytic compounds, pigments, and digestive substances may be harvested from certain varieties, though such work is hazardous and local knowledge matters greatly.

docs.title: Seaweed Fiend
docs.text:
A Seaweed Fiend is a mobile, nonsapient predatory Plant found in coastal shallows, tidal flats, wrecks, reefs, and other places where masses of seaweed can conceal an approaching creature.

Its body resembles a tangled heap of wet weed, roots, shells, driftwood, bones, and debris rather than a conventional animal. Seaweed Fiends move through water with surprising speed and can remain nearly indistinguishable from ordinary floating vegetation while waiting for prey.

They attack by enveloping, battering, or slashing victims with tough weed and the sharp fragments caught within their bodies. Rotting organic matter trapped inside them can produce an overpowering foul stench. Their waterlogged tissues make ordinary flame less effective than against many terrestrial plant creatures.

Seaweed Fiends possess only animal-like or lesser intelligence. They are dangerous predators, not a hidden aquatic people.

docs.title: Regional Creatures
docs.text:
This section provides a geographic path to creatures whose identity or significance is strongly associated with particular regions. It supplements the broader creature taxonomy rather than replacing it.

  • Jabber Birds — intelligent messenger animals closely associated with the Jabberer Islands.

See Bestiary and Bestiary Taxonomy for the wider creature reference.

docs.title: Jabber Birds
docs.text: Jabber Birds are extraordinarily intelligent messenger animals closely associated with the Jabberer Islands. The ordinary Meropolitan name of the archipelago derives from their presence there.

docs.title: Messages and Navigation
docs.text: Jabber Birds can learn destinations, carry written messages, and mimic short spoken messages. Their ability to navigate over long distances makes them particularly valuable in an island society where settlements, ports, and princely courts are separated by sea.

docs.title: Use Beyond the Islands
docs.text: Jabber Birds are used throughout the Hetaireian Princedoms and the Southern Cities. They are especially important to Meliti merchants and rulers, for whom reliable long-distance communication supports commerce, diplomacy, and maritime travel.

docs.title: Meliti Symbolism
docs.text: The Jabber Bird is a major Meliti cultural symbol. The shared Meliti badge depicts a Jabber Bird in flight above stylized waves, linking the islands' famous messenger animals with the navigational skill of Meliti sailors.

docs.text:
