  • Meliti
  • Dorado
  • The Hetaireian Princedoms
  • Great Cities

docs.title: Undead
docs.text:
Undead are beings existing in an undead or post-mortem state. Their present existence depends upon death rather than an ordinary living life cycle.

The category includes creatures whose identities, bodies, or continued existence persist beyond death in a form recognized by Loranian sages as undead.

Ghosts is the broad entry for post-death spiritual manifestations. It includes Echoes, Shades, Guardians, and Revenants according to the cosmological distinctions established in Souls and Death. Banshees are specialized Shades and belong there rather than among the Fey.

Zombies and Skeletons are the most familiar deliberately animated dead. Zombies animate substantially intact corpses, while Skeletons animate the bones after most or all flesh has been lost or removed. Both are broad families capable of substantial variation according to the corpse and the necromancy used to animate it.

Danse Macabre refers both to an intelligent skeletal Dance Master and the supernatural procession it creates, drawing living victims into a fatal dance and adding those who perish to its company of skeletal dancers.

Mummies are preserved corporeal undead. In the arid south they are generally called Mummies; the ice-preserved northern manifestation is known as the Draugr. Guardian Mummies are deliberately bound or created variants placed to defend tombs and other sacred or funerary sites.

Barrow Dwellers are intelligent corporeal undead strongly bound to a tomb, cairn, barrow, or other burial place. Northern traditions also preserve terms such as hagbui, haugbui, and cairn dweller for the same broad family of tomb-bound dead.

Drownlings are drowning victims returned as waterlogged Undead, haunting waters and places of drowning and seeking to drag the living into the same fate.

Undead Constructs are purpose-built undead manufactured from corpses or dead body parts. Rather than simply reanimating one corpse in its former shape, a necromancer may join bodies together, rearrange them into animal-like forms, animate individual tissues or limbs, or otherwise use the dead as raw material for a specialized servant.

Grave-Fetches are powerful necromancers' spirit familiars, usually appearing as faceless humanoid shadows. They serve as extensions of their masters' animating will and can coordinate and reinforce groups of lesser Undead.

The ancient Khemetian Undying are also undead, but they are a distinct Khemetian phenomenon rather than vampires. Any vampire-like mechanics used in legacy records are implementation reuse and do not establish their lore, origin, or nature.

See Bestiary Taxonomy for the broader classification system.

docs.title: Barrow Dwellers
docs.text:
Barrow Dwellers are ancient corporeal Undead bound to tombs, cairns, barrows, and other burial places. They are typically the preserved or partially preserved remains of people of unusual status in life: kings, queens, heroes, champions, retainers, priests, or other honored dead whose burial places became spiritually charged, cursed, or deliberately warded.

They are usually intelligent enough to remember at least fragments of their former lives, and many retain speech, habits, grudges, martial skill, ritual knowledge, or a powerful sense of ownership over the grave goods buried with them. Their minds may nevertheless be distorted by centuries of isolation, death, curse, or obsession.

Barrow Dwellers are strongly place-bound. Some cannot leave the burial place at all; others can range only a short distance before weakening or being compelled to return. This binding is one of the most reliable distinctions between a Barrow Dweller and a more freely wandering preserved undead such as a Mummy or Draugr.

docs.title: Tomb Guardians and Grave Goods
docs.text:
Many Barrow Dwellers act as guardians whether or not that role was consciously chosen. Some defend their own tombs, some protect the graves of rulers or kin, and others remain under commands or compulsions imposed at burial.

Their relationship with grave goods is often unusually intense. Ancient weapons, jewelry, coins, ritual objects, and funerary offerings may be treated as extensions of the tomb itself. A Barrow Dweller may ignore an intruder who has disturbed nothing yet react with immediate violence to theft.

In some cases this fixation becomes supernatural. Such Barrow Dwellers may sense precious objects, recover strength by reclaiming offerings, curse stolen treasure, or use apparently valuable objects as bait. These traits are not universal, but they are well suited to unusually powerful or deliberately cursed tomb guardians.

docs.title: Regional Names
docs.text: Northern traditions preserve several overlapping names for these dead. Hagbui or haugbui are archaic forms associated with barrow-dwelling dead, while cairn dweller is another descriptive term for the same broad phenomenon. The terminology is inconsistent between regions and periods and should not be taken to imply several clean biological species.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• Mummies
  • Ghosts
  • Undead

docs.title: Danse Macabre
docs.text:
A Danse Macabre is both an undead being and the terrible procession it creates. At the center of the phenomenon is a skeletal figure commonly called the Dance Master, usually described in gaudy or brightly colored robes and carrying pipes, flutes, or another instrument made from bone.

The Dance Master's music exerts a supernatural compulsion over mortals who hear it. Those who succumb are drawn into the procession and forced to dance for as long as the music holds them. The dance does not merely exhaust its victims: over time their flesh withers and rots away. Those who die within the procession rise as skeletal dancers and remain bound to it, swelling the Dance Master's retinue.

A Danse Macabre therefore grows as it travels. Existing skeletal dancers defend the Dance Master while newly enthralled victims are carried along until they escape the music or die within the dance. Accounts differ over where a Dance Master comes from, whether each is a distinct undead intelligence, and whether a particular procession can be permanently destroyed or only dispersed.

docs.title: Drownlings
docs.text:
Drownlings are the restless drowned: victims of drowning who return as waterlogged Undead with a compulsive urge to drag the living beneath the surface.

They generally retain the appearance they had at death, but their clothing remains perpetually soaked and their bodies carry the unmistakable pallor and heaviness of the drowned. They haunt coasts, riverbanks, flooded ruins, wells, marshes, wreck sites, and other places associated with fatal water.

Drownlings are not merely aquatic Zombies. Their defining behavior is an unnatural reenactment of their own death. A Drownling seizes a victim, clings with dead strength, and forces water into the victim's mouth and lungs even where ordinary drowning would be difficult. In open water they try to drag prey beneath the surface; on land, the same supernatural compulsion can leave a victim choking and filling with impossible water.

Most appear to possess little motive beyond repeating the violence of drowning and creating more death around the place that claimed them. Whether everyone slain by a Drownling can become one in turn, or whether additional conditions are required, remains uncertain.

docs.title: Related
docs.text: • Undead

docs.title: Ghosts
docs.text:
Ghost is the broad Umbratharian term for post-death spiritual manifestations associated with a dead person. Most ghosts are not the surviving soul itself. They are residues, patterns, or imprints shaped by memory, personality, attachment, emotion, manner of death, and place.

Sudden, violent, traumatic, emotionally unresolved, or unguided deaths are more likely to produce persistent ghosts, especially in spiritually turbulent places. Proper funerary rites and guidance reduce that risk, and many ghosts eventually dissipate on their own.

Ghosts vary enormously in awareness, temperament, and power. Loranian scholars commonly distinguish several recurring forms.

docs.title: Echoes
docs.text:
An Echo is weak, repetitive, or fragmentary, with little genuine agency. Many appear to reenact moments, gestures, words, or emotions from the life or death that produced them. Some are little more than supernatural recordings; stronger Echoes may notice disturbances, react briefly to intruders, or deviate from their familiar pattern without possessing the continuity of a living mind.

Echoes are often strongly bound to the place, object, remains, or circumstances that produced them.

docs.title: Shades
docs.text:
A Shade is a harmful, violent, predatory, or malign ghost. The term describes behavior and spiritual condition rather than a single fixed appearance or ability. A Shade may hunt the living, lash out from pain or hatred, drain vitality, inspire terror, or repeat the violence that marked its creation.

Banshees are a particularly dangerous form of Shade, traditionally associated with fear, grief, regret, and a devastating supernatural wail.

A Gravebane is a necromancer-derived Shade: the surviving predatory spirit of a dead necromancer that continues to animate corpses and feed through them. Gravebanes are not stable indefinitely. As memory, personality, and autonomous purpose erode, many eventually degenerate into simpler shadow-spirits that can be captured and bound by later necromancers as Grave-Fetches. This is a common fate rather than a universal life cycle; Grave-Fetches may also arise through other necromantic rites.

docs.title: Guardians
docs.text:
A Guardian is a benevolent or protective ghost, often anchored by love, loyalty, sacrifice, duty, or an enduring bond to a person, family, place, grave, relic, or oath. Guardians may warn the living, defend descendants or sacred places, resist hostile spirits, or repeat some protective act long after death.

A Guardian is still a post-death residue rather than necessarily the conscious surviving soul of the deceased.

docs.title: Revenants
docs.text:
A Revenant is fundamentally different from other ghosts. It is the actual soul of a dead person that, through extraordinary will, unfinished purpose, fate, magical circumstances, or other singular pressures, remains within the mortal-and-spiritual world instead of completing its departure.

Revenants are extremely rare. Unlike ordinary ghosts, they retain genuine continuity of identity and may be capable of learning, choosing new goals, and changing over time. Under some circumstances a Revenant may regain or acquire physical embodiment.

docs.title: Ghosts and the Wild Hunt
docs.text:
Ghosts may be swept into The Wild Hunt, appear among its riders or warriors, or accompany one of its regional manifestations. This does not make the Hunt itself Undead. Loranian sages classify the Wild Hunt among the Fey, albeit imperfectly, because it is better understood as a recurring spirit-world phenomenon—almost a kind of supernatural weather—than as a population of dead beings.

The distinction can be difficult for witnesses to make. A Hunt may contain genuine ghosts alongside characteristic Fey Hunters, spectral animals, and other spirits, so an individual manifestation can look overwhelmingly undead even when the phenomenon itself is not.

docs.title: Laying Ghosts to Rest
docs.text:
There is no universal method for ending a ghost. Because ghosts are shaped by the circumstances that produced them, resolution may require addressing those circumstances rather than merely attacking the manifestation. Proper burial, recovering or destroying remains, fulfilling an oath, exposing a crime, destroying an object of attachment, reconciling descendants, breaking a curse, cleansing a place, or confronting a stronger supernatural being may all matter in particular cases.

Different kinds of ghost can therefore demand very different remedies.

See Souls and Death for the broader cosmology of death, the liminal interval, and the departure of souls.

docs.title: Grave-Fetches
docs.text:
A Grave-Fetch is a powerful necromancer's familiar: a semi-autonomous necromantic spirit through which its master can extend command over the dead.

Grave-Fetches normally appear as roughly human silhouettes of deep, almost liquid darkness. Their outlines may suggest their creator, a dead person used in their making, or no recognizable individual at all. They are easily mistaken at a distance for a person standing in poor light, but close observation reveals no face or ordinary bodily detail.

Unlike an animal familiar, a Grave-Fetch is valued primarily as an extension of its master's supernatural authority. Where it moves among animated dead, Zombies, Skeletons, and other servants become unnaturally coordinated and difficult to disrupt. A necromancer capable of creating or binding one can therefore direct a large body of undead without remaining personally exposed among them.

The exact method of creating a Grave-Fetch varies among necromantic traditions. Some accounts describe a dead spirit bound into service; others claim the necromancer externalizes a portion of his own shadow or soul. These explanations may describe different rites rather than mutually exclusive theories.

One especially feared source of Grave-Fetches is the Gravebane: the predatory Shade left when a dead necromancer's spirit refuses to disperse and continues feeding through animated corpses. Gravebanes often lose memory, personality, and independent purpose as they persist. A common final degeneration is into a simpler shadow-spirit susceptible to capture and binding; once enslaved by another necromancer, such a remnant functions as a Grave-Fetch. Thus some Grave-Fetches may be the last, diminished state of sorcerers who once commanded the dead themselves.

Destroying a Grave-Fetch does not normally kill its master, but the severing of such a close supernatural bond is painful and can temporarily weaken, disorient, or otherwise impair the necromancer.

Grave-Fetches are generally associated with accomplished necromancers rather than apprentices. Their presence among a host of otherwise commonplace animated dead is therefore an ominous sign that a more dangerous intelligence stands behind them.

docs.title: Mummies
docs.text:
Mummies are preserved corpses that have become undead without first undergoing ordinary decay. In Umbrathar, the term is used most commonly in the arid south, where desiccation, burial conditions, salt, heat, and dry earth can preserve the dead for years or centuries.

Not every preserved corpse becomes a Mummy. Most remain dead. Those that rise are terrifying precisely because the process is irregular and poorly understood: some scholars blame incomplete funerary passage, others spiritual turbulence, curses, necromancy, or the persistence of violent emotion within a body that has not properly returned to the earth.

Mummies are typically stronger and more durable than ordinary Zombies. Their flesh has hardened rather than rotted away, and many remain clothed, armed, armored, or adorned as they were in life. Some lie inert for decades before awakening when a tomb is disturbed, while others wander ruins, caves, deserts, or burial grounds.

Although sorcerers can deliberately animate preserved dead, Mummy does not imply artificial creation. Natural preservation can itself produce the conditions under which such undead sometimes arise.

docs.title: Guardian Mummies
docs.text:
Guardian Mummies are preserved dead deliberately bound, awakened, or commanded to defend tombs, temples, reliquaries, royal burials, and similar places. Priests, soldiers, retainers, and other suitable corpses may be prepared for this role either during burial or through later necromancy.

Unlike naturally arising Mummies, Guardian Mummies exist because someone intended the dead to remain on duty. Their exact degree of memory and independence varies. Some are little more than tireless sentinels; others retain enough personality to interpret old orders, recognize sacred symbols, or distinguish rightful heirs from intruders.

Particularly elaborate guardian curses may bind the creature's behavior to the wealth it protects. Such a guardian might sense stolen grave goods, grow stronger when treasure is returned, curse objects taken from the tomb, or use tempting valuables as bait for thieves. These are exceptional curse traditions rather than universal Mummy traits.

docs.title: Draugr
docs.text:
In the frozen Clanlands, the same broad phenomenon is known as the Draugr. Here the body is preserved by severe cold rather than aridity. Frozen flesh hardens around the corpse, wounds remain visible, and armor, clothing, and weapons may remain trapped in ice or frost for generations before the dead stir again.

Draugr are therefore not a separate species of undead from Mummies, but the northern ice-preserved manifestation of the same phenomenon. They are particularly associated with frozen battlefields, lost travelers, snowbound ruins, burial cairns, glaciers, and other places where the dead can remain physically intact for long periods.

Northern stories often attribute additional powers to Draugr: unnatural cold, frostbite at a touch, unusual strength, resistance to ordinary injury, or a tendency to become dormant when removed from freezing conditions. Such traits vary between individuals and regions and should not be assumed universal.

docs.title: Regional Variants
docs.text:
Preservation by environment produces considerable variation. Southern Mummies may be desiccated, salt-preserved, sand-encrusted, or calcified; Draugr may be ice-locked, frost-hardened, or partially frozen. In either case, the preserved body itself is central to the creature's identity.

Necromancers sometimes seek out such corpses specifically because preservation leaves unusually complete remains to animate. This does not make every Mummy or Draugr a necromancer's servant, but it does make ancient tombs and frozen battlefields attractive resources to practitioners of corpse-magic.

docs.title: Screaming Skull
docs.text:
A Screaming Skull is a deliberately animated skull used as a minor Undead Construct and necromantic servant. It can fly under its own power, observe its surroundings, and unleash a terrifying supernatural scream.

Screaming Skulls are especially useful as spies, sentries, alarms, and messengers. They possess only limited independent intelligence, but a skilled creator can bind one to patrol a place, watch particular people, or alert its master to intrusion.

Some necromancers establish shared senses with a Screaming Skull, allowing the creator to see and hear through the servant at a distance. Destroying the skull can therefore blind an unseen observer as well as eliminate the immediate threat.

docs.title: Skeletons
docs.text:
Skeletons are among the simplest and most familiar forms of animated Undead. Necromancy animates a dead creature's bones and compels them to move and act despite the absence of living muscle, organs, or other tissues.

Most Skeletons are simple servants or guardians. They retain little or none of the identity of the dead creature whose bones they use and normally act according to the commands, bindings, or supernatural impulses that animate them. Their lack of flesh makes them physically different from Zombies, but both are common examples of deliberately animated dead.

Skeletons can be made from the remains of many creatures, not only humanoids. More elaborate skeletal creations may cross into Undead Constructs when a necromancer deliberately rebuilds, combines, or modifies the bones into a purpose-built anatomy rather than simply animating an existing skeleton.

docs.title: Undead Constructs
docs.text:
Undead Constructs are artificial undead assembled, surgically reshaped, or otherwise manufactured from corpses and dead body parts before being animated through necromancy or a comparable supernatural process.

They differ from ordinary Zombies and Skeletons mainly in design. A Zombie is usually a dead body made to move again in roughly the form it possessed in life. An Undead Construct uses the dead as raw material: bodies may be joined together, rearranged into an animal-like shape, stripped down to particular tissues, fitted with additional limbs, or otherwise rebuilt for a particular purpose before animation.

There is no single standard form. A necromancer might build a many-limbed climbing predator from several corpses, reshape one body into a quadrupedal hunting beast, animate an intact sheet of flayed skin as a strangling servant, or fuse a battlefield's dead into one growing mass. Such creations are best understood as products of necromantic craft rather than separate supernatural species.

The distinction from Golems is metaphysical as well as practical. Some golems are made from bone or corpse-flesh, but their dead material is merely construction matter animated as a Construct. Undead Constructs are genuinely Undead: necromancy grants unlife to the manufactured body. Outward appearance alone may not reveal which process was used.

docs.title: Common Construction Patterns
docs.text:
Known or plausible forms include:

  • Conglomerates — several corpses fused into one mass. Additional bodies may increase size, strength, resilience, or number of usable limbs. Some examples can incorporate new corpses after creation.
  • Corpse-Crawlers — bodies or torsos joined into long many-limbed forms that scuttle or climb like centipedes. Their numerous arms make them particularly effective at grappling and crushing prey.
  • Corpse Hounds — humanoid corpses surgically reshaped into low, fast quadrupedal hunting forms. Necromancers may modify jaws, tongues, limbs, senses, or internal anatomy to produce specialized trackers and attack beasts.
  • Flayed Servants — skin or other soft tissue removed intact and animated independently, often as crawling, enveloping, strangling, or smothering creatures.
  • Dismembered Servants — severed limbs, heads, viscera, or other body parts animated separately or designed to separate during combat. Creeping Hands overlap this pattern, although not every Creeping Hand is an Undead Construct. Screaming Skulls are a deliberate head-servant form used as flying sentries, spies, and alarms.
  • Visceral Servants — organs, vessels, or connected masses of soft internal tissue animated as independent guardians or predators. Such creations can be especially difficult to recognize as a single creature at first glance.
  • Skeletal Champions — deliberately modified or specially prepared skeletons built for elite martial service. Additional limbs, permanently fitted armor, retained intelligence, supernatural resilience, or binding oaths can distinguish them from ordinary animated skeletons.

These are construction patterns rather than canonical species. Individual necromancers may produce unique designs, and several traditions can independently arrive at similar solutions.

docs.title: Undying
docs.text:
The Undying are an ancient Khemetian form of undead. Unlike ordinary corpses raised by necromancy, they are associated with a deliberate transformation intended to preserve a person beyond mortal death.

They are a specifically Khemetian phenomenon and should not be treated as another name for vampires. The exact ritual, history, relationship to Khemetian Deathspeakers, and limits of the condition remain to be recovered or developed from the relevant Khemetian canon rather than reconstructed from older game statistics.

docs.title: Zombies
docs.text:
Zombies are corpses animated as Undead while retaining substantially the body and physical form they possessed at death. Alongside Skeletons, they are among the simplest and most familiar products of deliberate necromancy.

Most Zombies possess little or none of the identity, memory, or intelligence of the dead creature whose corpse they inhabit. They act according to the commands, bindings, compulsions, or supernatural impulses imposed by whatever animates them. Their continued movement does not imply that the original soul has returned to the body.

A Zombie can be made from the corpse of almost any creature with a sufficiently intact body. Age, decomposition, preservation, cause of death, the animating method, and deliberate preparation by a necromancer can all produce substantial differences between individual Zombies.

For that reason, Zombie describes a broad form of corporeal Undead rather than one narrowly uniform creature. Particularly distinctive methods of animation may produce recognizable variants with different physical or supernatural capabilities.

A corpse that has been extensively rebuilt, combined with other bodies, or deliberately reshaped into a new anatomy is normally better classified as an Undead Construct rather than a Zombie.

docs.title: Appendix
docs.text:
The Appendix collects supplementary material that sits outside the main setting chapters but remains useful as a player reference.

  • Player Characters — the principal player characters of the Gran Mago expedition to Devi.
  • Songs of the Sea — songs, shanties, boasts, and ballads of Umbrathar's sailors and maritime cultures.

docs.title: Player Characters
docs.text: These were the principal adventurers of the Gran Mago expedition from Tejago to Devi in 881–883 AA.

docs.title: Amaro Xacobo de Uviendo
docs.text:
Amaro Xacobo de Uviendo was an Atharite priest and Theurge living in Tejago. His studies included the Devi language and the magical plants and substances used in Theurgy, making him particularly useful for an expedition bound for Devi. He also had a strong personal interest in missionary work.

Amaro joined the voyage of the Gran Mago to Devi and survived the expedition, returning to Tejago in 883 AA.

docs.title: Bjorn “Hvítabjørn” Gohnson
docs.text:
Bjorn “Hvítabjørn” Gohnson, commonly called Gohn, was a Firelander mercenary and veteran warrior. He had previously fought alongside Raymundo Çizóm in a small war and later served as first mate aboard the Gran Mago.

Gohn joined the voyage to Devi and survived the expedition, returning to Tejago in 883 AA.

docs.title: Raymundo Çizóm
docs.text:
Raymundo Çizóm was a Tejagan sailor, naval veteran, and merchant captain. He had received commendations for bravery during his service in the Tejagan navy and later pursued a modest merchant career aboard the Gran Mago.

Raymundo joined the voyage to Devi and survived the expedition, returning to Tejago in 883 AA.

docs.title: Telvitri Damascus
docs.text:
Telvitri Damascus was a Devi warrior who had been betrayed and sold into pit slavery before eventually making his way to Tejago. He joined the expedition with strong personal reasons for returning to Devi.

Telvitri took part in the voyage of the Gran Mago but died in Devi before the expedition returned to Tejago.

docs.title: Ibn Sina al-Kabba
docs.text:
Ibn Sina al-Kabba was the son and representative of Sadiq al-Kabba, one of the financiers behind the expedition. He accompanied the voyage as his father’s agent and as one of its principal members.

Ibn Sina took part in the voyage to Devi and returned to Tejago ahead of the Gran Mago.

docs.title: Songs of the Sea
docs.text:
Collected here are a number of songs, shanties, boasts, and ballads heard aboard the ships and in the dockside taverns of Umbrathar. They are works of dubious provenance, sung by even more dubious men, and should not be mistaken for sober accounts of history, geography, theology, or anything else. Nevertheless, a sailor may tell you there is often more truth in a good song than in a scholar's book—and considerably more entertainment.

The songs themselves are part of the living culture of Umbrathar. Their claims are those of their singers: old names, exaggerations, prejudices, boasts, contradictions, and outright falsehoods may survive in a verse long after sober histories say otherwise.

docs.title: Round the Horn (of Rorania)
docs.text:
The Song of the El Gran Mago

Closely associated with the famous voyages of the El Gran Mago, this song became one of the best-known reminders of the dangers, discomforts, and rewards of the long sea-road around Rorania.

Verse 1

Sea serpents today, and far worse things tomorrow. Pray to Athar the sails will last, or the next day we will row!

Chorus

Goin' 'round the horn, 'round the horn of Rorania! If I don't die of disease, then at home port I shall see ya'!

Verse 2

Zamboulan spears, citymen food fighting off wicked Devi brood. Were I not pressed I'd be back in port, Carousing with familiar sort!

Chorus

Goin' 'round the horn, 'round the horn of Rorania! If I don't die of disease, then at home port I shall see ya'!

Verse 3

The riches big, but the dangers many Love for these places, I don't have any. Pirate nations, dead ahead words from the lookout, I do dread.

Chorus

Goin' 'round the horn, 'round the horn of Rorania! If I don't die of disease, then at home port I shall see ya'!

docs.title: The Jabberers Chaunty
docs.text:
By an Anonymous Crewman of the El Gran Mago

Sailin' outta the Jabberers and wasn't it a treat Winds were blowin' east-southeast to make the passage fleet You oughta see us runnin', the winds a-blowin' free On passage from the Jabberers to great Devi.

Chorus

Ay Gonzago, we are a doughty crew! Give a sheet an' let her slip, we're the boys to pull her through! You ought to see us runnin', the wind a-blowin' free! On passage from the Jabberers to Great Devi!

Our captain he's a Szovvy runt who likes to play the strings Our purser he's an Anwarese, he never says a thing! Our first mate he's a bearsarker, he comes from the Flamin' Isles! We've even got a Deviman who's full stark raving wild!

Chorus

Ay Gonzago, we are a doughty crew! Give a sheet an' let her slip, we're the boys to pull her through! You ought to see us runnin', the wind a-blowin' free! On passage from the Jabberers to Great Devi!

Our chemister is quite a stir, can't live without his ale. Our priest he is a holy fool who's never seen a sail! The crew has got its dullards and its drunkards and a whore! But we'd not trade a one of us for all the men ashore!

Chorus

Ay Gonzago, we are a doughty crew! Give a sheet an' let her slip, we're the boys to pull her through! You ought to see us runnin', the wind a-blowin' free! On passage from the Jabberers to Great Devi!

Ay Gonzago, we are a doughty crew! Give a sheet an' let her slip, we're the boys to pull her through! You ought to see us runnin', the wind a-blowin' free! On passage from the Jabberers to Great Devi!

docs.title: Devi Away
docs.text:
A Traditional Doradan Parting Song

Doradan sailors adapt this song to their destination, replacing "Devi" with whatever foreign shore awaits them. This version was sung on the voyage of the El Gran Mago to Devi.

Verse 1

Ooooh, La senorita, I miss her so But on the princes orders, to Devi I go. The journey's long, the waters, tough But the prince's favor, should be enough.

Chorus

To Devi away, my senora, she stay on the Golden shores of my home bay. Oh I hope to see her again some day But for now, to Devi, away.

Verse 2

On the map my home Dorado, Grows further away by the day! Oh I wish I could just simply go, back to my love, in Dorado.

Chorus

To Devi away, my senora, she stay, on the Golden shores of my home bay. Oh I hope to see her again some day But for now, to Devi, away.

Verse 3

The land of Devi, so unlike home But on crown's orders I must roam. The food is foul, the people strange.. On the journey back, my mood will change.

Chorus

To Devi away, my senora, she stay on the Golden shores of my home bay. Oh I hope to see her again some day But for now, to Devi, away.

docs.title: Even the Fishies Agree
docs.text:
An Albian Maritime Song

Verse 1

Oh sing, sing, the song of the sea! A jolly sea tune for you and for me! Out on the waves, not a troll in sight! And nary an ogre here to fight! We're heading out, to make the world better! Tea in every kettle, pet yer Erin setter!

Chorus

Albia, and the sea! Never a better pair would there be! Albian folk, the best around, even the fishies agree!

Verse 2

I talked to a fish once, 'ere's what 'e said, 'ad citymen tea once, wished I was dead! I gave 'im some tea, said would you rather try this? He took one little sip and was in permanent bliss!

Chorus

Albia, and the sea! Never a better pair would there be! Albian folk the best around, even the fishies agree!

Verse 3

Sing, sing me the song of the fish To be under our flag, is their every wish! Sing, sing me the song from their bubbles! We'll own the waves and solve all fish troubles! O prince,, treat them nicely, your new subjects pisces!

Chorus

Albia, and the sea! Never a better pair would there be! Albian folk, the best around, even the fishies agree!

docs.title: Albia Rules the Waves
docs.text:
An Albian Sailors' Song

Verse 1

Edward Taylor is a fine young sailor! Kenway knows his sails and stuff! Shamus cooks up all the grub! Albian sailors, mighty tough!

Chorus

The Seas shall belong to Albia 'tis truth Athar is planning on! Doradans feel they'll own the drink But that's quite plainly wrong to think

Verse 2

Take the spices, endure the wave, Albia's birthright we shall save! Send pretenders to the drink! Fly other flags? Then you'll sink!

Chorus

The Seas shall belong to Albia, 'tis truth Athar is planning on! Doradans feel they'll own the drink But that's quite plainly wrong to think

Verse 3

Gold from Zamboula, spices from the cities Alchemical re-agents from the lands of Devi! Albia's glory 'round the world will be known! Our flag'll be the one all the ports will see flown!

Chorus

The Seas shall belong to Albia 'tis truth Athar is planning on! Doradans feel they'll own the drink But that's quite plainly wrong to think

docs.title: Great Cities Serenade
docs.text:
A Great Cities Merchant's Song

Verse 1

Athar's love smiles warmly upon us, We claim the world's riches in surplus! Our cities build the finest boat! We've every single right to gloat!

Chorus

We shall have the biggest, fastest ship! The finest blades hung from our hip! Bound with gold, the timbers be! None shall grace the seas as we!

Verse 2

Zorah shipwrights, they're the best! Our opulence shines brighter than the rest! The other lands dearly wish to be fine as we! We embark to shame them upon the sea!

Chorus

We shall have the biggest, fastest ship! The finest blades hung from our hip! Bound with gold, the timbers be! None shall grace the seas as we!

Verse 3

What finer hat, than a jewel-decked turban? What better way than a well made trade plan? What better land than Roranian soil? What better purchase than slaves to toil?

Chorus

We shall have the biggest, fastest ship! The finest blades hung from our hip! Bound with gold, the timbers be! None shall grace the seas as we!

docs.title: Sea Wolves
docs.text:
A Reaver Clan Rowing Chorus

Verse 1

Let the others find what we desire, (Waste their lives to search and peruse!!) we'll take it all, put them to fire. (Burn down what we can not use!) Axes high, to cut them down! (And leave the cowards out to drown!)

Chorus

(Sail!) Wolves of the sea! To take what's ours and what belongs to thee! (Sail!) Wolves of the sea! The weak onto the shores do flee!

Verse 2

Illvith spare us, we'll be your wrath, (We are the storm that rides the waves!) Jorthi carry us into trade's path! (The lowlanders our distant slaves!) Reikal's tools we'll use them well! (Our ships are strong, our numbers grand!) Mordreyma, please, our way, to us do tell. (First out to them, then back to our land!)

Chorus

(Sail!) Wolves of the sea! To take what's ours and what belongs to thee! (Sail!) Wolves of the sea! The weak onto the shores do flee! (Sail!) (Sail!) (Sail!)

docs.title: Divine Wind
docs.text:
An Imperial Hymn of Conquest

Verse 1

Foam touches the shores, Begging the palace, to open its doors. The winds shall curl, and the sun shall climb As the Emperor commands them for all of time.

Chorus

Hizamazuke! (Kneel!) Before the dragon! Teishutsu suru! (Submit!) Far lands will be taken! Kō tōto-sa! (Nobility!) The Emperor embodies! Kuiaratameyo! (Repent!) Renounce your ways!

Verse 2

Resistance, yield! Barbarians, fall! The Dragon Emperor, conquers all! We are the shore that shall break your waves! The persistent river which carves its way!

Chorus

Hizamazuke! (Kneel!) Before the dragon! Teishutsu suru! (Submit!) Far lands will be taken! Kō tōto-sa! (Nobility!) The Emperor embodies! Kuiaratameyo! (Repent!) Renounce your ways!

Verse 3

All will kneel, before the Empire's might! Those who don't submit, get removed from sight! Samurai in the sun, shinobi in the night See the Emperor's power, and feel deep fright!

Chorus

Hizamazuke! (Kneel!) Before the dragon! Teishutsu suru! (Submit!) Far lands will be taken! Kō tōto-sa! (Nobility!) The Emperor embodies! Kuiaratameyo! (Repent!) Renounce your ways!

docs.title: Bring the Coins
docs.text:
A Traditional Al-Anwarese Merchant Song

Verse 1

Sadiq, bring your wallet! 'ahmaq, your debt, I do call it! Lending, ah what fun indeed! At interest yes, so good is greed!

Chorus

Bring your coin, outlander! With it I buy this splendor! Come buy this rug, come buy these silks! Don't buy from those eastern savage ilk!

Verse 2

docs.title: Historical and Heritage Peoples
docs.text:
Some identities remain important to Umbrathar long after their original political orders have changed, fragmented, or given rise to later peoples. This section collects peoples and heritage identities whose historical legacy continues to shape the present world.

  • Heryos
  • Heryoi
  • Heryan

See Realms and Peoples for the wider organization of contemporary realms and peoples.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Heryan are the southern descendants of the ancient Heryos, associated especially with Zorah and the southern imperial world.

They represent a settled cultural and linguistic branch of Heryos ancestry rather than an unrelated people.

docs.title: Language
docs.text:
The Heryan linguistic branch developed from the ancestral Heryos tongue toward the modern language of Zorah.

See Languages.

docs.title: Historical Role
docs.text: Heryan populations inherited the Heryos military and aristocratic legacy while absorbing the older urban cultures of the south. Their history is therefore part conquest, part assimilation, and part transformation by the cities they conquered.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Heryoi are the northern and Meropolitan descendants of the ancient Heryos who settled around Meropolis and the northern imperial world.

They are not a separate primordial people: the name describes one of the major settled cultural and linguistic branches that emerged as Heryos conquerors absorbed the civilizations they ruled.

docs.title: Language
docs.text:
The early Heryoi language developed from the ancestral Heryos tongue and eventually into modern Meropolitan.

Meropolitan is the native and civic language of Meropolis and also the principal transregional learned and clerical language of the Hetaireian Realms. It is not a universal everyday common tongue: local languages and dialects remain dominant across most communities outside the city, while clergy, scholars, record-keepers, and many elites use Meropolitan to communicate across political and cultural boundaries.

See Languages.

docs.title: Historical Role
docs.text:
Heryoi elites and institutions became closely entangled with Meropolis and the northern imperial tradition. Their later descendants form part of the cultural background from which the old imperial and Atharite political worlds emerged.

The Heryoi inheritance is institutional as well as genealogical. Imperial offices, administrative vocabulary, archives, roads, military traditions, civic institutions, legal forms, and aristocratic customs survived unevenly through Ardan's refoundation and the long contraction of the New Ardanic Empire.

Modern Hetaireian civilization does not treat that inheritance as the exclusive possession of one Heryoi successor. Meropolis preserves especially important archives, language, ritual, and institutional memory, but princely houses, cities, churches, and local communities across the Realms retain other fragments of the same past. Claims to “ancient Heryoi” authority can therefore be politically powerful without being uncontested.

docs.title: Horsemanship and the Vyrkar Tradition
docs.text:
The settled Heryoi retained an aristocratic memory of their Heryos equestrian ancestry. One archaic martial title, vyrkar, once denoted an elite mounted warrior of exceptional skill and status. Long after the word disappeared from ordinary military usage, it was revived as the name of the Pontifical Vyrkar Guard.

The Guard's later prestige helped transform the word into a broader Hetaireian label for Atharite steppe and frontier horsemen, ultimately contributing to the name of the Vyrkari of Khoryv.

docs.title: Heryos
docs.text:
The Heryos are the ancient steppe people whose conquests laid the foundations for the great western imperial civilizations.

They began as horse-lords, cattle herders, raiders, and builders of great burial mounds on the Eastern Steppe. Over generations they conquered and absorbed settled peoples around the Sea of Ardan, especially the urban cultures of the southern cities.

docs.title: Conquerors Conquered
docs.text:
The Heryos conquered the south militarily but were transformed by it culturally. They adopted writing, monumental stonework, settled government, and southern military organization while retaining an unusually strong aristocratic attachment to horses and cavalry.

As those populations settled and diverged, two major descendant identities emerged:

  • the Heryoi, associated especially with Meropolis and the northern imperial tradition;
  • the Heryan, associated especially with Zorah and the southern imperial tradition.

These are descendants and developments of the Heryos rather than unrelated peoples.

docs.title: Language Legacy
docs.text:
The ancient Heryos language diverged alongside its settled descendant populations rather than surviving unchanged.

The northern Heryoi branch eventually produced Meropolitan, the modern language of Meropolis and the transregional learned and clerical language of the Hetaireian world. The southern Heryan branch developed into the language of Zorah.

See Languages.

docs.title: Imperial Legacy
docs.text:
Heryos successor states produced the institutions from which the Old Empire eventually emerged. By the time of Ardan, centuries of conquest, settlement, administration, law, roads, taxation, military organization, civic government, and cultural borrowing had made the imperial order far more than a steppe conquest state.

Imperial expansion into the Northern Clanlands was never a simple line between conquered provinces and untouched wilderness. Direct control concentrated on valuable routes, crossings, forts, markets, and more accessible lowlands. Beyond those zones, northern rulers and communities could become clients, trading partners, military recruits, tributaries, hostage-givers, enemies, or diplomatic allies without being absorbed into ordinary provincial government.

This selective frontier left durable traces: roads and ruined forts, mixed border populations, old market sites, military traditions, imported scripts and prestige goods, and memories of both resistance and accommodation. Later imperial contraction disrupted these relationships and helped generate migrations, mercenary settlement, raiding, and new confederations across the north.

In its late period this civilization became increasingly entangled with diabolism from Devi and eldritch cults associated with Zamboula. Ardan overthrew its corrupt sacred and political order, but he did not discard every institution it had created. His refoundation was administratively conservative where inherited machinery could still serve human survival and the spread of Athar's Way, while being constitutionally and religiously revolutionary where the old structures were inseparable from corruption.

The resulting New Ardanic Empire therefore inherited much of the old imperial machinery under a new source of legitimacy. Its territorial government was organized through Principalities, whose Princes began as rulers or office-holders within the imperial system rather than as lesser kings.

The New Empire did not vanish in a single terminal collapse. It contracted over generations as military, fiscal, and regional autonomy accumulated through repeated crises. Central taxation, bureaucracy, infrastructure maintenance, and standing imperial military capacity fragmented faster than the transregional Atharite religious network.

Modern Hetaireian civilization consequently possesses a distributed imperial inheritance. Meropolis, the Hetaireia, princely houses, cities, religious institutions, and local communities preserve different fragments of Heryos and Ardanic law, office, archives, roads, boundaries, ritual, and political memory. No single modern institution possesses the whole inheritance, and rival claims of continuity may rest on genuine survival, Ardanic reform, later adaptation, revival, reconstruction, or fabrication.

docs.title: The Vyrkar Legacy
docs.text:
One surviving word illustrates the long afterlife of Heryos institutions. In old Heryos martial usage, a vyrkar was an elite mounted warrior of exceptional skill and status. The title eventually fell from ordinary use but was deliberately revived for the Pontifical Vyrkar Guard.

The Guard's prestige later caused the word to spread as a Hetaireian label for Atharite steppe and frontier horsemen. In eastern Khoryv, that later usage contributed to the name of the Vyrkari horse-host communities.

The modern Vyrkari are therefore not the ancient Heryos under another name. The semantic history is old Heryos martial title → Vyrkar Guard → wider frontier label → Khoryvian Vyrkari identity.

docs.title: Appearance
docs.text: The ancestral Heryos were famous for red hair and amber eyes. Amber eyes survive in some southern bloodlines, while red hair remains more strongly associated with northern descendants and is sometimes treated as a mark of destiny.
